News.title: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'
News.content:
A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to âchange the way they treat younger employeesâ.

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.

Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.

McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."

The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.

Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.

Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.

She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.

"I got the hell out of there," she says.

Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.

Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".

Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after.

"You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says.

"And why would you? That is literally a child still."

News.title: Leasehold system set to be scrapped in England and Wales
News.content:
The government is to introduce new laws to scrap the ownership rules for flats in England and Wales and cap ground rents at Â£250 a year.

Under the plans, which will not become law until at least next year, most new leasehold flats will eventually be banned and replaced with commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said the current leasehold system was "blighting lives" and was an "anachronism in the 21st century".

But the Residential Freehold Association says the plan is an "unprecedented abuse" of their rights, which will wipe billions from the value of pension funds, which have invested heavily in property.

The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, to be published on Thursday, is likely to contain further details on when the measures would come into force.

In order to become law, the bill would first need to be approved by both Houses of Parliament, a process that will take several months.

News.title: UK joins in GTA 6 frenzy as game becomes available worldwide
News.content:
After years of anticipation and delays, as well as controversy around worker rights, Grand Theft Auto 6 has completed its phased worldwide release and is available to gamers everywhere, including the UK.

There has been near universal praise from critics, with review aggregator Metacritic calculating its average score at 99 out of 100 based on 150 reviews., external

Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has held the top spot since 1998 - but Metacritic confirmed to the BBC that this has now officially been overtaken.

GTA 6 is set to become one of the world's most popular entertainment products ever, with fans booking time off work, and schools warning students not to bunk off.

Some schools have reminded parents and pupils to prioritise study over the game, which has an 18 rating, external for "strong graphic violence, strong sexual themes and use of illegal drugs".

One school in Essex incentivised pupils to attend with prizes such as vouchers, Christmas dinners and a pass to skip the lunch queue.

The UK rating means it can only be legally sold to an adult. It does not stop an adult letting their child play the game - instead it is meant to inform their decision.

News.title: Google rejects UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say
News.content:
Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.

The disgraced comedian is in prison after being sentenced to 10-and-a-half years following his conviction for rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Andy Burnham's official spokesperson said the PM believed "the public have heard enough from Russell Brand", and his victims "now deserve peace from him".

Google told BBC News in a statement it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".

It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."

On Sunday, Brand's wife Laura shared a video on their YouTube channel and read out a message from Brand in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

The Prison Service of England and Wales asked for the video to be taken down, on the basis it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.

A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said "it was only right" to ask for content that was "distressing for victims" to be removed, adding that while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".

Asked if the YouTube channel should be taken down, the prime minister's spokesperson said: "We hope and trust they will do the right thing."

News.title: Cleverly to run as Tory London mayor candidate
News.content:
Labour incumbent Lord Khan, first elected in 2016, is yet to confirm whether he will seek a fourth term.

Sir James, a former head of the London Fire Authority, was widely expected to win the nomination after he stood down from the shadow cabinet in August.

He said he would not seek re-selection as the candidate in his Essex seat at the next general election.

At the announcement of the result, he said Lord Khan was "letting London down".

Sir James added: "People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place - businesses, job creators, families leaving London - and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related.

"The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause. When I ask Londoners, 'Do you feel safe walking home at night?', the answer is no."

"It's shameful, it's a failure, and it's not just crime.

"We have had the worst period of housebuilding since the Second World War and only the highest-earning Londoners can afford the cheapest houses in London."

Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "James Cleverly has a record of failure and now wants to inflict his disastrous CV on London.

"He backed a no-deal Brexit and Liz Truss's disastrous mini-budget, voted for cuts to policing and youth services and opposed action to clean up London's air.

"Londoners should never forgive and never forget the damage the Conservatives did to our capital."

News.title: UK to provide Ukraine with 1,000 long-range strike drones
News.content:
In a statement released ahead of the latest meeting of the group of 36 countries committed to supporting Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire or peace agreement - the government said the UK is also building maritime, logistical and surveillance drones to help Ukraine's war effort.

Burnham, who is co-chairing the meeting, said the UK must do everything it can to make sure Ukraine can defend itself from Russian attacks throughout the winter.

The prime minister said: "Plunging millions of Ukrainians into the freezing cold and starving them of heat and warmth won't see Putin win this war, it will only cement our resolve to support Ukraine.

"That is why I am determined the UK will do everything we can to ensure Ukraine is able to defend itself from Russia's barrage of attacks and systematic striking of critical national infrastructure."

Before this latest support package was announced, government figures put the amount of support provided by the UK for Ukraine since Russia invaded the country in February 2022 at Â£35.5bn., external

In recent days, Ukraine has struck oil refineries in southern Russia, and has repeatedly hit the Crimean Bridge - a significant logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

Meanwhile, Russian forces have been focused on knocking out power in Ukraine before winter with attacks on critical infrastructure.

The UK is among a number of countries also supplying Ukraine with lightweight missiles which are being used to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

Ukraine's strike rate is now close to 70%, more than double what it was just a couple of months ago, Downing Street said.

The UK also pledged further air defence support this week and sanctioned Russia's 10 major oil producers.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the government was delivering on a promise for more support for Ukraine at the Budget.

"Ukraine's frontline is the frontline for freedom and democracy, and we will stand with them for as long as it takes," he said.

Meanwhile, on Friday Burnham will head to Brussels for a UK-EU summit, where both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.

News.title: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation
News.content:
Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds".

"The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg.

"Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."

The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming".

"I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."

She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again".

"I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."

Professor Heather Widdows from Everyday Lookism, external, which campaigns to end body shaming, told BBC News: "Pugh is right that we are in a place where 'beauty standards are changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with'.

"A global beauty ideal makes impossible demands and normalises what were once extreme," added Widdows, who is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Warwick.

"We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people's bodies... in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people."

News.title: Crew unaware of risks before Mike Lynch's yacht Bayesian sank, say investigators
News.content:
The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about critical safety risks that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily, killing seven people, British investigators say.

British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024.

The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said.

Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said.

"It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves. "The speed of events overtook the crew and prevented them from taking any other action."

The accident also led to the deaths of Morgan Stanley International bank chairman Jonathan Bloomer, 70, and his wife, Judy, 71; American lawyer Chris Morvillo, 59, and his wife Neda Morvillo, 57; and crew member Rick Thomas, 59.

News.title: Surgeon calls for corporate homicide probe over claims patients unnecessarily bled to death
News.content:
A consultant surgeon at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary has called for a corporate homicide investigation into claims of avoidable deaths among NHS Grampian patients over many years.

Dr Mohammed Habib, who is still a surgeon at the hospital, said he had been raising concerns for a decade, including with government ministers and police, but he had been ignored.

The whistleblowing medic also leaked an unpublished expert review from 2022 which found 19 avoidable deaths among 45 patients in liver and pancreatic surgery, including some who bled to death in the operating theatre because of mistakes by surgeons.

The allegations come a week after a scathing report found poor leadership and culture at the NHS Grampian board. The board's management is yet to comment on these latest public claims.

Last week, Healthcare Improvement Scotland (HIS) found "major deficiencies" across the region and revealed that a failure to learn from mistakes had caused "repeated and avoidable harm" to patients.

Health Secretary Angela Constance insisted facilities were safe and there would be "full transparency" at every level.

And in response to these fresh allegations, a Scottish government spokesperson said they recognised the "courage shown by this whistleblower" and reiterated that a "very significant level of intervention and an unprecedented level of support" was being given to NHS Grampian.

News.title: Badenoch defends amputee marathon runners claim in benefits cut row
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has defended her suggestion that because double amputees run marathons more disabled people should work instead of claiming benefits.

Badenoch had used the example when setting out her party's plans to cut welfare spending by Â£36bn a year.

Her comments were criticised by Paralympian Richard Whitehead, who accused her of "weaponising" his sporting success, while Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the Tory leader's words "crass and insensitive".

But in an interview with the BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Badenoch stood by the remarks, insisting that "if people even with significant problems can work, then those who have ADHD and mild anxiety should go to work".

Asked if she accepted the comments were insensitive, Badenoch said: "No, no, no. I do not accept it. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense.

"What I know is that if people can work, then we should encourage them to work."

Badenoch acknowledged she had used "extreme examples to illustrate things", but added: "If someone can do that, then yes, your condition of ADHD or anxiety is mild."

"I will say things as they are. People may disagree with things that I say, and that's fine, this is a free country, people are free to disagree, but they know where I'm coming from," she said.

"I start from first principles: If you can work, you should work, and the Conservative Party is going to help you get a job."

News.title: 'Inconceivable' that Irish government would not hold Omagh inquiry - Sir Chris Bryant
News.content:
Speaking to Irish broadcaster RTÃ's Morning Ireland, Sir Chris said: "I think it's almost inconceivable once we have completed our own inquiry in the UK, which is ongoing into the Omagh bombing, that the Republic will not, in the end, want to hold one of its own.

"I understand why, of course, we're two separate jurisdictions and I understand why there are difficulties in relation to that. I'm very grateful for the co-operation that has been shown already," he said.

The Irish government has agreed a co-operation arrangement via a memorandum of Understanding (MoU) which allows the inquiry access to material held by the Irish government.

John Fox, the solicitor for 54 families and survivors, said the inquiry in Belfast has no power of its own to compel witnesses or documents in the Republic, nor make findings regarding any failings by state agencies.

Fox Law wrote to the taoiseach on behalf of families, asking for a commitment to a full statutory public inquiry into the role of Irish State agencies.

Martin said "two parallel inquiries at the one time, to me, never made any sense", adding that there was a need to wait for the UK government "to adjudicate on that evidence and the totality of that evidence".

"We are co-operating 100% with the inquiry, and we've sent thousands of documents to the inquiry. And that to me is sensible," he told press in Dublin.

He said the "important point" is to let the inquiry get on with its work "and let the inquiry assess the evidence that's being presented to it and come to its conclusions".

News.title: 'Whole nation behind you' - Nessa delivers rallying cry for Wales rugby team
News.content:
Fresh off their historic victory against New Zealand's All Blacks, Gavin and Stacey's Nessa Jenkins has delivered a rousing message for the Wales men's team ahead of Saturday's game against Australia.

The popular character, played by Ruth Jones, delivered some straight-talking advice ahead of the team's Nations Championship fixture, reminding them that the whole nation is behind them.

"Oh what's occurin'? The question was rhetorical we all know what's occurin'... you are the heroes of Wales," Nessa said in the video.

Posted in collaboration with the Welsh Rugby Union, the caption read: "All Blacks? Done. Wallabies? Next up. Nessa's got a few words of inspiration for the boys."

Jones wore Nessa's distinctive black bob wig and red leather jacket to deliver the message.

"You're legends in your own time, you've got the whole nation behind you," she said.

Jones continued: "But I just wanted to remind you of everything I taught you in training, all right?

"On Saturday, when you face them Aussies, you've got to win the collisions, and you've got to edge the contact area. Yeah?"

"But the most important thing to remember is this - fire in the belly and heads in the fridge. You do that, you've got a damn good chance of winning. I'm proud of you boys.

"Go for it, alrigh'? Cracking."

The post was widely watched and shared on social media, with one user commenting: "As an Aussie, I almost want Wales to win! That's how much I love Nessa. Almost. Tidy."

Another said it was "lush to see Nessa once more".

More than 60,000 tickets have sold for Wales v Australia in Cardiff, following a surge in demand after Wales' historic 35-28 victory over New Zealand, which ended a losing streak against the All Blacks that went back to 1953.

"It's our last home game of this competition. The support that fans give to the players and staff has been incredible, and we can't wait to get back out at Principality Stadium," head coach Steve Tandy said after the New Zealand win.

News.title: Parents live in fear paedophile nursery worker harmed their children
News.content:
Parents are calling for mandatory CCTV in nurseries after a worker who looked after their children was later exposed as a paedophile.

Nathan Bennett was jailed in February for multiple counts of sexual abuse, including two counts of rape, against five boys at Partou King Street nursery in Bristol. His crimes were discovered after a CCTV review.

Bennett previously worked as an apprentice for 18 months at another nursery in the Somerset area - which the BBC is not naming â which does not have CCTV.

A number of parents whose children went there said they lived in fear about what could have happened to them at the nursery. The government said a panel was examining the use of CCTV in nurseries.

Warning: This story contains distressing details

Bennett's victims at Partou King Street nursery were two and three years old at the time of his offences. In February 2025, concerns were raised over his behaviour with the children, specifically a group of five who the prosecution said he would "favour".

He was suspended from the nursery after CCTV of him putting his hands down a boy's trousers was reviewed.

Avon and Somerset Police said they "are still supporting families, actively following lines of enquiry and assessing new information as appropriate".

Det Insp Lucy Forde, who led the investigation into Bennett's crimes, previously told the BBC she feared only a fraction of his crimes could be proven.

"He's worked in childcare and has had access to children for a number of years," she said.

"My worry is there will be other victims that we haven't been able to identify, that are too young to understand what's happened to them," Forde added.

After learning of Bennett's offending, a number of parents whose children went to the Somerset nursery shared their worries about what could have taken place. The BBC has changed their names to protect their children's identities.

Rachel, whose children attended the nursery, said she became suspicious of Bennett after witnessing him being overly tactile with her child in her opinion.

News.title: Anglo Saxon 'sand body' among new Sutton Hoo finds
News.content:
A mysterious "sand body" has been uncovered during renewed excavations at Sutton Hoo.

The site, near Woodbridge in Suffolk, is renowned for its royal burial ground and ship burials that have transformed historians' understanding of medieval England.

Now, yet more mysteries have been uncovered after the television archaeology series Time Team returned for a special dig in 2025, which has now been chronicled in a four-part documentary season.

These include an Anglo-Saxon grave and evidence of a second burial site beneath it, as well as beads, tweezers, a knife and a brooch.

News.title: Council wins legal fight against flags on lamp-posts
News.content:
Birmingham City Council has won a High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags being attached to lamp-posts and other highway infrastructure across the city.

The authority sought the order after thousands of St George's flags and union jacks were put up by supporters of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours from summer 2025 onwards.

Council lawyers argued the displays created safety risks and fuelled tensions, while campaigners said the move would restrict freedom of expression.

Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.

In her ruling, the judge said it would last until trial or further order of the court.

The order applies to Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.

It also grants a power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning police could arrest someone without a warrant if they are suspected of breaching the injunction.

The council said anyone who breaches the order could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court.

The local authority sought the injunction after thousands of St George's flags and union flags were attached to lamp-posts and bridges in Birmingham from summer 2025 onwards.

Lawyers acting for the council argued the displays could pose safety risks, obstruct visibility and contribute to tensions and disorder. The application also referred to reported incidents of alleged intimidation, harassment and obstruction connected to flags being put up in the city.

The court heard that, on one occasion, a man suffered a broken leg when he was struck by a cherry picker being used while flags were being installed.

The case followed similar legal action in Oxfordshire, where the county council secured a permanent injunction against four named individuals over flags attached to lamp-posts and other highway structures.

News.title: Will Jordan provides update on fitness ahead of England encounter
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Will Jordan has declared himself good to go after injury having been named to start for New Zealand against England.

Jordan appeared a major doubt for the game after tearing his hamstring in the All Blacks’ win over Scotland, but has trained this week and is set to take up his place on the right wing.

The 28-year-old became the All Blacks’ record try-scorer earlier this year and will look to add to his tally of 56 tries in his 65th Test.

“I guess off the back of the Scotland game, yeah, felt a weird grab in the hammy and we're just sort of taking it day by day since then,” Jordan said. “I was able to get running last week and I feel like I'm in a good position now to push for this week. So, yeah, pleased with how it's all come together.

“I think that run last week certainly gave the physios confidence that I might have a chance. Another run around this afternoon and hopefully I’ll be ready.”

Jordan will be part of a back three that also includes Beauden Barrett, who becomes just the second All Black and fourth player overall to reach 150 international caps.

“It’s been one of the great privileges of my All Blacks career, playing with Beaudy and being around his as teammates,” Jordan said of the full-back. “He’s someone I’d class as a good friend and certainly someone who took me under his wing since I’ve been in the team. He’s been like that with every player.

“One hundred and fifty Tests is a crazy feat of longevity. It feels like I’ve been around for a while now and I think it’s 65 [Tests] this weekend, so I’m not even halfway. I’ve got Damian McKenzie’s or Jordie Barrett’s full Test career to go before I get to Beaudy, which seems ridiculous.

“That shows his work ethic, his drive to get keep striving to get better every day and we’re super motivated to get a result for him on Saturday.”

News.title: Four foods to help you maximise your vitamin D levels this winter
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

As the days grow ever-shorter and winter threatens to begin in earnest, conversations about how to get enough vitamin D inevitably come to the surface, and with those discussions, questions about its role in overall health.

"Vitamin D helps support calcium and phosphorus absorption, so is really important for bone and muscle health," Katie Sanders, a Doctify-rated dietitian and nutritionist, said.

"It does seem to have a role in immune function as well."

Because sunlight is our primary source, it is widely termed the "sunshine vitamin".

"During the spring and summer, if we go outside regularly, our bodies can usually make enough vitamin D. However, due to the reduced exposure of UV rays and sunlight in the winter months, our levels tend to dip," Sanders said.

open image in gallery It’s normal for vitamin D levels to dip during autumn and winter ( Getty/iStock )

According to the NHS website, deficiency can cause bone deformities such as rickets in children, as well as adult bone pain from osteomalacia.

While certain foods are marketed as strong sources, questions remain over whether diet alone can maintain adequate levels during colder months.

When looking at daily requirements, Sanders said: "For children from the age of one and adults, the official NHS recommendation is 10 micrograms of vitamin D a day."

The NHS website notes this includes pregnant and breastfeeding women, plus those at risk of deficiency. "However, for infants under one, the recommendation is eight-and-a-half-to-10 micrograms."

So what foods are good sources of vitamin D?

Salmon

A fillet of salmon is one of the highest natural food sources of vitamin D.

Per 100g of steamed salmon, there are about 9.3 micrograms of vitamin D, according to the British Heart Foundation‘s website.

“Having oily fish like salmon a couple of times a week is really great for heart health,” Sanders said.

open image in gallery A succulent fillet of salmon is one of the highest natural food sources of vitamin D ( Getty/iStock )

There are many different ways to cook a salmon fillet, ranging from quick high-heat methods to gentle, low-temperature techniques.

“Personally, I like to poach salmon because it’s really quick and easy, but you could also roast or pan-fry it,” the dietitian said.

Cooking salmon in an air fryer is also super quick and gives you a crispy, golden exterior and a tender, flaky interior.

“Sometimes I just stick salmon fillets in the air fryer with a tiny drizzle of olive oil. You don’t have to do very much with it,” Sanders said.

Serve with new potatoes or over rice with an assortment of vegetables to add colour.

Mackerel

Another oily fish bursting with vitamin D that Sanders recommended is mackerel.

According to the British Heart Foundation, 100g of grilled mackerel provides an average of 8.5 micrograms of vitamin D.

“A simple, easy way to cook mackerel would be to grill it or pan-fry it,” Sanders advised.

“You could drizzle a little bit of olive oil over it or squeeze some lemon onto it.”

open image in gallery Another oily fish bursting with vitamin D that Sanders recommended is mackerel ( Getty/iStock )

Tinned mackerel could be a great, and much cheaper, alternative to salmon.

When serving mackerel, or any other protein, Sanders recommended splitting up your plate into thirds to help create a balanced meal.

“One third of your plate could be mackerel for lean protein, then another third is your starchy carbohydrate, which could be new potatoes, and the last third could be vegetables or salad,” Sanders suggested.

“If you always have those three things categories in mind and choose something that you like from each of the options, you’ll always have quite a good balanced meal.”

Eggs

One egg contains around 1.7 micrograms of vitamin D, according to the British Heart Foundation.

Eggs are incredibly versatile, and can be cooked and incorporated into many different meals.

“There are lots of simple ways to include more eggs into your diet,” Sanders said. “Some people like boiled eggs or scrambled eggs in the morning, or like a boiled egg as an easy snack during the day.”

She recommended using eggs to make a healthy omelette for lunch.

open image in gallery Eggs are incredibly versatile, and can be cooked and incorporated into many different meals ( Getty/iStock )

“I personally just do eggs, a little splash of milk, and some vegetables such as tomatoes or mushrooms with it too to make it more balanced,” says the dietitian. “You could also add a bit of cheese to it, too.”

Sanders said the more colour that you can add to your plate, the better.

“Get a bit of colour and variety into your meals because the different colours of vegetables represent different nutrients, vitamins and minerals,” she explained.

Fortified foods

While browsing the dairy and cereal supermarket aisles, you may have noticed that lots of products are marketed with “added vitamin D” labels.

“There are lots of food products that are fortified with vitamin D such as plant-based milk alternatives, breakfast cereals, yoghurts and spreads,” Sanders said.

While vitamin D isn’t naturally found in these fortified foods, adding it to everyday items helps boost your intake.

Is it possible to get enough vitamin D through diet alone?

“Although we can get vitamin D from food, we don’t get very much of it from food,” Sanders said.

“Most of the vitamin D that our bodies make is from the sunlight, but because there is a lack of the UV and sunlight in the winter months, a lot of us would need to probably consider taking a vitamin D supplement this time of year.”

The NHS website states that the government advises everyone to consider taking a daily supplement containing 10 micrograms of vitamin D during the autumn and winter.

Some people will not make enough vitamin D from sunlight because they have very little or no sunshine exposure.

“If somebody is at more risk of a vitamin D deficiency, for example somebody in a nursing home who doesn’t spend much time outside, they might need to take a vitamin D supplement all year round,” Sanders said.

“People with dark skin are also advised to take a supplement all year round.”

If you suspect that you have a vitamin D deficiency, you should speak with a GP or healthcare provider to discuss getting a simple blood test.

“There are cut-off levels for vitamin D insufficient and deficient,” Sanders said. “If somebody is clinically deficient and has a very low vitamin D, a GP might prescribe a high dose to bring levels back up to a normal range.”

News.title: No 10’s blunt response when asked if Burnham will be playing GTA 6
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Downing Street has confirmed that Prime Minister Andy Burnham will not be playing the new instalment of Grand Theft Auto himself, despite the launch dominating the headlines.

Grand Theft Auto VI, described by No 10 as “British success story”, went live for UK players at midnight on Thursday.

The release brought to an end a 13-year wait for the next installment in the franchise.

Rockstar's blockbuster series was largely developed by a team in Scotland, a point that Downing Street was keen to highlight.

A No 10 spokesperson said: “Rockstar Games is a British success story made in Edinburgh, and many fans are already saying GTA has been worth the wait.”

Asked whether the prime minister would be exploring Vice City, Rockstar's fictional take on Miami, the spokesperson said: “His diary is very full. He won’t be playing it.”

open image in gallery Andy Burnham’s ‘diary is very full’, No 10 says ( Getty )

The game carries an age rating of 18, and schools have urged pupils not to treat its arrival as a reason to miss lessons.

Some schools are even running prize draws for vouchers among pupils who do attend, in an effort to improve attendance.

The spokesperson said children “should be in classrooms today and tomorrow”, adding: “Every day in school matters.”

Players were quick to post their verdicts on social media after the midnight unlock.

The game has been overwhelmingly praised for its graphics and gameplay.

open image in gallery Grand Theft Auto VI has gone on sale ( AFP/Getty )

Critics have given GTA VI universally positive reviews, with the Guardian crediting Rockstar with creating “the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen”.

The Independent gave the game a five-star review, calling it an “absolute masterpiece”.

Gaming correspondent Jake Brigstock wrote: “This is the best gaming studio at the very top of its game; it has delivered not just the game of a generation, but the very best game of all time.”

A Uswitch poll commissioned earlier this month suggests some 2.8 million UK adults will play the game on launch day alone.

Many of those players are expected to call in sick to work, while others booked the day off as annual leave.

Reform UK marked the occasion by releasing a video of leader Nigel Farage playing a fake version of the game.

The spoof featured treasury spokesperson Robert Jenrick rugby-tackling a shoplifter at Brixton market in south London.

News.title: How genocide was proven in landmark Myanmar ruling by UN’s top court
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The United Nations' top court has ruled that thousands of killings, the destruction of homes and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar's security forces against its Rohingya Muslim minority in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

The decision by the International Court of Justice, seven years after the case was filed, marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the legal threshold to prove genocide had been met. It was the first time the court held a state responsible for genocide.

"The court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya," presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa said in a reading of the decision.

A panel of 15 judges found "that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine State."

It said "the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group, namely the Rohingya population in Northern Rakhine state," meeting the legal threshold for genocide.

The court's ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

open image in gallery International Court of Justice (ICJ) President Iwasawa Yuji reads the court's judgment ( AFP/Getty )

What is genocide?

Genocide has a strict legal definition cemented in humanitarian law after the Nazi Holocaust. The 1948 Genocide Convention defines genocide as crimes committed "with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such".

Five criminal acts can constitute genocide: killing members of the group, causing them serious bodily or mental harm, creating conditions calculated to destroy them, preventing births, or forcibly transferring children to other groups.

International courts have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including the slaughter in Cambodia of minority Cham and Vietnamese under Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s, during which some 1.7 million people died; the 1994 mass killing of Tutsis in Rwanda; and the 1995 Srebrenica massacre of about 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Bosnia.

How to prove genocide?

To determine that a state or individuals committed genocide, a court must find that at least one out of the five underlying criminal acts took place and that the victims were part of a distinct national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

open image in gallery Rohingya refugee children gather to watch the verdict by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ( Reuters )

Genocide is harder to prove than war crimes and crimes against humanity because it requires evidence of specific intent.

That intent can be established through direct statements or orders, but may also be inferred from a pattern of conduct.

When has genocide been proven?

The ICJ has issued judgments in two previous genocide cases, both stemming from the 1990s Balkan wars that followed the collapse of Yugoslavia. In 2007, it found that Serbia did not commit genocide but did violate the Genocide Convention by failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops in Srebrenica.

In 2015, it found genocide had not been committed in Croatia.

UN tribunals convicted dozens of perpetrators of genocide in Rwanda and Bosnia.

In 2018, a hybrid UN-Cambodian tribunal found two leaders of Cambodia's Khmer Rouge guilty of genocide, following years of debate about whether the "Killing Fields" constituted genocide.

What happened in Myanmar?

Myanmar's 2017 military crackdown drove more than 730,000 Rohingya Muslims into Bangladesh amid allegations of killings, rape and arson.

Witnesses told the court they saw mass killings, rapes and homes being burned.

UN investigations into both Myanmar's treatment of the Rohingya and Israel's conduct in Gaza said acts they described as genocidal had occurred. Both countries dispute the legal significance of those investigations.

How can the Myanmar ruling impact the Gaza case?

In 2023, South Africa filed a case at the ICJ accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza. Israel denies the allegation, saying it targeted Hamas militants. While a final ruling in that case is not expected before 2029, legal experts said they would closely watch how the court rules in the Myanmar case.

The Myanmar judgment said the acts of the military against the Rohingya, including thousands of killings, the burning of hundreds of villages and widespread sexual violence, amounted to genocide. The court ordered the state to enable their safe return and provide reparations.

Myanmar says its operations targeted an insurgency rather than the Rohingya as a group. Israel similarly says its military campaign is directed at Hamas militants, not Palestinians.

News.title: The new rights for homeowners as ‘feudal’ leasehold system to be scrapped
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The government is hoping to scrap what it has described as a “feudal” leasehold system in the biggest shake-up to the rules in a century.

The leasehold system has been in place for a thousand years with an estimated five million homes across England and Wales affected by it. The government has argued that homeowners currently face rising ground rents, expensive fees for basic requests to freehold owners, costly lease extensions and threats of losing their home over small debts.

Housing minister Matthew Pennycook said that the legislation was historic ahead of the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill’s introduction to parliament on Thursday.

“The leasehold system denies individuals control over the homes they live in, and have paid for, and routinely subjects them to excessive extraction,” he said. “It is blighting lives and it is an anachronism in the 21st century.”

“The publication of our historic Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill marks the beginning of the end for the feudal leasehold system.

“We’re laying the foundations for a commonhold future and transforming the experience of homeownership for existing leaseholders by giving them greater rights and protections, and providing them with easy and effective escape routes.”

open image in gallery Matthew Pennycook called the leasehold system ‘feudal’ ( Getty )

Here is how the bill will affect homeowners.

Ground rent and admin fees to be capped

Ground rent will be capped at £250 a year from 2028, as the government aims to cut bills for up to a million leaseholders. It’s expected that this will change to a peppercorn ground rent after 40 years as part of the bill.

Ministers will also have the power to cap excessive permission and administration fees such as asking permission to keep a pet or replace the front door.

Greater transparency around charges

By April next year, the government will enforce greater transparency for leaseholders around information about what they are paying for as well as how their building is managed, maintained, repaired and insured.

By November next year, private landlords will have to provide standardised bills, annual reports and accounts showing what leaseholders are paying for. Leaseholders will also more transparent information about how administration charges are calculated. In 2028, the government will apply this to social landlords as well.

An end to threats to take away people’s homes

The new bill will take away powers that can put a leaseholder’s home at risk over unpaid bills, such as disputed service charges. Mr Pennycook told the BBC that the government would introduce a “comprehensive new legal framework” and court-led system to tackle the issue.

The bill also looks to protect people living on freehold housing estates from threats to take over their home over unpaid estate maintenance charges.

open image in gallery The bill is expected to help the five million leasehold households across England and Wales ( PA )

Introducing the commonhold

As part of the bill, there would be no more leaseholds for new flats and homes. Instead, the government hopes to move from a leasehold system to a commonhold standard where buyers own their home outright forever and run their building jointly from day one.

More routes would be set up to help switch to a commonhold by dropping the threshold for existing blocks to convert from 100 per cent neighbour agreement down to 50 per cent support. This means that non-consenting neighbours could remain on modified leases until they sell, but holdouts could not block conversion for the rest of the building.

Making it easier to extend leases and purchase freeholds

Homeowners will receive help to buy 990-year lease extensions to stop them from having to pay their landlord’s expensive costs in most cases.

The bill will also scrap marriage value, an additional cost faced by leaseholders with 80 years or less remaining on their leases who are trying to extend. This cost represents the increase in a property’s market value that results from the extension.

The right to better broadband

Leaseholders will have better rights to request from their landlords a gigabit broadband connection. While landlords can currently ignore these requests, they will have to respond within set timeframes to calls for fast and reliable broadband.

News.title: Number of people seeking unemployment aid ticks higher yet still low historically
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Slightly more people applied for U.S. unemployment benefits last week, though layoffs remain low and most American workers enjoy solid job security.

The Labor Department said Thursday that jobless claims ticked up to 203,000 from a revised 202,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, rose 2,000 to 197,750.

Applications for unemployment aid are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. This year, claims have remained at a historically low level below 220,000.

The report suggests that most companies are confident enough in the economy and their sales to hold onto their workers. At the same time, hiring has been sluggish, resulting in a “low-hire, low-fire” job market.

Even so, job creation has improved in the past few months. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists forecast, while the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, from 4.2%.

News.title: Russian nuclear-capable bombers leave Vietnam as Putin meets world leaders in China
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Two Russian nuclear-capable strategic bombers left Vietnam on Thursday morning, in an apparent display of Moscow’s military reach across Asia even as Russian President Vladimir Putin met world leaders in China.

The two Tu-95 nuclear-capable strategic bombers, along with two support aircraft, were at an airport in the central Vietnamese city of Da Nang on Wednesday.

The meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping gave Putin a chance to portray Russia as one of the preeminent global powers. The bombers flew to Vietnam shortly before the summit. As Putin arrived in China, Russian television cameras focused on an officer accompanying him who carried a briefcase used to authorize the use of nuclear weapons.

After the bombers left Vietnam, Taiwan’s Defense Ministry said Thursday afternoon that it tracked two Russian Tu-95 military aircraft flying past the island’s eastern coast after approaching from the south.

The bombers also alarmed U.S. allies Japan and South Korea when they flew from Russia to Vietnam earlier in the week.

Japan protested to Moscow on Tuesday after the two Russian aircraft entered Japan’s airspace. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters that the aircraft violated Japanese airspace for about five minutes early Tuesday near Fukuoka, long enough for Japan to scramble fighter jets and send warnings.

“The violation of the Japanese airspace by the Russian aircraft is not only a serious violation of our country’s sovereignty, but also a threat to our safety,” Koizumi said.

South Korea’s military said several Russian military aircraft temporarily entered its air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan on Monday, though they did not violate South Korean airspace.

The last known use of a Vietnamese airport by Russian military aircraft was in 2014, when Russian refueling planes landed at Cam Ranh to support long-range bombers flying over the South China Sea, according to Vietnam’s state-controlled media.

Vietnam and Russia have had diplomatic relations since 1950. Evidence of the long-running relationship and its influence can be seen in Vietnamese cities like the capital, Hanoi, where Soviet-style apartment blocks are commonplace, although now dwarfed by skyscrapers.

A statue of Vladimir Lenin, the founder of the Soviet Union, stands in a park where kids skateboard every evening. Many in the Communist Party’s top leadership in Vietnam studied in Soviet universities.

Since the early 2000s, Russia has accounted for the bulk of Vietnam’s arms imports. This has been declining over the years due to Vietnamese attempts to diversify its supplies.

News.title: JD boss notes impact of ‘civil unrest’ across Europe on brand sales
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The boss of JD Sports Fashion has noted the impact of “civil unrest” across Europe on the brand’s sales through autumn.

JD Sports, founded in 1981, has 4,681 stores across 31 countries and operates brands such as Size? Go Outdoors, JD and Sport Zone.

The FTSE 100 company reported on Thursday that its comparable sales trends in the UK were boosted by the Fifa World Cup this summer, but have fallen in its third quarter to October 31.

Like-for-like sales fell 2.6% in the UK over the quarter.

But JD Sports noted that its overall organic sales trend across its global brands improved from a drop of 1.3% in the second quarter to growth of 1.1%, with like-for-likes down 2.6% against a 3.1% fall in the previous quarter.

Chief executive Regis Schultz said: “In the UK and Europe, cooler weather in October began to bring through some of the autumn/winter demand delayed by unseasonably warm weather earlier in the quarter, although trading in Europe was affected by civil unrest.”

Starting in September, Europe saw waves of protests which began as calls for more education funding in France and snowballed into unrest across the continent.

open image in gallery Protesters at Place De La Republique in Paris, set fire to a car during a march against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools (Lucy North/PA) ( PA Wire )

Mr Schultz went on to praise the “courage, professionalism and resilience” his colleagues showed across Europe during the unrest.

Across Europe, the company saw a drop in like-for-like sales of 2.7% and France was noted in particular for having been affected by civil unrest.

In the UK, the company saw a 4.2% drop in organic sales, which it said reflects store closures in JD and Outdoor.

It added that outdoor business had delivered a good performance while footwear performance softened, which reflected “end-of-cycle” products.

JD Sports said its overall group sales trends were “in line with our expectations” despite the unexpected unrest and warmer weather.

A senior retail analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, Charles Allen, said: “JD Sports may find that its efficiency projects – including bringing automation to its Heerlen distribution centre serving Europe – may only partly offset gross-margin pressure from continued sales weakness.”

He added: “A lack of industry acceptance that the athleisure footwear market is mature, likely influenced by a strong but small performance segment, translates into a surfeit of new product and market-share battles.”

The company said in its latest financial reports that while store footfall is down year-on-year, online sales growth, particularly in North America, has risen.

It also trimmed its full-year profit before tax guidance from a range of £700 million to £800 million to £700 million to £750 million.

Shares fell 4% in afternoon trading on Thursday.

Mr Schultz said: “Our multi-brand, multi-category model keeps us agile and quick to respond to changing customer trends and demand.

“We are raising the bar on our product ranges, bringing new launches to market faster, particularly in apparel, and investing in a stronger, more seamless experience across stores and online.

“With our technology re-platforming in Europe now complete, our new e-commerce platforms are live across all regions.

“We are also scaling our use of AI at pace across the business, from customer discovery to inventory management.”

News.title: Myanmar guilty of genocide, International Court of Justice rules
News.content:
Myanmar’s military junta has been found guilty of committing genocide in a ruling that could have implications for Israel and its war on Gaza.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, the UN’s highest court, said Myanmar had systematically attempted to destroy the Muslim minority Rohingya population. It is the first time in its 81-year history that the ICJ has found a state guilty of genocide.

The 2017 attacks led to the largest movement of people in modern history, with hundreds of thousands fleeing violence across the border to Bangladesh. The court said the attacks constituted more than an attempt to contain unrest in the region through military means.

The judges said: “The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations.”

News.title: England feast on Australia chaos to land early Ashes blow
News.content:
Good morning from idyllic Hobart, where there is not a cloud in the sky, and England are having a belting time batting first.

They zipped along all day in lovely batting conditions, moving to 137 for two from 20 overs.

The wickets to fall have been Tom Banton, well caught by a juggling Mitch Marsh running back from mid-off, and Joe Root, who had a horrible heave at Matt Renshaw, and was bowled. He has never made an ODI hundred on Australian soil and is unlikely to get another chance.

Ben Duckett initially cruised along in Banton’s slip stream, but has hit a blaze of boundaries since. He has feasted on some Australia’s bowling and fielding that has been pretty ordinary, as they say in these parts. Duckett was the beneficiary of a terrible drop at square leg by Alex Carey, who is back in the side but not keeping.

The other big talking point, inevitably, is sandpapergate. Usman Khawaja, who lit the fire for the reopening of the public debate, is here commentating, and Cricket Australia have announced an independent forum for players and staff from the tour of South Africa in 2018 to come forward and share their memories. CA will not be reopening the investigation, and or issuing any new punishments, though. They haven’t even decided how much of forum’s findings they will make public. So it is unclear exactly what the point of the whole thing is.

News.title: Households face back-to-back interest rate rises
News.content:
Mortgage borrowers face another rise in interest rates before Christmas after official figures showed inflation rose to its highest level in a year.

The Bank of England is expected to raise borrowing costs again in December, after increasing rates for the first time in three years earlier this month.

It comes after consumer prices index (CPI) inflation rose from 3.5pc in September to 3.6pc in October, according to the Office for National Statistics.

In a rare intervention after the publication of inflation data, the Bank underlined its commitment to slowing down the pace of price rises.

A spokesman for the Bank said: “The conflict in the Middle East has caused energy prices and inflation to rise in recent months, and inflation is expected to rise further by the middle of next year due to cost pressures already in the pipeline.

“The Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate two weeks ago to limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2pc target and stays there.”

Rob Wood of Pantheon Macroeconomics said it was a “very close call” over whether policymakers raise rates in December or February, but favoured a jump before Christmas.

Traders are betting there is a 74pc chance of a December rate rise, down from 77pc on Tuesday, after services inflation rose slightly less than expected to 3.7pc in October.

Mr Wood said: “The headlines provide some relief, but underlying inflation remains too high, and airfares may be beginning to show some effect from higher energy costs.

“We expect at least two further rate hikes and now bring our calls forward to December and February, from February and April.”

Inflation increased in October as a result of surging fuel prices for motorists.

The average price of petrol rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October to 174.7p, the highest level since August 2022.

The ONS said diesel rose by 7p to 199.5p per litre last month – the highest since records began in 1996.

News.title: ‘No guarantees’: Sierra Leone’s struggle to stop women dying in labour
News.content:
As she comes face to face with her newborn baby girl for the first time, young mother Adama Gomes smiles with relief.

Standing before a row of brand-new incubators in a spotlessly clean neonatal intensive care ward, Adama, 23, cradles her tiny one-day-old daughter with even more trepidation than most novice parents.

During an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems, she often doubted this blissful moment would happen.

Had she reached term a year ago, Adama, who has sickle cell anaemia, could have died from the significant complications she faced.

Adama Gomes, who has sickle cell anaemia, endured an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Thankfully, however, the first-time mum from a village in Sierra Leone’s Kono region gave birth at the recently opened Maternal Center of Excellence, a state-of-the-art hospital that would be the envy of the NHS.

As she bonds with her yet to be named first child, who has been kept in one of the incubators overnight, Adama and her tiny daughter embody the impressive transformation in Sierra Leone's maternal health over the last decade.

Maternity staff help Adama with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I am so happy that me and my baby are healthy,” she declares. “It was hard getting here for check-ups during the pregnancy but I’m so glad I did.

“I know that it’s only because of the treatment I received that I am here now. They checked my body very thoroughly and gave me the tablets that I needed.”

Midwife Gloria Nanah Kamara explains that Adama needed medication to prevent pre-eclampsia. The risk was great enough for doctors to insist her baby be delivered by caesarean section.

“Pre-eclampsia is very common, probably the leading cause of death during pregnancy in this country,” Kamara explains.

“The only way of ensuring that the mother and baby survive is to do a caesarean, which they cannot do in a local clinic.”

Adama Gomes watches over her newborn baby in an incubator Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Before the creation of the new hospital, which opened in February this year, the treatment Adama received would have been inconceivable for a mother from an underdeveloped region in Sierra Leone.

Two decades ago, amid the smouldering wreckage of a brutal war, the West African nation held the dubious distinction of having the worst maternal mortality rate in the world.

Around 2,000 women were dying for every 100,000 children born, a damning statistic for a country trying to rebuild.

Since then, the prospects for expectant mothers in the West African nation have improved dramatically.

Sullaymata Saffa with her one-day-old baby girl, after travelling across Sierra Leone to use the new maternal facility Credit : Simon Townsley

According to official figures from its Ministry of Health released last month, there are now only 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, a 74 per cent reduction.

While any progress is welcome, the latest data show that globally 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023. The vast majority of deaths in low and middle income countries are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia – and they are entirely preventable.

Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives. When a mother survives childbirth, her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

An expectant mother receives an ultrasound scan at an MSF hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Sierra Leone’s success is largely due to the roll-out of free healthcare to pregnant women and children in 2010, and a more recent push to reach zero preventable maternal deaths. The 300 days of Activism for Triple Zero campaign – which also aims to tackle preventable child deaths and unvaccinated children – began in March.

According to the government, maternal deaths have dropped by 31.4 per cent since last year. There remains, however, deep inequality for pregnant women, mostly because of geographical inequity.

The United States charity Partners in Health, the lead funder for the Maternal Center of Excellence, points out that women in Sierra Leone have a one in 74 chance of dying in pregnancy or childbirth in their reproductive years. By comparison, the risk for UK women is around one in 7,500.

Despite the unparalleled progress of recent years, the happy ending which Adama and her baby have experienced is by no means universal across Sierra Leone.

A mother and her newborn recover from birth at the Maternal Center of Excellence at the Koidu Government Hospital Credit : Simon Townsley

Accounts of pregnant women dying before reaching hospital are commonplace, with deplorable road conditions and poor facilities in rural clinics often to blame.

Last month, a woman in the remote Falaba district in the far north of the country died while being taken to the local state hospital.

The first ambulance dispatched to transport her became stuck on the road, forcing health authorities to send a second ambulance. Sadly, the woman died while being transported in the replacement vehicle.

During visits to villages in the diamond-producing Kono district, the Telegraph observed how the positive official statistics do not always reflect the reality on the ground.

The busy waiting room at Koidu Government Hospital, in the east of Sierra Leone Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

The contrast between the gleaming new hospital in the regional capital Koidu and the primitive clinic in the village of Ponduru is jarring.

Our journey provides a snapshot of how arduous it can be for expectant mothers living in distant communities to reach a decent maternity unit.

For the first hour, the spine-shaking terrain prompts me to contemplate how much more painful the same trip would be for a heavily pregnant woman.

Women wait for ante-natal examinations Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Afterwards, the churned-up mud track is so bad that we have to abandon the vehicle and walk the final mile.

Motorcycles skid and swerve through the sticky clay, but are the only form of transport for people living several hours further down the treacherous route, including pregnant women.

An ambulance that was due to visit the village during our visit never arrives because the driver is afraid it will get stuck.

It is evident that a woman needing a team of midwives and expensive monitoring equipment to assist with a complicated birth can be totally cut off during the rainy season.

On our hike, we pass women washing clothes in a flooded river while, further along, a group of men escapes the full blast of the sweltering heat in the shade of a mango tree.

Betty Abu prepares for the birth of her third child; Only two of Isha Sheriff’s four children survived Credit : Simon Townsley

Nine-months pregnant Betty Abu, 26, is sheltering inside the village clinic, preparing to give birth for the third time.

“I walked here from my own village because the road is so bad,” Betty tells me. “It took me three hours. I’ve been doing the same thing regularly for appointments because I’ve had a lot of pain.

“Even though it’s not great here it’s better than where I come from. Many women there have had miscarriages and stillbirths.”

Beside her, 29-year-old Isha Sheriff echoes this view, testifying that only two of her four children were born alive. Isha, like others, bears her tragedy with stoicism, recognising her own survival is entirely thanks to modern medicine.

Sebatu Kamara with baby Moses Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I had a blockage in my stomach, which caused the baby to die inside me. I also had sepsis,” explains Isha, a teacher in the village school. “They had to operate on me.

“My whole body was swollen. I could barely walk because I was so weak. But I know that I definitely would have lost my life without the treatment I was given in hospital.”

As we leave the village, I meet 23-year-old Sebatu Kamara carrying her eight-month-old baby Moses in a sling on her back.

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu faces the prospect of motorcycle transport Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I feel very lucky to have got through my pregnancy,” admits Sebatu. “There are no guarantees in a place like this. Now I can focus on my child.”

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu, 19, is less settled, desperately hoping that she can avoid an excruciating motorcycle trip to Koidu. She counts down the days to her admission into Ponduru’s delivery room.

If she does stay, the facilities in the clinic will be minimal. The village has a pump from a borehole, but no running water.

Community midwife Margaret Messie Seppeh admits the power supply is so unstable that she regularly depends on mobile phone torches to see during a nocturnal delivery.

The Maternal Center of Excellence is now the country’s main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

For those with the means to get there, the Maternal Center of Excellence, which is five and a half hours from the capital and biggest city Freetown, offers exemplary care.

Attached to the existing Government Hospital, it is now the main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies for the whole country.

From the six-bed delivery ward to the intensive care unit, every part of the hospital boasts the latest foetal and maternal monitoring technology.

The facilities are so much better than other regional delivery wards that some patients travel for days on the back of a motorbike taxi to use it, including some from neighbouring Guinea. Admission is free of charge, mostly thanks to financial support from Partners in Health.

The centre boasts state-of-the-art hospital facilities Credit : Simon Townsley

Nearly half of the 2,375 women to give birth in the Maternal Center of Excellence since it opened have had emergency caesarean sections, for which a blood transfusion is routinely required.

The reason for this is that many patients – often still teenagers – have had no check-ups, so potential complications are only identified as they go into labour.

Nurse Kamara says another significant challenge is that the majority of expectant mothers have been subjected to female genital mutilation, making a natural birth more problematic.

Midwife Fatu Josephine Musa with foetal heart-rate monitors in the centre’s delivery suite Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most mothers who come here have undergone this procedure,” she explains. “We can have up to 14 c-section operations a day, not including emergencies.

“Many of them had no antenatal appointments so when they arrive it is already too late for a natural birth.

“The young mothers often just don’t know what they are doing. They arrive here with a variety of obstetric problems. They are usually exhausted from the long journey too.”

A mother watches over her newborn in Sierra Leone’s first-ever neonatal intensive care unit Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Another issue which affects maternal health is the nutritionally limited diet of mothers who depend on staples like cassava and plantain. A lack of vitamins and minerals can increase the risk of anaemia, pre-eclampsia and complications after delivery.

Lack of income prevents many from making the long journey to Koidu. For them, motorcycle taxi fares are unaffordable.

But for now, the successful results of the facility mean pregnant women are gravitating there. With no equivalent anywhere nearby, it could soon be over-capacity.

In the antenatal ward, Kadiatu Jawara, 26, says it has taken her two days to reach the sanctuary of the region’s outstanding maternity hospital from her village in Guinea.

After suffering a miscarriage in her first pregnancy, she was desperate for the reassurance it provides.

“The pregnancy has been fine, but I know there is always risk,” admits Kadiatu. “I will need a caesarean, so I feel much more confident about it being here.”

Blood donors in Ponduru – including the village chief (centre) – play a crucial role in maternal healthcare Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At the heart of the multi-pronged approach to tackling maternal deaths in Sierra Leone is blood donation.

A scheme called Gi4SaveLife is addressing postpartum haemorrhage – when a mother loses a large quantity of blood after delivery – one of the leading causes of maternal death.

Clinics previously relied on blood donated by family members for transfusions.

Community blood donors in Ponduru Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

This precarious dependence was further complicated by cultural suspicion around blood donation in the rural areas where it is most needed.

Now, instead of desperately finding relatives willing to accompany a patient to give blood during an emergency, villages are building up their own supply.

Isatu Jimmysam, 27, discloses that she is alive only because she received two pints of blood from stocks donated by her neighbours when she delivered her baby boy Hassan earlier this year.

At a blood drive in another village outside Koidu, backed by the local Lifeline organisation, 28-year-old Kadaitu Balgale tells me she feels obliged to donate following her own experience during childbirth.

“I was given a transfusion because of complications when I had my baby,” she reveals. “My pressure went right up during labour and I collapsed. The nurses had to perform a C-section.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village after losing his sister to childbirth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Now my baby is three and we are both healthy. I was lucky. I’m very happy to give blood to make sure there is enough stock for other women who have the same problem.”

“I’m doing this to help save pregnant women and their children,” affirms Osman Kamara, 32. “I have been several times after the daughter of our village chief became very ill and needed blood during labour.”

In Sierra Leone’s most isolated places, however, keeping a stock of blood is simply not feasible.

Maya died aged 25, along with her infant, after losing too much blood to be resuscitated Credit : Collect

Refrigerated storage requires stable electrical power but 95 per cent of rural areas remain off grid. Solar panels are used but are not always reliable, especially during the rainy months.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village.

His sister Maya died aged 25 after losing too much blood to be resuscitated. She had been pregnant with her third child.

“Both her and the baby died,” states Moses. “She was very strong and healthy but developed serious complications which led to her bleeding profusely. There was nothing that could be done in time.”

The introduction of portable monitoring systems which enable rural midwives to assess maternal and foetal heart rates has also brought positive results. A trial of a device called the Cradle-5, backed by King’s College London and local NGO Wellbodi Partnership, improved detection of complications such as haemorrhage, sepsis and pre-eclampsia.

In the fishing village of Tombo, a complementary endeavour linked to the blood drives has led to a steep drop in maternal and perinatal deaths.

A pregnant teenager in the isolated Ponduru village, Kono district Credit : Simon Townsley

2YoungLives is a nationwide mentoring scheme for pregnant teenagers which recruits respected older women to mentor pregnant adolescents from pregnancy until a year after birth.

Mother mentors take girls to antenatal appointments, negotiate with families, recognise danger signs, accompany them during labour and help them return to education.

Before it started, many young women were ejected from their family homes after becoming pregnant.

Ostracised from the traditional support network, they were less likely to seek medical attention until too late.

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

Margaret Mansaray, 65, has been part of the mentoring scheme since it began Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most of these pregnant girls don’t want to go to clinic appointments because they are embarrassed, so one of our main jobs is to ensure that they do.

“We make sure they are tested for conditions like malaria and hepatitis, as well any issues with the pregnancy.”

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“There were so many girls dying in the past,” she continues. “My own niece died from bleeding because she was not taken to hospital in time.

“Because of that, I was very happy to do this. I knew there was a desperate need. We used to go into the communities to search for abandoned pregnant girls but now people are aware of us. They see us as role models. Some of the girls even name their children after me.”

Gathered around Margaret are the local teenagers whose lives she has protected. Mums Adama Sesay, 17, and Rahmatalai Bah, 16, sit on a stone wall holding their babies.

Although abandoned by the men who got them pregnant, they can at least look forward to watching their children grow up.

Additional reporting by Saidu Bah
