Petr Cech was just 22 when he made his Chelsea debut and went on to achieve legendary status. Alonso evidently didn't believe the Belgian international was ready at the start of this campaign but Penders has certainly given his manager something to consider.

2 - Inconsistent Chelsea's longest winning streak in the Premier League so far

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Carragher sits down with former team-mate and current Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso to discuss his start to life at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea have been consistently inconsistent so far. They bounced back from a poor draw with Hull and even worse thumping at Brentford by dishing out a 5-1 thrashing of Bournemouth, while losses to Spurs and Sunderland have tempered expectations. Three games in, their trip to the Emirates was billed as an opportunity to show they could be a real threat - potentially even title contenders. Instead, after 10 games, they're 11 points behind Arsenal and unlikely to trouble the Premier League champions.

They've won back-to-back league games just twice and have yet to demonstrate evidence of a clear identity forming. Injuries to key personnel have hampered Alonso. The Chelsea boss has continually stated his side will look different in May, compared to what we are witnessing now. However, the journey and the eventual destination isn't obvious. Yet in spite of four league defeats already, the Blues are relatively well-placed for Champions League qualification.

3 - Games in a row without a recognised striker

Image: Danny Welbeck has made just one Premier League start so far

We'll come onto Joao Pedro's brilliant start but Alonso's curious approach to his recent injury issue has sparked debate. Chelsea started without a recognised striker against Spurs, Man Utd and Sunderland, with Danny Welbeck given just a few minutes off the bench in the first two of those games before going on after an hour as Chelsea chased an equaliser at the Stadium of Light. With summer signings Welbeck and Emmanuel Emegha not trusted and Liam Delap, Nicolas Jackson and Marc Guiu sold, Chelsea look short up front.

Morgan Rogers and Pedro Neto have been used as false nines. The former Aston Villa man offers a presence when deployed there but Neto's usage is difficult to comprehend. Welbeck has been ineffective in starts against Brentford and Liverpool in the cup but Chelsea lack a focal point without a natural forward. They also have the biggest positive difference between goals scored (19) and Expected Goals (15.9). While that is the result of some stunning strikes, it also raises questions about the long-term sustainability of their attacking threat after blanks against Tottenham and Sunderland.

4 - Back four? Or back three?

In pre-season, there was much debate about whether Alonso would utilise the back-three set-up which served him so well at Bayer Leverkusen or go with a four as he did at Real Madrid. The answer is: a bit of both. There have been six matches when Chelsea have started with a four and four when they've gone with a three.

Alonso has been keen to stress that in-play shape is more significant than how the names are laid out in a graphic but his variations suggest he is still searching for the right formula - and Chelsea's inconsistent performances and results reflect that uncertainty. Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana have failed to convince at the start of this season and Maxence Lacroix is not injured. Academy graduate Josh Acheampong has been the only major positive defensively so far. He has mightily impressed.

Image: Chelsea in a 3-4-2-1 set-up

Image: Chelsea in a 4-2-3-1 set-up

Image: Chelsea went with a 4-3-2-1 set-up at Sunderland

5 - Times Chelsea have had more or less possession

Beyond formations, preconceptions about the style of play under Alonso have also been challenged in these opening 10 games. In half of them, Chelsea have had more possession than their opponents and bossed the ball. But it's been a different story in the other matches.

In fact, it was stunning to see Chelsea register just 26 per cent possession at home to Brighton in a game they won 4-3. They had just 31 per cent of the ball at home to Spurs. A performance which deeply frustrated the home support.

Part of the plan or a stat which speaks to deeper issues around controlling matches and winning midfield battles? Alonso has admitted that he wants his team to be better with the ball, a message he delivered at half-time to spark an upturn in performance against Manchester United.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at an awards ceremony with a difference - as Cole Palmer dishes out his awards for 2026 for Saturday Social

6 - Different midfield combinations

Alonso was a midfield maestro in his playing days and he has made no secret of declaring the central area as key to his team's success. But he has tried six different midfield combinations so far. Moises Caicedo's early-season injury problem was unhelpful, as was the subsequent Reece James lay-off. Romeo Lavia has at least been fit and impressed, while Jordan Henderson seems to have struck up a relationship with Caicedo. All three started in the defeat at Sunderland. It remains, though, an area of debate.

The sale of Enzo Fernandez late in the transfer window without an adequate replacement coming in has proved to be a problem. A January priority?

Chelsea's central midfield combinations under Alonso in Premier League Lavia, Gusto

Lavia, James

Henderson, Barco

Henderson, Caicedo

Caicedo, Lavia

Caicedo, Lavia, Henderson

7 - Goals from set-pieces and penalties - for and against!

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jordan Henderson and Cole Palmer reveal how they came to the decision for Henderson to take the free-kick against Bournemouth that ended up flying into the top corner

Such is the modern game, transfers of set-piece coaches is now a thing, and Chelsea's capture of Aston Villa's Austin MacPhee - an A-lister in the category - this summer drew attention. The results so far are best described as mixed. Only Brighton have scored more than Chelsea's six from set-piece situations, before you add in Cole Palmer's penalty against Man Utd. But no side has conceded more than their six from set-pieces, with Enzo Le Fee's penalty for Sunderland making the dead-ball for/against tally level.

Their resilient display at Everton suggested progress had been made. However, Alonso, MacPhee and Chelsea have work to do if they are to master this important department at both ends of the pitch.

8 - Still the number of Chelsea goals scored by Estevao

Image: Estevao lashes his shot into the net against Man Utd only for his effort to be ruled out by VAR

With JP Morgan (are we sticking with that name for Chelsea's first-choice front three?) making a flying start to the season, the knock-on effect has been reduced opportunities for Estevao. In fact, Alonso's persistent reluctance to throw the teenage Brazilian into the action has become a frustrating issue for Chelsea supporters, given the electric winger is a firm fan favourite. Like fellow 19-year-old Geovany Quenda - who signed an eight-year contract in the summer - Estevao has made just one Premier League start so far.

The absence of European football hasn't helped, with Chelsea's number of matches reduced this term, and Estevao was out to prove a point when he was given his shot against Man Utd. Despite his best efforts, he was unable to add to the eight goals he scored last season. A narrow offside call prevented him from adding to his tally.

He returned to the bench for the defeat at Sunderland. It's a situation Alonso needs to manage. Estevao has been seen as "untouchable" and unavailable for sale. However, the situation seems unsustainable if the Brazilian spends more time warming the bench than racing up the touchline.

9 - Curse of the No 9? What curse?!

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Joao Pedro scores Chelsea's first Premier League goal under Xabi Alonso inside ONE minute!

The Chelsea No 9 jersey has weighed heavy on its wearer for some time. From Radamel Falcao and Alvaro Morata a decade ago through to Romelu Lukaku, Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang and Liam Delap in more recent seasons, strikers have failed to repeat their prolificacy at other clubs when they've been marked out as Chelsea's main forward. But Joao Pedro has bucked the trend.

He has five goals and three assists in his six Premier League appearances so far and Chelsea's attack looks far better connected with him leading the line. Joao Pedro has emerged as perhaps Alonso's most important player. They need to keep him fit. Chelsea have scored just two goals in the four league matches he has missed - both coming in the win over United.

10 - Starts for in-form pair Palmer and Rogers

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Thomas Tuchel explains why Cole Palmer has failed to make his latest England squad

Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers are the only players to have started all 10 Chelsea Premier League games for Alonso.

Chelsea No 10 Palmer has shown glimpses of his best form and looks close to full fitness. He appears to have found his spark after his struggles last season, although his returns have been inconsistent. His three goals and three assists only tell part of the story. He looks a different player when he has Joao Pedro ahead of him. At times he has looked unplayable. Without the Brazilian striker, he has struggled to impact games as much. He let his frustration show with his sending-off against Spurs.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The REFCAM footage of Morgan Rogers' goal for Chelsea against Manchester United highlighted the woeful defending from Michael Carrick's men

His status as an England international remains a major topic of debate. A small injury forced him to withdraw from Thomas Tuchel's squad in September. He appears to have fallen down Tuchel's pecking order as a result.

Palmer's good friend Rogers has fiercely defended his desire to play for England and on the pitch they have worked well in tandem, too.

Sports.title: Joshua unable to see new baby daughter until after Fury fight
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua became a father for the second time after the birth of a daughter last weekend, although ongoing training for his fight against Tyson Fury means he is not able to see her until mid-December.

Joshua, whose son JJ was born in 2015, is currently in training camp in Marbella in preparation for his blockbuster all-British fight against Fury on December 11 at Cardiff's Principality Stadium, and was unable to be at the birth.

Joshua says the arrival of his daughter, who has not yet been named, is "amazing" and "a big blessing" as the 37-year-old paid tribute to Nicole, the mother of both children.

While he has been able to have "many" FaceTime calls with mother and daughter in recent days, Joshua says he wished he would have been able to be there but preparations for the Fury fight mean mean he is currently "on a mission".

"It's not ideal but she is in good hands," Joshua said in an interview with The Sun.

"She's got an amazing mother, she's got amazing family round her and the people at the hospital, I heard they were amazing. I spoke to them and said thank you, so I'm pretty content at the minute that she's in good hands. But, for me, it would have been much better if I was able to be there.

Image: Joshua is preparing to return to the boxing ring for just the second time in a year

"But I'm on duty at the minute and we're on a mission. I knew about this nine months ago so I made this commitment that I can't change, unfortunately, but there will be many more birthdays I'll be at, for sure."

Asked when he would likely meet her in person for the first time, Joshua said: "Probably December 12, December 13.

"I'll go and check in and rock her to sleep, let her hear my voice and let her feel my heartbeat, really. The basic stuff."

He said he would be a fully hands-on father.

"I'm going to do it all. I'm going to definitely do it all," he added.

"You might see me with some eye shadow on, some nail polish on, drinking some tea in a doll's playhouse just trying to do the right thing by her."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Michael Bridge has more on the timing for Fury and Joshua's fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on Friday 11 December - with the ringwalk expected to place at 1am in the early hours of Saturday

Joshua said he had wanted to become a father for a second time to "do something positive" after the "painful and traumatic" experience of last December's car crash in Nigeria that killed two members of his team, personal trainer Latif Ayodele, and strength and conditioning coach Sina Ghami.

"After the year that I'm coming off I wanted to do something positive," said Joshua, who was injured in the crash.

"I wanted to give JJ the opportunity to be an older brother. One day I won't be here and he'll have a sibling that he can turn to, be with and plan their future together. It's nice to have a sibling that they can lean on each other when needed, when me and his mum aren't here one day in the future."

The British boxer added: "Nicole is doing good. She is healthy. She said it was an amazing experience. She said it was easier than JJ and she's much prettier than JJ, so she's happy! She's already deeply in love with her."

Sports.title: Why Raya is the Premier League's best goalkeeper
Sports.content:
Welcome to The Radar, a Sky Sports column in which Nick Wright uses a blend of data and opinion to shed light on need-to-know Premier League stories. This week:

🔺Why Raya is the Premier League's best

🔺Newcastle's counter-pressing problem

🔺A player to watch this weekend

The qualities that make Raya special

Unai Simon was named goalkeeper of the year at the Ballon d'Or ceremony but the 20,000 professional players who vote on the FIFPRO World XI went for David Raya. In fact, his total of 10,278 votes was the highest of any player - goalkeeper or otherwise.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch a collection of David Raya's best Premier League saves for Arsenal

Raya had to settle for a supporting role during Spain's World Cup campaign. Simon started every game and remains Luis de la Fuente's first choice in the position. But Raya's FIFPRO vote share reflected his status in the eyes of his fellow players.

Arsenal see him in the same way. Their new contract for Raya will reflect his standing as one of the world's best; recognition of his vital role in last season's Premier League title win and reward for how he has flourished since joining from Brentford in 2023.

Raya is now a three-time Golden Glove winner who has kept clean sheets in nearly half of his 117 Premier League appearances for Arsenal. He has an even better success rate in the Champions League, with 21 shutouts in 40 games in the same timeframe.

Raya's reflexes are key to his shot-stopping. The quality of his positioning is another factor. According to Gradient's analysts, he hasn't made a single positional error when facing a shot this season.

Raya is of course well protected. Arsenal have the best defence in the Premier League and maybe Europe. But those defenders benefit from Raya's presence as much as he benefits from theirs.

When interviewing him for Sky Sports in 2024, Raya highlighted the importance of another of his best attributes: his ability to claim crosses, which he credited to Iñaki Caña, the goalkeeping coach who followed him from Brentford to Arsenal.

"If you watch highlights from me when I was back at Blackburn, you will see a 'keeper that just stood on the line, not coming for anything, rarely going for a cross, rarely going outside the box, rarely anticipating, just waiting to make that save," he said.

"When I signed for Brentford, Iñaki just completely changed my style of being a goalkeeper, to be more proactive and anticipate stuff that has not happened yet. So, if you can go for a cross, just go for it. Don't wait for the save. Instead, avoid the chance."

Raya's proactivity can backfire.

Brentford fans will recall him being caught off his line by Joe Byram's long-range free-kick in the 2020 Championship play-off final. Arsenal fans will remember him failing to reach a high ball before Brian Brobbey's 94th-minute equaliser away to Sunderland.

But the rewards comfortably outweigh the risks overall.

This season, Gradient's data for crosses caught, factoring crosses caught at waist height or above, shows him top among goalkeepers, with 13. And that despite facing roughly 20 per cent fewer crosses than the two goalkeepers closest to his total.

Raya's dominance from crosses acts as a pressure release valve for Arsenal when defending their box. His efforts this season help to explain why the Gunners have one of the lowest opponent cross completion rates among Premier League sides.

Raya is shorter than the average goalkeeper at 6ft 1in, instead relying on his spring and athleticism when commanding his box. In possession, meanwhile, he benefits from vision that once prompted Jurgen Klopp to say he "should have number 10 on his back".

According to Gradient, Raya has completed the joint-most line-breaking passes of Premier League goalkeepers with this season. His total of 33 puts him level with Aston Villa's Zion Suzuki but with a higher success rate at 87 per cent to Suzuki's 79 per cent.

Suzuki stands out in the data as another goalkeeper who offers proactivity on crosses as well as progressive passing ability. But the Villa goalkeeper has conceded five saveable goals already this season, nearly as many as Raya in the last two combined.

It is that completeness, in shot-stopping, cross-claiming and distribution, that separates Raya from the rest in the Premier League. And while the Ballon d'Or voting went another way, it gives him a strong case to be considered one of the world's best too.

Jaissle's pressing problem

Arsenal next test comes at St James' Park, live on Sky Sports on Saturday, where Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle could really do with a result. He has only won one out of five five Premier League home games since arriving from Saudi Arabian club Al Ahli.

Speaking to him while at Red Bull Salzburg, where he won back-to-back Austrian titles between 2021 and 2023, provided an insight into his philosophy. Jaissle is an advocate of quick, vertical attacks. But what came across most strongly was the overarching importance he places on out-of-possession work.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Carragher said earlier this month that a tough season lies ahead for Newcastle

"The mentality is important, to see the nature of the player," Jaissle told Sky Sports. "Does he really want to chase the ball, to win it back? We also have a saying that mentality eats talent."

Jaissle likes to his teams to channel their intensity into Jurgen Klopp-like counter-pressing, which is defined as attempting to win the ball back within a few seconds of losing it. The idea is to capitalise on an opponent's disorganisation in the moments after regaining the ball, ideally high up the pitch.

Image: Matthias Jaissle's only home Premier League win at Newcastle came against Hull

Jaissle's Red Bull Salzburg excelled on this front. In their 2021/22 and 2022/23 Champions League campaigns, they ranked ninth and seventh respectively among the 32 competing sides for possessions won in the final third per game. But his Newcastle players have so far struggled to make the same tactics work.

According to Opta, Newcastle sit 17th among Premier League sides for high-intensity counter pressures this season.

Brighton, Arsenal and Manchester City, the Premier League's top three, also feature low on the list. But that is largely because they dominate the ball, averaging roughly 60 per cent possession, meaning there are fewer opportunities to counter-press. Newcastle, by contrast, only average 50 per cent possession.

Sports.title: Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’
Sports.content:
The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under-21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one.

Time to talk, so let’s start with tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and reckons he might have liked law, yet even that wasn’t his chosen field.

Hayworth’s family was from Seville province. “I know she was a great actress but I’m afraid I have to admit I’m not one for old films,” García concedes in an even tone. “My uncles played rugby for Ciencias and practically all of them were in the national team together. They tried to get me to play with my cousins, but I was always more into football.” He was good at it too: another Spain international, the Club World Cup’s top scorer, playing for Real Madrid.

Then this summer, with opportunities limited, he joined Fulham, his introductory interview conducted in impeccable English. Having joined Madrid aged 10, he was leaving home for the first time, as Fulham’s record signing, at 22. He had the language and intelligence to embrace it. As for being uprooted, he was used to that, growing up in Argentina and Chile as well as Spain.

“From very little my parents impressed upon me the importance of study, learning languages,” García says. “I’m at Villanueva university [in Madrid]. I started with dual honours business and analytics although that became difficult with my profession. Now it’s just business, and I’m trying to arrange with the university how best to handle it [from London]. My parents considered it fundamental to speak English and I was always at international schools.

View image in fullscreen Gonzalo García plays football for Spain’s under-21s but his uncles were international rugby players. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

“Every two or three years we would change city. Obviously, there would be phases when I felt: ‘Pfff, again?!’ Having to move home because of my parents’ work. But I look back and feel grateful because, seen with perspective, it gives you opportunities to meet new people, see new places, learn. I’ve always had foreign friends with whom I spoke English.”

García has been joined at Fulham by César Palacios and Manuel Ángel from Madrid’s academy. Three 22-year-olds, like your very own Erasmus course. “Nah,” García says, laughing. “I wouldn’t call it an Erasmus because we’re talking about a big, ambitious career step. We’re grateful for the trust placed in us. I’ve been pleasantly surprised by London, a huge city with people from all nationalities and cultures and Fulham fit the situation I was in, the desire to grow.

“Álvaro Arbeloa explained the project, convinced me. I’d worked with him in Madrid. He knows me perfectly, how far he can push me. Equally, I know what he wants of me. That helps … [Arbeloa] told me it was a project that it will take time but that he needed me. I’m very, very happy. It’s one of the world’s best leagues, if not the best.”

And the toughest? Is English football as wild as it looks? “Yes!” García replies. “They had told me it was demanding, hard, but …” He cracks up. “I have to admit it still surprised me. That first game against Chelsea, I finished really, really tired. It was box to box, intense, a lot of running. Bit by bit I’m adapting. The intensity and pace is very different.

“Spain is more tactical, a bit more technical. English football is pace. You can’t lose concentration for a second, not a second. Anything can happen any moment. How many Premier League games are decided late? Suddenly there’s a goal in the 90th minute and again on 93. It’s your corner and their chance. The level of concentration, that constant transition, is what most sets the Premier League apart.”

Despite defeat on that opening day against Chelsea, García scored. A superb goal followed against AFC Wimbledon in the Carabao Cup. “It was super special to do it at Craven Cottage – I love how close the fans are; they can reach out and touch you. But I don’t consider myself someone who’s easily satisfied. I’m not like that. I always want more, more, more.”

View image in fullscreen ‘Álvaro Arbeloa explained the project at Fulham, he convinced me,’ says Gonzalo García. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

García hasn’t scored since and Fulham went five league games without a win, pressure building. Which is where the calmness comes in. By the time they faced Hull, Arbeloa appeared on the edge of the sack, questions asked about his signings, García especially. Were three Madrid academy kids really what Fulham needed? Was the coach’s relationship with them not such a good thing after all?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

No player is impermeable to what is said, García admits, but he insists: “We treat that as outside noise. And we all knew that the beginning wouldn’t be easy. There’s a change of cycle: the coach goes, a new coach comes, there are signings, a different system, idea. Everyone has to adapt: those already at the club and those of us who are new. We’re young too. Results weren’t going our way but we had good intentions: to play good football, build, apply the manager’s ideas bit by bit. We had to remain calm.”

Fulham go into Saturday’s game at Manchester City unbeaten in four in the league, the sense of them shifting towards something more pragmatic not shared by García. “I don’t think we changed anything against Hull,” he says of a game Fulham won 1-0. “We didn’t do anything we weren’t already doing. Nothing. Maybe we controlled the small details that hurt us but the idea was the same. The players were very clear what the manager asked, very firm: it was just a question of time. You have to be patient. If you watch Fulham, you see the manager’s idea: have the ball, construct attacks well, show maximum intensity constantly with and without the ball. Aggressive, ambitious.”

View image in fullscreen Gonzalo García has not scored for Fulham since August: ‘I know strikers are measured by goals.’ Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

Chances are coming for García but goals aren’t. He has started every league game but not scored or assisted since the opening day. Yet if there is a sense of a man feeling the pressure, that’s not repeated here; instead there’s an evenness, an ease. And a smile when another, more welcome, stat is raised: he has made more off-the-ball runs into the area than anyone. Something to hold on to, perhaps, a process that will pay off. “Really?” he says. “Well, I’m happy for people to see that a striker can help the team without the ball. In the end, it’s about following the manager’s instructions.”

In the end though, teams will be judged on results and strikers on goals, price too. He knows: this is what he does, the path he chose. “Pressure depends on how you look at it, really,” García says. “Football is [very psychological]. It happens fast: it doesn’t give you time to enjoy good moments or linger on bad ones. It’s a rollercoaster: up there, down here. It’s not flat, but you maintain balance, work daily, improve: go in, focus, repeat.

“It’s not that I don’t ‘care’ about the price, it’s that the market is the market; it doesn’t depend on me. Calmness always, perspective … I know strikers are measured by goals but, well, the days I don’t score I’m completely sure I will be able to walk off the pitch and say that, no matter what happened, I helped my team, doing a load of other things. It is what it is.”

It is also time. A head peers around the door, the bus is going. García holds out a hand, apologises again. “It’s been a pleasure,” he says.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino calls for Manchester United to show no fear against Liverpool
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield on Sunday for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start.

United are 18th in the Premier League and Liverpool fourth but the head coach will not accept nerves. Pochettino is known for being attack-minded and will bring those ideals, but will have had only three days with the players since replacing Michael Carrick.

“We are going to go there to Anfield with the idea to win and be brave and to be Manchester United,” Pochettino told the club’s website. “The history talks for us, and what we need to expect, and we are going to expect in Manchester United. We need to be sure that we are brave and we are protagonists and go there with no fears and challenge a very good team like Liverpool.”

Pochettino arrived in Manchester on Wednesday after an overnight flight, having taken charge of his final USA match against Haiti. He toured the training ground and held meetings with senior staff and players not on international duty. Members of Pochettino’s staff were in place earlier in the week as they seek to revitalise a team with one league win.

“We need to go little by little, step by step,” Pochettino said. “We cannot go too fast but also we need to, at the same time, attack the priorities to build something.”

He said it was important he and his staff adapt to the culture of the club. “And then, with this sense of knowing the history of the club, try to create all together, because we are all different, a culture, a philosophy that can respect that identity, the history of the club. But at the same time, performing. If we don’t perform, the responsibility is mine.”

Pochettino has coveted the United job and is a keen admirer of Sir Alex Ferguson, who he describes as “the best coach in history”. Since the Scot’s retirement in 2013, United have failed to match his success but Pochettino said he was looking at “the potential of the club”. The weight of past achievements has hindered individuals over the past 13 years.

“The players need to express their talent,” Pochettino said. “We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now: it’s to work with them and try to take the pressure.

“Pressure needs to bring energy, responsibility needs to bring energy. Because if not, it’s too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back. When you connect with the game, you connect through your talent when you feel freedom, when you feel happy, when you want to play for your teammates, when you want to play for your family, when you want to play for your club, your fans.”

He sounded an upbeat note, saying: “With the power of this club and the fans supporting us, I think we will get in the place that we deserve to be.”

United on Thursday reported a quarterly ⁠net loss of £18.1m, compared with £6.6m ​in ​the same period a year earlier. Revenue rose 4% to £146m in the three months ​to the end of ​September.

Sports.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden
Sports.content:
It’s injury time at the Emirates on the 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Spurs. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and on to the post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs fans before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it.

But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”.

It’s just a noise, but it’s unmistakingly Danny Kelly. He regains the power of speech and follows it up with: “Gooooaaaal … Goalll Stan Goalll at the Emirates.” Reporter Ian Abrahams and Stan Collymore join the excitement, before Danny comes back: “I LOVE FOOTBALL, STAN, I LOVE IT.” It is such a brilliant piece of radio. From one of the absolute greats.

Danny died last week. In a beautiful tribute on the Spurs podcast he hosted – A View From The Lane – Charlie Eccleshare pointed out the irony that for someone so articulate and erudite and able to do so much more than just “the football”, his most iconic moment is so simple. Even the opening noise – not even a real word – is perfect in that context.

Words such as pioneer and trailblazer often get thrown out in moments like this. But Danny really was. I first met him at BBC London more than 20 years ago. As someone who’d listened to him and Danny Baker as a teenager, I couldn’t really believe I was in the same office as them.

His career was ridiculous, editing the NME and Q magazine, setting up Football365, but it was radio where I knew him. He understood the absurdity of life and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living by talking about football.

I remember at TalkSport one World Cup – 2018 perhaps – wandering in and he was hosting a live match, watching a game on the TV just marvelling at the fact that this was a job, and that this was his job.

And he was funny. Blimey he was funny – what an ability to be blessed with. I listened to a best of Baker and Kelly Upfront from the old Radio 5 on YouTube the other day; amazing calls about Arthur Cox locking a disgruntled fan in his office for two and a half hours, a man playing football with a pig’s head in a sausage factory in Peckham: “I used to like the volleys when the eyes used to pop out.” Anyone who has tried to make funny football content, of any kind – radio, TV, podcasts, social media – owes a debt of gratitude to him.

View image in fullscreen Danny Kelly on television in 2013. Photograph: Steve Meddle/Shutterstock

Last Wednesday afternoon Charlie Baker and I had to try to do him justice on TalkSport. Afternoon UK time, midnight til 3am for me in Australia. I was asleep when my phone rang and instantly presumed I’d slept through my alarm and missed the show. A millisecond of internal panic surged through me as I jumped up and cracked a shin on the bedside table. Danny would appreciate the ridiculous scene of me hopping around in the dark trying not to wake the kids while one of the bosses gave me the incredibly sad news.

If you’ve broadcast for any amount of time, you will be confronted with having to host shows just after someone has died. Jack Charlton, Terry Venables, Jimmy Greaves – but never before have I had to pay tribute to a friend.

Paul Hawksbee’s voice cracks and we all go. There are West Ham and Chelsea fans calling admitting they listen to his Spurs podcast because it’s him. There are all manner of texts recounting hilarious stories they heard on his shows over the last 30 years: the man who took a TV to a game in Northern Ireland so they could watch the FA Cup final, having to move around holding the aerial to keep the signal.

There’s a moment I think Danny would have found so funny, when I’m being sad – because it is sad, and I am sad – and into the break I read the sponsor’s lines: “This show is brought to you by Toolstation, first stop Toolstation” in such a maudlin way it’s as if I’m delivering a eulogy, just one sponsored by a hardware store. I catch myself just in time.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

But most importantly there are so many messages from people who never met Danny, who never knew him, but who felt as if they knew him. We believed he would have wanted a bit of fuss made of him.

He definitely knew the enduring power of radio, even as the broadcasting landscape changes so quickly. It connects in a way nothing else can. And nothing said that more than messages we received from listeners who at one time or another were struggling and going through incredibly hard times and Danny’s energy, wit and joy were an escape and a tonic.

There will be a million people more important in Danny’s life than me. Our paths crossed a great deal, but never for very long. I was a minuscule cog in his world – but Danny had so much love to give. Voice notes about how to broadcast remotely or celebrating Spurs’ win in Bilbao; the tributes showed he had almost infinite time for others.

It always feels such a bland cliche to say it’s impossible to consider someone so full of life not being there – we all know that we have a sell-by date. At the start of October he had been given a choice: to ebb away slowly over a couple of years or have a big but very risky operation. Danny never ebbed.

He sent a big group WhatsApp voice note to many friends and colleagues, and I don’t think he would mind me writing what it said.

“I want you to know that I’ve enjoyed being around you, I’ve learnt from you, I’ve enjoyed working with you, you know how much I love my work – the fact I’m pretty good at it is secondary to how much I enjoy it, but look I’m very much hopeful that the boffins and my own determination will get me through this and we can all laugh about this message. But know how I care about you, how much you have meant in my life and on Thursday night or Friday morning when you look at the sky or feel the wind against your face, think about me and what’s happening and hopefully we’ll all have a pint and a laugh about this somewhere down the line.”

From “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH” to that – his words just hit the right tone every time.

Sports.title: Race for the Fifa presidency: lineup revealed to challenge Gianni Infantino
Sports.content:
Fifa has confirmed that Gianni Infantino will face challenges from Philippe Diallo of France and Japan’s Kozo Tashima in March’s presidential election.

The president of the French Football Federation and honorary president of the Japan Football Association submitted nomination letters with endorsements from five member associations by Wednesday night’s midnight CET deadline. The former Switzerland and Tottenham defender Ramon Vega has not met that threshold, despite repeatedly saying he would stand.

“The candidatures have been forwarded to the electoral committee for examination and for passing a decision on the admission of the candidate,” Fifa said.

The election in Rabat on 18 March will be the first time Infantino has faced opposition since he was first elected in 2016, when he defeated the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88.

Infantino had been expected to be re-elected unopposed for a third time after declaring his candidacy in April and had received more than 200 letters of endorsement from national associations by the time of last summer’s World Cup, but the emergence of his Fifa Forward Enterprise plan has led to a haemorrhaging of support.

Uefa has led a campaign to unseat him since July with backing from Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, and initially the AFC, but with Infantino conducting a global tour to rally support from smaller nations they have struggled to put up an alternative candidate.

Tashima was the first to declare last month in defiance of the AFC, which after criticising the FFE proposal is backing Infantino, having come under pressure from the region’s two major financial powerhouses, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

As revealed by the Guardian on Monday, Diallo was belatedly chosen last weekend as the Uefa candidate after a complex selection process. The 63-year-old’s emergence was a surprise because Uefa had initially hoped to field a more high-profile candidate, such as Arsène Wenger. The Hungarian banker Sandor Csanyi, the president of his country’s FA, had strong backers owing to his close relationship with Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Diallo and Tashima may yet join forces in an attempt to defeat Infantino amid concerns of splitting those opposed to the president among the 211 Fifa members. Were that to occur it is expected Tashima would stand aside, a development that would be supported by Uefa.

All three candidates will be vetted by Fifa’s governance, audit and compliance committee, chaired by the Infantino ally Bruno Chiomento, before the nominations are confirmed on 18 February.

Sports.title: Washington Spirit v Kansas City Current: where the NWSL Championship will be won and lost
Sports.content:
This year’s NWSL Championship blends recurring themes with some newness. For the familiar: the Washington Spirit are in the final for the third straight year, hoping the third time’s the charm after back-to-back 1-0 defeats in their past two attempts. Slightly familiar, too, is Kansas City Current playing the championship game at Washington’s Audi Field, where they lost the final to Portland in 2022 and where they will contend again Saturday.

For the novelty? Neither Kansas City nor Washington, despite their modern dominance in the NWSL table, have won the championship since 2021 (when Washington won). With Gotham’s bid for a two-peat stymied by the Current in the semi-final, here are five things that will decide a new winner in 2026.

Washington’s defensive pressure Washington have allowed the second-fewest goals in the NWSL this year. Through the season and into the playoffs, the center-back pairing of the English defender Esme Morgan and Tara Rudd, the Scottish goalkeeper Sandy MacIver (fourth-highest save percentage in NWSL) and the defensive midfielder Andi Sullivan have been tough to break through for even the league’s most elite attackers. Further up the field, the Spirit’s defense begins with an attacking unit fond of forcing mistakes that lead to goals, with the late-season addition of Clara Luvanga (who has seven goal contributions in seven games for the Spirit) a key impact.

Kansas City, who have scored more goals than any other NWSL team this year, will be a challenge. Defending set pieces will be a space to watch, as they provided the only goal Utah scored against the Spirit in the semi-final, and all the goals Kansas City scored against Gotham.

View image in fullscreen Tara Rudd of Washington Spirit clears under pressure from Kate Del Fava of Utah Royals. Photograph: Scott Taetsch/NWSL/Getty Images

Bethune on a mission against former team This season’s Midfielder of the Year is representing a team in the NWSL Championship for the third straight year (her second with availability to play). But this will be her first not representing the Spirit. After leaving Washington for Missouri in February, Bethune is facing her former team for the chance to win her first championship trophy.

A bit more poetry: Bethune nearly broke the NWSL’s all-time single-season assists record during her 2024 rookie season for the Spirit. (A torn meniscus cut short her streak, but she still was named Rookie of the Year.) She finally broke it this season with Kansas City. Her creative influence in the Current’s midfield has been crucial to unlocking their goal-scoring capabilities. Bethune’s ability to pull apart Washington’s laudable defensive structure could prove crucial in the final.

View image in fullscreen Kansas City Current star Croix Bethune was named this season’s Midfielder of the Year. Photograph: William Purnell/Imagn Images/Reuters

Kansas City’s attacking depth Temwa Chawinga is a two-time NWSL MVP for a reason, but she wasn’t the sole source of Kansas City’s 54 goals in 30 regular season games. The Current’s past nine goals (across five games including the playoffs) were scored by six different players, with Haley Hopkins (tied with Chawinga for goal contributions in the regular season) notching four of them. Chawinga enters the Championship with only one goal contribution in five games and no goals since 3 October, but she can break through at any moment. If not, the Current’s surrounding cast of contributors – Hopkins, Michelle Cooper, Bethune and Debinha – seems prepared to make the difference.

View image in fullscreen Temwa Chawinga could be due for a breakout game in Saturday’s final. Photograph: Ira L Black/Getty Images

Rodman is the Spirit’s gamechanger The Spirit also have attacking depth, but Rodman is a gamechanger whose impact is more lopsided. Her 20 goal contributions in the regular season were more than double the goal contributions of any teammate, and that’s without quantifying the space she frees up for fellow goalscorers with her calculated off-the-ball movements.

In the postseason, Rodman has four goal contributions in two games – two goals and two assists. Coming at the end of one of her best club seasons, a big performance in the final will be essential for a Spirit victory. It would also further solidify her as one of the deserved main characters (and highest-paid player) in the NWSL.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Will Rowdy Audi make a difference? Stadium squabbles were an unexpected storyline of this year’s postseason. Gotham and Washington faced scheduling hurdles that called into question their home-field advantage and/or forced them to play on less-than-ideal pitches for their semi-finals. But this Saturday, the Spirit will still have home-field advantage at Audi Field, where they’ve earned the trust of a robust home crowd. Whether Washington can turn that familiar, friendly space into the perfect scene for actually lifting the trophy in their third straight final would be a poetic end to the postseason’s stadium woes.
