Sports.title: Maine Road offer non-league haven to fans of scandal-hit Manchester City
Sports.content:
It began with a timely message on social media. “We’ve seen the posts. We’ve read the comments. If all the recent conversation has made you curious about the other team in Manchester playing in sky blue, come and see us.”

It was a direct response to the news of a guilty verdict in the Premier League’s financial fair play case against Manchester City and it came from the 10th-tier (step six) club Maine Road, who carry City’s colours and a near-identical badge, as well as the name of City’s previous home.

Maine Road stadium was demolished in 2003-04 and replaced by houses but two miles away, in a corner of Chorlton-cum-Hardy, Maine Road FC are playing in front of about 100 people on a cool November Saturday. The high-stakes surroundings of the Premier League seem a fair distance away, but Maine Road – founded in 1955 in Rusholme as a Manchester City supporters’ club team – have never professed to be City.

“There is FC United and Manchester United, who are intrinsically linked in terms of why that club exists,” says Rob McKay, Maine Road women’s head coach, watching as a fan as the men’s side draw 0-0 with Halewood Apollo in the North West Counties League First Division North. “This is not a protest club. The links with City have ebbed and flowed over the years. It’s just that they were playing out of the Maine Road social club when it formed.”

The chair and director Alex Simmonds, who arrived in the summer, has big ambitions for Maine Road. He believes the fallout from City’s legal battle with the Premier League could help attract a new audience.

“It was a bit of a statement,” Simmonds says of that social media post. “We came across a lot of comments when the news came out and a lot were saying: ‘Well, we’ll stop watching City if they get relegated or if anything happens, and we’ll just go to Maine Road.’ That came up in quite a few conversations online.”

View image in fullscreen A Maine Road player takes a throw-in as supporters watch on. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

Simmonds admits there has not yet been a huge rise in crowd numbers, with City fans, perhaps understandably, staying defiantly loyal to their club, who have appealed against the independent commission’s verdict. His priority is to regenerate Maine Road. “For me coming into the club, it was about trying to get people to see that we are here,” he says. “To get in touch with the community and to get fans down here, so no matter who you support in the Premier League or Championship or whatever, we are here.”

Maine Road offer free entry to anyone with a season ticket for a Premier League or EFL club, hoping to boost numbers during international breaks or when other Greater Manchester teams play away. Simmonds is helping to fund a multimillion-pound renovation of St Margaret’s Community Centre, which serves as Maine Road’s clubhouse. The club are also launching a new website and a scheme to hand out thousands of free tickets to local primary schools.

View image in fullscreen Alex Simmonds, the Maine Road chair, is hoping to welcome new fans to the club. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

Will that, combined with potential disillusionment after any City punishment, bring fans flocking to Maine Road? “I think it will,” Simmonds says, “but only if people know that there’s a difference between a Premier League Man City and a Maine Road at step six. If they come with ideas that we are going to be a City or even one of the bigger semi-pro teams … we’re not quite there yet. But their support would help.”

Non-league football in Greater Manchester has enjoyed a significant surge in popularity since Covid, so Maine Road find themselves in a crowded marketplace. McKay says: “West Didsbury and Chorlton are down the road and they get 1,000. Droylsden get huge crowds, Ashton United get huge crowds, Curzon Ashton are getting reasonable crowds. There’s so much football.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen A supporter casts a late-afternoon shadow on the Maine Road dugout. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

Simmonds believes the connection with City, however loose, should help Maine Road gradually gain a foothold. City’s former training ground at Platt Lane is a stone’s throw from Brantingham Road, where Maine Road play. City’s academy teams have played at Maine Road’s ground, as well as at nearby St Bede’s College.

Another connection is the fact Maine Road are managed by a former City player in Leon Mike, who made his only City start at the old Maine Road in 2001 under Kevin Keegan.

View image in fullscreen Leon Mike, the Maine Road manager, shouts instructions from the sidelines. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

“People make jokes about the Etihad not being full, but genuinely, a lot of times you speak to City fans, they’ll say it’s too expensive,” says Mike. “Premier League, FA Cup, League Cup, Champions League, that’s a lot of games to go to. Whereas on a Saturday here it will cost you £6 to attend and you can have a pint and some food.”

There is optimism among those most closely connected with Maine Road that the club will soon experience growth. “We gained 9,000 followers across the platforms just on the back of that one social media post,” Simmonds says. “It was surprising – I didn’t think it would do that – but social media is really powerful. We’re definitely going to try and stay in that conversation and get people coming through.”

Sports.title: Inside women’s football’s difficult rise in Syria: ‘A joy that everyone in the country needed’
Sports.content:
In December 2024, Syria’s under-18 women’s football team boarded a last-minute bus at midnight from Aqaba, bound for Damascus. The players had been in Jordan preparing for their final match of the WAFF women’s championship, where a win against Saudi Arabia would have kept their hopes of winning the title alive. Syria pulled out amid fears that the border would close.

Back home, a war that had been largely frozen for four years was suddenly moving at pace. Rebel forces had swept out of the northwest, taking Aleppo and were pushing south towards the capital, 350km away, threatening to topple the now-former president, Bashar al-Assad. Players from the provinces around Damascus made their way home. But those from Hasakah, in the country’s far north-east, spent the next three days stranded at Damascus airport, as airline staff fled and planes sat idle on the tarmac, until a bus was finally able to take them home.

Scared, exhausted and running on adrenaline, the team had lived through another episode of disruption; but in truth they had rarely known stability. For Syrian women’s footballers, navigating uncertainty had been part of the game long before the country’s political upheaval reached its latest turning point. “My generation was burned away and completely lost,” said Noor Jumaa, a former national team goalkeeper. “It was like everything that was being built just disappeared.”

After 14 years of war, Syria has much to rebuild. Women’s football is among the institutions trying to recover from a conflict that erased an entire generation of players, interrupted the development of the game itself and left its infrastructure struggling. Yet, in recent years, Syria’s youth teams have emerged as one of the country’s more unexpected sporting success stories, winning regional titles and producing players who are beginning to make their mark abroad.

Syria’s women’s national team played their first international match in 2005. By 2011, plans were under way for an 11-a-side women’s league. Then the uprising began, and all plans were abandoned. For the next six years, women’s football in Syria effectively stopped. There were no international fixtures at any level, only occasional futsal tournaments. More than six million people eventually fled Syria, including hundreds involved in the sport, leaving an already small pool of players scattered across the world.

Men’s football, by contrast, continued. The national team played matches abroad after Syria was barred from hosting fixtures in 2011 on security grounds. The Assad regime used its successes to project an image of normality, even welcoming the squad to his palace after their 2012 WAFF Championship victory. Fifa, despite its rules against political interference, stayed silent.

Girls growing up in those years had no women’s team to watch. “I was watching a match of Syria’s men’s national team, and I was really upset. I would say, ‘God, if only they’d make a national team for girls,’” recalled Raneem Abo Lateef, a 21-year-old goalkeeper for Syria. The opportunity came unexpectedly after her family moved houses, and a girl next door told Abo Lateef that a relative was starting a girls’ club. “Girls’ football? Wow,” she said. “It was like dreams coming true.”

View image in fullscreen Raneem Abo Lateef makes a save in the Syrian women’s league Photograph: Ibrahim Janoudi / SFA

Similarly, international teammate Julnar Mustafa spent hours playing with boys in her neighbourhood in Hasakah. Born in 2008, so too young to remember the beginning of the uprising, she filmed herself dribbling and performing tricks on her phone, uploading the videos to Facebook. A regional coach came across them and invited Mustafa to join his team.

But finding an opportunity to play was only part of the challenge. “In our society, especially in the north, in Hasakah, sport is completely off-limits for girls,” Mustafa told the Guardian. “Not football, not anything”.

While a new generation of girls were finding their way into football, the national team was attempting to return to international competition. In April 2017, Syria entered the Asian Cup qualifiers in Vietnam, assembling a squad after six years without any activity. The federation announced tryouts on Facebook, and players were given about a month of preparation. Syria went on to lose every match, including a 14-0 defeat by Myanmar. “Honestly, it was one of the worst teams in Syria’s history,” said Jumaa, who was part of that squad. “We lost by terrifying scores.”

Maha Al-Katreb, also in the squad at the time, remembers the criticism that followed. Players were ridiculed despite having had little preparation. At the tournament, she saw opponents arrive with larger coaching staffs and younger players training alongside their senior teams. The gap between Syria and their regional competitors was difficult to ignore.

With injuries ending her career early, Al-Katreb fell into coaching by chance and turned towards building a programme that could develop the next generation. She later joined the Syrian Football Association (SFA), taking on administrative and coaching responsibilities.

A six-team women’s senior league was established in 2019, followed by the development of youth national teams. This year the country held an inaugural edition of its youth league. Al-Katreb developed Syria’s first women’s football strategy, submitted to Fifa, that set out a longer-term plan for expanding participation and creating a pathway into the national teams. “You have to start building from the bottom if you want to see results after these 10 years,” Al-Katreb said. “So that we don’t burn one generation after another.”

In 2022, women accounted for only 1,000 of Syria’s 25,000 registered footballers. The women’s football strategy, seen by the Guardian, aimed to increase female participation by 150% over four years, including through 33 school training centres across 11 provinces, with capacity for 1,650 girls by 2026.

View image in fullscreen Julnar Mustafa stands for the national anthem. Photograph: Syria Football Association

The government has also outlined plans to rehabilitate the country’s sporting infrastructure. Rami Alsubea, an adviser at the Ministry of Sport and Youth, said in a statement that 48 sports facilities had been rehabilitated in 2025, with plans to rehabilitate about 150 more and build about 20 new ones by 2028. Restoring infrastructure is in part to meet hosting criteria set by Fifa and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

Al-Katreb left the federation more than a year ago. Jumaa is now part of a two-woman team leading its women’s football department, appointed after the arrival of the federation’s current president, Feras al-Teet. Several players have criticized the federation’s leadership and the pace of progress. The Guardian reached out to Al-Teet for comment. He declined.

Among the players who have been vocal about the shortcomings is 26-year-old Rona Aizouk, one of the most experienced members of the current generation. Named after Brazilian footballer Ronaldinho, she made history in 2023 when she became the first Syrian-born woman to sign a professional contract, joining Saudi side Najmat Jeddah. Her performances in Syria had attracted the club’s attention, but securing the move proved difficult. Visa refusals and paperwork complications delayed her arrival until two days before the season began. Her time in Saudi Arabia lasted only a few months, and she was unable to extend her stay.

“Honestly, I went there not wanting to come back,” said Aizouk. “There’s no comparison. Everything is better, the treatment, the training, the facilities. It’s just different.

“The most important thing is the players’ comfort. Here in Syria, we have to endure psychological pressure and torment. As a player, I have to fight the world just to achieve even a little bit of success.”

After returning to Damascus to complete her studies, Aizouk quickly received interest from multiple clubs in Jordan, where she now plays. For her, being in situ abroad is about more than personal progression. “I want to be a message that I, who came out of hard circumstances and out of a war, still managed to succeed.”

View image in fullscreen Rona Azouk in training with Syria. Photograph: Syria Football Association

Aizouk’s exposure to regional excellence has shown her that Syria is still many years behind. At the forefront is financial restriction that has left the sport bare-boned. International sanctions and banking restrictions imposed on Syria left millions of dollars in development funding from Fifa inaccessible to the SFA, preventing it from fully benefiting from programmes such as Fifa Forward.

Although broad economic sanctions have since been lifted, an estimated $11.5m in funds remains inaccessible to the federation. Both the SFA and Fifa insist they are working to establish a mechanism through which the money can be transferred. For now, the support has been seen in training equipment.

The financial strain is felt directly by players as both the national team and regional league are operated by the SFA. Clubs frequently go months without paying wages, and when payments do arrive, players say they can fall short of the amounts agreed. International call-ups offer little relief: during national team duty, including training camps, players receive a daily allowance of $20, capped at $200 for the length of their stay, regardless of how long it is. Some say the costs of travelling and playing can exceed what they receive.

Several clubs have folded since the domestic league’s launch in 2019, citing financial difficulties and the continued disruption caused by the war and ongoing conflicts. Those that remain often struggle to provide even basic resources.

Al-Hilal, now renamed Qamishlo Sport, have become one of the country’s most successful women’s sides, currently reigning as senior and youth league champions. But their achievements have not translated into financial security, according to head coach, Daleel Khalid. “There’s an absence of adequate support from all sides and the parties responsible for Syrian women’s sports, whether in terms of training camps and preparation, or the capabilities and infrastructure needed to develop the game,” he said.

The club’s campaign at the 2026 WAFF Women’s Clubs Championship was a big test. The tournament brought together league champions from six regional competitions. Despite having only a short training camp at home, Al-Hilal reached the final against Saudi champions Al-Nassr. Abo Lateef and Mustafa were among those who represented them, and their performances offered a reminder that Syrian teams can compete with the region’s best, even when their opponents have considerably greater resources.

There was also individual recognition. Al-Hilal’s Mai Al-Jani was named the tournament’s best player after a series of standout performances, an achievement she was quick to share with those around her. “The award I won is a source of pride for me, for the club and for the players. I see it as a team award,” she said. “It belongs to the staff, the players, and every Syrian girl living through these difficult circumstances.”

Born in 2006 in a small village in Homs province, Al-Jani has emerged as one of Syria’s promising attacking talents. She won the league’s Golden Boot in the 2024-25 season and has continued to impress for both club and country. She was also named the best player at the 2023 WAFF under-17 championship, when Syria won their first international title in women’s football. Al-Katreb, who was an assistant coach, saw the victory as evidence of what the country could build with the right support.

The WAFF under-17 triumph was repeated at the 2026 edition with a completely different squad. “It was joy that everyone in the country needed,” said Jumaa. “We were completely outnumbered in technical and admin staff, with only nine of us managing everything. Other teams had double the number of staff, with gameplay technology we can’t get our hands on.”

For Abo Lateef, the greatest risk is allowing another generation of players to lose the chance to compete. The senior women’s national team, for instance, has not played in over two years, with no reason given to players. “We need competition, regardless of the level,” said Abo Lateef. “I’m afraid a day will come when I’m made to sit at home, as was the case with the ones before us. A friendly fixture is a good start. Anything.”

Aizouk’s message to those responsible for the future of the women’s game was more direct. “Save Syrian football,” she said. “Save the generations. Save us.”

Sports.title: Veerle Buurman scrambles late WCL winner to push blunt Chelsea past PSG
Sports.content:
Chelsea were made to work hard for three Champions League points against a resilient Paris Saint-Germain side but their patience paid off, Veerle Buurman squeezing the ball in at the near post to put them, temporarily at least, at the top of the table in the league phase.

Buurman had stolen the show in Chelsea’s defeat of Manchester City at the weekend, coming on 12 minutes in and nullifying Khadija Shaw’s threat to be named player of the match, and she was the hero under the lights with Chelsea doing everything but score prior to her goal.

“She is a top, young talent and is so mature on and off the pitch,” said Sonia Bompastor. “She is a confident player and a really complete player.”

Bompastor’s side were frustrated by Häcken last week, held to a 0-0 draw by the Swedish side and falling out of the top four automatic qualification places. There was a desire to put things right at AFC Wimbledon’s stadium and they did just that, albeit in not the prettiest of encounters.

“Sometimes in football you need to find a way to win and the result tonight was really important for us,” said Bompastor.

Quick Guide WCL roundup: City subs Hemp and Shaw see off Häcken Show Lauren Hemp and Khadija Shaw both scored off the bench to earn Manchester City a 2-0 Women’s Champions League victory over Häcken in Gothenburg. The first half ended goalless with City's best chances coming just before the break. Aoba Fujino was put through on goal but she hit her effort straight at Häcken keeper Jennifer Falk, who made saves from Grace Clinton and Rebecca Knaak to keep the hosts on terms at the interval. Hemp and Shaw were both introduced at half-time by Andrée Jeglertz, and the England winger opened the scoring after 55 minutes. It was a fortuitous breakthrough, with Emma Östlund's clearance ricocheting off Hemp's shin and into the net [pictured]. Mary Fowler appeared to have added a second soon after, but her strike was ruled out for offside against Yui Hasegawa. Soon after Hemp was denied her second goal when her shot hit the post, she turned creator by passing to an onrushing Shaw, who tucked home for City's second in the 77th minute. The visitors could have had a third, but Falk saved Fowler's stoppage-time penalty after a VAR intervention. Signe Bruun also made the difference off the bench on Wednesday, scoring two late goals as Real Madrid wore down 10-woman Internazionale to win 3-1. The Danish forward put Madrid ahead five minutes of time before adding a late penalty to secure all three points. Lineth Beerensteyn got the hosts off the mark in Madrid after 28 minutes, and Inter faced an uphill battle after Karolina Vilhjalmsdottir was sent off three minutes before the break. The visitors got an unexpected equaliser when Michela Cambiaghi headed in from a corner, and held on until Bruun's late double. City and Real Madrid are both unbeaten after five league phase games, winning two and drawing three matches each as they bid to finish in the top four and avoid the playoffs. Juventus join them on nine points after late goals from Annamaria Serturini and Matilde Pavan earned a 2-0 home win over Leuven. PA and Guardian sport Photograph: Declan Lloyd/Manchester City FC Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

PSG had lost 2-1 at home to Bayern Munich after three draws and one win in the competition before their trip to London. Denied a point late on, they remain 10th and dangerously close to slipping out of the playoff places with one game to play.

Chelsea had been thrillingly gutsy and diligent in their 1-0 win over City on Saturday and against PSG they were similarly solid at the back, but they lacked spark in attack. Ellie Carpenter became the focal point of their forward play from the right, with the striker Melvine Malard injured in the game against City.

PSG nullifying the threat of Carpenter blunted Chelsea, and despite their dominance of the ball, amassing 64% possession in the first half, Chelsea struggled to carve a way through the visitors’ backline. They had seven attempts on goal to PSG’s six at the break, despite 33 attacks to 10.

Chelsea have historically performed well against PSG, winning three of their four Champions League meetings prior to this penultimate fixture of their league phase campaign. In the 2018-19 quarter-finals they earned a 2-0 home win and, after a 2-1 away defeat, progressed to the semi-finals; in the 2022-23 season they won both group meetings with an overall score of 4-0.

The visiting team’s first attempt on target arrived after the break, with Merveille Kanjinga forcing a near-post save from Hannah Hampton. While Chelsea still dominated, PSG had more forays forward in the second half.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Aggie Beever-Jones is beaten to a header by her Chelsea teammate Wieke Kaptein (right) in what was a close game against PSG. Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty Images

Erin Cuthbert, Maika Hamano and Lucy Bronze arrived at the hour mark as the home team sought to deal the killer blow their dominance required. It increasingly felt like it would take something special to break the deadlock, akin to the sublime effort that Sandy Baltimore had delivered against City.

Aggie Beever-Jones was replaced by Sjoeke Nüsken late on and the German instantly made a difference, forcing a sublime save from Katarzyna Kiedrzynek. The breakthrough came from the resulting corner, and it was far less sublime than Saturday’s effort, Buurman somehow squeezing the ball in at the near post after PSG failed to clear Cuthbert’s ball in.

“The main feeling is one of frustration,” said the PSG manager, Paulo César. “We defended well, we just lacked a bit of clarity on the transition and I have mixed feelings. I’m proud of my team but it shows that there are very fine margins that we need to rival a big team like Chelsea.”

Ultimately, the goal was the bit of luck Chelsea needed and they look increasingly formidable.

Sports.title: Man City v Fulham live commentary with incredible record on the line
Sports.content:
Man City v Fulham live commentary with incredible record on the line

Manchester City will hope to move to within three points of Premier League leaders Arsenal when they host Fulham this weekend.

Top-flight football will return at the Etihad on Saturday lunchtime following the final international break of the year.



3 Maresca's Man City face Fulham this weekend Credit: Getty

And City need to get back to winning ways having lost their last three games before the hiatus.

Enzo Maresca’s men have lost to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest in recent weeks to allow Arsenal to take a firm grip on the title race.

But with the Gunners facing a tricky trip to Newcastle on Saturday evening, City will hope to put some pressure on.



Fulham, meanwhile, head into the match in 15th in the table, just two points outside the relegation zone.

But they are unbeaten in the last four Premier League matches and will hope to capitalise on City’s recent wobble.



Man City v Fulham live on talkSPORT

This top-flight clash will take place on Saturday, November 2.

Kick-off at the Etihad is scheduled for 12:30pm.

talkSPORT will have exclusive live commentary from Manchester with Reshmin Chowdhury, Sam Matterface and former England captain Stuart Pearce.

3 Arbeloa's Fulham are only two points outside the drop zone Credit: Getty



Listen talkSPORT through the website or find us on DAB digital radio through your smart speaker and on 1089 or 1053 AM.

Download and listen to all our live commentaries via the talkSPORT app, whilst talkSPORT is also available to watch on Samsung TV Plus.

Subscribe to the talkSPORT YouTube channel for news, views and analysis plus our regular goals show and for more, 

For the latest odds and bet boosts for every big event, visit talkSPORT BET.



Man City v Fulham team news

City winger Antoine Semenyo remains sidelined with a knee injury and is not expected to return until mid-December.

Marc Guehi and Josko Gvardiol face late fitness tests for hip and fatigue issues respectively.

Abdukodir Khusanov pulled out of Uzbekistan's recent international fixtures with an undisclosed knock but should be fine.

Elliot Anderson is eligible to play on Saturday, as his red card for England against Spain only triggers a suspension for his next Nations League match.



For Fulham, captain Tom Cairney is the visitors' only notable injury concern as he recovers from a knee issue, though he could return to the matchday squad.

Playmaker Josh King has also been dealing with fatigue problems recently but should start in midfield.

Rodrigo Muniz is pushing to replace Gonzalo Garcia up front after scoring off the bench against Newcastle last time out.

3 Man City have a remarkable record against Fulham Credit: Getty



Premier League Matchweek 11 fixtures Saturday, November 21 Manchester City vs Fulham, 12:30 - LIVE on talkSPORT

Aston Villa vs Sunderland, 15:00

Bournemouth vs Nottingham Forest, 15:00

Chelsea vs Leeds, 15:00

Coventry vs Crystal Palace, 15:00

Tottenham vs Ipswich Town, 15:00

Newcastle vs Arsenal, 17:30 Sunday, November 22 Hull vs Brighton, 14:00

Liverpool vs Manchester United, 16:30 Monday, November 23 Brentford vs Everton, 20:00 - LIVE on talkSPORT

Man City hope to extend all-time record Fulham

City enter this weekend’s clash holding an incredible 20-game winning streak across all competitions against the Cottagers.

That run is the longest in English football history and dates back to February 2012.

It includes 17 consecutive Premier League victories plus two in the FA Cup, and one in the League Cup.

City have also scored at least two goals in all 17 of those top-flight wins while Fulham have not kept a clean sheet against the Citizens since March 2004.



City beat Fulham 3-0 at home last season after a 5-4 thriller in their favour in west London.

City last dropped points against Fulham in September 2011 when a Vincent Kompany own goal earned the Cottagers a 2-2 draw.

Fulham have not beaten City since a 3-2 win in Manchester in April 2008, 28 games ago.

Sports.title: £3.5bn finance giant targets Premier League clubs in new venture with deal already in place
Sports.content:
£3.5bn finance giant targets Premier League clubs in new venture with deal already in place

Nottingham Forest sponsors Marex are set to offer financing to clubs in the Premier League and Championship.

The London-based firm plan to offer the chance to access cash before certain revenues arrive.



3 Marex have announced plans to offer financing to Premier League and Championship clubs Credit: Getty

It is expected the proposed funds could help clubs manage cash flow or fund investment going forward.

Marex plans have seen them announce a new specialist football finance operation with sports investment advisor Pinto Capital.

As part of the move, clubs in the Premier League and Championship will be offered financing against future revenue streams.



These include broadcasting revenues, sponsorship payments, transfer-fee receivables, matchday income and season-ticket sales.

In a statement, Marex's chief strategist and CEO of capital markets Paolo Tonucci said: "Football clubs are increasingly sophisticated businesses with significant and growing financing requirements, yet their access to capital can be limited.



"We see an opportunity to provide football clubs with a unique suite of services that meet these requirements, from financing, credit and risk management, to FX, payments and structured solutions.

"Through our partnership with Pinto Capital, we have an opportunity to give clubs more flexibility in managing their financial commitments and investing in future growth."



Who are Marex?

Marex are a global financial services group founded in 2005 with their current headquarters located in London.

They offer market access, infrastructure services and liquidity to clients around the world.

According to City AM, Marex's customer base sits at more than 3,000 global clients.

3 Marex proposals are expected to help clubs manage cash flow Credit: Getty



The firm is listed on Nasdaq with a reported market capitalisation of approximately £3.5billion.

Meanwhile, they already have a direct connection to the Premier League this season.

Marex were announced as Forest's front-of-shirt sponsors back in August.

The deal is worth £25million over three years, with Marex set to remain as the club's sponsor until 2029.



Their partnership sees the firm's branding appear on both the men's and women's kits.

As for Pinto Capital, who have partnered with Marex on the newly-announced operation, they are also based in London.

3 Marex became Forest's shirt sponsor in August in a three-year deal worth £25million Credit: Getty

The advisory company has previously brokered investments in multiple different sports.



Those include deals at varying levels of football and cricket in England.

Sports.title: Man United ready to take legal action over JJ Gabriel exit
Sports.content:
Manchester United are reportedly willing to take legal action if they find out JJ Gabriel had been approached illegally.

Gabriel announced that he had left the club earlier this week, but Man United have still not been officially informed of his exit.

2 Man United are ready to take legal action if any club approached Real Madrid-bound Gabriel while he was still contracted with them Credit: Getty

The 16-year-old sensation revealed the bombshell news that he wanted to leave the Red Devils in September and he is now understood to be on the brink of finalising a switch to Real Madrid.

However, according to ESPN, United could take a legal route if it's found out that he had been contacted while under contract at the club.

In the Premier League and EFL, interested clubs are not allowed to approach or induce a player that is registered with another academy without getting permission from the player's current team.

Gabriel is currently still registered with Man United, despite him releasing an emotional social media announcing his departure.

The Premier League giants have not been contacted by any governing body about transferring his registration to a new team.

And they believe the teenager's family and representatives could have been holding talks with others sides as early as last summer, according to ESPN's sources.

If they find that Real Madrid, or any other club, had approached Gabriel, then they are said to be prepared to take legal action.

That could well lead to a review and then sanctions being handed out, or a potential compensation package being paid to United.

talkSPORT's Jason Cundy labelled Gabriel's situation as the same as when Rio Ngumoha joined Liverpool from Chelsea's academy.

Ngumoha's transfer also led to a huge legal dispute, that eventually led to the Blues receiving £2.8million in compensation from the Reds, who were ordered to pay their rivals following a tribunal.

2 United reportedly believe that Gabriel's representatives were in talks with other clubs from last year, with him eventually asking to leave this September Credit: Getty

Where is JJ Gabriel?

Gabriel's transfer saga has been in the headlines over the last couple of months, but where has he been?

It is reported by ESPN that Man United's staff have not been able to get in touch with the forward's family since his request to leave.

He has not been back to Carrington since the bombshell news.

Gabriel has still been active on social media though, sending out his goodbye message to the Red Devils this week.

As well as that, he has switched agents, signing with Epic Sports, who released a promotional video unveiling his signature.

That clip has since faced huge backlash, with the Gabriel saga expected to continue, even potentially after he joins Real Madrid.

Sports.title: Rob Edwards eyed up for Swansea job alongside sought-after Premier League assistant
Sports.content:
Rob Edwards is among the list of contenders to replace Vitor Matos as Swansea manager, talkSPORT understands.

The Welsh side are on the hunt for a new boss after Matos was announced as the new Strasbourg manager.



2 Matos' decision to leave his job as Swansea boss for Strasbourg has come as a complete shock to the club Credit: Getty

Swansea legend Ashley Williams will take charge of the Championship match against West Brom on Saturday as part of a three-coach interim set-up.

Edwards has been out of the game for five months after being sacked by Wolves in June and recently held talks with Burnley.

Liverpool assistant manager Tommy Elphick is another potential option for the Championship side.



Elphick rejected both Bristol City and Burnley in the summer but is keen on becoming a manger.

Swansea's contingency plan

The Swans made an electric start to this Championship campaign but lost four of the last five games under Matos.



He had successfully steered the club away from the threat of relegation after being appointed in November 2025.

Swansea currently sit sixth but the surprise departure of their manager, who signed fresh terms in the summer and got significant backing in the transfer market, has threatened to throw their season into disarray.



talkSPORT's Wales correspondent Mora said on Tuesday: "When I woke up this morning and saw a few messages on my phone, I thought: 'Hang on a second... what is this all about?'

"I spoke to someone at the club who's in a good position, and he said to me: 'At this time yesterday, this was not on my radar at all'.

"So, it has taken them completely by surprise at the club.

2 Liverpool assistant Elphick also worked at Bournemouth as Andoni Iraola's assistant Credit: AFP

"He signed a new contract, an improved deal, in the summer. He's been given the biggest transfer budget that any Swansea manager has had since they got relegated from the Premier League.



"So, the club are quite bemused at what's happened and the decision being made there."

After the West Brom game, Swansea face another promotion contender in Middlesbrough next Tuesday before a Welsh derby against Cardiff.

The clash between the bitter rivals will be live on talkSPORT 2 next Sunday, with commentary from Nigel Adderley and Chris Iwelumo.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino facing two FIFA presidential rivals after botched $4.2bn deal
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino facing two FIFA presidential rivals after botched $4.2bn deal

Add us as preferred source

Gianni Infantino has discovered his opponents in the FIFA presidential election.

The incumbent president will run for a fourth term at the 77th FIFA Congress in Rabat on March 18, 2027.

3 Kozo Tashima is one of two candidates running against Infantino Credit: Getty

FIFA have confirmed Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will contest the election alongside Infantino.

It comes amid mounting pressure on the current president, who has been in the position since February 2016.

Infantino has lost considerable support since announcing his own candidacy at the 76th FIFA Congress in April.

His botched FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal has led to mounting pressure on the 56-year-old.

Plans to raise $4.2billion by selling private equity in tournaments including the World Cup prompted the threat of a boycott from UEFA members.

Meanwhile, the FA were amongst those to withdraw their endorsements of Infantino's re-election bid.

Although he later scrapped the FFE plans, his future as FIFA president remains in doubt ahead of the upcoming election.

Who is running for FIFA president?

French Football Federation president Diallo has been selected as the UEFA representative.

The 63-year-old has the unanimous endorsement of the UEFA Executive Committee.

Diallo has also been backed unanimously by the European members of the FIFA Council.

3 French Football Federation president Diallo has the unanimous backing of UEFA members Credit: Getty

All 55 UEFA members will have a vote in the FIFA presidential election, with 211 member nations selecting their preferred candidate.

Arsene Wenger had been the preferred choice for UEFA to run against Infantino.

However, the former Arsenal manager, who is now FIFA's chief of global football development, reportedly declined to stand in the election.

Tashima will complete the three-man race for the presidency.

The Japan Football Association's honorary president is already a member of the FIFA Council.

He is expected to split the vote from Asian member nations, with the AFC having 46 member nations.

3 Tashima is expected to split the votes of AFC member nations Credit: AFP

Tashima has also previously served as president of the East Asian Football Federation, holding the position between 2016 and 2018.

Candidates needed the support of at least five member nations in order to submit their nominations for the election.

Sports.title: The five most underrated footballers ever with Roy Keane favourite
Sports.content:
Some players take all the praise, all the credit, all the plaudits - well now's the time to celebrate those who deserve more.

In the latest edition of Max Scott's Mount Rushmore or Less, the talkSPORT host picks whom he believes are the five most underrated footballers ever.

6 Mount Rushmore - the iconic carving of four influential US president in South Dakota - is often used by fans to rank things, with talkSPORT's Max Scott arguing that sometimes, four just isn't enough Credit: AFP

But doesn't Mount Rushmore only feature four US presidents?

Yes it does, but sometimes there are just so many names that you can't afford to leave some out of the list, hence the 'more or less'.

So, here are the most criminally underrated and influential players that deserve to receive much more credit than they do...

An underrated great of the game

"A Manchester United legend who won seven Premier League titles, made 500 appearances and is declared by Roy Keane to be the best full-back he has ever played with," Max began.

Who is that legendary full-back? It's Denis Irwin.

"Irwin, for me, doesn't get enough credit. He falls into a period of history where we conveniently forget about it because the back end of his career was when the Premier League became the global behemoth that it is today and we all started tracking stats and performances.

"Irwin had the longevity, leadership and the versatility where he could play right-back and left-back. He also won seven Premier League titles.

"So, for someone with that amount of honours and silverware, playing in one of the greatest teams we have ever seen in Europe, I don't think he gets enough plaudits.

"He's a great of the game. And I know Gary Neville was brilliant, but Keane will tell you that Irwin was a stratosphere ahead.

"We've got to give him his flowers. He's incredibly underrated but incredibly influential."

6 Irwin, right, won seven Premier League titles and a Champions League with Man United, playing more than 500 games for the club over his 12 years at Old Trafford Credit: Getty

What is Mount Rushmore? The faces of George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln are carved into the stone in South Dakota, chosen for their representation of the most important events in the United States' history. As a result, fans use the idea to create their own version to list the most influential or iconic games and people that define their selected categories. Here, though, talkSPORT argues five is not enough, so more or less this is Mount Rushmore.

Klose to being among the best

"Miroslav Klose was hugely influential, he won a World Cup with Germany in 2014," Max then said, picking his next player.

Klose retired from football in 2016 at 38 years old, bringing an end to a stunning career that some may think deserves a little bit more hype.

"I think that because he didn't play in the Premier League, he isn't seen in the same stratosphere as Harry Kane and Robert Lewandowski, and he deserves to be.

"He scored more than 50 goals for four different clubs, most notably Bayern Munich and Lazio.

"He won a World Cup and held the record for the most goals scored at a World Cup for 12 years, and he's been overtaken by who? Lionel Messi and then Kylian Mbappe.

"He's in rarefied air. He scored 71 goals for Germany, won trophies in Germany and Italy and, I think if he played in the Premier League, we'd be talking about him being one of the best ever strikers to come out of Europe."

6 Klose won the World Cup with Germany and was the tournament's greatest ever scorer for 12 years before Messi toppled hm Credit: Getty

The miniature giant

Next up is a man that has already been mentioned in the Mount Rushmore or Less for best midfield trios - Claude Makelele.

A two-time Premier League winner and a Champions League winner, the Frenchman quite literally made his position his own.

"Previously, the position was known as CDM (central defensive midfielder), now it's called the Claude Makelele role.

"Players like Ballon d'Or winner Rodri, Arsenal title winner Declan Rice, Manchester City's Elliot Anderson and France World Cup winner N'Golo Kante stand on the shoulders of the miniature giant that is Makelele.

"Jose Mourinho needed one man to intercept play, break up play, simple passes to allow the likes of Frank Lampard or whoever it was to go and do their magic further up the pitch.

"The position is named after him, for crying out loud, and I still don't think he's given enough credit for redefining the tactical revolution we have seen in the Premier League."

6 Former Chelsea and Real Madrid midfielder Makelele was that good of a player that his position and playstyle was named after him Credit: Getty
