NewsFeed Putin says US-China-Russia can strengthen global stability

Russia, China, and the US can strengthen global stability if they cooperate constructively, President Putin has said in his opening remarks at the trilateral summit in Shenzhen. The Russian leader said he had also discussed Ukraine with Trump during their closed-door meeting.

World.title: Denmark parliament approves security deal with Greenland and US
World.content:
All 109 Danish lawmakers present approved the deal, easing tensions over Trump’s desire to annex the Arctic island.

Share Denmark parliament approves security deal with Greenland and US on social media

The Danish parliament ⁠has unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States covering Greenland, aimed at bolstering security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.

Thursday’s decision to approve the deal signed in September eases tensions over US President Donald Trump’s desire to annex the Arctic island.

In the 179-seat parliament, known as the Folketing, the 109 members present voted in favour of the text, which was adopted without opposition or abstention.

The vote, which followed the second reading of the text, went through without any debate or opposition.

In early November, Greenland’s parliament had passed it by 16 votes, with seven abstentions.

The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September to resolve tensions after Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of ⁠the mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory home to 57,000 people.

The deal is not subject to a vote by the US Senate. The executive ‌agreement, following Thursday’s vote in Copenhagen, will enter into force once the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs informs the US in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete.

Signed in New York on September 22, the agreement supplements a 1951 accord on the US military presence in Greenland.

It allows the US to build two military bases in Greenland and blocks countries outside the European Union and NATO from strategic sectors, in order to stop China or Russia from gaining influence over the territory, particularly through investments.



Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark, but the deal is to remain in force even if Greenland gains full independence.

Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that the US needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and other partners.

The shortest route ‌from ‌Europe to North America runs via strategically located Greenland, where the northernmost US military base is located.

World.title: This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
World.content:
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.

For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.

Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.

And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.

Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.

His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.

But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.

World.title: Dozens missing after boat carrying 100 migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
World.content:
Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast.

Initial reports said that one person had died, but some local media have reported that at least four bodies have been recovered. Dozens of people are still missing.

Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.

This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.

Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).

"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.

A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.

Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.

At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.

He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.

Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.

Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.

The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.

It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.

World.title: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
World.content:
Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (Â£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.

Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.

The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.

Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.

The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

World.title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
World.content:
It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.

The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (Â£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.

Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.

Four other owners then had the painting.

The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

World.title: Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
World.content:
Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.

Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.

Commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors."

The collapse of the Crimean Bridge's arch was the worst damage to be inflicted onto the structure in several years.

The bridge had long been in Ukraine's sights because it represents Moscow's pretensions over sovereign Ukrainian land, and because of its logistical importance in supplying Russian troops in the occupied Ukrainian southern regions.

It was built and unveiled to great fanfare in 2018, four years after Russia illegally annexed Ukraine's Crimea.

Thursday's strike was carried out with Neptune cruise missiles, Ukraine said. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. Train services on the bridge were suspended but resumed in the afternoon.

Car traffic, however, will be prohibited for the foreseeable future as a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was dragged below into the sea when missiles hit the arch on Tuesday.

President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

The seven-stage operation first required the destruction of air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets which protected the bridge. Missiles and drones then dealt the structure the final blow.

World.title: Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's ouster
World.content:
The United States and Venezuela have re-established military ties less than a year after US forces seized the then-leader of the South American country, NicolÃ¡s Maduro, in a raid on the capital, Caracas.

The interim government led by Delcy RodrÃ­guez, Maduro's former vice-president, signed a military co-operation agreement with US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.

Few details about the deal have been released so far but Hegseth said that Venezuela had "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner" in less than 12 months.

Interim President RodrÃ­guez said the deal would help confront "common threats".

Military co-operation between the two countries was terminated in 2005 by Hugo ChÃ¡vez, Venezuela's left-wing president at the time.

ChÃ¡vez alleged that US military personnel sent to Venezuela to train their counterparts had made disparaging remarks about his government.

He also accused the US military office located in Fuerte Tiuna, Venezuela's largest military complex, of being "an organ of the CIA... conspiring against the government".

Under NicolÃ¡s Maduro, who succeeded ChÃ¡vez after the latter's death from cancer, relations between the two countries deteriorated further.

They reached rock bottom late last year when the US doubled its reward for information leading to Maduro's capture to $50m (Â£38m) and eventually seized him on 3 January in a military raid.

Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now in custody in New York on charges of drug-trafficking and conspiracy to commit torture, which they deny.

Hegseth addressed the change in the two countries' relationship since Maduro was seized in his speech at the US embassy in Caracas on Wednesday.

"It's a great honour to be here as the first United States Secretary of War this century to set foot in Venezuela. The weight of this moment does not escape me," he said.

"Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable," he added before recalling a public appearance by then-President Maduro which had angered the Trump administration.

"Exactly one year ago today, the indicted narco-terrorist fugitive NicolÃ¡s Maduro, the man who spent more than a decade handing Venezuela's borders and territory to terrorists from all over the world, stood on a stage, not too far from here, and yelled mockingly: 'Come and get me!'. Well, we answered that call."

World.title: US consortium wins huge Kenya mining deal, beating Chinese rivals
World.content:
A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.

The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (Â£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.

Frontier Minerals says its proposal aims to keep more of the economic benefits in Kenya through "processing and refining of minerals in-country".

The deal comes as Washington seeks greater access to Africa's minerals, aiming to strengthen US supply chains and compete with China.

Frontier Minerals brings together three US companies - Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation. The consortium combines expertise in mineral resource development, critical materials supply chains and advanced refining technologies.

A central part of its proposal is to develop mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya. Brad Marnett from Frontier Minerals said the company wanted the country to capture more value from its mineral resources.

Mrima Hill is located in Kwale County, near Kenya's Indian Ocean coastline. The site covers about 390 acres of forest.

The prospect of mining in the area has raised concerns among local residents, who fear the project could damage the forest and threaten their ancestral heritage.

There are also questions over whether communities living near the site will benefit from the investment.

Marnett was keen to reassure Kenyans that they would benefit: "We intend to create lasting opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy through capacity-building and targeted investment, while prioritising environmental management and performance."

The consortium must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet the necessary regulatory requirements before the project can proceed.

The tender decision has drawn objections from competing bidders.

Reuters news agency reports that two rival companies intend to challenge the selection, with Australia's RareX alleging that Frontier Minerals missed an earlier submission deadline.

Kenya's government has maintained that the process was open and transparent.

The project comes as US strives to secure alternative sources of critical minerals and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the processing of several key minerals.

Washington has been pursuing partnerships with mineral-rich African countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, as it seeks to strengthen supply chains for industries ranging from electric vehicles to defence technology.

Kenya's mining ministry says the sector is an important part of its plans to diversify the economy beyond traditional sources of revenue such as tourism, agriculture and financial services.

World.title: Survivors of Uganda's deadly landslide seek justice at the UN
World.content:
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.

The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.

Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.

The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.

At least 33 of the 53 people who died in the 2019 landslide were children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.

William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family.

"My quest should be a lesson," he said.

"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."

Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.

Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18m Ugandan shillings ($4,300; Â£3,300) to help them move to safer areas.

But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.

Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8m shillings, plus 10m shillings towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.

The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.

The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.

The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.

"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.

The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.

They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.

Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters.

"Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.

The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.

In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.

The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people.

"Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change â and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.

She said poorer countries, which have contributed relatively little to global emissions, are bearing some of the heaviest consequences of climate change and need greater financial support.

"High income countries must provide financial assistance and ensure that sufficient money goes directly to countries like Uganda, so they can roll out life-saving adaptation measures," she said.

The complainants say relocation must involve more than moving people out of danger.

They want the government to protect their livelihoods, respect their land rights, and take account of individual needs.

The case is now before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which will ask the Ugandan government to respond within six months.

World.title: After 28 years, NFVCB secures permanent headquarters, pursues name change
World.content:
The National Film and Video Censors Board (NFVCB) has said it secured a permanent headquarters after operating without one for 28 years.

The Executive Director and Chief Executive Officer of the board, Shaibu Husseini, announced the development at the sixth Peace Anyiam-Osigwe Nigeria Digital Content Regulatory Conference in Lagos on Wednesday.

Mr Husseini described the acquisition as a major step toward strengthening the agency’s operations and improving the discharge of its statutory responsibilities.

“One major achievement is the securing of a permanent headquarters for the NFVCB after 28 years without one,” he said.

“This milestone provides institutional stability and a stronger foundation for improved service delivery and the effective discharge of our statutory responsibilities.”

The NFVCB boss did not disclose the headquarters’ location, its cost or when the agency would begin operating from the facility.

The conference, themed “Film and Content Production in the Digital Era: Balancing Regulation and Innovation,” brought together regulators, filmmakers, investors and other stakeholders in Nigeria’s creative industry.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Proposed name change

Mr Husseini also disclosed that the NFVCB was pursuing an amendment to its enabling law to remove the word “Censors” from its name.

He said the proposed change would reposition the agency as a classification-focused regulator and reflect its evolving approach to film and digital-content regulation.

According to him, the board has increasingly emphasised classification rather than censorship since March 2024.

“Another important reform is our effort to secure, through the National Assembly, an amendment to the board’s enabling law to remove the word ‘Censors’ from its name and reposition the institution as a classification-focused regulatory organisation,” he said.

“Classification informs audiences, supports informed viewing choices, protects consumers and gives filmmakers a clearer framework for responsible creative freedom.”

Mr Husseini said the proposed change formed part of a broader shift toward audience empowerment, professional standards, technological responsiveness and the sustainable development of Nigeria’s creative industry.

He added that the board would continue engaging the National Assembly and other stakeholders on the legislative process.

Regulatory reforms

The NFVCB chief said artificial intelligence, streaming platforms, social media and digital distribution had transformed how films and other audiovisual content were produced and consumed.

He noted that the changes had created opportunities for filmmakers but also raised concerns about intellectual property, authorship, ownership, content standards and consumer protection.

Mr Husseini said the board had strengthened its cooperation with other institutions, including the Nigerian Communications Commission, to address challenges associated with digital distribution, classification, monitoring and licensing.

He also said a technical review committee was examining the NFVCB’s classification, exhibition and distribution guidelines to ensure they remained relevant to current industry realities.

The agency, he added, had initiated discussions with Goethe University on a possible partnership to digitise and preserve its audiovisual classification archive, which dates back to 1994.

Mr Husseini also highlighted the implementation of the 2024 Regulation on the Control of the Promotion and Glamourisation of Tobacco, Narcotics, Ritual Killing and Money Ritual in Film and Video Works.

He said the regulation reflected the agency’s position that creative freedom should be protected without allowing content to promote practices capable of causing harm.

“The NFVCB is not opposed to innovation and does not seek to create unnecessary obstacles for filmmakers, investors or digital operators,” he said.

“We want an industry where filmmakers tell compelling stories, investors earn reasonable returns, distributors and exhibitors run viable businesses, and audiences enjoy diverse, quality content.”

RMD cautions regulators

Delivering the keynote address, veteran actor Richard Mofe-Damijo urged regulators to protect audiences without creating an environment in which filmmakers were afraid to explore difficult subjects.

Mr Mofe-Damijo, popularly known as RMD, said regulation should provide clarity and confidence while encouraging innovation rather than punishing it.

He argued that storytelling had always challenged assumptions, questioned authority and examined uncomfortable realities.

“Responsible storytelling must not become an excuse for controlling storytelling,” he said.

“We must avoid creating an environment in which every difficult subject is regarded as a threat or every uncomfortable narrative is treated as an act of disobedience.”

The actor said classification, age-appropriate access, clear content guidelines and transparent regulatory processes could help protect vulnerable audiences without intimidating filmmakers.

He also urged Nigeria to begin developing safeguards around the use of artificial intelligence in filmmaking.

According to him, AI has created new opportunities in script development, visual effects, editing, animation and translation but had also raised questions about consent, authorship and ownership.

“What happens when an actor’s image or voice is replicated digitally without permission?” he asked.

“Who owns a creative work generated with artificial intelligence? What protections exist for writers and artists whose work may be used to train AI systems?”

He warned that Nigeria should not wait until such abuses became widespread before responding.

Creative financing

In her remarks, the Minister of Art, Culture, Tourism and the Creative Economy said the federal government was working to transform the creative economy from a largely talent-driven sector into a structured, investment-ready and globally competitive industry.

She said the Creative Economy Development Fund was providing financing opportunities for creative businesses through debt, equity and grant windows.

According to her, the fund’s extended second phase was accepting applications from eligible creatives.

She also said the government was pursuing audiovisual co-production partnerships with countries including South Africa and France to encourage investment, skills transfer and wider distribution for Nigerian productions.

The minister urged filmmakers, regulators, investors and digital platforms to work together to develop practical recommendations that would strengthen regulation without restricting innovation.

World.title: Gully erosion threatens power transmission structure in Cross River
World.content:
An advancing gully ravaging some part of Osok Community in Odukpani, Cross River State, has put a major electricity transmission structure at the risk of collapse

The Cross River State Emergency Management Agency (CR-SEMA) and the Nigerian Red Cross Society made the observation during an assessment visit to erosion-impacted sites in the community on Thursday.

The News Agency of Nigeria reports that the erosion has destroyed some residential buildings and severely degraded the surrounding terrain.

The development has also raised concerns over the safety of residents and critical infrastructure in the community.

The Director-General, CR-SEMA, Efa Nyong said the ravaging gully was threatening a major high-tension electricity transmission. He said the threat has possible consequences for power supply.

Mr Nyong expressed concern over the scale of destruction and assured residents that the Governor Bassey Otu-led government would intervene.

“The state government will give the matter its deserved consideration, particularly because of its potential consequences to lives, property, and critical infrastructure,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the assessment became necessary to establish the extent of the damage and determine appropriate interventions to contain the advancing erosion.

“Assessing the situation is important in determining necessary measures to protect residents, their property, and the threatened electricity transmission facility,” he said.

Agbor Okim, the disaster management officer, Nigerian Red Cross Society, Calabar Division, recorded the losses in the community.

Mr Okim said the documentation would assist in further evaluation of the disaster and facilitate the provision of appropriate support to affected residents.

World.title: Anambra govt explains removal of billboard featuring Peter Obi
World.content:
The Anambra State Government has admitted pulling down a billboard bearing an image of the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi.

There were reports suggesting that the Anambra State Government pulled down a billboard in Anambra State because it featured Mr Obi’s image.

The billboard belongs to the Anambra Central Senator and the NDC candidate for the district, Victor Umeh, whose photograph also featured alongside Mr Obi’s.

But in a statement on Thursday, the Commissioner for Information in Anambra State, Law Mefor, denied the allegations.

“This claim is false, misleading, and a deliberate distortion of the facts.

“For the avoidance of doubt, the billboard was not pulled down because of Peter Obi’s image,” Mr Mefor said.

The commissioner explained that the billboard was pulled down by the state government because although Mr Umeh paid, Mr Obi, whose image also appeared on the billboard, did not pay.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Rather than ensure compliance, the distinguished senator decided to use his billboard to campaign for the NDC presidential candidate, in clear contravention of the Anambra State Signage Act, 2010, a law enacted by the Peter Obi administration itself.

“The enforcement action was therefore carried out strictly in accordance with the law, and not on account of any person, personality, or political affiliation,” he said.

Mr Mefor vowed that the state government would not hesitate to pull down any other combined billboard involving a candidate or candidates who failed to pay the approved signage fee.

“The Anambra State Government remains firmly committed to the fair, transparent, and even-handed enforcement of all extant laws, without fear or favour.

“We will continue to uphold process and ensure a level playing field for all in the regulation of outdoor advertising across the state,” he stated.

Background

PREMIUM TIMES reports that Governor Soludo’s administration, in May, announced a signage fee for deployment of outdoor campaign materials in the state.

Presidential candidates, according to the government, must pay N50 million while senatorial candidates seeking to deploy similar campaign materials will pay N20 million.

Similarly, House of Representatives candidates will pay N5 million, while candidates for the Anambra State House of Assembly will pay N1.5 million.

Local government chairmanship candidates will pay N2.5 million while councillorship candidates will pay N100,000 before deploying outdoor campaigns in the state.

This was not the first time the Anambra State Government announced permit fees for deploying campaign materials in the state.

Before the 2023 general elections, the state government announced various fees for deploying campaign materials.

At that time, presidential candidates were asked to pay N10 million each to the state government.

Senatorial candidates were asked to pay N7 million, while House of Representatives candidates were told to pay N5 million to paste their campaign posters in the state.

Similarly, candidates for the state assembly were expected to pay N1 million for the same purpose.

The removal of the billboard featuring Mr Obi sparked widespread debate online, coming amid ongoing political friction between Governor Soludo and the NDC presidential candidate.

The governor, though a member of the All Progressives Grand Alliance, has continued to openly declare support for the re-election of President Bola Tinubu, a member of the All Progressives Congress.

Aside from supporting Mr Tinubu, Mr Soludo has been campaigning against Mr Obi’s presidential ambition ahead of the 2027 general election.

World.title: Police recover stolen truck in Cross River, hunt suspect
World.content:
The Police Command in Cross River State has recovered a stolen Toyota Hilux belonging to the National Inland Waterways Authority (NIWA).

The truck was reportedly stolen in Anambra State.

Sunday Eitokpah, the police spokesperson in Cross River, disclosed this in Calabar on Thursday.

Mr Eitokpah, an assistant superintendent of police, said the vehicle, with registration number NIWA 19E-68-FG, was recovered on Wednesday at Uko-Ma Petrol Station, opposite Picolo Junction, near the Spaghetti Flyover in Odukpani Local Government Area.

According to him, the recovery followed a report received by the Divisional Police Officer (DPO), Odukpani, at about 11:30 a.m. from a NIWA official in Calabar.

He said the official informed the police that the vehicle had been stolen in Anambra and was being tracked towards Calabar.

“Acting on the information, the Commissioner of Police, Ajo Ordue, directed the mobilisation of relevant operational units to track the vehicle.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“At about 3 p.m., the police located the Hilux abandoned at the petrol station, while an individual suspected to be connected with the vehicle reportedly fled on sighting the operatives.

“The vehicle was subsequently taken to the police station for safekeeping, while investigations commenced to establish the circumstances surrounding its theft and movement,” he explained.

Mr Eitokpah said efforts were ongoing to identify and apprehend the fleeing suspect.

According to him, the police commissioner commended the officers involved for their prompt response and effective coordination.

Mr Ordue reiterated the command’s commitment to intelligence gathering, inter-divisional collaboration, and proactive policing to prevent criminal activities.

He warned criminals against using Cross River as a hiding place or transit route, assuring residents that the police would continue to track down offenders and bring them to justice.

(NAN)

World.title: COP31 carbon removal push could threaten African farmland, fisheries, activist warns
World.content:
An environmental justice activist has warned that proposals to expand carbon dioxide removal technologies under consideration at the COP31 climate negotiations could threaten African livelihoods, worsen food insecurity and divert scarce climate resources from adaptation projects.

Kwami Kpondzo, an official of the Global Forest Coalition and co-coordinator of the Africa Working Group of the Hands Off Mother Earth (HOME) Alliance, said large-scale deployment of technologies such as bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) and marine carbon dioxide removal could impose significant costs on communities already vulnerable to climate change.

In an interview with PREMIUM TIMES in Antalya, Türkiye, Mr Kpondzo argued that the growing emphasis on carbon removal risks allowing major polluters to continue emitting greenhouse gases instead of reducing pollution at its source.

His concerns come as negotiators consider provisions in the first draft of the COP31 cover decision that encourage the expansion of carbon capture and carbon dioxide removal technologies.

The draft calls for efforts to accelerate carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) to at least 500 million tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2035, while encouraging countries to work towards removing between 1.3 billion and 2.5 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide annually by the same year.

Although the draft recognises that carbon dioxide removal may be needed to return global warming below 1.5 degrees Celsius, it also states that such measures should complement, rather than replace or delay, deep emissions reductions.

The proposals have, however, raised concerns among some environmental groups about the environmental and social consequences of deploying technologies at scale.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Threat to land, food security

Mr Kpondzo said BECCS, which involves growing biomass, burning it for energy and capturing the resulting carbon dioxide for storage, could require extensive areas of land if deployed on a large scale.

He warned that this could put pressure on land used by rural communities for farming, particularly in African countries where smallholder and family farming remain important sources of food and household income.

“If BECCS should work, it needs a huge amount of land. Africa’s economy is based on agriculture, and people need land to cultivate and have food. If land is taken from communities, it means they will not have access to land to cultivate,” he said.

He added that the consequences could extend beyond food production to household income, education and housing, particularly where families depend on small-scale farming to pay for their children’s schooling and meet other basic needs.

Mr Kpondzo also raised concerns about the possible displacement of communities and the use of chemicals in large-scale biomass production, arguing that these could affect soil quality, water resources and biodiversity.

He described the potential consequences as human rights concerns, including the rights to food, water, housing and a safe environment.

Concerns over marine carbon removal

The activist also criticised proposals to explore marine carbon dioxide removal, which involves using the ocean or marine ecosystems to absorb and store more carbon dioxide.

He said some approaches being promoted for further research, including ocean alkalinity enhancement and ocean fertilisation, could affect marine ecosystems and the livelihoods of fishing communities.

Ocean alkalinity enhancement involves adding alkaline materials to seawater to increase its capacity to absorb carbon dioxide, while ocean fertilisation seeks to stimulate the growth of marine organisms, such as phytoplankton, which absorb carbon dioxide through photosynthesis.

Mr Kpondzo warned that experiments and eventual deployment could expose fishing communities to risks if they disrupt marine ecosystems.

He questioned why governments should commit substantial resources to researching technologies whose environmental consequences remain uncertain when vulnerable communities urgently need support to adapt to climate impacts.

“We are here to find a solution to the climate crisis, not to put more burden on the community,” he said.

He argued that funding for such research would be better directed towards adaptation projects and community-led practices that work with nature.

Climate finance concerns

Beyond the possible effects on land and marine ecosystems, Mr Kpondzo said expanding investment in carbon removal could further complicate the long-standing demand by African countries for more climate finance, particularly for adaptation.

He argued that funding for carbon removal technologies and carbon market projects should not be treated as a substitute for financial obligations by wealthy countries to support developing nations dealing with climate impacts.

“We need climate debt to be paid, not climate finance,” he said, arguing that countries with greater historical responsibility for greenhouse gas emissions should fulfil their obligations rather than rely on carbon markets to demonstrate climate action.

He said Africa needed more direct investment in initiatives such as agroecology, sustainable forest management and community-led adaptation.

Agroecology applies ecological principles to farming, including practices that improve soil health, protect biodiversity and reduce reliance on chemical inputs.

Mr Kpondzo said funding directed towards carbon capture and removal projects could instead support these approaches, which he believes would provide more immediate benefits to communities.

Nigeria’s energy challenge

Mr Kpondzo also questioned whether continued investment in oil and gas extraction would address Africa’s energy access challenges.

He cited Nigeria as an example, pointing to persistent electricity shortages despite decades of oil and gas production.

“Every time I go to Nigeria, I experience power cuts. It is terrible,” he said.

He argued that communities in oil-producing areas continued to bear the consequences of extraction through pollution, gas flaring and black soot, while many people still lacked reliable electricity.

For Africa, he said, the energy transition should prioritise clean, accessible and community-centred electricity rather than systems that continue to depend on fossil fuels or serve primarily the interests of wealthier countries.

He also raised concerns about the extraction of critical minerals needed for renewable energy technologies, saying the process could create new environmental and social pressures on African communities if not governed responsibly.

“We need electrification that will benefit the Global South, not electrification that will benefit the Global North,” he said. “It should be from clean energy, people-centred and democratised.”

A disputed proposal

The debate over carbon removal is part of wider discussions at COP31 about how countries can respond to the risk of global warming exceeding the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold.

READ ALSO: COP31 carbon capture target raises fears of prolonged fossil fuel dependence

While some proponents argue that carbon removal will be needed alongside emissions reductions to address residual emissions and remove carbon dioxide already in the atmosphere, critics warn that relying on the technologies could weaken pressure on governments and industries to move away from fossil fuels.

The COP31 draft cover decision is not yet an agreed outcome. In a note accompanying the 16 November draft, the presidency said the text was intended to facilitate further negotiations and did not represent consensus among parties.

Mr Kpondzo said African countries should resist proposals that could delay emissions reductions while increasing pressure on communities and natural resources.

He called for governments to prioritise direct cuts in fossil fuel emissions and invest in solutions such as agroecology and forest management.

“We can’t be doing the same thing and expect something different as a result,” he said.

World.title: Court strikes out suit challenging Yahaya Bello’s APC senatorial candidacy
World.content:
The Federal High Court in Abuja on Thursday struck out a suit challenging former Kogi State Governor Yahaya Bello’s emergence as the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate for Kogi Central Senatorial District in the 2027 elections.

Judge Inyang Ekwo held that the plaintiff, Momoh Obaro, failed to exhaust the party’s internal dispute-resolution process before filing the suit.

Ruling on Mr Bello and the other defendants’ preliminary objection, the judge found the case premature and struck it out.

The court also found that the results Mr Obaro presented were not signed by the chairman and secretary of the committee that conducted the primary.

Speaking to journalists after the ruling, Mr Bello’s lawyer, Paul Daudu, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), said the court could not give the documents “probative value in law.”

He added that Mr Obaro’s case was based on documents the court considered not genuine, describing them as a “scam.”

Mr Daudu said the ruling meant Mr Bello remained the APC candidate for the senatorial election.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Obaro, through his lawyer, Kimi Appah, had instituted the suit against the APC, Mr Bello and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) on 29 May.

He asked the court to declare him the lawful winner of the 18 May primary, having scored the highest number of valid votes, and direct the party to forward his name to INEC as its candidate.

He also sought an order restraining the APC from submitting Mr Bello’s name to INEC as its candidate for the 2027 senatorial election.

In an affidavit he personally deposed to, Mr Obaro alleged that Mr Bello was neither screened nor cleared to contest the primary and said he was surprised when he learnt that the former governor had been declared the winner and his name forwarded to INEC.

Bello, APC, INEC opposed the suit

PREMIUM TIMES reported that when the matter came up for final arguments on 28 September, Mr Bello, the APC and INEC urged Judge Ekwo to dismiss the suit.

In a preliminary objection, Mr Bello asked the court to dismiss the case in limine, arguing that it was fundamentally defective, incompetent and did not vest the court with jurisdiction to hear it.

He maintained that, contrary to Mr Obaro’s claim, he scored the highest number of lawful votes, while the plaintiff came a distant third. He said he polled 72,999 votes, compared with Mr Obaro’s 188.

Mr Bello also argued that Mr Obaro failed to present the authentic result sheet issued by the duly constituted primary election committee. He explained that he was screened, cleared and certified as qualified to contest the primary, contrary to the plaintiff’s allegation.

The APC and INEC, in their separate court filings, also urged the court to dismiss the suit, maintaining that Mr Bello won the primary with the highest number of valid votes.

Bello’s Emergence

The APC National Assembly screening committee had cleared Mr Bello, who governed Kogi State from 2016 to 2024, to contest the party’s Kogi Central senatorial primary.

A document circulated within the party initially listed him as “not cleared,” but the party later released another list that included his name among the aspirants cleared to contest the primary, against Momoh Obaro and Ibrahim Adoke.

The direct primary was held across the five local government areas that make up Kogi Central Senatorial District on 18 May.

The returning officer, Sadiq Mohammed, declared Mr Bello the winner at the collation centre in Okene. He noted that the former governor polled over 70,000 votes, while Mr Adoke scored 319 votes and Mr Obaro polled 188 votes.

Notwithstanding his emergence as the party’s candidate, Mr Bello remains involved in two separate criminal trials over alleged financial misconduct during his tenure as governor of Kogi State.

The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) is prosecuting him on 19 charges involving the alleged diversion of N80.2 billion belonging to Kogi State in a money laundering scheme before the Federal High Court in Abuja.

The trial has continued, with prosecution witnesses giving evidence about transactions allegedly linked to the case, but it may suffer a setback following the recent elevation of the presiding judge, Emeka Nwite, to the Court of Appeal. He was sworn in alongside others on Tuesday.

Mr Bello is also facing a separate 16-count case of fraud and criminal breach of trust before the FCT High Court in Abuja, alongside Umar Oricha and Abdulsalami. They are accused of diverting N110 billion belonging to Kogi State. Mr Bello has denied all the allegations.

In April 2024, the EFCC declared him wanted after an attempt to arrest him at his Abuja residence.

In June, the FCT High Court dismissed Mr Bello’s application seeking to stop the N110.4 billion trial. Judge Maryanne Anenih held that the court had jurisdiction to hear the case and directed that the trial should continue.

World.title: Jos hospital denies negligence in nursing student’s death
World.content:
The National Orthopaedic Hospital, Jos, has denied allegations of medical negligence following the death of a nursing student, Raphael Bilat.

In a statement on Wednesday, the hospital’s management said its medical team immediately activated emergency response procedures and administered life-saving interventions.

Some of the deceased’s colleagues had claimed that he did not receive adequate medical attention.

The hospital said Mr Bilat was brought to its Accident and Emergency Unit at about 6:05 p.m. on Monday, 16 November, after collapsing during a football match.

Mr Bilat’s death sparked outrage among colleagues and members of the nursing community, with allegations of inadequate emergency facilities and delays in medical intervention at the orthopaedic hospital and the Jos University Teaching Hospital (JUTH), where he was subsequently transferred.

One of his colleagues, Ifeoma Onyibe, alleged that essential emergency supplies, including oxygen, were unavailable when the student was brought to the hospital.

She also claimed that the students waited for about two hours without access to the doctor on duty.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The hospital, however, gave a different account, saying the student was already in an extremely critical condition when he arrived.

According to the statement, Mr Bilat was accompanied by a large group of student nurses following his sudden collapse on a football pitch.

The hospital said he was clinically unresponsive, pale and cold to the touch, with fixed and dilated pupils and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3/15, indicating profound unresponsiveness.

It said nurses on duty immediately commenced resuscitation while the doctor on call was notified.

The medical team established an intravenous line and conducted a random blood sugar test, which returned a reading of 8.4 millimoles per litre.

The attending doctor reportedly confirmed that the patient was unresponsive following cardiac arrest, prompting continued cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), administration of intravenous fluids and 200 milligrams of hydrocortisone.

The hospital said cardiac monitoring showed a body temperature of 31 degrees Celsius, while his pulse, blood pressure and oxygen saturation could not be recorded.

It added that intravenous adrenaline was administered and supplemental oxygen provided, but the patient remained unresponsive.

Hospital alleges interference with resuscitation

The hospital further alleged that efforts to resuscitate the student were disrupted by a large crowd of student nurses who overwhelmed its Accident and Emergency Unit.

It said the crowd obstructed medical specialists from taking full control of the patient’s management despite repeated appeals by hospital personnel.

According to the management, some students insisted on performing endotracheal intubation themselves and administering what it described as unapproved doses of emergency medications, including up to six ampoules of intravenous adrenaline and atropine, against the attending physician’s advice.

The hospital said the situation overwhelmed its internal security personnel and operatives of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps deployed to the facility.

Despite the alleged disruption, the management said its medical team continued resuscitation efforts.

It added that the students subsequently requested an ambulance to transfer Mr Bilat to JUTH for further treatment.

At the time of the request, the hospital said his body temperature had dropped to 30 degrees Celsius, his oxygen saturation was 42 per cent, while his pulse and blood pressure remained unrecordable.

A second doctor on call reportedly managed to reach the patient through the crowd, reassessed his condition and explained the critical prognosis to the students before authorising the transfer.

The hospital’s ambulance was deployed at 8:59 p.m. and departed at 9:05 p.m., accompanied by a nurse, a porter and student representatives.

The statement said resuscitation continued throughout the journey, with the patient remaining unresponsive and his oxygen saturation at 42 per cent.

He was handed over to the Accident and Emergency team at JUTH at 9:20 p.m., while the ambulance returned to the orthopaedic hospital at 10:05 p.m.

Hospital defends emergency response

The management maintained that it provided emergency care in accordance with national healthcare directives, insisting that life-saving medications, intravenous fluids and emergency drugs were deployed as required.

It also disclosed that another student from the same group was brought to its Accident and Emergency Unit during the incident in critical condition.

According to the hospital, its medical team attended to the second student and successfully stabilised her before she regained consciousness.

While expressing condolences to the family of the deceased, his colleagues and the wider nursing community, the hospital appealed for calm and urged the public to respect medical protocols during emergencies.

It said attempts by people without clinical authority to take over emergency procedures and administer restricted medications could compromise patient care.

However, the hospital’s statement did not independently establish the cause of Mr Bilat’s collapse or address all the specific allegations concerning the availability and functionality of emergency equipment, including reported concerns about a defibrillator.

The conflicting accounts have raised questions about emergency preparedness, the availability of critical equipment and coordination between medical personnel and accompanying students during life-threatening situations.

There are also questions surrounding the circumstances of the student’s transfer between the two federal hospitals.

The orthopaedic hospital said Mr Bilat was handed over to JUTH at 9:20 p.m. on Monday, while earlier accounts placed the time he was pronounced dead at about 9 p.m.

World.title: NCTC-led AgriShield Initiative works with NECSOB to address farmers’ concerns
World.content:
The Network of Civil Society Organisations in Borno State (NECSOB) is working with the National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC), Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) to strengthen engagement with farming communities to ensure that their security and livelihood concerns are heard and addressed through the NCTC-led AgriShield initiative.

At a recent AgriShield town hall in Maiduguri, organised by NECSOB in partnership with the NCTC, farmers and community members came together to discuss the challenges affecting their daily lives.

The event attracted strong community participation, with interactive discussions and community drama helping to highlight the difficulties faced by local farmers.

Participants raised concerns about ongoing insecurity preventing access to farmland, increasing competition for limited agricultural land and the destruction of crops by cattle entering farms.

These concerns have been brought to the attention of the NCTC, which is taking steps to coordinate with relevant government ministries and security agencies to help identify appropriate responses.

Through its network of more than 200 civil society organisations, NECSOB is supporting the delivery of AgriShield by connecting communities with the NCTC and security services, gathering local insights and ensuring that community concerns inform government coordination and decision-making.

The Director of Administration, Network of Civil Society Organisation (NECSOB) in Borno State, Dr Abdullahi Maina, said: “AgriShield demonstrates the importance of government and civil society working together.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He added that the National Counter Terrorism Centre is leading efforts to strengthen cooperation between communities and security services, while our role is to ensure that the voices of those most affected are heard.

Farmers have raised important concerns about their safety and livelihoods. By working closely with the NCTC, we can help bring these issues to the attention of the relevant authorities and support practical steps to address them.”

The engagement reflects AgriShield’s wider whole-of-society approach, recognising that improving community security requires government, security agencies, civil society and citizens to work together.

NECSOB will continue supporting the NCTC-led initiative through community engagements, radio programmes and public information activities, encouraging communities to share security information, follow local security advice and participate in efforts to create safer conditions for farming.

If you have any security concerns, you can report them toll-free on 112.

World.title: Remi Tinubu seeks N70bn to complete National Library
World.content:
Oluremi Tinubu

By Joseph Erunke, Abuja

The First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, has said an additional N70 billion is required to complete the National Library headquarters in Abuja, disclosing that her 65th birthday fundraising initiative has so far generated N25.6 billion for the project.

Tinubu made the disclosure on Thursday as construction work formally resumed on the long-abandoned National Library headquarters, a project conceived decades ago but stalled by funding challenges and repeated interruptions.

The First Lady launched the fundraising campaign in December 2025 to mark her 65th birthday. She said the contributions came from wealthy Nigerians, women’s groups and other individuals who shared her vision of a world-class national library.

While appreciating the donors, she acknowledged the challenge of raising the remaining funds, given the enormous resources required to complete the facility.

She, however, urged Nigerians to contribute to the project, saying even modest donations would make a difference.

“I have told the Minister that every contribution counts, even if it is just N10. Let everyone have an opportunity to say, ‘I contributed to the construction of the National Library’,” she said.

Tinubu said the National Library was not merely a government construction project but a national monument belonging to all Nigerians.

She urged students, individuals, organisations and other citizens to support the project, noting that collective participation would strengthen public ownership of the facility.

Explaining her personal attachment to the project, the First Lady said libraries played an important role in shaping her life and deepening her appreciation of education.

She recalled her years in the Senate, particularly during the 7th, 8th and 9th National Assemblies, when she consistently sought membership of the education committee because of her background as a teacher and passion for the sector.

Tinubu said she and President Bola Tinubu understood the struggles associated with humble beginnings and believed education remained one of the most potent instruments for breaking the cycle of poverty.

She recalled visiting the Qatar National Library in Doha in October 2025, where she saw how a modern library could serve beyond book storage to become a centre for research, technology, innovation, cultural preservation and lifelong learning.

The experience, she said, reinforced her determination to see Nigeria’s National Library transformed into a modern knowledge institution capable of serving generations.

She commended President Tinubu for renewing the government’s commitment to the project and urged contractors and consultants to deliver a world-class facility within the stipulated timeframe.

The Minister of Education, Dr Maruf Tunji Alausa, said the National Library headquarters, conceived and commenced in 2006, had suffered repeated setbacks before being abandoned for 16 years.

He said the project remained stalled until President Tinubu renewed the government’s commitment to its completion, describing the intervention as a demonstration of the administration’s resolve to prioritise education and human capital development.

Alausa said the National Library was a critical national asset for preserving Nigeria’s documentary heritage, providing access to knowledge and supporting research, education and national development.

He commended the First Lady for dedicating proceeds from her 65th birthday fundraising initiative to the project, describing the gesture as a personal celebration converted into an enduring public investment.

The minister assured Nigerians that the Federal Ministry of Education would work with the National Library management, contractors, consultants and relevant government agencies to ensure transparent oversight, quality execution and compliance with approved standards.

“The confidence invested in this project must be repaid through responsible and timely delivery,” he said.

Alausa charged the contractors and consultants to adhere strictly to project milestones, maintain rigorous supervision and promptly address challenges that could undermine delivery.

He said the completed facility would provide students with access to learning resources, support researchers, authors and publishers, and offer reliable information to policymakers and other stakeholders.

The minister also urged young Nigerians to cultivate reading habits, explore new ideas and harness knowledge to solve societal problems.

Providing an account of the project’s history, the National Librarian and Chief Executive Officer of the National Library of Nigeria, Professor Chinwe Veronica Nwakaego Anunobi, said efforts to establish a befitting headquarters began in 1981, when the institution engaged Odele International Associates to design the facility.

She said the construction contract was awarded to Reynolds Construction Company Nigeria Limited in March 2006 under former President Olusegun Obasanjo, with work commencing in April that year.

However, the project suffered major interruptions between 2008 and 2010 and again from August 2014, eventually grinding to a halt after reaching only 48 per cent completion.

Anunobi said the 11-storey complex, covering approximately 82,941 square metres, represented a significant national investment that had remained unrealised for too long.

She disclosed that construction resumed on October 21, 2026, following efforts by the Minister of Education, with work now being undertaken in phases.

The revised design, she said, incorporated modern facilities, including preservation and conservation laboratories, a digitisation laboratory, an innovation and research hub, and a children’s library.

According to her, the facilities would reposition the National Library as a centre for intellectual development, research, education, innovation, social engagement and economic advancement.

Anunobi also said the First Lady’s visit to the Qatar National Library, alongside education ministers, inspired a renewed vision for Nigeria’s National Library and culminated in the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding between Nigerian and Qatari library institutions in August 2026.

She said the agreement provided for knowledge and heritage sharing, exchange of expertise and collaboration in adopting international best practices in library management and development.

Describing the N25.6 billion raised by the First Lady as a major contribution towards Nigeria’s intellectual future, the National Librarian commended the President, Tinubu, Alausa and the Minister of State for Education, Professor Suwaiba Sa’idu Ahmad, for their roles in reviving the project.

She assured Nigerians that the National Library management was committed to delivering a world-class facility, stressing that the project was about more than completing a building.

According to her, it represents an effort to restore a national institution, preserve Nigeria’s intellectual heritage and safeguard knowledge for future generations.

N200,000 support for elderly, PWDs

In a related development, Tinubu announced plans to provide N200,000 each to elderly citizens and persons with disabilities across the country’s senatorial districts in December.

She said the initiative would cover 250 beneficiaries in each senatorial district, with the money intended to support small businesses or meet personal needs.

The First Lady said persons with disabilities would receive the support on December 3, in commemoration of the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, while elderly beneficiaries would be celebrated on December 17.

She described the initiative as part of her longstanding commitment to improving the welfare of vulnerable Nigerians.

Tinubu urged senators to work with her team to ensure effective implementation and encourage eligible beneficiaries to register through their respective senatorial representatives.

She said the programmes were being expanded to reach more Nigerians, acknowledging that the country’s large population required sustained efforts to extend support to different categories of vulnerable people.

The resumption of construction on the National Library headquarters offers an opportunity to complete an institution expected to serve as a major pillar of Nigeria’s educational, research and knowledge infrastructure after decades of delays.

World.title: Germany, France, Britain meet with Ukraine after Trump-Putin-Xi talks
World.content:
Ukraine President, Zelensky

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Berlin Thursday for a “Coalition of the Willing” summit where Kyiv’s allies were to signal steadfast support and push for a European role in any future peace talks.

The meeting – co-hosted by the leaders of Germany, France and Britain – was being held shortly after unprecedented three-way talks in China between US President Donald Trump, Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping.

The goal of the Berlin summit was to boost Europe’s role in any efforts to end the continent’s worst conflict since World War II, in a process so far dominated by Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.

Zelensky wrote on X that “we are doing everything we can to ensure that Europe’s presence in the negotiation process is fully represented”.

A so-called E5 core group – made up of Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland as well as EU officials – is expected to represent Europe in any potential peace negotiations.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff also arrived at the chancellery for the summit, expected to bring more than 25 European leaders as well as EU and NATO chiefs.

The US envoys were expected to face questions on the China talks, where the three presidents agreed a brief “peace declaration” that touched on “strategic stability” but made no mention of the war in Ukraine.

Putin, speaking later in China, said Russia had invited European officials, through diplomatic channels, to Moscow to discuss whether they should participate in US-led talks on ending the Ukraine war.

“We understand that discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans,” Putin told a press conference.

However, he also said Moscow could not accept any kind of military ties between Ukraine and Europe as part of a deal to end the war.

Billions needed for arms

Kushner wrote on X that he and Witkoff hoped “to further strengthen our close coordination with Ukraine and Europe, work toward a unified position on the key elements of a lasting peace, and to jointly prepare the agenda and proposed format for the next round of multilateral negotiations”.

He added that the talks would also explore how the coalition “can contribute to post-war security arrangements, including credible guarantees for Ukraine and a broader framework that strengthens European stability and reduces the risk of future conflict”.

Germany has emerged as the biggest provider of military aid to Ukraine since Trump scaled back US support and is also rapidly rebuilding its own military to deter a hostile Russia.

Merz has insisted that all 27 EU member states help finance Ukraine as it faces a 70-billion-euro ($77-billion) funding shortfall next year.

The European Union on Wednesday proposed members give Ukraine an extra 45-billion-euro loan to help plug the finance gap.

Russia has sought to link an end to the Ukraine war with a complete overhaul of the European security architecture that would push NATO further away from its borders.

Merz, speaking last week, dismissed that idea: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that, it already exists.”

The Germany summit comes as the war enters its fifth gruelling winter, with Russian strikes hammering Ukraine’s energy and transport infrastructure.

Ukraine is in urgent need of interceptors, especially US-made Patriot missiles, at a time when the Middle East war has deepened a global shortage.

Ukraine has meanwhile targeted Russian oil facilities and again attacked the bridge connecting annexed Crimea to Russia on Thursday, the third time in a week the key transport artery had been targeted.

Putin, speaking in China after the trilateral summit, vowed that “we will respond to these attacks. Our response will be far more painful than Kyiv’s attack on the bridge.”
