World.title: Ebonyi gives shanty shop owners 15-day ultimatum to remove structures
World.content:
By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki

The Ebonyi State Government has given owners and operators of shanty shops at Quarry Junction, Abakaliki, 15 days to dismantle and remove their structures over safety concerns.

The Commissioner for Capital City and Urban Planning, Chief Richard Ugo Idike, issued the directive during a routine inspection exercise aimed at ensuring compliance with urban planning regulations and protecting lives and property in the state capital.

Idike expressed concern that the makeshift shops were located directly beneath high-tension electricity lines, describing the situation as a serious threat to traders, customers and other members of the public.

He said the government’s intervention was necessary to prevent possible accidents, electrocution and loss of lives, stressing that commercial activities would not be allowed to continue in locations considered dangerous to public safety.

The commissioner directed all owners and occupants of the affected shops to dismantle their structures within 15 days, warning that failure to comply would attract enforcement action by the ministry.

He said the state government’s urban renewal and development agenda was not limited to creating a beautiful and well-organised capital city but also included ensuring that residents operated businesses in safe and approved locations.

Idike reiterated the ministry’s commitment to regular monitoring, inspection and enforcement of building and urban planning regulations across Abakaliki metropolis.

He urged residents, traders, property owners and developers to obtain the necessary government approvals before erecting structures or engaging in commercial activities.

The commissioner assured that the ministry would continue to take proactive measures to prevent avoidable disasters and promote orderly development across the state capital.

World.title: Treat gunshot victims first; police report can wait – IGP Disu to doctors
World.content:
Inspector General of Police (IGP), Olatunji Disu

By Enitan Abdultawab

The Inspector General of Police, Tunji Disu, has urged hospitals and healthcare workers across the country to treat gunshot victims immediately without demanding police reports, warning that delays could cost lives.

Disu also called on members of the public to assist injured persons in accessing medical attention, assuring them that they would not face punishment for helping victims.

The IGP made the appeal in a sensitisation message by the National Orientation Agency (NOA) in collaboration with the Nigeria Police Force, shared by the police on its X account on Thursday.

Addressing Nigerians, police officers and medical personnel, Disu described the treatment of gunshot victims as a matter of life and death, stressing that no police documentation was required before emergency medical care could be provided.

“Fellow Nigerians, I am here to address a matter of life and death – the treatment of gunshot victims in our hospitals.

“To my fellow officers, to my medical personnel across the nation, and to every Nigerian listening, treating gunshot victims does not require a police report.

“When a gunshot victim is brought to any hospital, the law does not require a police report before treatment,” he said.

He urged doctors and other healthcare workers to prioritise saving lives rather than allow administrative procedures to delay emergency treatment.

“To our doctors and healthcare workers, you are enjoined to treat gunshot victims immediately without waiting for a police report. Our duty is not to create fear but to protect lives. We wish to reassure citizens of their safety at all times,” Disu added.

The police chief also appealed to Nigerians not to hesitate to help people who sustain gunshot injuries, emphasising that the law protects those who assist victims.

“To the members of the public, if you see someone injured, do not hesitate to help. You will not be punished for helping.

“Again, to my officers and medical personnel, please uphold the law because every second counts. Treat first, save lives,” he said.

In a related message accompanying the video, the Nigeria Police Force warned that refusing or delaying medical attention for gunshot victims was punishable under the Compulsory Treatment and Care for Victims of Gunshots Act, 2017.

According to the police, the legislation requires all public and private hospitals to provide immediate treatment to gunshot victims, regardless of whether they have police reports or clearance.

The police further warned that violations of the Act could attract imprisonment of up to 15 years and other penalties, depending on the offence.

The law provides that every hospital in Nigeria, whether public or private, must receive and provide immediate and adequate treatment to anyone with gunshot wounds, with or without police clearance.

It also places a responsibility on members of the public, including security personnel, to assist victims and ensure they are taken to the nearest hospital for treatment.

Under the Act, hospitals are required to notify the nearest police station within two hours of commencing treatment, allowing investigations into the circumstances surrounding the shooting to begin without delaying medical attention.

The legislation further protects volunteers and other helpers from unnecessary or embarrassing interrogation for their efforts to save the lives of gunshot victims.

World.title: Burna Boy, Asake, Seyi Vibez feature on GTA VI soundtrack
World.content:
A woman holds a copy of Grand Theft Auto VI during a pre-launch party in Miami, Florida, on November 18, 2026. Gamers around the world got their first taste of “Grand Theft Auto VI” on Wednesday, as critics heaped praise on one of the most anticipated video game releases ever. (Photo by Marco BELLO / AFP)

By Enitan Abdultawab

Nigerian music stars Burna Boy, Asake and Seyi Vibez have secured spots on the soundtrack of the highly anticipated video game, Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI).

The Nigerian artistes are among several international performers featured on the game’s soundtrack, which was recently unveiled by Rockstar Games, the developer of the popular gaming franchise.

Some of their songs will feature on AfroBank FM, an in-game radio station dedicated to African music, including Afrobeats, amapiano, African classics and 3-step sounds.

Burna Boy is also set to co-host the station alongside British DJ and record producer Palms Trax, who appears in the game under the name Palmsy.

Among the Nigerian tracks featured on the station are Asake’s ‘Joha’ and ‘Giza’, a collaboration between Burna Boy and Seyi Vibez.

The station’s previewed playlist also includes ‘Gye Wani’ by Pat Thomas featuring Ebo Taylor, as well as ‘Shay’sana’ by DJ Lag and Robot Boii featuring Kamo Mphela.

Burna Boy also makes a separate contribution to the game’s official soundtrack with his song ‘Bigger’.

Other international artistes featured on the soundtrack include Travis Scott, Dua Lipa, Cardi B, Gunna, Young Thug, Kodak Black, Don Toliver, Zara Larsson, Camila Cabello and Lana Del Rey.

The development marks another international gaming appearance for Nigerian music, as Afrobeats continues to gain visibility across global entertainment platforms.

GTA VI is the latest instalment in Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto series, one of the world’s most popular video game franchises.

World.title: UDUS medical academics threaten five-day warning strike
World.content:
By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto

The Nigerian Association of Medical and Dental Academics (NAMDA), Usmanu Danfodiyo University, Sokoto (UDUS)/Usmanu Danfodiyo University Teaching Hospital (UDUTH) Chapter, has threatened to embark on a five-day warning strike over alleged irregularities in salary payments, partial implementation of professional allowances and outstanding promotion arrears owed to its members.

The association, at a press briefing in Sokoto on Thursday, said the unresolved welfare and remuneration issues had persisted despite several rounds of consultations, formal correspondence and peaceful engagements with the university management.

It warned that its members might be left with no option but to embark on an indefinite strike if the issues were not addressed.

Speaking at the briefing, presided over by Professor Usman Bello, NAMDA said its members had exercised considerable patience and goodwill through sustained dialogue with the relevant authorities, but expressed regret that the engagements had not produced the desired results.

The association said its concerns centred on the continued partial implementation of professional allowances under the revised Consolidated Medical Salary Structure (CONMESS), unexplained salary disparities among members on the same grade levels and steps, and the non-payment of promotion arrears covering 2017 to 2024.

It also alleged that some eligible members were excluded from the payment of 2025 and 2026 promotion arrears, describing the situation as an administrative and financial burden that had continued to affect the welfare and morale of medical academics.

According to the association, comparable institutions in both Northern and Southern Nigeria had fully implemented the revised CONMESS, a development it said had heightened concerns among its members over disparities in remuneration.

NAMDA recalled that it had pursued several avenues to resolve the dispute, including meetings with university authorities, submission of formal letters and supporting documents, and interventions by senior colleagues and elders.

However, it said those efforts had yet to yield the desired outcome.

The association also raised concerns over the migration of experienced medical professionals, including senior consultants and professors, to other countries in search of better working conditions.

It described the development, popularly known as “japa”, as a threat to medical education and healthcare delivery in the country.

“Mr President is aware of the ongoing exodus of highly experienced academic staff, including senior consultants and professors, to other countries, a trend popularly known as ‘japa’,” it said.

NAMDA added that the Federal Government’s decision to increase the admission quota for medical students had placed additional pressure on the declining number of medical teachers.

It warned that increasing student intake without corresponding investment in recruiting and retaining qualified medical lecturers could undermine the quality of medical education.

The association said medical teachers, under NAMDA, the Medical and Dental Consultants Association of Nigeria (MDCAN) and the Nigerian Medical Association (NMA), had continued to discharge their responsibilities despite the challenges.

“Despite these challenges, medical teachers have continued to impart knowledge and skills without compromising quality or professional standards,” it said.

NAMDA further disclosed that the Minister of Education had directed vice-chancellors to ensure the payment of outstanding arrears owed to medical teachers in compliance with a presidential directive.

It said several other universities had implemented the directive, but alleged that the management of UDUS had yet to act on it despite sustained engagements.

The association said its congress had consequently resolved to issue a 21-day ultimatum to the university management, effective November 3, 2026, demanding the resolution of all outstanding welfare and remuneration issues before the notice expires on November 24.

It warned that failure to address the concerns would trigger a five-day warning strike.

“Should these concerns remain unaddressed at the expiry of the notice on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, members shall commence a five-day warning strike from 12 midnight on Wednesday, November 25, 2026,” it stated.

The association added that it would review the situation after the warning strike, including the possibility of embarking on an indefinite industrial action if the dispute remained unresolved.

Despite the planned action, NAMDA appealed for urgent intervention and constructive engagement, saying it remained willing to work with the university management towards a lasting resolution in the interest of medical academics, students and patients who depend on the institution’s services.

World.title: China, US, Russia issue ‘peace declaration’ after first summit
World.content:
From left: Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump, arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China. Win McNamee/ Getty Images.

China, the United States and Russia issued a “peace declaration” Thursday following an unprecedented leaders’ summit, almost five years into the Ukraine war and with Donald Trump bogged down in Iran.

The statement after Xi Jinping, Trump and Vladimir Putin met in China, said that they wanted to reform the United Nations, to protect diplomatic immunity and boost supply and production of refined petroleum products.

“The three heads of state engaged in an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed themselves to upholding strategic stability and international security,” said the statement published by Chinese state media and the Kremlin, but not yet by the White House.

The three-way meeting took place with Russia’s years-long offensive in Ukraine grinding on, mayhem in the Middle East in the wake of Trump’s attacks on Iran, and an ascendant China looking to strengthen its hand in East Asia.

“Our countries have many converging interests when it comes to resolving regional conflicts, including, of course, the conflict in Ukraine,” Putin said at the start of the meeting, adding they had a “shared responsibility for maintaining international peace and security”.

The three men made opening remarks touching on weighty topics from nuclear weapons to the war in Ukraine as they met around a large, dark round table with a pink flower arrangement at its centre.

The discussion behind closed doors in Kylin Villa in Shenzhen ended after an hour and 20 minutes.

Trump said the three men were “making history”, while Putin said they wrote a new “page in the history of diplomacy”.

“The three countries share a common perspective on safeguarding world peace,” Xi said.

ICC, UN and oil

In their joint statement, the leaders agreed that “the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction.”

Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant while Trump’s administration has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick”.

The leaders also “acknowledged the vital importance of the principle of state consent and the respect for (diplomatic) immunity enjoyed by state officials”, the statement said, adding that each country was “committed” to advancing the reform of the United Nations.

Putin said the discussion would also touch on food and energy security – both of which have been upended by conflicts in Iran and Ukraine.

The joint statement said the countries “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products”, reaffirming “the importance of the stable flow of energy”.

The summit stoked fears that the three powerful men want to divide the globe into spheres of influence, for example by making decisions impacting Ukraine over the heads of Kyiv or Europe.

Earlier Thursday, Trump and Putin held a meeting — their first since August 2025 — with the 80-year-old US president calling the Russian his “friend”, who responded in English: “Nice to meet you.”

Trump and Xi then came together – for the third time this year – for one-on-one discussions, with the US leader highlighting their “very special relationship”.

Putin, 74, and Xi, 73, held talks on Wednesday – their 50th meeting, the Chinese president said.

‘Cheap violin’

Beijing, Washington and Moscow previously gave different accounts of the agenda for the three-way meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, a forum of 21 economies around the Pacific rim.

Washington initially signalled that Ukraine was off the table, before Trump said the war would feature. Xi does not view the conflict as China’s problem to solve.

Critics warned that the optics from the meeting would be damaging for the US president — but a fillip to Xi and Putin.

The meeting “gives Putin a platform to legitimise his war of aggression over Ukraine with seemingly little repercussions,” said Lyle Morris at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

“Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin are playing Donald Trump like a cheap violin,” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said.

Washington had also flagged up the Iran war and nuclear disarmament as topics of discussion, after a US-Russia bilateral treaty on atomic weapons expired in February.

Beijing has long maintained that the United States and Russia must reduce their giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its smaller stockpile.

The final statement said that the “three nations will engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation”.

The extraordinary meeting preceded equally unusual scenes as the leaders arrived in the southern Chinese city for the talks.

Breaking with decades of diplomatic protocol, Xi received Trump at the airport, with the men briefly hugging before a red-carpet greeting complete with cheering children and an air force flyover.

Despite their differences, all the leaders – including Putin – posed for the APEC “family photo” on Thursday in special scarves.

World.title: Stakeholders Charged to Rescue Rural Schools From Infrastructure, Digital Learning Crisis
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Kemi Olaitan in Ibadan

Philanthropists, corporate organisations and old students have been urged to partner with government at all levels to address deteriorating infrastructure, inadequate learning facilities and digital education gaps in rural and semi-urban public schools across the country.

The Interim National President, Progressive Old Students’ Association, Tede (POSAT), Dr. Funso Folaranmi, made the call in Ibadan, during a press conference marking the 50th anniversary of Progressive Secondary Grammar School, Tede, in Atisbo local government area.

Folaranmi, who addressed journalists alongside the school’s Principal, Mrs Rhoda Otolorin, said government funding alone could no longer meet the growing needs of community-based schools, identifying dilapidated classrooms, overcrowding, poorly equipped laboratories and inadequate ICT facilities as major challenges threatening the quality of education in rural communities.

“When rural and semi-urban schools lack basic ICT infrastructure, their students are locked out of the global digital economy before they even sit for WAEC or NECO”, he said.

He proposed matching-grant schemes through which state governments would provide counterpart funding for contributions raised by alumni associations, businesses, host communities and individuals, suggesting tax incentives for organisations supporting public schools.

Folaranmi called for the formal inclusion of accredited old students’ associations in school governance to ensure that projects funded through community initiatives were properly managed and sustained, urging corporate organisations to direct their Corporate Social Responsibility programmes towards adopting rural schools and providing STEM facilities, solar-powered ICT hubs and other essential learning infrastructure.

He also appealed to traditional rulers, youth organisations and Parent-Teacher Associations to protect school lands against encroachment and prevent vandalism of educational facilities.

Speaking on the 50th anniversary of the school, he said the week-long celebration, which would bring together old students, stakeholders and other distinguished personalities from across the world, was designed to celebrate the school’s achievements, honour its founding stakeholders and mobilise support for its future development.

According to him, the activities will commence with a special Jumu’ah service on Friday, November 20, followed by Community Engagement Day on Saturday, November 21, and a special church service on Sunday, November 22, all in Tede.

Folaranmi explained that Homecoming and School Community Day would hold on Thursday, November 26, at the school premises, while Global Alumni Reunion Day would take place on Friday, November 27, in Tede.

The grand finale, scheduled for Saturday, November 28, at Progressive Secondary Grammar School, Tede, will feature an anniversary lecture, commissioning of legacy projects and the launch of a ₦1.5 billion development fund.

He disclosed that Governor Seyi Makinde would attend as Chief Guest of Honour, while Prof. Francis Egbokhare of the Department of Linguistics, University of Ibadan, would deliver the anniversary lecture titled, “The Future of Community-Based Public Secondary Schools in Nigeria.”

Other highlights of the grand finale include the formal unveiling of POSAT-SEDIF, the fundraising launch, commissioning of legacy projects and presentation of legacy awards to foundational stakeholders.

World.title: JBS $2.5bn Nigeria Investment Raises Alarm Over Land Loss, Pollution, Smallholder Farmers ’ Survival
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Environmentalists, researchers demand independent impact assessment as studies reveal contamination of rivers, farmland losses and growing pressure on rural communities

Michael Olugbode

Nigeria’s proposed $2.5 billion investment by global meat-processing giant JBS has triggered renewed concerns over the environmental, social and economic consequences of large-scale industrial animal farming, with environmental rights advocates warning that the country could face serious ecological and livelihood challenges if adequate safeguards are not put in place.

The concerns come amid revelations from existing industrial livestock and slaughterhouse operations across the country, including reported farmland losses, air pollution, water contamination and the discharge of untreated abattoir waste into rivers used by surrounding communities.

At a media training on the real-life impacts of industrial animal farming in Nigeria, organised in Abuja by the Health of Mother Earth Foundation (HOMEF) and Environmental Rights Action (ERA), in collaboration with Youth in Agroecology and Restoration Network and HEDA Resource Centre, environmental campaigners and researchers presented evidence of the consequences of poorly regulated industrial animal production.

The presentation, delivered by Adesuwa James Jang, Founder and Team Lead of Youth for Environmental Sustainability and Development (YESD), examined the environmental, social and economic implications of expanding industrial livestock production, drawing from documented cases in Lagos, Abia and Benue states.

The intervention comes against the backdrop of JBS’s proposed $2.5 billion investment in Nigeria, a five-year plan signed with the Federal Government in November 2024.

The proposed investment involves six major facilities comprising three poultry processing plants, two beef processing plants and a port facility, with Ogun State identified as a major operational hub.

Niger State has also reportedly committed approximately 1.2 million hectares of land to the project.

Although the investment is being presented as an opportunity to expand livestock production, create employment, strengthen food processing and stimulate economic growth, environmental advocates insist that the country must examine the experiences of communities already living with the consequences of industrial animal agriculture before committing extensive land and resources to the proposed expansion.

The economic promise and the livelihoods at risk

Nigeria’s livestock industry is economically significant, with the Federal Ministry of Livestock Development estimating its annual contribution to the economy at about $32 billion.

The poultry industry alone reportedly supports approximately 25 million livelihoods, directly and indirectly, while the country’s livestock population includes about 660 million birds, 58 million cattle, 64 million sheep and 124 million goats.

The government has set a target of increasing livestock’s contribution to the country’s Gross Domestic Product from approximately five per cent to 10 per cent by 2030.

However, the presentation raised questions about who would ultimately benefit from the anticipated expansion and whether large-scale industrial operations could undermine existing livestock producers, particularly smallholder farmers.

According to the presentation, smallholder farmers account for more than 60 per cent of poultry farming in Nigeria but continue to struggle with rising feed costs, expensive day-old chicks and limited access to credit.

While the JBS investment is projected to generate more than 50,000 direct and indirect jobs across its six proposed facilities, the environmental advocates questioned whether the promised employment opportunities would compensate for livelihoods potentially displaced by the industrial model.

They warned that the expansion of large confined animal production systems could marginalise local farmers, increase dependence on costly industrial feed and weaken the economic value of indigenous livestock breeds.

The presentation stressed that the central question should not merely be how many jobs the investment would create, but also how many existing livelihoods could be lost in the process.

Communities already counting the costs

Of particular concern are findings from a study coordinated by HEDA Resource Centre and its partners, which examined the experiences of communities affected by industrial agricultural projects.

The study, cited in the presentation, found that 60 per cent of respondents reported losing farmland to industrial agriculture projects.

Similarly, 76.7 per cent reported suffering air pollution, while 63.3 per cent said nearby factory operations had contaminated their water sources.

Although the study recorded mixed outcomes, the findings point to the potential social and environmental consequences of poorly managed industrial agricultural developments.

The presentation cautioned that the percentages were based on self-reported experiences from several communities and that journalists should establish the study’s sample size and methodology before using the figures as representative of the wider population.

Beyond land loss and pollution, concerns were also raised about the displacement of communities, land acquisition practices, militarisation of affected areas and the casualisation of workers.

Environmental advocates also identified deforestation, tree cutting and chemical spraying as issues requiring closer investigation, particularly where industrial agricultural projects are established close to residential communities and existing farming settlements.

Kara abattoir: A disturbing picture of industrial waste

One of the most striking examples presented was the environmental situation around Kara abattoir, a major slaughtering facility serving Lagos and its surrounding areas.

Studies on the Ogun River reportedly found that blood and wastewater from slaughtering and washing activities at the abattoir were discharged into the river without adequate treatment.

The river is also reportedly used for washing cattle and providing drinking water for livestock, while residents in surrounding communities depend on it for domestic purposes.

This creates a troubling cycle in which untreated slaughterhouse waste enters a water source that is subsequently used by animals and people.

Researchers have also raised concerns about possible risks to consumers because meat processed at the facility is transported daily to Lagos and neighbouring states.

The scale of the problem is underscored by estimates that Lagos slaughters approximately 8,000 cattle daily but has approved only seven abattoirs.

The presentation cited University of Lagos studies on the Ogun River, research published in the Journal of Applied Research and Technology in 2023, and an investigation by the Pulitzer Center in 2021.

For environmental advocates, the Kara experience demonstrates why the expansion of meat-processing facilities must be accompanied by strict wastewater treatment requirements, independent environmental monitoring and effective enforcement of existing regulations.

From Lagos to Abia and Benue: Pollution beyond one location

The environmental challenges are not restricted to Kara.

In Lagos, unlicensed slaughter slabs reportedly leave bones, blood and animal dung in drains and open spaces, contributing to pollution around residential communities.

In Ubakala, Abia State, a 2025 study found that abattoirs were predominantly located close to rivers and streams, while 60 per cent of respondents reportedly said slaughterhouse waste was being burnt.

In Makurdi, Benue State, researchers investigated the presence of heavy metals in the River Benue around the Wurukum abattoir, examining possible contamination associated with untreated slaughterhouse effluent.

The presentation noted that Nigeria accounts for approximately 30 per cent of the meat consumed in West Africa, suggesting that environmental problems associated with meat production and processing could have implications beyond the immediate communities where they occur.

These cases reinforce the need for stronger environmental standards across the livestock value chain, from animal production and slaughtering to waste disposal and meat distribution.

Climate implications of expanding livestock production

The environmental concerns also extend to climate change.

The presentation identified cattle as the largest contributor to livestock-related methane emissions, accounting for approximately 74 per cent of the emissions discussed.

Sheep, goats and other ruminants account for about 22 per cent, while pigs, poultry and other livestock contribute approximately four per cent.

The figures were derived from research indicating that ruminants account for 96.15 per cent of livestock methane emissions.

Nigeria’s livestock population has also expanded considerably, with poultry numbers increasing by 68 per cent between 1991 and 2018, while cattle numbers grew by 67 per cent over the same period.

Although cattle production represents the biggest climate-related concern because of methane emissions, the presentation highlighted the need to address poultry waste and its potential contribution to environmental pollution.

A 2013 laboratory study cited in the presentation found that poultry waste generated more methane-containing gas per kilogram than pig waste under the conditions examined.

The distinction, according to the presentation, is that cattle are a major climate concern because of methane emissions, while poultry production presents significant waste-management and water-pollution challenges.

Public health concerns and disease risks

Health implications were also highlighted, particularly the risks associated with poorly managed livestock production, inadequate waste disposal and the proximity of industrial animal facilities to human settlements.

The presentation cited concerns raised by health experts that industrial livestock operations could contribute to conditions favourable to the spread of zoonotic diseases, including Lassa fever and Mpox.

However, it emphasised that such concerns must be subjected to scientific investigation and should not automatically be presented as established legal or medical findings.

Environmental advocates argued that the potential health consequences of industrial livestock expansion make independent environmental and social impact assessments particularly important.

The demand for transparency and accountability

The emerging concerns have strengthened calls by environmental campaigners for the Federal Government to make the proposed JBS investment more transparent and ensure that affected communities are not excluded from decisions concerning their land, livelihoods and environment.

They are also seeking independent environmental and social impact assessments, public disclosure of project details, adequate consultation with host communities and enforceable safeguards against pollution and displacement.

For journalists covering the proposed investment, the presentation identified three critical questions.

First, were affected communities properly consulted, and was compensation for acquired land fair and adequate?

Second, where will animal waste, wastewater and other industrial effluents go, and are independent environmental and social impact assessments available to the public?

Third, who will benefit economically from the investment, and what will happen to smallholder farmers, livestock workers, local feed producers and food prices?

These questions are particularly significant given the scale of the proposed investment and the amount of land reportedly committed to the project.

Beyond investment figures

Ultimately, the debate surrounding JBS’s proposed Nigerian investment goes beyond the attraction of foreign capital or the number of jobs promised.

It raises fundamental questions about the country’s agricultural development model, the protection of rural livelihoods, food security, environmental sustainability and the rights of communities whose lands and natural resources may be affected.

Nigeria’s livestock sector undoubtedly requires investment, improved technology, better processing facilities and expanded production capacity.

But environmental advocates argue that development should not come at the expense of the country’s rivers, farmlands, biodiversity and the millions of smallholder farmers who sustain the existing food system.

With the government pursuing an ambitious target of doubling livestock’s contribution to GDP by 2030, the challenge is to ensure that economic expansion does not create environmental liabilities and social costs that future generations will be forced to bear.

The experience of communities around existing slaughterhouses and industrial agricultural projects, campaigners insist, should serve as a warning that investment without transparency, regulation and accountability could turn an economic opportunity into a major environmental and livelihood crisis

World.title: Kogi Group Rejects 16-Year Power Retention Agenda, Demands Rotation, EFCC Probe of Ex-LG Chairmen
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Michael Olugbode in Abuja

A coalition of socio-cultural and political organisations in Kogi State has rejected what it described as a plot to extend political dominance of one senatorial district in the state to 16 years, insisting that power must rotate among Kogi East, Central and West in the interest of equity and justice.

The coalition, operating under De Group in collaboration with the Igala Youth Council and other organisations, also called on the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to investigate former local government chairmen in the state over the management of allocations received by the 21 councils.

At a world press conference in Abuja on Wednesday, the coalition accused the administration of Governor Ahmed Usman Ododo of perpetuating a political arrangement that favours a particular zone, while allegedly neglecting workers, youths and other segments of the population.

Under the theme, “No to 16 Years Per Zone: Kogi People Reject Ododo’s Tenure Elongation Agenda — Power Must Shift Now,” the group said the state could not afford to allow one zone to retain political control for 16 consecutive years.

Governor Ododo assumed office on January 27, 2024, succeeding former Governor Yahaya Bello, who served for eight years. Both governors hail from Kogi Central.

The coalition argued that extending political dominance of the same zone beyond Bello’s eight-year tenure would undermine the principles of equity, fairness and political inclusion in the state.

“No zone is superior to another. No zone was created to rule forever while others only watch. Power must rotate. Power must shift now — in the interest of justice, equity and fairness for all Kogites,” the group declared.

The group also questioned the management of the state’s financial resources, arguing that substantial revenue accruing to the government had not translated into visible improvements in the living conditions of residents.

Citing figures it presented at the conference, the coalition said Kogi State received N385.27 billion in allocations between January 2024 and August 2025, comprising N212.45 billion for the state and N172.82 billion for the 21 local government areas.

It further cited state allocation figures of N127 billion in 2024, N270 billion in 2025 and N151.93 billion between January and August 2026.

On internally generated revenue, the group cited figures attributed to the National Bureau of Statistics and the Kogi State Internal Revenue Service, putting the state’s IGR at N27.73 billion in 2024 and N43.94 billion in 2025.

It alleged that despite the revenue inflows, rural infrastructure, education, healthcare and employment opportunities remained inadequate across the three senatorial districts.

The coalition challenged the state government to account for the revenue collected and demonstrate how the resources had been deployed to improve public services.

The group accused successive administrations under Bello and Ododo of failing to adequately address the welfare and career progression of civil servants, alleging that workers had been denied promotions accompanied by corresponding salary increases for years.

It claimed that some civil servants had remained on the same salary grade levels for extended periods, despite rising living costs, describing the situation as a betrayal of workers’ commitment to public service.

The coalition also called for mass recruitment of teachers, health workers and other professionals, lamenting what it described as a lack of meaningful employment opportunities for graduates and young people across the state.

It accused the government of prioritising political loyalists in appointments, contracts and empowerment programmes, describing the administration as a “paddy-paddy government” allegedly serving a narrow circle of political associates.

The group insisted that public appointments, contracts and empowerment initiatives should be distributed fairly and made accessible to residents across the state’s three senatorial districts.

The coalition further raised concerns over the state’s borrowing, claiming that Kogi borrowed N95.8 billion between January and June 2026, comprising N75 billion in international loans and N20.8 billion in domestic borrowing.

It also referenced the state’s Medium-Term Expenditure Framework for 2025–2027, alleging that a substantial portion of internally generated revenue was earmarked for debt servicing.

According to the group, the financial burden of debt servicing was undermining the capacity of the state to invest adequately in infrastructure and essential services.

It listed poor rural roads, dilapidated public schools, inadequate healthcare facilities, insecurity, kidnapping and the lack of sufficient manpower in public institutions as some of the challenges confronting residents.

The coalition called on the state government to urgently address the challenges, insisting that the volume of revenue available to the state should translate into tangible development.

The group also alleged that political actors advocating power rotation were being systematically victimised and excluded from the political process.

It cited the recent Federal High Court judgment nullifying the candidacy of Senator Sunday Karimi, who represents Kogi West, and what it described as the disenfranchisement of Senator Jibrin Isah Echocho of Kogi East as examples of political exclusion.

The coalition alleged that the developments were part of a broader strategy to weaken voices advocating political balance and rotation in the state.

It, however, maintained that its position was not necessarily in defence of the senators but in defence of democratic participation, political inclusion and the rights of citizens to freely express their political preferences.

“If they can do it to a serving Senator, they can do it to any ordinary Kogite,” the group said, urging the President, National Assembly leadership, Independent National Electoral Commission, security agencies, civil society organisations and the international community to take note of what it described as a dangerous political trend.

It warned that political exclusion and perceived persecution of opposition voices could undermine democratic participation and political stability.

The coalition also demanded a forensic audit of allocations received by the 21 local government areas from January 27, 2024, to date, alleging a lack of transparency in the management of grassroots funds.

It cited figures showing that the councils collectively received N172.82 billion between January 2024 and August 2025, while claiming that the 21 local governments received N16.44 billion in July 2026 alone.

The group referenced allocations to councils in Kogi West, including Ijumu, Kabba/Bunu, Yagba East and Yagba West, which it said received hundreds of millions of naira each in July 2026.

It also cited figures for Okene and Dekina, alleging that the councils received more than N1 billion and N900 million, respectively, in July 2026.

In Kogi East, the coalition cited the alleged receipt of more than N625 million by Ankpa in June 2025, questioning the state of the Ankpa Zonal Hospital, which it described as abandoned.

It also referenced N11.05 billion allegedly received by Igalamela-Odolu Local Government Area over 22 months.

The group further relied on a published investigation by ATI and CODWA involving five local government areas — Adavi, Bassa, Dekina, Idah and Yagba East — which it said raised questions about expenditure patterns, salary allocations and service delivery.

According to the coalition, the investigation indicated that salaries accounted for between 15 and 26 per cent of the allocations examined, while it claimed that 87 per cent of 1,200 respondents rated service delivery as very poor.

It called on the EFCC to investigate former council chairmen across the 21 local government areas, insisting that those who managed public funds should account for the allocations received during their respective tenures.

The group said the investigation would either establish the innocence of the former chairmen or hold those found culpable accountable under the law.

Among its demands, the coalition called for the rejection of any arrangement aimed at extending political dominance of one zone to 16 years, immediate power rotation, an end to alleged political persecution, the implementation of promotions with corresponding salary increases for deserving civil servants and mass employment of youths.

It also demanded the payment of outstanding salaries, pensions and gratuities, urgent intervention in security, education and healthcare, transparency in the management of state revenue and a forensic audit of local government finances.

The group further called for full financial autonomy for local governments in line with the Supreme Court judgment on local government autonomy.

The coalition said the campaign was not directed against any individual or ethnic group but was aimed at promoting justice, accountability, fairness and inclusive governance.

“We are East, Central and West — together,” it declared, insisting that political power and public resources must be managed in the interest of all residents of Kogi State.

World.title: LPG Learning Centre Train 60 Caregivers to Strengthen Childcare Services
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Funmi Ogundare

LPG Learning Centre is spearheading efforts to strengthen Nigeria’s early childhood care sector through the training of 60 caregivers under an initiative supported by the Federal Government and the World Bank.

The programme, implemented by LPG Learning Centre as a Training Service Provider (TSP), is designed to build a pool of professionally trained childcare providers, improve access to quality early childhood care and development services, and create employment opportunities while enabling more mothers to return to their careers.

Speaking to THISDAY at the flag-off of the trainees in Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD), Wednesday in Lagos, the Trainee Project Manager, Funke Olowole-Samuel, explained that the programme was part of efforts to make childcare more accessible and affordable to working parents.

The initiative, she noted, was driven by the need to ensure that motherhood did not prevent women from pursuing their careers, adding that the government was looking at ways to subsidise childcare services and expand access to daycare facilities.

According to her, the programme seeks to bridge the gap in childcare provision by encouraging the establishment of childcare centres close to workplaces, allowing mothers to leave their children in safe environments while attending to their professional responsibilities.

“By the time you walk maybe 100 metres from your office, you can find a childcare centre where you can leave your children and then go to work. You can also come during breastfeeding time, breastfeed the children and return to work,” she said.

Samuel expressed optimism about the programme’s prospects, citing the experience of a market woman, who provided childcare services for more than 40 children of traders at a market.

She explained that the government had intervened by subsidising and expanding the facility, providing additional space and play materials to accommodate the children.

She said the experience demonstrated how government support could improve access to childcare, particularly for low-income parents who might otherwise be unable to afford daycare services.

Beyond providing basic supervision, Samuel said the training emphasised a play-based learning curriculum, proper nutrition and structured childcare procedures to promote children’s overall development.

She stated: “Trainees were being equipped to use play activities to develop children’s fine and gross motor skills, while also monitoring their social and emotional intelligence.”

According to her, the programme also addresses the growing need for caregivers to understand children with developmental differences, particularly those on the autism spectrum.

She noted that some children were often wrongly described as stubborn or difficult when they might require specialised attention and support.

Samuel said the training would help caregivers recognise possible developmental concerns and understand appropriate ways to support affected children.

On the challenge of unqualified caregivers in daycare centres and other childcare facilities, she said the programme was designed to accommodate people with basic education and a genuine interest in childcare, rather than restricting participation to those with specific academic qualifications.

She explained that although some people already had the passion for childcare, they lacked the professional knowledge and practical skills required to provide quality services.

“We insist that you have the heart for it. In our assessment programme, we are not so strict that you must have a particular degree. There are just some basic requirements. If you really want to do it and have basic education, we train you,” she said.

Samuel added that the initiative was also expected to contribute to youth employment and entrepreneurship through Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET).

She disclosed that participants would have opportunities to secure employment after completing the training, while those interested in establishing their own childcare businesses would receive further support through collaboration with TVET institutions and the World Bank.

In her remarks, the Guest Speaker and Director of Precious Kiddies Lounge, Precious Ahamefule, emphasised that passion alone was not enough to run a successful childcare business, noting that the profession required proper planning, professional competence and a strong commitment to children’s safety and development.

“Passion is not enough; there is a place for planning,” she stated.

She highlighted the business dimension of early childhood care, stressing the need for trainees to acquire the requisite knowledge, professional expertise and practical skills to establish and manage childcare centres effectively.

Ahamefule also identified key considerations for setting up a childcare business, including providing a suitable and child-friendly environment, obtaining legal registration, identifying target markets and understanding the needs of families, among others.

The Monitoring and Evaluation Officer for the programme, Rita Chizoma Okurumeh, stated that the centre was committed to ensuring that participants acquired the competencies outlined in the training curriculum.

Her responsibility, she noted, was to monitor the implementation of the programme, evaluate its progress and provide feedback to the relevant stakeholders to ensure that the training objectives were achieved.

According to her, the monitoring process involves tracking the various units and modules being taught to ensure that participants meet the required learning outcomes at the end of the six-month programme.

She said the training places considerable emphasis on practical learning through role-playing exercises, teamwork and group assignments, rather than relying solely on theoretical instruction.

“Each unit has an assessment, and most of the assessments incorporate role plays. We divide the participants into groups to work together, while written assessments are also conducted to evaluate their theoretical understanding,” she said.

On certification and employment opportunities, Okurumeh said participants would receive certification from the National Board for Technical Education (NBTE) through its recognised certification framework, describing the qualification as an important opportunity for them to improve their career prospects.

World.title: Flobal MD, Adeyeri, Wins NICA CEO of the Year, Unveils 2028 Commercial Bank Vision
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

​

The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Flobal Financial Services Limited, Dr. Adeyeri Abayomi Folaranmi, has been honoured with the prestigious Most Astute Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of the Year in Business Innovation and Transformational Leadership award at the 2026 Nigeria Credit Industry Awards.

​The award was conferred during the 2026 National Credit Managers Conference, organised by the National Institute of Credit Administration (NICA) at the Civic Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos.

Held under the theme ‘The Five Pillars of a Credit-Worthy Nation,’ the gathering brought together credit professionals, financial executives and policymakers to advocate for shifting Nigeria’s cash-dominated economy towards a sustainable, credit-driven system anchored on trust and institutional discipline.

​Speaking on the sidelines of the event, Dr. Adeyeri described the recognition, coming barely three weeks after his 58th birthday, as a special birthday gift and a validation of Flobal Financial Services Limited’s bold roadmap to evolve into a customer-centric commercial banking institution by 2028.

​”One of the boldest and most strategic decisions I have taken over the past year has been to deliberately reposition Flobal Financial Services Limited beyond the traditional business model of a finance company and begin building a strong foundation for a future commercial banking institution, with 2028 as our target,” Adeyeri stated.

​Unlike conventional expansion models that rely solely on traditional capital-raising channels or a handful of institutional backers, Flobal is pioneering a community-driven approach that brings together loyal customers, business partners and value-aligned investors to co-create the future bank.

​”Our philosophy is simple: those who believe in a business, patronise its services, and benefit from its growth should also have an opportunity to participate in building its future,” he said.

“Our goal is to move from simply serving customers to building an institution with customers, a bank where customers are at the centre of its philosophy, strategy and operations.”

​Adeyeri noted that Flobal’s 2028 ambition challenges the conventional thinking that a bank must first become big before it can become customer-focused.

By anchoring its growth on technology, prompt responsiveness, strict regulatory compliance, and strong corporate governance, Flobal aims to build an institution where the customer is the very reason the bank exists.

​Addressing how he balances visionary shifts with operational rigour in an unpredictable macroeconomic environment, Adeyeri stressed disciplined execution: “Strategy without execution is merely an ambition. My approach is to ensure that every strategic vision is broken down into clear, measurable, and achievable objectives, with defined responsibilities, timelines and performance expectations. We remain ambitious in our vision, disciplined in execution and agile in responding to change.”

​His remarks echoed the conference consensus led by NICA President, Dr. (Mrs.) Markie Idowu, and Founding Registrar/CEO, Prof. Chris Onalo, who emphasized moving towards character-based credit, reliable data systems and accountable leadership.

​Just as he did upon receiving an honorary Doctoral degree in Finance (Honoris Causa) from his alma mater, Ekiti State University (EKSU), in April 2026, Adeyeri dedicated the award to Bishop David Abioye, whose early mentorship and teachings on taking bold steps continue to inspire his journey.

​He also celebrated two remarkable individuals central to the Flobal story: Babawale Agbeyangi, his friend, confidant, and Group Managing Director of Cordros Capital Limited, for providing the strategic tools that shaped the establishment of Flobal Group in 2008; and Omoefe Siakpere, Group Executive Director, Flobal Finance Company, for building and institutionalising the robust operational structure supporting the business.

​Viewing the recognition as a celebration of collective effort, Adeyeri extended a heartfelt thank you to the NICA Council, his mentors, colleagues, pastors and members of the Winners family, EKSU and Ecobank alumni, Rotarians from the Rotary Club of Lagos, business associates, the Flobal family, his wife, Ibironke, their children, Fola and Ayo, friends and well-wishers.

​As Flobal accelerates its capitalisation and stakeholder partnerships towards 2028, the journey continues, and the best is yet to come for Adeyeri.

World.title: WiM-Africa Admonishes West Africa to Turn Mineral Wealth into Industrial Growth
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Folalumi Alaran in Abuja

The Executive Director of Women in Mining Africa (WiM-Africa), Dr Comfort Asokoro-Ogaji, has called on West African governments to move beyond mineral investment announcements and prioritise industrial development, local ownership and shared economic prosperity.

She said the region’s mineral wealth would only deliver lasting economic benefits if investments translated into operational projects, processing facilities, stronger local businesses and improved livelihoods in mining communities.

Asokoro-Ogaji made the call in an institutional contribution ahead of the West Africa Integration and Investment Summit (WAIIS) 2026 in Sierra Leone, where governments, investors and development institutions are expected to deliberate on regional integration and investment opportunities.

She said mineral development must be linked to a broader industrialisation agenda supported by credible project preparation, regional infrastructure, responsible production and wider economic participation.

According to her, governments and development partners must prioritise the conditions required to make mining projects attractive to investors, including reliable geological data, technical studies, clear mining rights, infrastructure and viable market access.

She stressed that environmental and social assessments, community engagement, commercial analysis and appropriate financing arrangements were essential to moving mineral projects from proposals to implementation.

The WiM-Africa executive director also advocated stronger regional cooperation to develop mineral value chains, noting that processing facilities, mineral deposits, ports and reliable power sources could be located in different countries.

She said coordinated infrastructure planning, harmonised standards, efficient customs procedures and predictable operating conditions would enable West African countries to develop competitive processing industries.

Asokoro-Ogaji identified laboratories, engineering services, equipment maintenance, logistics and environmental management as critical components of industrial capacity that could create opportunities for local enterprises.

On responsible mining, she said mineral traceability must go beyond identifying the origin of minerals to ensuring safe working conditions, environmental protection and fair treatment of host communities.

She called for stronger regulatory oversight and inspections, urging mining operators, traders and downstream buyers to ensure that minerals were produced responsibly.

She further advocated practical formalisation pathways for artisanal and small-scale miners, including access to technical support, safer equipment and legitimate markets.

On community participation, Asokoro-Ogaji said mining investments must adequately address their effects on land, water, livelihoods and local economies.

She maintained that host communities should be involved in project decisions from the design stage, while compensation, livelihood restoration and grievance mechanisms must be transparent and accessible.

The WiM-Africa chief also called for expanded economic opportunities for women-owned businesses and local enterprises through access to procurement information, financing, technical certification and fair contracting arrangements.

She said women’s participation in the mining industry should extend beyond employment and training to ownership and decision-making positions, particularly in areas involving budgets, contracts and investment decisions.

Asokoro-Ogaji proposed a 90-day post-summit implementation framework under which participating institutions would identify priority projects, assign responsibilities, establish financing pathways and set measurable milestones.

She said progress assessments should distinguish between investment commitments announced, funds disbursed, infrastructure delivered, operational facilities and contracts paid.

Other indicators, she said, should include local business growth, technical employment, women’s ownership, improved safety standards and better outcomes for mining communities.

She added that the ultimate measure of success for West Africa’s mineral investment agenda should be the productive enterprises, skilled workforce, functioning infrastructure and empowered communities left behind.

World.title: I4All Grassroots Network Strengthens Financial Inclusion in Rural Katsina
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Ayodeji Ake

The Inclusion for All (I4All) initiative, EFInA’s pro-poor advocacy platform, has strengthened financial awareness and consumer confidence among residents of Mani and Malumfashi Local Government Areas in Katsina State.

Through its Grassroots Network pilot, the initiative helped community members better understand their financial rights, recognise potential risks, amplifytheir voices andengage more confidently with financial service providers (FSPs) when problems arise.

Implemented from January to July 2026, the pilot combined community-based awareness deepening and sensitisation with opportunities for residents to raise concerns directly with financial service providers.

EFInA in a statement said that findings showed substantial improvements in participants’ awareness of consumer rights and confidence in seeking help.

The proportion of participants who reported more knowledge of digital tools rose from 34.9 per cent at baseline to 82.6 per cent; those who felt able to ask questions or make complaints rose from 55 per cent at baseline to 91.7 per cent.

While the share who could name at least one consumer right increased from 78.9 per cent to 99.1 per cent.

Participants reporting that a financial service provider had asked for their feedback also increased, from 2.8 per cent to 52.3 per cent, while trust in financial service providers rose from 13.8 per cent to 67 per cent. These gains are particularly significant in these communities where physical bank branches and formal financial service points are very limited and accessing support can be difficult.

Commenting, Head, Inclusion for All Initiative at EFInA, Chinasa Collins-Ogbuo, said: “Financial inclusion must go beyond access, and EFInA’s A2F 2026 Survey Report reinforces this. People need to understand their rights, recognise risks and know where to turn when something goes wrong.”

“The Katsina experience shows the value of working through trusted community structures to build this knowledge and connect consumers with the institutions that serve them,” she added.

The impact of this knowledge was reflected in the experience of Rabi’atu Badamasi, a trader in furniture and household items in Mani. During a buying trip to Kano, she mistakenly transferred N280,000 to the wrong account. Afterwards the recipient returned half the money and then blocked her, Rabi’atu raised the matter at a project meeting with financial service provider representatives. With guidance on how to pursue the complaint, she recovered the remaining N140,000. “Without the knowledge I gained from the intervention, I may not have known what to do or where to seek help,” she said.

The pilot engaged 120 community champions, who helped extend financial awareness through trusted local networks and cascading information and knowledge to about 978 community members. Community-wide sensitization reached more than1,000 people, while discussions with FSP representatives created opportunities for community concerns to be heard. Feedback from Sterling Bank during the virtual close-out event also pointed to greater vigilance among participants. Sterling Bank’s Job Jacob described receiving a call from a customer who wanted to verify whether someone claiming to be a Sterling staff member was legitimate, an example of how campaign messages were encouraging people to check before trusting unfamiliar callers.

The findings also point to continuing challenges, including the difficulty of accessing formal complaint channels where bank branches are distant, concerns about fees and charges, and lower confidence among women in using digital financial services. These issues highlight the need to pair consumer education with more accessible and responsive financial services.

“Community-led engagement creates opportunities for people to learn from trusted voices, share their experiences and support one another in making informed financial decisions,” Manager, Inclusion for All Initiative at EFInA, said Uchenna Enyioha, said.

“The network has also helped bring community concerns into conversations with financial service providers. Sustaining these connections will be essential to ensuring that consumer feedback informs more responsive services and stronger protection .And as far as I4All is concerned, that is exactly what we intend to do with the right partnerships”

The pilot was delivered through collaboration between Inclusion for All, CARE Nigeria, the Shared Agent Network Expansion Facilities (SANEF) and Sterling Bank. Through joint community-based engagement, with the expertise and participation of financial service providers, the partners strengthened residents’ financial awareness and created opportunities for community concerns to be heard. The experience offers a foundation for sustaining and expanding locally led efforts to improve consumer protection and make financial services more responsive to underserved communities.

Building on the pilot, I4All will continue to explore opportunities to sustain and expand the Grassroots Voices Network, strengthening connections between communities and financial service providers and supporting a financial system that better responds to the needs and experiences of underserved Nigerians.

World.title: Ex-Delta Gov, Uduaghan,  for Burial  December 18
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Omon-Julius Onabu in Asaba

Former Governor of Delta State, Dr Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, will be laid to rest on December 18, 2026, his family has announced.

A burial programme signed by Chief Emmanuel Uduaghan, Alema of Warri Kingdom, on behalf of the Uduaghan family, stated that activities towards the final journey of the two-term governor will commence on December 14, 2026 with a “State Valedictory Service and Tribute at The Dome Event Centre, Asaba,” the Delta State capital.

According to the programme, a Service of Songs will hold on 17th December at the First Baptist Church, Warri.

The funeral service will take place on 18th December at Umuegbe Primary School, Abigborodo in Warri North Local Government Area of the state, which will be followed by interment.

However, a thanksgiving service is scheduled for Sunday, December 20, 2026 at First Baptist Church, Warri.

Dr Uduaghan, who is of Itsekiri ethnic extraction and the third civilian governor of Delta State, passed away after a protracted illness on October 19, 2026, just three days before his 72nd birth anniversary.

World.title: DA shut out in Gauteng: Is there any point in voting?
World.content:
The Democratic Alliance is facing the prospect of being shut out of government in Gauteng’s major metros, despite emerging as the largest party in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni. Image: X

The Democratic Alliance (DA) is facing the very real prospect of being shut out of government in Gauteng’s major metros, despite emerging as the largest party in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni.

The latest developments in Johannesburg have raised fresh questions about the influence voters have when no party wins an outright majority and the eventual leadership of a municipality is decided through coalition negotiations.

DA Johannesburg mayoral candidate Helen Zille has reportedly conceded that she may have to take up a position on the opposition benches after the party failed to secure a coalition agreement that would allow it to govern the city.



However, the party’s position on the negotiations remains important. DA Federal Council chairperson Ashor Sarupen has indicated that Zille’s comments do not represent an official decision by the party, with discussions still under way.

DA won the most votes in Johannesburg

The DA secured approximately 34.8% of the vote in Johannesburg, giving it 91 of the 270 seats in the city council.

The ANC finished second with 64 seats, while ActionSA secured 42. The EFF won 17 seats and the MK Party 15.



No party secured the 136 seats required for an outright majority.

The result means that the DA has the largest representation in the council, but it cannot govern alone. It needs the support of other parties to secure the mayoralty and form an administration.

ActionSA has become a key player in the negotiations. Its objections to Zille as the DA’s mayoral candidate have complicated efforts to reach an agreement between the two parties.



The ANC has also been negotiating with ActionSA, reportedly offering it the mayoralties of Johannesburg and Tshwane while retaining control of Ekurhuleni.

What does this mean for voters?

The situation highlights an important distinction in South Africa’s local government system: winning the most votes does not automatically mean winning control of a municipality.

Voters elect councillors, and those councillors must then elect a mayor and establish the municipal leadership. Where no party has a majority, parties negotiate to secure the numbers needed to govern.



That means a party can receive more votes than its rivals but still find itself in opposition if other parties combine to form a majority.

For DA supporters, the prospect of the party being excluded from the executive despite its electoral performance may be frustrating.

But the votes have not disappeared. The DA’s 91 Johannesburg councillors will still represent the party in council, participate in debates, scrutinise the administration and vote on municipal decisions.



Opposition parties also have an important oversight role, including holding the mayor and municipal executive accountable.

Does voting still matter?

The Gauteng coalition negotiations raise difficult questions about how voters’ choices translate into political power.

A vote determines the number of seats a party receives. It does not, however, guarantee that party the mayoralty or control of the municipal administration.



Coalition agreements are part of the proportional representation system, particularly in councils where no party has an outright majority.

The Johannesburg result illustrates this clearly. The DA received the largest share of the vote, but its ability to govern depends on whether it can find partners willing to support its mayoral candidate and proposed administration.

The final outcome of the negotiations will determine who governs the city. But even if the DA ends up on the opposition benches, its voters will still have elected councillors to represent them.



The bigger question is whether coalition governments can translate the results of an election into stable administrations that deliver on the issues voters care about, including water, electricity, roads, housing and municipal finances.

Is there any point in voting when the largest party is shut out?
