World.title: The unusual Kruger viewpoint where three countries meet
World.content:
The Limpopo River at the border between South Africa, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. Image: Arthur Chapman / Flickr

Deep in the northern reaches of the Kruger National Park is a place with an unusual geographical location and an even more colourful history.

Known as Crooks’ Corner, the remote viewpoint sits at the confluence of the Limpopo and Luvuvhu rivers, where South Africa meets Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

Today, it is a scenic spot for visitors exploring the Pafuri region. However, its name comes from a time when the area was known as a refuge for fugitives, smugglers and other people seeking to evade the law.



Where exactly is Crooks’ Corner?

Crooks’ Corner is located in the far north-eastern section of Kruger, in the Pafuri area.

It’s positioned where the Luvuvhu River flows into the Limpopo River. Across the water are Mozambique and Zimbabwe, making it possible to look towards two neighbouring countries without leaving South Africa.

The area forms part of a diverse landscape of riverine forests, floodplains, fever trees, palm-lined waterways and baobab-covered ridges.



It’s also an important ecological area, with the nearby Makuleke Wetlands recognised as a Ramsar wetland site.

BUT why is it called Crooks’ Corner?

The name dates back to the early 20th century, when the area was used by people attempting to escape law enforcement.

The remote location and its position near three territories made it particularly useful to fugitives.



At the time, the region bordered the Transvaal, Southern Rhodesia and Portuguese East Africa, which are now South Africa, Zimbabwe and Mozambique respectively.

Ivory poachers, gunrunners and labour recruiters were among those associated with the area.

People could cross into a neighbouring territory to avoid authorities pursuing them from another jurisdiction. The location became notorious as a place where those on the run could disappear across a border.



One story associated with Crooks’ Corner describes fugitives standing on a boundary marker at the river confluence, effectively placing themselves in a disputed or awkward position for law enforcement.

The area’s reputation eventually gave it the name it still carries today.

Today, Crooks’ Corner is better known for its scenery, birdlife and wildlife than its criminal past.



The viewpoint offers a look across the rivers towards the neighbouring countries, while the surrounding Pafuri landscape is one of Kruger’s most distinctive areas.

Visitors exploring the region may encounter:

Fever tree forests: Tall trees with distinctive pale trunks grow along the river systems.

Tall trees with distinctive pale trunks grow along the river systems. Baobabs: The rocky ridges and surrounding landscape are dotted with these iconic trees.

The rocky ridges and surrounding landscape are dotted with these iconic trees. Riverine forests: The waterways support dense vegetation and a variety of bird species.

The waterways support dense vegetation and a variety of bird species. Wetlands and floodplains: The area provides important habitat for wildlife and birds.

The area provides important habitat for wildlife and birds. Wildlife: Elephants, zebra, kudu, nyala and other species occur in the wider Pafuri region.

The northern part of Kruger is also known for its bird diversity, making the area particularly appealing to birdwatchers.



How to visit Crooks’ Corner

Crooks’ Corner can be reached through the Pafuri area in northern Kruger.

Visitors can enter through Pafuri Gate for a day visit, while Punda Maria Rest Camp is one of the accommodation options to consider when exploring the northern section of the park.

The route to the viewpoint follows the S63, but visitors should check current road conditions and access arrangements with SANParks before setting out.



This is particularly important following seasonal flooding or heavy rainfall, which can affect roads in the far north.

The journey is best treated as part of a wider Pafuri outing rather than a quick detour. Visitors should allow enough time for the drive, wildlife viewing and the return journey before the gates close.

World.title: Good news for Kruger visitors as popular rest camp gate reopens
World.content:
A temporary access arrangement at one of Kruger's busiest rest camps is coming to an end this week. Image: file

Visitors to Kruger National Park will once again be able to use the Skukuza Rest Camp Gate from Friday, 20 November 2026, following the completion of structural repairs.

South African National Parks (SANParks) confirmed that the gate would reopen after repair work was successfully completed.

The work was carried out to ensure the continued safety, functionality and convenience of access for guests, visitors and operational staff at one of the park’s busiest rest camps.



Temporary access arrangements at Kruger come to an end

During the repair period, visitors had to follow temporary directional signage and alternative access arrangements to enter and exit the rest camp.

SANParks thanked guests, tour operators, staff and other stakeholders for their patience and cooperation while the work was underway.

The organisation also praised visitors for following the temporary traffic arrangements, saying their cooperation helped minimise disruptions and maintain road safety during construction.



With the repairs now complete, the reopening will restore normal access through the Skukuza Rest Camp Gate from Friday.

The update comes ahead of the busy festive season, when Kruger National Park attracts large numbers of local and international visitors.

World.title: How much should you pay your domestic worker for their Christmas bonus?
World.content:
Christmas bonuses for domestic workers in SA are customary, but are they compulsory? Image: Flickr

For many South African households, December comes with an unwritten tradition: giving domestic workers and cleaners a little something extra for Christmas.

Whether it’s a cash bonus, a grocery hamper or both, the gesture has become commonplace. But how much is enough? And what does the law say?

Unfortunately, there is no prescribed amount. However, there are some useful guidelines employers can follow…



Christmas bonus: What does the law say?

Domestic workers in South Africa are covered by the Basic Conditions of Employment Act (BCEA), the National Minimum Wage (NMW) Act and Sectoral Determination 7, which specifically regulates the domestic-worker sector.

However, none of these establishes a compulsory Christmas bonus or a minimum amount that employers must pay.

According to Izwi’s Employing a Domestic Worker: A Legal and Practical Guide, published with the Socio-Economic Rights Institute (SERI), “An employer is not obligated to provide a domestic worker with a bonus at the end of the year.”

However, the guide acknowledges that “domestic workers have come to expect a bonus” because it is widely practised by South African employers.

It also states that “bonuses are generally based on the employee’s performance during the year and whether the employer can afford to provide them with a bonus.”

There is an important caveat. Labour Guide South Africa notes that consistently paying a bonus over several years can establish a condition of employment through what is known as ‘custom and practice.’



This could make its continued payment contractually enforceable, and employers should avoid suddenly withdrawing an expected payment without a discussion.

Also, grocery hampers and other gifts are welcome gestures, but they cannot replace wages owed to an employee. In fact, this is backed by Section 5 of the NMW Act.

How much is your ‘Christmas bonsela’ for your domestic worker?

There is no official industry benchmark or recommended amount for Christmas bonuses, but a useful starting point is to base the bonus on your domestic’s normal earnings.

For full-time employees, one possible reference point is the equivalent of a 13th cheque, or an additional month’s salary. This is a generous option for households that can afford it.

However, it is not a statutory entitlement or a prescribed domestic-worker bonus.

Many South Africans also employ domestic workers on a part-time basis, paying them a daily rate for one or two days a week.

A more practical approach then is to consider your domestic worker’s usual daily earnings and the number of days they work for you.

For example, someone earning R400 per day/ week could receive a week’s wages (R400) as a modest bonus, R800 for two weeks’ pay, or more if the household can afford it.

A Useful Guide:

One week’s salary: A modest Christmas bonus, particularly for households with tighter budgets or where the employment relationship began during the year.

A modest Christmas bonus, particularly for households with tighter budgets or where the employment relationship began during the year. Half a month’s salary: A more substantial gesture and a useful middle-ground benchmark.

A more substantial gesture and a useful middle-ground benchmark. A full month’s salary: The equivalent of a traditional 13th cheque, and a generous option for households that can afford it.

For example:

Suggested Christmas bonus (approx.) If weekly salary (for one day’s work) is R400 If weekly salary (for two day’s work) is R800 One week’s pay (modest) R400 R800 Half a month’s salary (benchmark) R800 R1 600 One month’s salary (generous) R1 600 R3 200

Remember, these are salary comparisons and suggested benchmarks, not industry standards.

Minimum wages

There is also the national minimum wage (NMW) to consider. Since 1 March 2026, domestic workers must earn at least R30.23 per ordinary hour worked.

The Department of Employment and Labour also stipulates: “An employee or a worker who works for less than four hours on any day must be paid for four hours work on that day.” This is covered by the NMW Act.

For daily-rate employees, the hourly rate is calculated by dividing their daily wage by their ordinary hours worked. Transport allowances are excluded from this minimum wage calculation.

The Department adds: “The NMW does not include allowances (such as transport, tools, food or accommodation).”

Ultimately, a Christmas bonus is an opportunity to recognise someone’s contribution throughout the year. Even if a full month’s salary isn’t affordable, a smaller cash payment and a grocery hamper can still make a difference.

In related news, the agency has clarified its stance on a SASSA Christmas bonuses for 2026. Read more here.

World.title: Kaizer Chiefs attacking duo in contention for Sundowns clash
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs duo of Langelihle Phili and Elias Mokwana in contention for Sundowns clash. Image: Kaizer Chiefs WhatsApp Channel

World.title: ‘Almost 19 approved months with no dates’: SRD applicants still waiting on SASSA
World.content:
Some Social Relief of Distress (SRD) grant applicants say their applications show “approved”, but no money ever arrives.

They described their frustration under a post on The South African’s Facebook page, where several said they had been waiting for months.

Approved but unpaid SRD GRANT

Bongani Mtuntwana said he has a long list of approvals and nothing to show for it.



“I have almost 19 approved months with no dates. Every time I contact the SASSA office on the phone, they say I must wait maybe until the 15th of every month, but nothing appears in my bank,” Mtuntwana said.

Desiree O’Rie said the problem feels uneven. “They get approved but others dont even get a date,” she wrote.

‘Source of income identified’

Approval is not the only obstacle. Some applicants say SASSA flags them for income they do not have.



Tumelo Dire said a single status has followed him for nearly two years. “A source of income has been identified since January last year,” Dire wrote.

SASSA checks SRD applicants against bank records and other government databases every month. If the agency detects money flowing into an applicant’s account, it may decline that month’s application, even when the deposit was a once-off transfer from family or friends.

What applicants can do

Applicants who see an approval but no pay date should first check their status on the official SRD website. Banking details that are outdated or entered incorrectly can hold up payments, so applicants should confirm that the account is in their own name and still active.



Applicants who receive a decline, including one for “source of income identified”, can ask for a reconsideration through the same website.

For people like Mtuntwana, though, the longer the wait, the harder it becomes to believe the money will ever arrive.

World.title: Big change to TIPPING in restaurants in South Africa
World.content:
South Africans dining out do not have to pay an automatically added 10% service charge simply because it appears on a restaurant bill. Image: File

South Africans dining out do not have to pay an automatically added 10% service charge simply because it appears on a restaurant bill, following an important consumer rights ruling against a Pretoria restaurant.

The National Consumer Tribunal found that Tribeca Standard, a restaurant at Lynnwood Bridge in Pretoria, had engaged in prohibited conduct by automatically adding a 10% service charge to customers’ bills.

The restaurant described the charge as discretionary and told diners they could ask for it to be removed if they were unhappy with the service.



READ | Major fried chicken chain from Korea opens its first store in South Africa

However, the Tribunal ruled that customers should not have to challenge an automatically added charge to avoid paying it.

Speaking to Stephen Grootes on The Money Show, consumer rights expert Wendy Knowler explained why the decision matters for restaurants and diners across the country.

Restaurant added 10% to every bill

Tribeca Standard’s menu stated that a discretionary 10% charge would be added to customers’ bills.

Diners were told to notify management if the service was not up to standard, with the restaurant promising to remove the charge.

However, the fee was automatically applied to all bills, with the restaurant confirming that approximately 200 service-charge transactions were processed daily.



The National Consumer Commission considered this a systemic practice rather than an isolated incident.

Knowler said customers were increasingly encountering service charges that were added automatically, sometimes without being clearly communicated before the bill arrived.

She explained that many diners simply look at the final amount and may not realise that a service fee has already been included before adding their own tip.

Why the Tribunal ruled against the restaurant

The restaurant defended its policy by arguing that the charge was disclosed on its menu, was discretionary and could be removed at a customer’s request.

It also said the money was paid to waiters as tips and that no customer had complained about being refused a request to remove the charge.

However, Knowler said the central issue was that consumers could not be compelled to pay more than the displayed price.

Section 23 of the Consumer Protection Act (CPA) prohibits suppliers from requiring consumers to pay more than the displayed price for goods or services.

The Tribunal also found that the restaurant’s approach effectively required customers to pay extra for good service or negotiate a lower bill if the service was poor.

Knowler said consumers already have a legal right to good-quality service.

A genuinely voluntary gratuity is one that a customer freely chooses to pay. It is not an amount automatically added to a bill and removed only if the customer challenges it.

The Tribunal clarified that restaurants are not prohibited from charging for additional services. However, they must specify what those services entail and display the full price upfront so customers can decide whether to accept the offer before ordering.

Restaurant escapes R1 million fine

The National Consumer Commission asked the Tribunal to impose a R1 million administrative fine on Tribeca Standard.

However, the restaurant was not fined.

The Tribunal declared the conduct prohibited but decided that imposing a financial penalty was not in the interests of justice.

Knowler explained that several factors worked in the restaurant’s favour.

These included that there was no evidence of bad faith, that the service charges had genuinely been paid to waiters and that the restaurant had not profited from the arrangement.

No specific financial loss was presented to the Tribunal.

The restaurant also cooperated with the investigation and removed the disputed wording from its menu.

Knowler contrasted the outcome with an earlier case involving a Gauteng restaurant group, which was fined R1 million in 2024 after the Tribunal found that it had charged undisclosed service fees and failed to cooperate with proceedings.

Can restaurants still charge a 10% service fee for large tables?

The discussion also considered whether restaurants should be allowed to add service charges to larger bookings.

Knowler acknowledged that a waiter may spend much of an evening attending to a single table of eight or 10 people.

Restaurants can decide whether to accept large bookings and can charge for additional services, provided the charges are properly disclosed and customers agree to them before ordering.

However, she said blanket charges applied to every bill, including those for a single diner, were particularly problematic.

Customers should also be told clearly when a service fee has already been included rather than discovering it when the bill arrives.

What should you do if a restaurant adds 10% to your bill?

Knowler advised diners to check their bills before adding an additional tip.

If a service charge appears that they did not agree to, they can ask for it to be removed.

Importantly, customers do not have to complain about the quality of the service to justify refusing an unwanted charge.

If a restaurant refuses to remove the fee, consumers can report the matter to the National Consumer Commission.

The ruling does not mean restaurants can never charge for additional services. It reinforces the importance of transparent pricing and allowing customers to make an informed decision before ordering.

For South African diners, the message is clear: a tip is voluntary, and a restaurant cannot simply make an automatically added charge compulsory by describing it as discretionary.

World.title: Rand tanks making festive-season travel more expensive
World.content:
The rand has lost nearly 2% against the US dollar, trading around R17.25 as rising inflation and US interest-rate expectations put pressure on the currency. Image: Pexels.

The rand has come under renewed pressure, losing nearly 2% against the US dollar to trade at around R17.22 as at the time of publishing, as global interest-rate concerns and South Africa’s rising inflation add to uncertainty ahead of the Reserve Bank’s final monetary policy announcement of 2026 on Thursday afternoon.

The currency’s latest weakness comes as investors increasingly expect the US Federal Reserve to keep interest rates higher, or potentially tighten monetary policy further, to contain inflation.

Higher US interest rates tend to make dollar-denominated investments more attractive, supporting demand for the greenback and putting pressure on emerging-market currencies such as the rand.



The South African currency also weakened to its lowest level of the year during Thursday’s early trading session, with Reuters reporting that it had reached R17.3450 against the dollar.

US dollar strength puts pressure on the rand

Expectations of further US monetary tightening have strengthened the dollar, with recent Federal Reserve commentary reinforcing concerns that interest rates may remain elevated.

The pressure on the rand is not limited to US monetary policy.

Lower precious-metal prices have also weighed on the currency, as gold is an important South African export. Uncertainty surrounding local government coalition negotiations has added another domestic risk for investors.

The combination of global and local factors has made the rand more vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment.

Inflation rises to 5.2%

The currency’s decline comes a day after Statistics South Africa reported that annual consumer inflation had accelerated to 5.2% in October, up from 4.5% in September.



The increase of 0.7 percentage points marked the highest headline inflation reading since May 2024.

Fuel was a major contributor to the increase. Annual fuel inflation surged to 42.9% in October, compared with 27.9% in September.

Transport inflation reached 15.2%, while food and non-alcoholic beverage inflation increased for a third consecutive month to 1.4%.

The latest figures add to concerns about the cost of living, particularly as higher fuel prices can feed through to transport, distribution and other household expenses.

All eyes on the Reserve Bank

Attention is now turning to the South African Reserve Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), which is scheduled to announce its final interest rate decision of the year on Thursday.

The repo rate currently stands at 7.25%, following a 25-basis-point increase at the previous MPC meeting in September. The prime lending rate is 10.75%.

Most economists expect the MPC to leave interest rates unchanged, although the latest inflation figures have revived debate about whether another increase could be necessary.

The Reserve Bank must weigh rising domestic inflation against the risks posed by a weaker rand, higher global interest rates and the impact of previous rate increases on the economy.

A decision to hold rates would give policymakers more time to assess whether the latest inflation increase is temporary or likely to become more persistent.

However, the market will also be watching Governor Lesetja Kganyago’s comments for clues about the direction of interest rates in 2027.

What a weaker rand means for South Africans

A weaker rand makes imported goods and commodities more expensive in local currency terms.

This can add pressure to fuel prices, particularly because South Africa imports much of its crude oil and refined petroleum products.

It can also increase the cost of imported food, machinery, electronics and other consumer goods, depending on how much of the currency movement is passed on to local prices.

For consumers, the combination of a weaker rand and higher fuel inflation is an unwelcome development as the country heads towards the festive season.

The Reserve Bank’s decision on Thursday will therefore be closely watched by borrowers, investors and businesses looking for clarity on the outlook for interest rates and the economy.

World.title: SA Reserve Bank keeps repo rate unchanged
World.content:
PRETORIA - The South African Reserve Bank has kept the repo rate unchanged.

Reserve Bank Governor Lesetja Kganyago delivered the final Monetary Policy Committee statement of the year.



Kganyago says four members preferred no change, while three members preferred an increase of 25 basis points.



The interest rate will stay at 7.25%.



The prime lending rate remains at 10.75%.

"After two policy adjustments this year, and with a moderately restrictive policy stance, we decided to pause for now," Kganyago said.

"We are mindful of risks, and will not hesitate to raise rates if needed, to return inflation to target over the policy horizon.

"Our decisions will continue to be taken on a meeting-by-meeting basis, with careful attention to the outlook, data outcomes, and the balance of risks."

Kganyago says 2026 has been a challenging year with inflation being much higher than expected at the start of the year, and growth has been lower, with unemployment rising.



"We trace this mainly to negative supply shocks from geopolitical conflicts," he said.



"It is unclear how conditions will evolve from here – but we remain committed to steering inflation back to the 3% target. With lower inflation, an improving fiscal position, and ongoing structural reforms, South Africa has clear potential to achieve higher growth in the years ahead.

World.title: Tennis world number one Zverev to defend himself against new lawsuit
World.content:
LONDON - Lawyers for world number one Alexander Zverev have told the BBC he will defend himself against a fresh action which alleges he misrepresented the outcome of his domestic abuse trial.

Former partner Brenda Patea is seeking damages and an injunction against him making similar comments in future.

In October 2023 Zverev was issued with a penalty order for bodily harm against Patea, with whom he has a daughter.

He challenged the order, having always denied the charges, and a public trial was under way in Berlin in June 2024 when the court terminated the proceedings.

A separate settlement between Zverev and Patea was agreed.

But in September it emerged lawyers for Patea had filed a civil complaint in Berlin about an interview Zverev gave to French sports newspaper L'Equipe in June the day after he won his first Grand Slam title at Roland Garros.

According to the complaint, L'Equipe reported Zverev, who also won this year's US Open, allegedly said "my innocence has been proven".

The lawsuit asks the 29-year-old German should be ordered "on pain of a fine of up to 250,000 euros (£209,000)" not to repeat the claim, and also seeks damages for the impact these statements have made on Patea.

"He was not found guilty, but he was not acquitted and they signed an agreement in which he committed not to talk about this case any more," Patea's lawyer Michael Scheele told the BBC.

Zverev is being represented by Berlin law firm Schertz Bergman.

They told the BBC: "Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law."

The out-of-court settlement in Berlin in June 2024 came on the day Zverev reached the French Open final for the first time.

Zverev, asked then if he had any reservations about missing an opportunity to clear his name completely, replied: "That's what dropping the case is. That is innocence."

He added: "We move on. I never ever want to hear another question about the subject again. That goes out to everybody."

- AFP

World.title: 'Almost all' Fed policymakers saw further interest rate hikes as likely
World.content:
WASHINGTON - "Almost all" participants of the US Federal Reserve's interest rate-setting meeting in October thought that further rate hikes would be necessary to fight stubbornly high inflation, minutes of the meeting showed Wednesday.

The meeting's minutes, released after a customary three-week lag, showed that according to almost all policymakers' baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further rate hikes "would likely be appropriate" to bring prices back under control.

The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at its last meeting in late October, even as its Chairman Kevin Warsh said inflation remained "too high."

The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 and 4.00 percent, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.

Two voting members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, had dissented in favor of an immediate 25-basis-point hike.

- 'Broad-based' inflation -

The Fed has a dual mandate of keeping inflation to its long-term two-percent target while ensuring maximum employment.

The unemployment rate in the United States has been relatively steady over the last year, even as job growth has seesawed. That stability is due to demographic changes and lower immigration.

Inflation, on a downward trajectory since hitting a pandemic peak, has reignited in the last year, driven by US President Donald Trump's tariff policies and the energy price spike caused by his war on Iran.

The massive investments in infrastructure to support the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout have also led to increased prices.

Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index inflation, the Fed's preferred gauge, hit 3.6 percent in September, far above the central bank's target.

At the meeting in October, participants "acknowledged that inflation remained elevated."

"Most remarked that inflation pressures in the economy were broad-based," indicating they saw price increases as having spread beyond skyrocketing energy prices into other sectors.

Still, 10 of the committee's 12 voting members called for rates to be held steady.

"These participants cited the need to assess the durability of AI-related investment demand, the evolution of financing conditions, the transmission of the September rate increase to the economy, or geopolitical developments," the minutes said.

Those who dissented from the majority decision in calling for a 25-basis-point hike said they saw inflation as "too high" and "saw few signs of it abating."

"They judged that the current policy stance was not sufficiently restrictive, and a few of them warned that further delay risked allowing high inflation to become entrenched or necessitating a larger and more disruptive tightening later."

- 'Concerned' -

Speaking to US broadcaster CNBC on Wednesday morning, before the minutes were released, Fed Governor Chris Waller said he was "very, very concerned" about inflation and now saw the need for a 50-basis-point hike at the Fed's next meeting in December.

"If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking more aggressive actions," he said.

He said the Fed may need to go beyond the December rate hike he prescribed in order to meaningfully fight inflation.

Fed Governor Michael Barr, speaking at an event in New York on Wednesday, also said he saw the need for further rate hikes.

World.title: Tropical Fiji declares El Niño drought 'crisis'
World.content:
WELLINGTON - South Pacific nation Fiji has declared a national state of disaster as a drought fuelled by the El Niño weather phenomenon reaches "crisis" levels.

Drought in Fiji is strongly linked to the El Niño pattern, which dries up the tropical rains that typically keep its islands lush and green.

El Niño warms surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in wind, heat and rain.

The current El Niño is expected to become one of the most powerful on record, experts have warned.

The Fiji government said "the ongoing El Niño drought has reached crisis thresholds", forcing the declaration of a nationwide disaster.

"Families across Fiji are concerned about the availability of water and the impacts of prolonged dry conditions on their daily lives," Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said on Wednesday.

"Farmers are worried about their crops and livestock. These concerns are real."

Under the emergency measures, the Fiji government has the power to ration water, force evacuations and reallocate public funds to disaster assistance.

Water sources across much of the country have dropped to worrying levels, local media reported, with scores of trucks dispatched to re-supply parched villages.

"We cannot control the climate, but we can act early, use our resources responsibly and stand together through its impacts," Rabuka said.

World.title: Who said what since revelations reignited 'Sandpapergate' scandal
World.content:
MELBOURNE - The 2018 "Sandpapergate" ball-tampering controversy has engulfed Australian cricket since retired Test star Usman Khawaja reopened old wounds with the release of his bombshell autobiography this month.

He said the whole team knew about the plot to alter the ball in a Test at Cape Town, despite a Cricket Australia probe finding only captain Steve Smith, deputy David Warner and opener Cameron Bancroft were responsible.

AFP Sports looks at the key quotes since the scandal erupted again:

November 7

"It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us."

-- Khawaja on who knew about the plan.

November 7

"I don't think everybody would have known."

-- Darren Lehmann, who quit as coach after the scandal.

November 8

"I haven't thrown anyone under the bus. These three guys (Smith, Warner and Bancroft) took the blame for all of us.

-- Khawaja.

November 9

"Uzzie, I throw my full support behind you. I thank you for what you've done. It's 100 percent accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."

-- Warner.

November 10

"We don't see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this again. I don't think there's anything that can be gained from that."

-- Cricket Australia chief Todd Greenberg.

November 11

"All I've ever wanted for us is to take accountability as a team. This has never been a witch hunt for me."

-- Khawaja.

November 11

"I guess I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers but, where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed, my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021."

-- Bowler Mitchell Starc, referring to a joint statement from the four main bowlers denying any knowledge.

November 12

"To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false."

-- Former batting coach Graeme Hick.

November 13

"When he says we all knew, if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 percent wrong."

-- Current Test captain Pat Cummins.

"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."

-- Cummins.

November 14

"It looks like they (Cricket Australia) had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea. That stinks of a cover-up."

-- Warner.

November 15

"I believe that everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used."

-- Bowler Chadd Sayers, who was on the 2018 tour.

November 18

"We believe it is time for a circuit-breaker. This is not about litigating the past."

-- Cricket Australia interim chairman David Boon in announcing a forum for players to share their version of events.

"We recognise the pain and hurt that events surrounding Sandpapergate have caused. Let's be honest, the game is hurting at the moment."

-- Greenberg.

November 18

"It was not just the three of us -— Steve Smith, David Warner and I -- who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team."

-- Bancroft.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference. It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone."

-- Bancroft.

November 19

"Pat's position hasn't changed in eight years. He's been consistent and adamant from day one. There is nothing he hasn't answered. And that includes in response to what Cam has now said."

-- Cummins' manager Neil Maxwell.

World.title: Safaricom dispute leaves Vodacom billions in limbo
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Vodacom is unable to access more than R1 billion linked to its Safaricom deal in Kenya.

Around R1.15 billion in dividends has been frozen while a legal battle over the transaction continues.

The money comes from an agreement that gave Vodacom the rights to future dividends from the Kenyan government's remaining stake in Safaricom.

The dispute follows a September ruling by Kenya's High Court, which declared the government's sale of a 15% stake in Safaricom to Vodacom unconstitutional and ordered that the shares be returned.

READ | Vodacom reaches 250 million customers across Africa

The ruling also affected Vodacom's funding agreement with Stanbic Bank Kenya.

As a result, the bank account holding the dividend money has been placed under a standstill arrangement.

Vodacom has agreed not to withdraw the funds while the matter is being resolved.

The company is appealing the court ruling and says it remains confident that the deal will stand.

World.title: LIVESTREAM | IMC on migration gives update
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Inter-ministerial Committee on Migration is expected to outline government's approach to managing migration.

This as concerns mount over undocumented migrants and conditions at the Lindela Repatriation Centre.

A recent High Court inspection exposed serious challenges, including deportation delays and a shortage of interpreters.

Government now faces the problem of enforcing immigration laws while upholding constitutional and human rights.

World.title: Ruto accuses Uhuru of neglecting Western region
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during commissioning of projects in Webuye West Constituency, Bungoma county. [Jackline Inyanji,Standard]

President William Ruto has taken a swipe at former President Uhuru Kenyatta, former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua and opposition leaders, accusing them of neglecting Western Kenya during their time in power and lacking the moral authority to dictate the region’s political direction.

The President said residents of the region should not allow outsiders to determine their political choices, insisting that the people of Western Kenya have the right to decide their leaders and political future without intimidation or manipulation.

Speaking in Kakapel, Teso South, Busia County, during a development tour, Dr Ruto challenged residents to reject what he termed attempts by some politicians to undermine the region, saying his administration was committed to ensuring equitable distribution of development projects across the country.

“Some people were in positions of authority for a long time but did not even know where Teso was located. Now they are the ones trying to organise the people of Teso. Will you allow other people to organise you, or will you organise your own affairs?” he posed.

He added: “There is no small community in Kenya and there is no big community. We are all Kenyans and every part of this country deserves development.”

The President appeared to target former leaders and opposition figures whom he accused of attempting to influence Western Kenya's political choices despite having failed to address the region's development needs when they held power.

He said residents should not be intimidated by politicians claiming to control millions of votes, insisting that the electorate had the final say on who should lead them.

Ruto cited ongoing and planned infrastructure projects as evidence of his administration's commitment to the region, announcing that the road connecting Amukura, Machakuzi and Kocholia would be extended to Kakapel following demands by residents.

He said he had agreed with area MP Mary Emase and other local leaders to extend the project beyond Kocholia to Amakoro and Kakapel.

“I am going to tell the contractor immediately where the people of Kakapel want this road to reach. I have agreed that it will not end at Kocholia but will come through Amakoro up to Kakapel. I will add money to ensure the road is constructed,” he said.

On housing, Ruto announced plans to construct 6,000 affordable housing units in Busia County, saying Malaba would also be transformed into a smart city.

He questioned why Malaba should be excluded from the country's urban transformation programme while other towns, including Nairobi, Kakamega, Eldoret and Kisumu, were benefiting from modern infrastructure.

“Why should a building being constructed in Nairobi not be constructed in Malaba? If we are building in Kakamega, Nairobi, Eldoret and Kisumu, Malaba must also be developed,” he said.

The President also pledged to complete the ongoing Ngurai market within two months, saying the facility would provide traders with a decent working environment and protect them from harsh weather conditions.

He said the Sh400 million Malaba market was also progressing, adding that his administration was constructing 17 markets across Busia County.

Ruto further announced that the government had allocated Sh200 million towards the construction of hostels at KMTTC to support students from the Teso region.

He said the development agenda would also prioritise roads, electricity connectivity, education and other essential services, insisting that no community should be left behind.

The President defended the broad-based political arrangement between UDA and ODM, saying cooperation between the two parties was intended to promote national unity, development and equitable resource distribution.

He urged residents to reject tribalism and political hatred, arguing that every Kenyan deserved equal opportunities regardless of their community or geographical location.

World.title: Ruto lists measures to lower cost of living, put more money in Kenyans' pockets
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during his State Of The Nation Address at Parliament, Nairobi. November 18th, 2026. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

President William Ruto has outlined a raft of government interventions aimed at reducing the cost of living, increasing household incomes and creating more employment opportunities for Kenyans.

Addressing Parliament during the 2026 State of the Nation Address on Wednesday, Ruto said his administration had prioritised lowering the cost of essential goods and services while increasing earnings across key sectors of the economy.

“Our economic proposition was simple: Reduce the cost for families and increase the income from what they do,” he said.

On food prices, the President cited the government’s fertiliser subsidy programme, which has reduced the price of a 50-kilogramme bag of fertiliser from Sh7,500 in 2022 to Sh2,000 this year.

He said the government had distributed 38.5 million bags of subsidised fertiliser to farmers, contributing to an increase in maize production from 44.3 million bags in 2022 to 71 million bags last year.

Consequently, maize imports declined from 9.9 million bags to 3.3 million bags, while the average price of a two-kilogramme packet of sifted maize flour dropped from a high of Sh230 in September 2022 to Sh152 in September this year.

Ruto also highlighted gains in the tea, coffee, dairy and sugar industries, saying government interventions had helped improve production and increase farmers' earnings.

He said the Cherry Advance Revolving Fund had disbursed Sh15.07 billion to 684,000 coffee farmers, while tea export earnings increased from Sh163 billion in 2022 to Sh187 billion in 2025.

In the dairy sector, milk production rose from 4.5 billion litres to 5.52 billion litres, while average earnings for farmers increased from Sh32 to Sh60 per litre last month.

Sugar production, he added, increased by 60 per cent between January and October, with cane crushing rising by 57 per cent. The industry is projected to produce more than 900,000 tonnes by the end of the year, with Sh1.2 billion in bonuses expected to be paid to sugarcane farmers.

On healthcare, Ruto said the Social Health Authority (SHA) was designed to ease the financial burden of medical expenses on households through a shared health financing system.

In education, he said the government had employed 100,000 teachers and was preparing to recruit an additional 20,000 to address staffing shortages and reduce the burden on parents who pay teachers hired through Boards of Management.

He added that 23,000 classrooms had been constructed, while 1,600 laboratories were being built and equipped.

The President said the annual education allocation had increased from Sh521 billion in the 2022/23 financial year to Sh784 billion in the current financial year.

"These investments improve the quality of education while progressively reducing the need for Kenyans to finance education," he said.

On affordable housing, Ruto said more than 313,000 homes were at different stages of construction across the 47 counties, with over 1.37 million Kenyans registered on the Boma Yangu platform and more than 18,000 homes already allocated.

He said households could work towards homeownership through monthly payments starting at Sh4,000, which he argued would help ease the burden of rent.

The housing programme, according to the President, had also generated more than 1.1 million employment opportunities and reserved orders worth over Sh61 billion for Jua Kali artisans.

On employment, Ruto said 350,000 Kenyans had secured jobs through the digital economy programme, while another 707,000 had obtained employment abroad through international labour mobility initiatives.

He also cited the Hustler Fund, saying more than seven million Kenyans had established credit records through the programme, with cumulative borrowing reaching Sh94 billion.

Under the NYOTA programme, more than 133,000 young entrepreneurs had received training, mentorship and Sh50,000 each in start-up capital, he said.

The President further announced proposed tax measures aimed at increasing disposable incomes, including exempting workers earning Sh32,333 or less per month from Pay As You Earn (PAYE).

Other proposals include scrapping stamp duty on land transactions valued at Sh1 million or less and removing the 25 per cent import duty on mobile phones.

On pending bills, Ruto said the government had approved the settlement of 28,726 verified claims amounting to Sh27.8 billion, covering debts of Sh50 million and below dating back to 2005.

He added that Sh18 billion owed to public universities and another Sh16 billion owed to public and private hospitals under the former National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) had been approved for payment and were undergoing Treasury processing.

“These are not isolated interventions, but parts of one comprehensive undertaking,” Ruto said.

He maintained that the government's economic strategy was anchored on reducing household expenditure, increasing incomes and expanding opportunities for Kenyans.

World.title: After 22 years of waiting, woman welcomes quadruplet boys
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Samuel Langat speaks to journalists outside St Clare's Kaplong Mission hospital in Sotik Subcounty, Bomet county after his wife Lily Langat gave to quadruplets at the hospital. [Kiprono Kurgat, Standard]

After 22 years of waiting to become a mother, a woman has welcomed quadruplet boys in a rare and joyful birth that has brought immense happiness to her family.

Lily Langat delivered the quadruplets through a Caesarean section at St Clare’s Kaplong Mission Hospital in Sotik Sub-County on November 14, 2026.

The four boys arrived after more than two decades of waiting for a child in what the family described as a double blessing.

The 43-year-old mother could not hide her joy, saying the arrival of the four babies was an answer to years of prayer.

“I am very grateful to God for giving me four babies at once. This is a great blessing to my family. I thank the hospital staff for ensuring I got to see these bundles of joy,” she said.

“I have been praying and waiting upon God to give me double for the trouble. I have been childless for a long time, and God could not have given me a better gift than this,” she added.

She said she had been looking forward to the moment after doctors informed her early in the pregnancy that she could be carrying quadruplets.

Hospital staff celebrated the successful delivery, describing it as a rare occurrence at the facility.

A nurse who spoke with The Standard said the mother and her four newborns were in stable condition.

“We were delighted to deliver the babies. The mother faced some difficulties because of the combined weight of the four babies, but both she and the newborns are now stable,” she said.

The nurse said the babies had been placed in the nursery for observation and were doing well.

“This is a rare case in this hospital. We have had twins before, but this is different. None of the babies has developed complications so far, and we expect them to be discharged once they are fully stable,” she said.

She added that the mother was also recovering well and was expected to be discharged once doctors were satisfied with the condition of the newborns.

Lily's husband, Samuel Langat, appealed to well-wishers to support the family as they prepare to raise the four children.

“Raising four babies at once is no easy task. I am calling on well-wishers to lend a helping hand as we begin this extraordinary journey,” he said.

“Our four precious miracles have arrived safely, and while our hearts are overflowing with gratitude, the reality of caring for four newborns at once has brought challenges,” he added.

Naturally conceived quadruplets are extremely rare, although the likelihood varies depending on several factors, including maternal age and fertility treatment.

The birth marks a remarkable new beginning for the Langat family after 22 years of waiting for a child.

World.title: TSC picks Cheptumo Ayabei as new Chief Executive Officer
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Teachers Service Commission headquarters in Nairobi. [File, Standard]

The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) has picked Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer, making him the first person with a disability to head the commission.

Ayabei emerged top in interviews conducted on Monday, beating four other candidates, including the commission’s acting chief executive, Dr Evaleen Jesang Mitei, to become the country’s top teachers’ employer.

His selection ends a prolonged search for a substantive head of the commission, which has operated under acting leadership since the departure of former CEO Nancy Macharia in June 2025.

Ayabei, who hails from Baringo County, is currently TSC’s Director of Finance, having served at the commission for more than two decades. He joined the institution in 1999 as a Finance Officer before rising through the ranks to become Director of Finance in 2009.

His elevation marks a significant milestone for the representation of persons with disabilities in the country’s public institutions.

Ayabei was the first candidate to face the selection panel at 9am at the commission’s headquarters in Upper Hill, Nairobi. He was followed by Mitei at 10am, Robert Odette at 11am, Lawrence Ngai Kaburu at noon and Farah Abdi Saman at 1pm.

The five candidates were shortlisted from 124 applicants who responded to a fresh  issued on September 29. Applications closed on October 30.

Ayabei holds a Bachelor of Education degree in Mathematics and Economics from Kenyatta University and a Master’s degree in Finance and Banking from the University of Stirling in the United Kingdom. He is also a Certified Public Accountant.

Before joining TSC, he worked at the Ministry of Education between 1990 and 1999.

He takes over at a critical time for the commission, which oversees the employment, deployment, promotion and discipline of teachers across the country. He will inherit mounting pressure over teacher shortages, recruitment, promotions, transfers and the management of the teaching workforce.

The recruitment process had faced legal challenges, with a petition filed at the Employment and Labour Relations Court in Kisii seeking to halt the exercise.

The case, filed by Evans Morara Nyangongo under Cause E038 of 2026, challenged the fresh recruitment and raised questions about Mitei’s participation in the process while serving as acting CEO and seeking the substantive position.

Nyangongo sought to stop the commission from proceeding with the appointment until the issues raised in the petition were determined.

However, the court dismissed both the application and the suit, with no orders as to costs, clearing the way for the interviews.

In its defence, TSC maintained that the decision to advertise the position had been made collectively by the commission’s board and not by the acting CEO.

In a replying affidavit, TSC chairman Jamleck Muturi John maintained that Mitei had neither participated in the board’s deliberations on the recruitment nor influenced the process.

The fresh recruitment followed an earlier court decision that nullified the previous exercise over procedural irregularities, forcing the commission to restart the search for a substantive chief executive.

World.title: Thwake Dam project reaches 94pc completion
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Thwake Multipurpose Dam, which is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment.[File,Standard]

Thwake Dam is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment as residents seek a review of alleged construction-related damage claims.

Principal Secretary for Water and Sanitation Julius Korir told the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Blue Economy, Water and Irrigation that construction had reached 94.2 per cent.

The dam is being built at the confluence of the Athi and Thwake rivers along the Makueni-Kitui border. It is designed to provide water for domestic use, irrigation and electricity generation.

Martin Kimeu, a resident of Wote, said the project would improve access to water for farming in the region.

“Ukambani is fertile. Water has been the biggest impediment to the realization of our agricultural potential. Thwake Dam water is the clear solution to this,” he said.

Kimeu also defended the compensation process, saying he had followed the project since its inception and believed the exercise had been conducted properly.

Jacob Mwanzia, a resident of Madangi Village, said households in his area had been assessed and compensated. He argued that outstanding complaints should be addressed without delaying the project.

Mariam Mwikali, another resident, said assessments had been conducted on affected properties and residents given an opportunity to raise concerns.

However, some households have complained that construction-related blasting damaged their homes. Residents have reported cracks in walls, windows and foundations as well as dust, noise and ground vibrations.

In August 2026, residents from villages in Mavindini Ward, organised under the Thwake Dam Blasting-Affected Community Committee, sought an independent review by the African Development Bank (AfDB).

The residents alleged that some properties had been left out of assessments and compensation. They also sought access to assessment reports, photographs, measurements, valuation records and estimates for repairs or reconstruction.

A project official said the dam's safety department invited competitive bids for an independent assessment of properties potentially affected by blasting. Agile Consulting was selected to conduct the exercise.

The official said the consultant assessed 330 households within a two-kilometre radius of the construction site and submitted its report to the project implementation team. A large proportion of those assessed were satisfied with the exercise, the official added, without giving a breakdown.

Ben Mwongela, a director at Agile Consulting, said the assessment reviewed blasting records, vibration data and compliance with regulatory standards.

The exercise also involved documenting households, classifying structural defects and preparing bills of quantities and cost estimates for repairs or reconstruction, he said.

The AfDB conducted a field mission to the project between September 21 and 25, with its report published on October 21, 2026.

The bank's team, led by project task manager Nancy Ogal, met residents whose homes had been affected by blasting and identified outstanding health, safety, environmental and social issues, including homeowner grievances.

The bank called for timely compensation and continued monitoring of the project's environmental and social performance.

During a stakeholder engagement visit to Mavindini in October, Korir said the government had secured additional funding after the project experienced cash-flow constraints.

“When we ran short of cash, we engaged with our development partners, and they allocated additional funding, and this money will now go towards total completion of the project,” he said.

In June 2026, the AfDB approved additional financing of €68.39 million to support completion of the first phase, alongside funding from the Kenyan government.

The bank said the financing would support engineering refinements and safety works, including strengthening foundations, raising the dam and constructing two additional saddle dams.

The project has four phases. The first involves construction of the dam, while the subsequent phases cover hydropower generation, water supply and sanitation infrastructure, and irrigation.

The dam is approximately 80.5 metres high and has a planned storage capacity of 688 million cubic metres.

Once the water supply component is operational, the project is expected to provide 150,000 cubic metres of treated water daily to an estimated 1.3 million people in Makueni and Kitui counties and Konza Technopolis in Machakos County.

The irrigation scheme is designed to cover 40,000 hectares, equivalent to about 100,000 acres of agricultural land.

The project is also designed to generate 20 megawatts of hydropower.

The water supply, irrigation and hydropower components require infrastructure beyond the dam structure, including treatment and distribution networks and power generation facilities.

World.title: Love under watch: How technology is fuelling intimate partner abuse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Your enemy is closer than you think. For many Kenyan women, the person who demands a phone password, reads private messages and tracks their movements through a screen is not a faceless troll. He is the man they live with, or the one they used to.

That is the uncomfortable picture painted by the recently released 2025–2626 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey (KMDHS), which measured technology-facilitated gender-based violence, abuse committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified through digital tools.

The most common form of abuse is online control, reported by 19 per cent of women, followed by hacking at 5 per cent and online sexual harassment or cyber sexual abuse at 3 per cent. Most of it happens on platforms women use every day.

“Sixty-seven per cent of women who experienced digital gender violence say it happened on social media, with Facebook cited by 59 per cent. Messaging apps follow at 47 per cent, with WhatsApp at 26 per cent. Among girls aged 15–19, 77 per cent reported abuse on social media.”

The report shows how widespread the abuse is. “Twenty-six percent of women age 15–49 have ever experienced technology-facilitated violence from any perpetrator,” the report says, and 21 per cent experienced it often or sometimes in the 12 months before the survey. Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced it at the hands of a current, most recent or previous partner.

The burden is not spread evenly, the report states that Nairobi City records the highest lifetime experience from any perpetrator at 33 per cent, followed by Murang’a and Baringo at 32 per cent each.

“For abuse by an intimate partner, Homa Bay 36 per cent and Baringo 35 per cent lead, while in the 12 months before the survey Trans Nzoia topped the list at 31 per cent. At the other end, Mandera and Wajir report just 3 per cent, a figure that may say as much about silence as about safety,” the report says

The picture is similar among young people. A 2024 rapid study by the Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, working with the UNFPA and Women Economic Empowerment, found that nearly 90 per cent of young adults enrolled in three Nairobi tertiary institutions had witnessed TFGBV, and 39 per cent had experienced it personally.

Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced gender violence committed by a current, most recent or previous partner, and 22 per cent did so in the past year. When women were asked who was responsible, the answer was blunt. Current husbands or intimate partners accounted for 61 per cent of perpetrators, former partners for 22 per cent and strangers for just 13 per cent.

Women who have never been married or had a partner face a different threat. For them, the most common perpetrators are strangers at 45 per cent, online attackers at 23 per cent and friends or acquaintances at 20 per cent.

Warning signs

Control is the common thread. The report describes such behaviours by a male partner as “important early warning signs that may escalate into violence within a relationship.”

Sixty-one per cent of ever-partnered women say their current or most recent partner has shown at least one controlling behaviour, and 27 per cent report three or more. Half say he has been jealous or angry when they spoke to other men, and 36 per cent say he insists on knowing where they are at all times. Others describe partners who demand passwords or read messages without consent.

Age and marital status matter. Technology-based gender violence is lowest among girls aged 15–19 at 10 per cent and highest among women aged 20–24 at 37 per cent. Forty-one per cent of divorced, separated or widowed women have experienced it, compared with 27 per cent of married women and 19 per cent of the never married.

Yet the digital rights advocate Cherie Oyier, a programmes officer at the Kenya ICT Action Network (KICTANet), says the low figures in some places should not be read as safety. Much of the abuse happens where nobody can see it.

“Closed applications, meaning like WhatsApp, those are the ones that most people, intimate partners will usually use,” she says. “Even as you are scrolling the internet to look for these instances, we may not be able to catch it. But it does not mean that it is not happening or that it is at a lower level.”

Culture also silences women. “Most women are told just endure, this is what marriage is about,” Oyier says. “Sometimes they don’t know, it’s so overt, like it doesn’t come out clearly that this is abuse. So most of the times, it is not reported.”

Online, abuse has been turned into entertainment. “It has become banter,” she says. “Even the people who are experiencing it have trivialised it. It’s now ingrained to you, like this is something that happens, you should expect it actually. If you post a picture, one of the things that you are thinking about is what kind of comments am I going to get.”

A 2023 report by KICTANet found that more than 30 per cent of Kenyans have experienced some form of TFGBV, while 90 per cent have witnessed it. In 2025, KICTANet and Equality Now released survivor testimonies showing how deceptive online job offers, grooming and image-based abuse leave women exposed, and how many had never received counselling despite years of trauma.

The stakes are not only digital. The 2025 Report of the Technical Working Group on GBV Including Femicide, cited in the KMDHS, indicated that many cases of homicide of women and girls, and of sexual and physical harm directed towards them, “are preceded by online and offline harassment using digital tools.”

For survivors, the law offers little comfort. “The technology is moving at a very fast pace compared to the laws,” Oyier says. In an attempt to bolster the gaps, Kenya has many fragmented laws. “You’ll have the Data Protection Act, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Children’s Act, that to some extent touch on online issues, but they don’t really cohesively cover the different instances of TFGBV.”

The police, she says, often do not know either. “Just imagine you’re a woman who is in a village, for example, a village in Siaya, and you encounter violence. For you to even understand which law apply is very stressful.”

“You’re going through psychological stress and depression, and you’re also supposed to figure out which law applies in your situation. It causes even more problems for victims and survivors.”

Flagging abusive language

Artificial intelligence is adding a new layer. Even so, Oyier cautions against writing it off. “We should not vilify AI completely,” she says. KICTANet has built a lexicon to help flag abusive language and runs a tracker for online gender-based violence. “One person cannot sit down and look at everything on social media. When AI is able to pull every post that has this word, a human content moderator is able to look through it with local context and see is this TFGBV or not.”

The KMDHS findings further show that exposure to TFGBV varies across age groups and digital platforms.

“Younger women are particularly exposed on social media, with 77 per cent of women aged 15–19 and 72 per cent of those aged 20–24 who experienced TFGBV reporting abuse on social media platforms, compared with 50 per cent of women aged 40–49.”

However, messaging applications tell a different story. Women aged 40–49 reported the highest exposure through these platforms at 54 per cent, compared with 30 per cent among teenagers aged 15–19.

Wealth also influences where women encounter online abuse. Exposure on social media increases from 45 per cent among women in the lowest wealth quintile to 74 per cent among those in the highest. Conversely, women in the lowest wealth quintile report greater exposure through messaging applications, at 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent among those in the highest wealth quintile.

These differences suggest that TFGBV cuts across age and economic backgrounds, although the platforms through which women experience it vary.

World.title: Not so fast: Court slams brake on ARA over wealth forfeiture
World.content:
Felix Mecha Nyakundi could not provide a plausible explanation for how he amassed his wealth.

The Court of Appeal has ruled that the government cannot go after a person’s wealth without prior investigations to establish reasonable grounds for suspecting that the property constitutes proceeds of crime.

In a landmark judgment, Justices Patrick Kiage, Jamila Mohammed and Nduma Nderi said that although it does not require a person to be charged for a crime for the Asset Recovery Agency (ARA) to come knocking, it bears the responsibility to link the wealth or cash to a crime.

World.title: Back to sender: Aisha Jumwa returns to UDA
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto welcome former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa has returned to President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA), ending a three-month political fallout with the ruling party that saw her join opposition outfit Wiper Patriotic Front and declare support for the one-term movement ahead of the 2027 General Election.

President Ruto welcomed Jumwa back into UDA at State House, Mombasa, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in a political reunion that could reshape alignments in Kilifi County and the wider Coast region as parties position themselves for next year's elections.

The reunion comes barely three months after Jumwa dramatically announced her departure from UDA, accusing the party leadership of frustrating her political ambitions and failing to support her quest for the Kilifi gubernatorial seat.

On July 30, 2026, Jumwa announced her resignation during a press conference at her Kakuyuni home in Malindi, saying her attempts to have her grievances addressed by the President had repeatedly been unsuccessful.

Among her concerns was what she described as humiliation and rejection within the ruling party, including an alleged incident in which she was chased out of State House during a meeting between Ruto and Coast leaders.

She also accused sections of the ruling coalition of undermining her gubernatorial ambitions, claiming that the political arrangements being pursued in Kilifi were designed to deny her an opportunity to contest for the county's top seat.

President William Ruto recieve former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Jumwa, who was among UDA's founding members and one of Ruto's most vocal mobilisers at the Coast during the 2022 elections, said her loyalty to the people of Kilifi outweighed her allegiance to any political party.

"My loyalty to the people of Kilifi will always be greater than my loyalty to any political party. The voice of the people of Kilifi is louder than the voice of UDA," she declared during her exit announcement.

Her departure marked a significant political shift, particularly given her central role in mobilising support for Ruto in the Coast region.

In August, Jumwa turned to the opposition, where she was warmly received by Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka, who visited her at her Kakuyuni residence on August 14 alongside a delegation of party leaders, including Nyali MP Mohamed Ali, Kitui Senator Enoch Wambua and Wundanyi MP Danson Mwashako.

Kalonzo subsequently proposed Jumwa for the position of Wiper Deputy Party Leader, citing her political experience and influence, while also backing her ambition to contest the Kilifi governorship on a Wiper ticket.

Jumwa embraced the new political alliance, declaring support for the one-term movement and threatening to mobilise UDA supporters in Kilifi to deregister from the ruling party and join Wiper.

"We are the ones who registered UDA members in Kilifi, and we are embarking on a grassroots campaign to deregister them from UDA and join Wiper," she said at the time.

On September 8, she attended a meeting involving Wiper leaders and Coast gubernatorial aspirants, including Mohammed Ali and Danson Mwashako, as the party intensified efforts to expand its influence in the region.

However, the political alliance has now taken another turn, with Jumwa returning to the party she had accused of frustrating her ambitions.

Announcing her return, President Ruto welcomed the former Cabinet Secretary back into UDA, signalling renewed efforts to consolidate the ruling party's support in the Coast region.

"I look forward to working with her to advance the party’s transformation agenda at the Coast and across the country. We remain committed to uniting leaders and Kenyans around our shared vision of a united, inclusive and prosperous Kenya," the President said.

Her return comes as Ruto steps up political mobilisation in the Coast region ahead of the 2027 elections, with Kilifi emerging as an important battleground for competing political formations.

Jumwa's political journey has been characterised by shifting alliances. She previously served under the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), representing Malindi in Parliament before becoming Kilifi's first Woman Representative between 2013 and 2017.

She later became one of Ruto's key political allies and served in his Cabinet.

World.title: Ancient late period, Ptolemaic, early Roman necropolis uncovered in Menoufia
World.content:
An Egyptian archaeological mission affiliated with the Supreme Council of Antiquities (SCA) has uncovered an ancient necropolis at Tell Kom Abu Billo in Menoufia Governorate, featuring tombs and burials dating to the end of the Late Period, the Ptolemaic era, and the early Roman period.

The site contains hundreds of stone and pottery coffins some anthropoid and others bearing caricatured human features alongside wooden coffin remnants, vaulted mud brick tombs, and a limestone-lined tomb.

Preliminary studies indicate the open-courtyard necropolis likely served the middle class during the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE, reflecting funerary traditions linked to deities such as Osiris, Isis, Hathor, and Renenutet.

Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sherif Fathy emphasized the discovery’s importance in illustrating the evolution of ancient Egyptian burial practices.

SCA Secretary-General Hisham el Leithy noted the unprecedented scale of burials at the site, which lies within the ancient city of Terenuthis (modern Tarrana) near Wadi El Natrun—historically known for supplying natron salt for mummification.

Despite past looting and quarrying damage, excavations revealed human remains with traces of mummification resins and painted cartonnage.

Recovered artifacts include gold tongues, gold jewelry and foil, inscribed faience ushabti figurines, offering tables, schist and lapis lazuli scarabs, Wedjat eyes, amulets, small sphinx and Horus statues, terracotta figurines of Isis-Aphrodite, and two falcon burials.

Excavations and scientific documentation are ongoing to further uncover the history of the necropolis and ancient Terenuthis.

World.title: Egypt, US discuss strategic partnership, regional stability in Washington
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty met on Wednesday, November, 18, 2026, with US Representative Lois Frankel, Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs, during his current visit to Washington.

According to Foreign Ministry Spokesman Ambassador Nader Zaki, Abdelatty commended the strategic cooperation between Egypt and the US, affirming Egypt’s commitment to fostering communication and coordination with members of both chambers of the US Congress.

Abdelatty expressed Cairo’s appreciation for Frankel’s positions in support of bilateral relations.

Meanwhile, Frankel expressed appreciation for the US-Egypt partnership, applauding Egypt’s role in supporting peace and stability in the Middle East.

She also recalled her previous visit to Egypt, and said she took pride in her meeting with President Abdel Fattah El Sisi as part of a congressional delegation.

The meeting addressed regional and international developments, with Abdelatty emphasizing the importance of joint action to enhance regional peace and stability.

As regards the crisis with Iran, Abdelatty called for prioritizing political tracks and diplomatic solutions to contain tensions and prevent conflict escalation, reiterating Egypt’s rejection of attacks on Gulf states.

On the Horn of Africa, the minister underscored the need for regional stability, preserving state sovereignty and territorial integrity, and supporting national institutions, while ensuring freedom of navigation to prevent disruptions to international trade, global supply chains, the world economy, and Egypt’s economy.

World.title: PM attends launch of Nevera Egypt project to boost tourism, investments in West Cairo
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly affirmed the Egyptian government’s commitment to supporting strategic projects that advance sustainable development, strengthen the competitiveness of the national economy, and create genuine opportunities for future generations. Speaking at the signing and launch ceremony of the Nevera Egypt city project, held at the government headquarters in the New Capital, Madbouly described the project as a major addition to Egypt’s tourism and economic growth efforts.

He said the project falls within the framework of Egypt’s National Strategic Plan for Urban Development, which aims to achieve a balanced distribution of economic activities and make optimal use of the country’s available resources and potential.

Madbouly highlighted West Cairo as one of Egypt’s promising development regions, given its unique tourism, archaeological, and cultural assets, which position it to become an integrated destination for tourism, entertainment, and services, as well as a gateway for economic development in western Egypt.

He emphasized that the project builds on major national infrastructure investments carried out in recent years, including the development of the Tourist Road and Ring Road, the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system, and the high-speed electric rail network linking Ain Sokhna, Alamein, and Aswan.

The prime minister also pointed to the government’s comprehensive vision for developing the area extending from the Giza Pyramids and Saqqara to Sphinx International Airport.

The plan aims to maximize the area’s tourism and archaeological potential and accommodate expected growth in visitor numbers, he said.

He explained that the government had brought in specialized international consultancy firms to prepare a comprehensive study on the area’s development.

The study identified key priorities, particularly increasing hotel capacity to accommodate the expected rise in tourist numbers and meet growing demand for different types of tourism, he noted.

Madbouly described Nevera Egypt as one of the main strategic projects for developing West Cairo and strengthening its position as an emerging tourism, entertainment, and economic hub.

He added that the project land is owned by the state through contributions from several companies and economic entities, whose role is to prepare the land for development and offer the project for partnerships with the private sector.

The project, he concluded, represents an important step toward attracting investments, supporting the national economy, and opening new opportunities for development in West Cairo.

World.title: Egypt, Denmark discuss developments in Horn of Africa, Sahel
World.content:
Egypt and Denmark held political consultations in Copenhagen on developments in Sudan, the Horn of Africa and the Sahel, focusing on regional security and closer cooperation on African affairs.

The talks were attended by Egypt’s Assistant Foreign Minister for African Affairs Ambassador Mohamed Karim Sherif and Denmark’s Director of Africa, Development Policy, and Financing (AFRPOL) at Denmark’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs Kettel Karlsen.

Egyptian Ambassador to Denmark Mohamed Mounir and a number of Danish officials also attended the meeting.

Karlsen welcomed the development of Egyptian-Danish relations following the Egyptian presidential visit to Denmark in December 2024 and expressed interest in expanding cooperation under the two countries’ strategic partnership.

The discussions covered developments in Sudan, the Horn of Africa and the Sahel, as well as opportunities for trilateral cooperation.

Both sides reviewed the outcome of the October 2026 Alamein African Forum and Summit and the Alamein quadrilateral summit, including their discussions on Sudan, the Horn of Africa and opposition to the militarisation of the Red Sea.

Egypt and Denmark agreed to maintain political consultations and coordinate more closely on African issues.

Egypt also invited Denmark to hold the next round of consultations in Cairo.

World.title: Russia and China are not America’s friends. Why does Trump think they are?
World.content:
It’s fine for presidents to meet leaders of US adversaries. But Donald Trump’s summits with authoritarians are so odd because he treats them as friends.

This jarring dynamic may reemerge in his landmark summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in southern China on Thursday. He hopes to complete a trifecta of tyrant check-ins by also meeting with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.

The symbolism of the three-way talks in Shenzhen is stark. Three great powers, each of which stakes a hegemonic claim in its wider geographical orbit, will send a signal of dominance that deliberately excludes smaller, weaker nations.

The optics would be less striking if Trump acted as the leader of the free world facing down ruthless strongmen. But the president shows contempt for US allies and admires the iron rule of Xi and Putin. He frequently excuses their conduct or seeks to avoid upsetting them.
