World.title: Nike unveils plan that suggests its days of putting politics ahead of sports may be numbered | Matt Calkins
World.content:
I'm rooting for Nike.

The world is better when the most iconic sports brand in history is on top of its game.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

This is the company that brought us "Bo Knows," "It's gotta be the shoes" and "Chicks dig the long ball."

It gave us Tiger Woods juggling a golf ball, Andre Agassi and Pete Sampras trading forehands in the middle of a New York City street and Charles Barkley going one-on-one with Godzilla.

These ads made you want to pick up a baseball bat or a 5-iron — not a picket sign. And there are encouraging signs that Nike wants to be that company again.

NIKE CEO MAY HAVE JUST ADMITTED THE COMPANY WENT TOO WOKE AS STOCK HITS 12-YEAR LOW

At Nike's first Investor Day in nine years Tuesday, CEO Elliott Hill unveiled a long-term turnaround strategy dubbed "Full Stride Ahead." With the Swoosh's stock having lost half its value over the past two years, Hill emphasized a return to the company's roots.

"Nike is at its best when we start with the athlete and bring the full power of the company together around sport," Hill said in a statement.

Yes. Sport. This is what made Nike a juggernaut in the first place.

There are myriad reasons for the company's dramatic decline — its stock price hit a 12-year low last month. It oversaturated the market with retro sneakers, damaged relationships with retailers by prioritizing direct-to-consumer sales and ceded ground to competitors such as Hoka and On. Its business in China has been reeling, too.

But it's impossible to ignore that, somewhere along the way, Nike seemed to prioritize activism every bit as much as athleticism.

As I wrote last month, this is the company that made Colin Kaepernick the face of its 30th anniversary "Just Do It" campaign. It released a "For Once, Don't Do It" commercial in 2020, telling Americans not to turn their backs on racism. And in 2023, it enlisted transgender influencer Dylan Mulvaney to promote women's leggings and sports bras.

FROM COLIN KAEPERNICK TO DYLAN MULVANEY, NIKE'S DECADE OF LEFT-WING ACTIVISM HAS FINALLY CAUGHT UP TO IT

It's hard not to wonder if the higher-ups were more focused on appeasing the employees inside the building than courting customers outside it. But it sounds like those days might be over.

In an Oct. 1 memo, Hill wrote that "over the past year, we've put sport at the center of everything we do." I wondered at the time if that was as much a confession as it was a mission statement.

Hill struck a similar tone Tuesday, outlining five priority sports — running, training, soccer, basketball and outdoor — while emphasizing a return to athlete-centered marketing.

"Start with the athlete and the problem that we are solving. Bring product and storytelling together around the athlete," Hill said during his presentation.

That second sentence is particularly encouraging. Few companies in the history of advertising have been better storytellers than Nike. And the beauty of those stories was that you didn't have to be a Republican or a Democrat to appreciate them. You just had to love sports.

NIKE FORGOT THAT REPUBLICANS BUY SNEAKERS, TOO, AND NOW IT'S GETTING BOOTED FROM THE S&P 100

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Plus, it wasn't just executives taking the stage Tuesday. Caitlin Clark, reigning NBA MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Olympic gold medalist Sha'Carri Richardson were among the athletes Nike showcased at its headquarters.

What's more, given how long it took Nike to get Clark's signature shoe to market, the company revealed that the Caitlin 1 was the largest women's signature shoe launch in its history.

Turns out there's quite a market for celebrating athletic excellence.

That's not to say Nike should abandon its pursuit of cultural relevance. But there is a difference between shaping culture and fighting a culture war. Nike was at its best when it was doing the former.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

I miss that Nike. And for the first time in a while, I'm optimistic we're getting it back.

What are your thoughts on Nike's plan? Let us know at matthew.calkins@outkick.com

A homeowner’s lucrative rental property investment within an affluent Pacific Northwest community was allegedly hijacked by the very property manager he hired, sparking a months-long squatter standoff that ended with a $1 deed, a shooting on the property and the manager behind bars.

Ellis Cameron shared his story with Fox News Digital and says he hired Junior Patrick Adelbai to manage property he purchased and renovated in Edgewood, Washington. Instead of managing the rental, the homeowner said the alleged squatter decided to move his family in, causing a months-long legal battle for the homeowner and making him unable to sell it.

The homeowner intended to have Adelbai rent out the property for $6,500 a month. After the pair reached an agreement, Cameron changed the locks to prep it for renters.

SQUATTER NIGHTMARE TURNS DC APARTMENT BUILDING INTO 'DRUG HAVEN' AS LEGAL BATTLE DRAGS ON: 'THERE'S NO HELP'

"The very next day, he broke the locks, went into the house, and brought his wife and his two kids, and instead of doing [things] according to our agreement, he decided that he would just squat there, live there for free."

The homeowner said Adelbai moved his family in and lived in the house without running water for nearly two months – and made a mess of the inside and outside of the property, as depicted in a series of photos he shared with Fox News Digital.

NYC LANDLORD PLEADS FOR HELP AS '9-YEAR-SQUATTER' CONTINUES TO DRAIN HIM DRY IN COURT SAGA: 'TWILIGHT ZONE'

Cameron said he was left paying the mortgage without the rental income he was anticipating to cover the payments.

He asked the family to leave on numerous occasions, enlisting the help of law enforcement at times, but was told the dispute was a "civil matter" that would have to be resolved through the court system.

'TOXIC COCKTAIL' OF RENTER PROTECTIONS DESTROYED $39M AFFORDABLE HOUSING INVESTMENT AS DEM CITIES FOLLOW SUIT

"You have squatter-friendly laws that protect the squatters," Cameron said. "In Washington state, especially Pierce County, it's a high-risk agreement to decide to rent your place out because if something doesn't go right, it's going to be problematic for you. In Washington state, you can't turn off the squatters' utilities, you can't threaten them."

ALLEGED MALIBU SERIAL SQUATTER FEATURED IN NEW DOCUSERIES AFTER YEARS OF HOMEOWNER COMPLAINTS

State law says landlords cannot evict tenants on their own. Instead, they must notify law enforcement, give proper notice and let courts handle the removal.

Making matters worse, the homeowner said Adelbai's wife weaponized law enforcement against him when he tried to show the home in hopes of selling it.

"She held my place sabotaged for months because the law protected her," he said.

HOMEOWNERS TERRORIZED BY PRO SQUATTERS TURNING DREAMS INTO NIGHTMARES IN PALM-LINED PARADISE, EXPERTS SAY

Cameron went on to say, "I had a real estate agent [give] a 48-hour notice to the squatter, and she called the police when [the agent] showed up and [she told police] she didn't want to show the place."

The situation reached a breaking point when Adelbai allegedly shot at someone on the property in March, claiming self-defense while simultaneously claiming he was the homeowner, Cameron said.

HIS HOME CHANGED HANDS FOR $5. COULD IT HAPPEN TO YOUR FAMILY?

The situation escalated March 19, when records show a quitclaim deed prepared and signed by Adelbai was filed with the Pierce County Auditor’s Office, KIRO7 reported.

Adelbai claimed he owned the property in the document and transferred ownership to his wife, Karmaleen Issac, for $1.

ARIZONA MAN SAYS HE LOST $475K HOME TO HOA FORECLOSURE OVER LESS THAN $1,000 IN UNPAID DUES

When asked how a fraudulent deed could be approved, the Pierce County Auditor’s Office told Fox News Digital that their hands are tied by state law, which dictates that they cannot legally refuse to record a document—or assess its legality—as long as it meets basic formatting criteria.

"Title fraud is devastating, and the law needs to change. More protection is needed in Washington state and nationwide," Pierce County Auditor Linda Farmer said.

FLORIDA REAL ESTATE SEES SURGE FROM WASHINGTON HIGH EARNERS FLEEING NEW MILLIONAIRE INCOME TAX

The auditor's office noted they are currently co-chairing a statewide workgroup tracking national models to propose new measures to the Washington State Legislature. In the interim, Pierce County has launched a free "Owner Alert" service, which notifies homeowners of suspicious filings so they can take rapid legal action. Over 7,000 residents have already signed up.

Meanwhile, Adelbai is currently in jail with a list of pending charges. The Pierce County Sheriff's Office confirmed the suspect's arrest to Fox News Digital, but did not provide details into the incident or shooting.

Cameron said following the arrest, the family moved out – and left the home behind in a state of disrepair.

He said, "Florida's laws changed to get the squatters out and they [are] not only getting them out of there, but they [are] charging them criminally for squatting."

He went on to say, "They have the tougher laws there."

World.title: Popular cruise ship rocked by illness outbreak as nearly 150 passengers and crew fall victim
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Caribbean cruise has taken an uncomfortable turn for nearly 150 passengers and crew members who have fallen sick with stomach illness symptoms — with an infectious disease expert providing important insight into a very "common" issue.

A total of 148 people aboard Princess Cruises' Caribbean Princess — 134 passengers and 14 crew members — have reported the symptoms, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The ship departed Nov. 11 and is not scheduled to return until Nov. 23. It is carrying 2,936 passengers and 1,132 crew members, the CDC said.

HIGHLY CONTAGIOUS NOROVIRUS SPREADS ON CRUISE SHIP, SICKENING OVER 100 PASSENGERS AND CREW

Its 12-night round-trip voyage from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, includes scheduled stops in Aruba, Colombia, the Panama Canal, Costa Rica and Grand Cayman, according to the ship's itinerary.

Princess Cruises reported the outbreak to the CDC's Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) on Nov. 15. It also confirmed the situation in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Princess Cruises can confirm that a limited number of guests aboard Caribbean Princess have reported mild gastrointestinal illness," the company said in its statement.

"Our crew responded promptly by implementing enhanced sanitation protocols across the ship, including comprehensive cleaning and disinfection measures."

It concluded, "While most guests remain unaffected, we are continuing to closely monitor the situation."

Test results are still pending, and the CDC said it is monitoring the ship's cleaning efforts and response.

Those affected have experienced vomiting and diarrhea, though health officials have not yet determined what caused the illness.

In response, the CDC said the cruise line and crew have taken several steps to limit the spread of illness on board.

CRUISE BUFFET GUESTS FACE SURPRISE CHARGES FOR TAKING FOOD BACK TO CABINS

Those steps include more frequent cleaning and disinfecting, keeping sick passengers and crew members away from others, and working with health officials on cleaning procedures and reporting cases.

Crew members also collected stool samples from sick individuals to help identify the cause of the outbreak, the agency said.

Test results are still pending, and the CDC said it is monitoring the ship's cleaning efforts and response.

Fox News Digital reached out to the CDC for further details.

Health officials say it can take time to figure out what is making people sick on a cruise ship. While norovirus is a common cause of stomach illnesses on cruise ships, the CDC said it is not always clear what is causing an outbreak when it's first reported.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

The agency also noted that the 148 cases of illness were reported over the course of the trip so far — so not everyone became sick at the same time.

To help prevent stomach illnesses, the CDC recommends washing hands often, especially after using the bathroom and before eating.

‘Very, very common’

"This is not the first time we've seen this with cruise ships," said Dr. Tyler Evans, an adult infectious diseases and addiction medicine physician who is also CEO, founder and chief medical officer for Wellness Equity Alliance in California.

"Cruise ships, I often say, are sort of floating Petri dishes. They're these massive congregate facilities on the sea."

CLICK HERE TO 

He said gastrointestinal illnesses on ships are "very, very common." A main reason is the food, he said — especially buffet set-ups, he noted.

For anyone connected to this particular incident, he said individuals should look for "any sudden onset of vomiting and watery diarrhea. I know it's not glamorous to talk about," he added, "but if you are on the toilet more than five times a day, that is definitely an indication this is not normal and should be checked out by a primary care provider."

Those with at-risk health conditions, particularly older adults, should be seen very promptly by doctors, he also said.

Pregnant women as well as children need to be treated urgently as well, he said.

Other cruise ships report similar illnesses

The Caribbean Princess outbreak comes as other cruise ships have also reported similar illnesses this year.

In March, 65 passengers and 11 crew members fell ill aboard Holland America's Westerdam during a February voyage in Asia, Fox News Digital previously reported.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Those affected reported diarrhea, vomiting and fever. Tests conducted by the ship's lab found that stool samples from seven patients were positive for norovirus.

Health officials in Hong Kong boarded the ship on March 1 to investigate the outbreak.

The cruise line said it increased cleaning and disinfection efforts, while authorities inspected the vessel before allowing new passengers and crew members to board.

Jessica Mekles of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

World.title: Trump urges nuclear arms control in historic meeting with Putin and Xi
World.content:
SHENZHEN, China — It’s unclear what decisions may come from this historic meeting.

But the spectacle of President Donald Trump’s meeting with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping may be what delivers the defining image.

On Thursday, Trump, Putin and Xi met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen. Sitting around a huge, doughnut-shaped table at the Kylin Villa resort were leaders of three of the world’s most powerful nations: the U.S. with its largest economy, Russia with its biggest nuclear arsenal, and China its largest standing army and manufacturing sector.

“We are really making history,” Trump said.

The sight of Trump expressing such warmth toward two authoritarian strongmen will have left many American allies outside the room dismayed. After Trump called Putin his “friend,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted to X, “God, protect us from such friends.” Russia has invaded Ukraine and waged a yearslong campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and misinformation against the West.

Others were concerned about the prospect of a “Yalta 2.0,” a reprise of the 1945 Yalta Conference in which the U.S., Britain and the then-Soviet Union met to carve up the postwar world.

After Thursday’s meeting finished, Russia and China issued a brief statement that was light on detail or major announcements. The U.S. did not immediately release a version.

The “China-Russia-U.S. Declaration on Peace” agreed to “reform” the United Nations “so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges.” (Russia and China have long sought to shift the body away from Western human rights concerns, while Trump has been a strident critic of the world body.) The declaration agreed to boost the production and supply of petroleum products, which have been disrupted by the Ukraine and Iran wars, and it rebuked the International Criminal Court not to abuse its power. (The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Putin.)

The final point was that the leaders vowed to take steps to avoid nuclear war, although no specifics were mentioned.

The last remaining treaty between Washington and Moscow, New START, lapsed in February, but China, which has a far smaller nuclear arsenal than the other two, has resisted calls to be included in a new agreement.

“As the world’s three largest nuclear powers, by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” Trump said in the public section of the meeting.

“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard to not have them, it’s very hard to give them up,” he added. “That’s the way life works.”

World.title: Sen. Elissa Slotkin fires back at DOJ official’s ‘sham’ investigation
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A Democratic senator repeatedly targeted by the Trump administration for potential prosecution due to her political remarks is firing back at a Trump-appointed Justice Department official over what she called a “baseless” inquiry into her rhetoric about congressional oversight.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., is one of five Democratic members of Congress who have been the subject of letters that the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, Aaron Reitz, has posted on social media. In one of the letters, which have come under scrutiny from legal experts, Reitz suggested that Slotkin’s comments about congressional oversight potentially acting as a “deterrence message” to people considering joining the Trump administration could amount to a criminal civil rights offense.

“I made those statements consistent with my basic right to freedom of speech, a right that every American enjoys under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution,” Slotkin wrote Wednesday in a letter to Reitz obtained by NBC News. “In addition to my First Amendment rights, as a United States Senator, oversight is an important constitutional responsibility.”

“The Constitution’s Speech or Debate clause bars prosecution of a legislator for conducting an investigation or performing other legislative acts,” she wrote. “As such, your threat of investigation is baseless, and you should withdraw your letter immediately.”

Slotkin went on to say that Reitz’s “public threats” violated Justice Department policy, and that his decision to publicly post the letter rather than providing it to her, her attorney or the Senate legal counsel “is evidence that your threat of investigation is more about publicity and your political ambitions than any sort of legitimate inquiry.”

Reitz, 39, previously worked as chief of staff for Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and became U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas over the summer after placing fourth in the Republican primary for state attorney general.

Reitz also posted letters on X to Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif.

He told NBC News this week that he was “not interested in chilling free speech.”

Aaron Reitz on Capitol Hill last year. Chip Somodevilla / Getty

Slotkin and five other sitting Democratic lawmakers were separately targeted by the Trump administration earlier this year over a video they posted to social media that sought to remind members of the military and intelligence communities that they should not obey unlawful orders. Allies of the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, tried to indict the six Democrats for their speech in that video, but federal grand jurors unanimously rejected the indictment attempt.

Slotkin’s attorney, Preet Bharara, had previously written a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche cautioning him against following President Donald Trump’s public instruction to look into Slotkin’s political speech, which he dubbed a “criminal act.”

Blanche has conceded that Slotkin’s words alone were “absolutely not a crime” and said at a press conference last week that there were “no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said.”

Slotkin wrote in her letter that Reitz appeared to be “seeking attention” for himself and the Justice Department, or was “unaware” of basic constitutional rights.

“Given all of this, your threats are frivolous and a violation of your ethical duties as an attorney,” she wrote. “I reserve all rights to take appropriate actions in the future as it relates to this sham investigation.”

World.title: Takeaways from the Trump-Xi-Putin summit and ‘GTA VI’ launches to rave reviews: Morning Rundown
World.content:
Trump touts his friendships with China’s Xi and Russia’s Putin at a historic three-way summit. Workers whose employers dropped GLP-1 coverage scramble to pay out-of-pocket costs. And the highly anticipated “GTA VI” goes on sale.

Here’s what to know today.

Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic summit

President Donald Trump has wrapped up historic three-way talks with the leaders of U.S. rivals, Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping.

This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox.

What these three men might decide has the potential to reverberate across the globe. But the spectacle of Trump’s meeting with Putin and Xi, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, may be what delivers the defining image.

Sitting around the table were three of the world’s most powerful leaders: The U.S. with its largest economy, Russia its biggest nuclear arsenal, and China its largest standing army and manufacturing sector. “We are really making history,” Trump said before the talks began.

Trump called Xi and Putin “friends,” but it was unclear what exactly had been accomplished during the 90-minute meeting. Still, comparisons have already been drawn with the Yalta Conference of 1945, in which President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin sat down to carve up the postwar world.

Trump focused on calling for new curbs on nuclear weapons, after the last remaining nuclear treaty between Washington and Moscow lapsed this year, and China, whose arsenal is smaller than that of the other two, has resisted calls to be involved in a new one.

The Russian leader said it was up to them to “strengthen the system of international law” (Russia has been accused of war crimes in Ukraine) as well as work on issues such as food and energy security. Xi meanwhile stuck to broader themes.

Post-summit identical statements released by China and Russia — but not yet the U.S. — also called for the three countries to increase their energy production and supply, which would fuel Russia’s oil-driven war economy.

As well as nuclear issues, the leaders said they would discuss Iran, economics and trade. But the optics of the meeting, the diplomatic ballet of three strongmen leaders operating in close quarters, was just as gripping to foreign policy observers.

Takeaways from the summit.

Follow the latest news and analysis on our liveblog.

Related coverage:

In an exclusive interview with NBC News’ Richard Engel, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the U.S. and China could end the war in Ukraine if they “put sanctions, or will say that they will put sanctions, stop export-import trade” with Russia.

Workers scramble as employers cut GLP-1s from health coverage

Jacob Hege for NBC News

Workers signing up for next year’s health insurance plans might notice a glaring difference, as an increasing number of employers cut coverage for GLP-1s for weight loss. An industry survey shows the share of companies providing insurance coverage for the medication fell from 72% last year to 60% this year. Among the companies that have recently ended insurance coverage or will do so in 2026 are Starbucks, UPS, PepsiCo and Comcast, the parent company of NBC News.

Caitlin Mendoza, a Starbucks employee who has lost 60 pounds, said she faces a monthly bill of $299. Her doctor said the only way her insurance would cover the medication is if she developed diabetes. Doctors and advocates for patients who spoke to NBC News pointed out the double standard for patients with obesity, with one advocate saying “we just don’t see that happen to other people living with different conditions.”

Why it’s easier for employers to cut GLP-1 coverage.

‘Grand Theft Auto’ is back

The 13-year wait is over. “GTA VI” is live, welcoming gamers to Miami-inspired Vice City. As of Tuesday, the game had sold nearly 16 million copies, earning Rockstar Games more than 1.5 billion, one analysis found. And it has already garnered rave reviews, scoring 99/100 on Metacritic.

For the first time, players will be allowed to toggle between the perspectives of the game’s main characters, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos. Completing the game’s missions will likely take 50 hours, according to the publication Insider Gaming, though it’ll likely be closer to 200 hours if you want to achieve “platinum” status. And that doesn’t include time players can spend in the game’s world doing activities like working out, gambling, petting animals, robbing banks or jetskiing.

So, don’t be surprised if you don’t hear from your loved ones (or employees) today — or maybe for a few weeks.

Here’s what else to know about GTA VI, and follow our live blog for reactions and updates.

Elon Musk says he is ‘not MAGA’

Elon Musk spent nearly $500 million in contributions to Republican campaigns and allies of President Donald Trump in the lead-up to the midterm elections — but he’s “not MAGA,” he insisted. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO’s remarks were made while he was in China as part of Trump’s delegation at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

“I’m not MAGA,” Musk said in an interview for the New York Times DealBook Summit. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.” Musk also said he expected Democrat Gina Hinojosa to be “quite moderate” when she takes office as Texas governor. He also claimed to spend big on campaigns because “it’s good to have some balance of power.”

Read more about Musk’s comments.

More politics news:

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries won House Democrats’ nomination for speaker, putting him on track to be the first Black lawmaker elected to the position. A full House vote will be held on Jan. 3.

Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin fired back at a Trump-appointed DOJ official over what she called a “baseless” inquiry into her comments about congressional oversight.

World.title: Trump, Xi and Putin sit down for rare 3-way meeting in China
World.content:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down for a meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday — a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries.

All three made brief opening statements before meeting behind closed doors for about an hour and a half. The leaders did not offer joint or separate statements to reporters after the sit-down, and Mr. Trump immediately left for the airport to return home.

Putin's senior aid Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it said was a statement jointly agreed on by all three leaders characterizing the talks.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, center, President Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin take part in a meeting at Kylin Villa, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 19, 2026. Mandel NGAN/AFP/Getty

The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the Kremlin readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."

They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the "International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."

Finally, the Russian government said the leaders had "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."

The White House did not offer an immediate readout of the meeting, but indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.

The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.

Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.

"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."

As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."

Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."

After the trilateral talks, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.

"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."

Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.

Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."

Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."

He said he intended to discuss ending the Ukraine war with Xi and Putin.

Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons, with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.

Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program, ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year.

China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi, however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."

The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.

A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence.

President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping arrive for the plenary meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. Ng Han Guan/POOL/AFP via Getty

The summit is taking place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang, whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."

Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed, is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.

Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.

Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence.

"We do not want to do anything to destroy the tremendous potential of this technology," he said. "We have to watch it, we have to be careful, we have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements."

Beyond AI, the U.S. and China have sought to stabilize their economic relationship over the last year, following a tit-for-tat trade war that sent tariffs above 100% in 2025. A tariff truce between the two countries is set to expire on Jan. 10 of next year.

Mr. Trump said in his APEC speech the U.S. is committed to "growth and stability" in the Asia-Pacific region, and argued the American economy is "thriving like it has never thrived before." He also said the U.S. is negotiating "numerous trade agreements" and expects to sign some agreements with APEC members in the near future.

During Xi's remarks earlier in the session, the Chinese leader called on countries in the region to "look out for each other" and "expand our shared interests," including on free trade and economic growth.

President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping after leaders posed for a group photo during the summit on Nov. 19, 2026. Greg Baker/POOL/AFP via Getty

Foreign conflicts loom large during the Trump-Putin-Xi talks. Iran is one contentious area, given China's status as one of the largest customers of Iranian oil, and Russia's ties with Iran.

The White House previously said the war in Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said he expected the issue to come up, calling it "my favorite subject."

Taiwan is another frequent discussion topic between the U.S. and China. During the U.S. president's visit to Beijing in the spring, Xi reportedly delivered a stern warning about the island, which he has long vowed to reintegrate with mainland China, floating potential "clashes and even conflicts" if the issue isn't "handled properly."

And Mr. Trump was expected to press Xi to release two detained Americans during his visit to China, CBS News has reported. Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release.

World.title: Does your credit card already provide travel insurance? Here's how to tell
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

Your credit card could provide valuable travel insurance benefits, potentially saving you money on coverage. d3sign/Getty Images

Travel can get expensive long before you ever reach your destination. Between the high cost of airfare, hotel reservations, rental cars and other prepaid expenses, even a relatively short trip out of town can require a substantial financial commitment upfront. And when something goes wrong with your travel plans, whether it's a canceled flight, lost luggage or an unexpected medical emergency, the resulting costs can add up quickly.

That's one reason travel insurance can be worth adding to your vacation or travel budget. A travel insurance policy can help protect the money you've invested in a trip while providing financial assistance when unexpected disruptions occur. But purchasing a separate travel policy adds another expense to an already costly undertaking, and in some cases, travelers may be paying for protections that they already have access to.

In fact, certain credit cards come with travel insurance benefits that cardholders may not even realize exist. Depending on the credit card, those benefits could provide coverage without requiring a separate insurance purchase. However, the protections can vary significantly, and understanding exactly whether your card offers coverage, and what it covers, is essential before relying on it for your next trip.

Compare your top travel insurance options and protect your trip today.

How to tell if your credit card already provides travel insurance

Not every credit card offers travel insurance, and even cards that advertise travel protections may only cover certain situations. Here's how to determine whether your card provides coverage and what that coverage actually includes:

Check your credit card's benefits guide

The easiest place to start is your credit card's guide to benefits, which typically outlines the insurance protections available to cardholders. You can usually find this document through your card issuer's website or via your online account. Look for a section labeled "travel benefits," "travel protection" or "insurance benefits." Depending on the credit card, you may find you have coverage for:

Trip cancellation and interruption: This coverage offers reimbursement for eligible prepaid, nonrefundable travel expenses if you must cancel or cut a trip short for a covered reason.

This coverage offers reimbursement for eligible prepaid, nonrefundable travel expenses if you must cancel or cut a trip short for a covered reason. Trip delay: This type of coverage offers reimbursement for certain additional expenses, such as meals or lodging, when a covered delay exceeds the required waiting period.

This type of coverage offers reimbursement for certain additional expenses, such as meals or lodging, when a covered delay exceeds the required waiting period. Baggage delay or loss: This is coverage for qualifying purchases when luggage is delayed or reimbursement when belongings are lost or damaged.

This is coverage for qualifying purchases when luggage is delayed or reimbursement when belongings are lost or damaged. Rental car coverage: With rental car coverage, you get protection against certain theft or collision-related costs when renting an eligible vehicle.

With rental car coverage, you get protection against certain theft or collision-related costs when renting an eligible vehicle. Travel accident insurance: This coverage offers benefits for certain serious injuries or accidental deaths involving covered travel.

Some premium credit cards offer several of these protections, while others provide only one or two.

Learn more about the travel insurance options available to you now.

Call your card issuer to confirm your coverage

If your credit card benefits guide leaves questions unanswered, contact the number on the back of your credit card and ask about your travel insurance protections. Request clarification about which benefits are active, who qualifies for coverage and whether your upcoming trip meets the eligibility requirements.

It's also worth asking how claims are handled. Some benefits are administered by third-party insurance providers rather than the card issuer itself, and you'll generally need documentation to receive reimbursement. Getting these details before departure can help prevent costly surprises later.

What else to know about credit card travel insurance coverage

If your credit card includes travel insurance, there are often important restrictions and limitations to understand before you rely on those benefits. Here's what to consider:

Find out whether you need to book with your card

Having travel insurance benefits doesn't automatically mean every trip you take is covered. Many credit card protections require you to pay for some or all of the eligible travel expenses using that specific card.

For example, trip cancellation coverage may require you to charge at least part of your transportation costs to the card, while rental car coverage generally requires you to pay for the rental with the card and decline the rental company's collision damage waiver. Certain credit cards may also extend coverage to eligible trips booked using rewards points, though the requirements vary.

So, before booking any travel, take time to review the payment requirements carefully. Otherwise, you could discover that your card's travel insurance doesn't apply when you need it.

Review the coverage limits and exclusions

If your card provides travel insurance, the coverage may be more limited than what you'd receive through a standalone policy. For example, a credit card might reimburse up to a specified amount for trip cancellation, but only when the cancellation results from an explicitly covered event, such as certain illnesses or severe weather conditions. Credit card travel insurance also regularly excludes situations involving preexisting medical conditions, certain high-risk activities or changes in travel plans made for personal reasons.

And, one particularly important distinction involves medical coverage. Many credit cards don't provide comprehensive emergency medical insurance or medical evacuation benefits, which can be especially important when traveling internationally. That's why it's important to check the maximum reimbursement amounts, covered reasons, exclusions and claim-filing deadlines before deciding whether your existing benefits are sufficient.

Compare your benefits with standalone travel insurance

Once you understand what your credit card covers, compare those protections with the coverage available through a separate travel insurance policy. Pay particular attention to medical emergencies, evacuation expenses, trip cancellation limits and coverage for circumstances your credit card excludes.

If your card already provides substantial protection for a relatively inexpensive domestic trip, purchasing additional insurance might offer limited value. However, an expensive international vacation or a trip involving significant nonrefundable expenses may warrant broader coverage.

The bottom line

Your credit card could already provide valuable travel insurance benefits, potentially saving you money on coverage you would otherwise purchase separately. But those protections aren't universal, and the eligibility requirements, exclusions and reimbursement limits can make a significant difference in how useful they are. Before purchasing a standalone policy, take a few minutes to review your card's benefits and identify any gaps. That way, you can avoid paying twice for overlapping protections while making sure you're adequately covered if your travel plans go wrong.

World.title: Are CDs worth it? When they beat savings and money market accounts
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

Each interest-bearing account comes with different trade-offs related to returns, flexibility and access to your cash. Andrii Yalanskyi/Getty Images

Right now, savers have an important decision to make about where to keep their money. Interest rates on certificates of deposit (CDs), high-yield savings accounts and money market accounts remain competitive, giving them a few ways to earn meaningful returns without taking on significant risk. But opting for the account with the highest advertised rate isn't necessarily the best strategy to use, particularly when the interest rate environment could change over the coming months.

That's because each interest-bearing account option comes with different trade-offs related to returns, flexibility and access to your cash. CDs, for example, offer something that variable-rate savings accounts generally can't: the ability to lock in a guaranteed return for a set period. Whether that advantage makes a CD worth opening, though, depends on when you'll need your money, what other accounts are paying and how much flexibility you're willing to sacrifice.

Find out how much you could earn with the right CD account today.

CDs vs. savings, money market accounts and Treasury bills

CDs, high-yield savings accounts, money market accounts and Treasury bills can all help you earn interest while limiting risk. However, they differ in several ways, which could have an impact on which option makes the most sense for your savings goals.



CD High-yield savings Money market account Treasury bills Top rates Up to 5.00% APY Up to 4.27% APY Up to 4.17% APY 4.01% to 4.50% investment yield Access to money Early withdrawal usually triggers a penalty Withdraw anytime Withdraw anytime; some offer checks or debit cards Hold 4 to 52 weeks or sell early Rate lock Fixed for the term Variable Variable Fixed return at maturity Taxes Federal and state Federal and state Federal and state Federal only; exempt from state and local taxes Protection FDIC/NCUA insured up to applicable limits FDIC/NCUA insured up to applicable limits FDIC/NCUA insured up to applicable limits Backed by the U.S. government

Rates reflect selected competitive offers and recent Treasury auctions as of October 28–29, 2026. Treasury yields are not APYs, and rates vary by term and institution.

Compare your top CD account options and find the right fit now.

CD vs. high-yield savings account

The biggest difference when comparing a CD versus a high-yield savings account is flexibility. A CD guarantees your rate throughout its term, while a savings account allows withdrawals without an early withdrawal penalty but pays a variable rate. As a general rule, emergency savings belong in a high-yield savings account so it's readily accessible, while money earmarked for a specific future expense may be better suited for a CD.

CD vs. money market account

Money market accounts offer interest rates that are comparable to high-yield savings accounts, but often come with check-writing privileges or debit card access. However, some money market accounts require higher minimum balances to earn their best rates or avoid fees. A CD, on the other hand, generally makes more sense when you don't need frequent access to your money and want to earn predictable returns.

CD vs. Treasury bills

Treasury bills offer another low-risk alternative, with an important tax advantage: Their interest is exempt from state and local income taxes. That means a Treasury bill could provide a better after-tax return than a CD offering a slightly higher rate, particularly for residents of high-tax states.

CD vs. bonds

Bonds can offer higher yields than CDs, depending on the type and risk. However, bond prices fluctuate, meaning you could lose money if you sell before maturity. With an insured CD, your principal is protected within FDIC or NCUA coverage limits, although withdrawing before maturity generally results in an interest penalty.

When a CD makes sense

CDs can be particularly valuable when you want predictable earnings and can comfortably leave your deposit untouched. You may want to consider opening one if:

You have a known expense coming up: A CD that matures before a home down payment or tuition bill can help you earn interest until the money is needed.

You expect interest rates to fall: Locking in a competitive rate protects your returns if banks subsequently reduce their savings account yields.

You struggle to leave savings untouched: Early withdrawal penalties can discourage unnecessary spending.

You're approaching retirement: CDs can provide predictable returns on money you'll need in the relatively near future, without exposing it to stock market volatility.

When a CD doesn't make sense

Despite their advantages, CDs aren't always the best place for your savings. You may want to consider alternatives if:

You're building an emergency fund: Unexpected expenses require quick access to cash without penalties.

You might need the money early: Withdrawing before maturity could erase a meaningful portion of your interest earnings.

You expect rates to rise: Locking into today's rate could mean missing better offers later.

You're investing for long-term growth: Stocks generally offer greater growth potential over longer periods, although they carry substantially more risk.

Inflation exceeds your CD rate: Even with guaranteed interest, your money could lose purchasing power if inflation outpaces your returns.

How to get the most from a CD

To maximize your earnings, compare offers from online banks and credit unions, which frequently pay more than traditional banks, and review the latest best CD rates to see what's available. You can also explore what constitutes a good CD rate and consider building a CD ladder, which spreads your deposits across different maturity dates to provide regular access to your money without sacrificing the benefits of fixed rates.

World.title: Anthropic's IPO set for blastoff in key test for AI boom
World.content:
Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector.

"This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at investment bank Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."

Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. ET.

What the stock price will tell us

In an announcement on Wednesday night, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 each.

The company said that 956,351,354 shares are being sold by Anthropic. The remaining shares are being sold by certain selling stockholders, from which Anthropic said it will not receive any proceeds.

Sources told CBS News before the announcement that Anthropic would likely price its shares above $80 due to strong demand.

The company also plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.

The market debut is expected to value Anthropic at up to $1.5 trillion, short of the $2 trillion valuation that some IPO experts projected earlier this year. Still, the AI developer — which launched only in 2021 — is on track to stage what could become the second-largest IPO ever. Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $75 billion and was valued at roughly $1.7 trillion when it went public in June.

Kennedy thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading, an increase that would represent a "solid pop," he said. If the stock rises closer to $140, "that would tell me that AI enthusiasm has come roaring back," he added.

Great expectations

Although many investors appear eager to own a piece of Anthropic, the IPO comes amid growing concerns about whether the torrid spending on AI will deliver the expected productivity and profit boom.

AI-related stocks have fluctuated in recent weeks following subpar earnings and the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance data center construction. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors, with the chipmaker's stock now down more than 35% from its October all-time high.

"The whole AI sector has sold off from its July peak. Investor enthusiasm was greatest then," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, told CBS News.

Although Anthropic has yet to turn a profit, the company has shown explosive revenue growth over its short time in business. Anthropic raked in nearly $17 billion in the third quarter this year, up 45% from the second quarter, a recent regulatory filing shows. Given that heady rate of expansion, Ritter expects Anthropic to reach profitability quickly.

To justify its projected trillion-dollar valuation, however, the company will need to sustain that momentum while operating under Wall Street's unsparing gaze. Compounding the challenge is how quickly the AI landscape itself is changing. For instance, Anthropic could struggle to maintain its growth rate as consumers shift from pricier AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to cheaper open-source models, Ritter noted.

Anthropic also will have to spend heavily to keep developing its AI models and stay ahead of rivals, from OpenAI, Alphabet and Meta to Chinese platforms. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Meanwhile, the company has committed to spending nearly a trillion dollars on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045, according to a securities filing.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a Congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.

"The company is likely to be very successful, but the market is pricing in very lofty expectations," Ritter said. "It could be hard for management to execute."

Wall Street analysts said Anthropic's share offering has broader ramifications for the AI sector, with the IPO's pricing setting a benchmark for other tech companies planning to go public.

Even if Anthropic's stock soars on the first day of trading, it won't necessarily create a swarm of IPO activity, Kennedy said. Still, it could reinvigorate markets, he added.

Meanwhile, by going public, Anthropic is effectively asking investors to discount the threats that Anthropic founder Dario Amodei himself has identified as posed by AI. In September, he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after a former Anthropic researcher warned of the existential threat AI poses to humanity.

World.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, U.N. top court rules
World.content:
The Hague, Netherlands — In a landmark judgment, the United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.

International Court of Justice President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar "has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention."

The 15-judge panel of the World Court rejected Myanmar's defense that the 2017 campaign was a legitimate operation against insurgents.

Iwasawa said that "the court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers."

Judges led by International Court of Justice (ICJ) President Yuji Iwasawa preside over a hearing at the Peace Palace, the seat of the ICJ, in The Hague, Netherlands,on Nov. 19, 2026, as the court delivers its judgment in the case brought by Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority. Mouneb Taim / Anadolu via Getty Images

The decision marks the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide.

"This is a great day for the Rohingya, and it is a great day for all oppressed people, everywhere, who have been told that their suffering does not count and that no one is listening," said Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the court's ornate, wood-paneled Great Hall of Justice for the three-hour reading of the ruling.

The intent to destroy a group in whole or in part is a key element in establishing whether crimes amount to genocide under international law.

The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya.

The Muslim-majority African nation of Gambia launched the proceedings at the International Court of Justice in 2019, asking it to rule that Myanmar breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order the nation to end any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished.

The judgment comes as the World Court also is handling genocide allegations linked to the Gaza conflict and the war in Ukraine.

"Genocides have similarities in how they are committed so this decision will have an impact on other cases," said Melanie O'Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia.

In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.

Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya "in whole or in part."

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox's Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

Gambia has asked for reparations for the Rohingya, including ordering Myanmar to grant them full citizenship and the right to return home.

The court's rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.

In a previous judgment in 2007, the court said that Serbia "violated the obligation to prevent genocide" in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in the Bosnian town.

Judges at The Hague-based court have also been asked to weigh in on other allegations of genocide.

South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the Genocide Convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion.

Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya human rights activist who fled Myanmar as a young child with her mother in the 1990s, said the demands in the Myanmar case are rooted in her community's desire for recognition and dignity.

"Because so far, we've just been pushed around into this limbo state," she said. "It's been almost 10 years now that Rohingya have been living in very, very precarious conditions across the Asia-Pacific."

In March 2022, then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken said Myanmar's treatment olf the Rohingya amounted to genocide, in a declaration intended to generate international pressure and lay the groundwork for potential legal action.

"The day will come when those responsible for these appalling acts will have to answer for them," Blinken said at the time.

World.title: Obama gives pep talk to freshman House Democrats in surprise visit
World.content:
Washington — Groups of newly elected Democratic members of the House of Representatives rushed to board buses outside the Capitol on Wednesday bound for a meeting with a "special guest."

When they arrived at their destination, they learned the guest was none other than former President Barack Obama.

"I did not know who the special guest was, but I knew it was going to be someone special," Representative-Elect Johnny Garcia, of Texas, told CBS News. "And then obviously we get here, and we get to see it's President Obama!"

The meeting was arranged by House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, fresh off his nomination to become the next House speaker. If elected in January, he would make history as the first African American to serve in the role.

Former President Barack Obama and presumptive House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries at a suprise meeting with newly-elected House Democrats in Washington on Nov. 18, 2026. Hakeem Jeffries Instagram account (@repjeffries)

"We're excited about the opportunities that are in front of us to deliver big, meaningful bold progress to the American people," Jeffries said as he introduced Obama to cheers and chants of "four more years."

"I believe in the Constitution, people," Obama quipped.

The former President engaged in a broad discussion, moderated by Jeffries, about the challenges and opportunities of the next Congress. Obama addressed practical matters, like having robust constituent services, and bigger picture policy goals such as lowering costs, making health care more affordable, and creating accessible housing, his office said. He also told the freshman class he was deeply proud of them, and encouraged them to stay connected to their communities.

Representative-Elect Patty Garcia said the former president answered a "mix of questions" from new members including his advice to them, his message after this month's election victories, what the party can build on and immigration.

Garcia first met Obama when he was a senator and she was a student at the University of Illinois. The incoming congresswoman said the event with the former president was a "full circle" moment as she prepares to represent a Chicago-area district.

"I think being able to see him in different roles, and you know, very encouraging message, of you know, 'You all represent different constituencies, very diverse, and at the end of the day, you need to kind of find a common ground that can help deliver for everyone as much as possible and make an impact,'" Garcia said.

Texas Representative-Elect Katy Padilla Stout worked for the Obama administration as an intern at the Department of Education.

"I think it was just the pep talk everyone needed to come hear and remind us why we're here, who sent us here, and the importance of the work that we have here to do," Padilla Stout said.

Since leaving office, the former president has worked to lift up a new generation of leaders and relishes his role transitioning from player to coach, according to a source familiar with his thinking. He often counsels candidates and new members and welcomes opportunities to serve as a sounding board for those entering public service.

"He said, you know, he thinks everyone who plays a part in American history, it's like a relay and you're always, you know, passing it off to the next generation," Padilla Stout said. "He did denote that like half the people that came through were like, 'You're the first person I voted for!' ... He was like, 'It just makes me really proud to know that we planted those seeds and they're coming to fruition."

New York Representative-Elect Claire Valdez said Obama offered a unifying message even as the party faces divisions over its leadership. The Democratic Socialist was one of 11 members who voted against Jeffries for speaker but noted "we're in ongoing negotiations and continuing to have meetings with him."

"What is unifying for our freshman class is taking money out of politics, taking on corruption, taking on corporate greed, and really fighting for an economy that works for working people," Valdez told CBS News. "And I think that's something that's really unifying from people who are from, you know, Montana to Tennessee to Texas to New York."

She said the former President shook "every single incoming member's hand" calling it a "beautiful" gesture.

As Michigan's Christina Hines exited the event, she described it in one word.

"Life-changing."

World.title: Danish lawmakers OK Greenland security deal with U.S.
World.content:
Copenhagen — Denmark's parliament on Thursday unanimously approved a hard-wrought agreement with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.

The vote follows months of pressure by President Trump seeking to control Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of Denmark, a NATO ally.

The trilateral deal among Mr. Trump and Danish and Greenlandic leaders paves the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eases tensions over Mr. Trump's repeated calls for the vast, mineral-rich island to become part of the U.S.

The 109-0 vote in the Folketing amounts to a final step: The deal was expected to enter into force once Denmark and Greenland had signed on.

Denmark Foreign Minister Lars Loekke Rasmussen at the first of two readings of an agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S., at Christiansborg Castle, in Copenhagen, Denmark, on Nov. 12, 2026. Thomas Traasdahl / Ritzau Scanpix via AP

Greenland's parliament approved the deal earlier this month, also with no opposition.

The deal isn't technically a treaty so doesn't need a green light from the U.S. Senate.

The text of the agreement says it will become effective once Denmark and Greenland inform the U.S. "in a diplomatic note" indicating that their parliaments had completed all necessary steps.

The U.S. ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the "strong support" in the Danish parliament for ratification of the deal "paving the way for it to enter into force."

"The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernizes our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of NATO," he wrote on X.

The aim is to bolster the U.S. military presence on Greenland but keep the self-governing island under Danish control. It would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.

Mr. Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed the deal in September in New York, after months of quiet, behind-the-scenes negotiations to address his security concerns and Danish and Greenlandic fears of a possible U.S. takeover.

Under the deal, which builds on a defense agreement dating to 1951, the United States can expand its military presence on the island and "modernize and expand" its activities at the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest.

The U.S. can also set up "defense areas" at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east of Greenland, and can establish additional defense areas in the territory and strengthen its military operations or sites.

World.title: Top U.N. court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
World.content:
Top U.N. court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya

toggle caption i Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during its 2017 military operations in northern Rakhine State.

Delivering the judgment, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said the scale and nature of the military's actions went "well beyond what would be required to punish the population" and were instead "characteristic of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group."

toggle caption i JEROEN JUMELET/ANP/AFP via Getty Images

The judges estimated that around 815,000 Rohingya lived in northern Rakhine State before the operations, and concluded that around 10,000 were violently killed during the 2017 clearance campaign.

toggle caption i SALAHUDDIN AHMED/AFP via Getty Images

The court found that Myanmar's security forces "acted with genocidal intent." Judge Iwasawa said the operations were preceded by an atmosphere of anti-Rohingya hate speech, with the community portrayed as "sub-human" and "a violent threat."

This is a developing story that will be updated.

World.title: Yahoo for the loo! An ode to the commode! Dotty for the potty! It's World Toilet Day!
World.content:
Yahoo for the loo! An ode to the commode! Dotty for the potty! It's World Toilet Day!

toggle caption i John Poole/Ryan Kellman/NPR

Twenty-five years ago, Jack Sim was flush with excitement. (Please pardon the pun.)

The Singapore entrepreneur was looking for a meaningful project and came upon this thought from the prime minister: "He said we should measure our graciousness according to the cleanliness of our public toilets," Sim recalls.

Thus was born World Toilet Day. The goal was more than cleanliness. It was access, too — billions of people do not have a safe and sanitary toilet to use.

Enshrined as an official U.N. day in 2013, World Toilet Day aims to get people talking and thinking about a topic that maybe is a taboo in polite conversation.

toggle caption i NOAH SEELAM/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

Let's eschew the euphemisms

World Toilet Day is all about peeing, pooping and addressing menstrual hygiene in a clean and safe manner — followed by the "conveyance" of excreta to a sanitary disposal system, notes Kate Olive Medlicott , the sanitation and waste team leader within the WASH team at the World Health Organization. Human diseases are shed in sewage, so a top-notch sanitation system is critical, says Medlicott. Cholera is linked to sewage. Polio is, too.

Sponsor Message

This year's World Toilet Day theme is "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures." Even though everyone suffers when they can't find a toilet, the menstrual cycle creates additional complications. If schools or offices lack a safe and sanitary place to attend to period needs and to dispose of period products, girls and women may opt to stay home.

There is another gender issue. Sofia Calltorp , the U.N. Women global head of humanitarian action, says: "When women and girls do not have access to safe toilets," they leave their home and look for a public toilet or a secluded space to do their business, often venturing into unsafe areas. "There is a huge impact in terms of being exposed to harassment or violence," Calltorp says. She points to refugee camps as a place where this issue often arises, with unlit toilets that aren't differentiated by gender.

toggle caption i DefeatDD

toggle caption i Haag/ullstein bild/via Getty Images

toggle caption i Kristina Ketelsen

Now you might well ask: Has World Toilet Day made a difference?

The toilet titans we interviewed say yes, it has, just by talking about toilets in the public arena. The U.N. has stated that access to safe sanitation is a human right. And in just about every country, progress has been made in improving access to sanitary facilities. Since 2015, 1.2 billion people have become part of the world of safely managed sanitation systems.

Sponsor Message

What are the next steps? Kellogg Schwab , who specializes in water and wastewater contaminants of public health concern at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, stresses that governments should be a force for change but that it shouldn't be top down. It should also be … oh, forgive me again … bottom up. Schwab suggests giving money to communities to figure out what solutions they can come up with to improve the toilet and sanitation situation. There will be flops. But there will be successes that can be scaled up.

toggle caption i NurPhoto/via Getty Images



So maybe one day — Medlicott of WHO thinks in 50 years or so —- Earthlings will look back and say, How curious that in a world of wealth there were not enough safe and secure toilets.

A toast to toilets

Let's end by reflecting on the present day.

"World Toilet Day is my favorite day of the year," says Medlicott. "People find it fun and funny but it's really important to celebrate and act on something we take for granted."

If you're among the population where toilets are plentiful, she suggests pausing to think of a moment — it's happened to all of us — when you needed a bathroom and couldn't find one. Maybe that incident has turned into a funny story you share with friends. Now imagine if it were to happen every day.

I am deeply thankful that all I need to do is walk down the office hallway to find a clean and private loo.

World.title: Anthropic raises more than $100B in IPO. And, Dems nominate Jeffries for House speaker
World.content:
Anthropic raises more than $100B in IPO. And, Dems nominate Jeffries for House speaker

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has received the House Democrats' nomination to become speaker when the party regains the majority in the new year. This nomination, confirmed by a closed-door vote of 251 to 11, marks the start of the formal selection process for speaker. It will culminate in a House floor vote on Jan. 3, at the start of the new Congress. If successful, Jeffries will make history as the first Black Speaker of the House. Jeffries said after the closed door vote that he is committed to addressing cost-of-living issues, pledging to fight for lower costs in groceries, gas, housing and healthcare.

toggle caption i Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

🎧 Jeffries, who has served as the top Democrat in the minority since 2023, ran unopposed for the speaker position. But that is not the case in the Senate, NPR's Elena Moore tells Up First. Current minority leader Sen. Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen for majority leader. Van Hollen has positioned himself as an anti-status quo, progressive leader. Both Van Hollen and Schumer have served in Congress for decades. The vote for that Senate position is set for early December.
