World.title: Xi-Trump-Putin summit concludes with joint statement warning world bodies to not 'abuse their jurisdiction'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin released a joint statement following an unprecedented three-way meeting on Thursday in Shenzhen, urging reform at the UN, committing to increased fossil fuel production and warning that 'the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.'

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met for an unprecedented three-way meeting on Thursday, concluding their talks after more than an hour.

Earlier, the leaders of the world's biggest nuclear powers, sitting at a round table in a villa nestled among wooded hills beside a lake in the southern ‌Chinese city of Shenzhen, described their meeting as a historic moment.

Trump soon left for the Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport, where he engaged in a brief conversation with China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi before departing on Air Force One en route to Washington.

"We are really making history," Trump said at the onset of the trilateral meeting. "The three of us have a great deal to discuss."

"No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement."

Before their meeting, Trump met Xi and Putin separately, referring to both as friends.

China's President Xi Jinping, left, President Donald Trump, right, and Russia's President Vladimir Putin, centtre, hold a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Andres Martinez Casares/The Associated Press)

Leaders say UN needs reform

A joint statement was released after Xi, Trump and Putin met, in which the leaders "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought." The countries pledged to hold a dialogue on reducing nuclear risk and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

Other parts of the joint statement might make the leaders of European Union and NATO countries uneasy.

The three heads of state "concurred that the International Criminal Court (ICC) and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction," and said they were committed to reform of the United Nations so that it "can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security."

The United Nations Security Council is expected to hold another secret ballot this week to pick the next UN chief, ‌but after eight rounds of voting, the council’s five veto-wielding members have not agreed on a successor ahead of Antonio Guterres's last day on Dec. 31. France and Britain are the other two veto powers.

Trump, left, speaks during a meeting with Xi Jinping on Thursday. With Trump on the American side of the table are, from left to right, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. (Andres Martinez Casares/The Associated Press)

With respect to the ICC, the statement read that the leaders "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance." Putin faces an international arrest warrant from the ICC over the war in Ukraine.

While other U.S. administrations have criticized the Hague court, the Trump administration has unleashed a suite of sanctions on it, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying the U.S. wanted to "dismantle the ICC, piece by piece."

Finally, the three countries stressed the importance of stable energy flows and "plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations." Trump's decision to wage war on Iran with Israel on Feb. 28 has led to monthslong issues for commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, raising global oil prices.

Trump said both he and Xi felt strongly about oil having to flow through the Strait of Hormuz. Xi did not mention Ukraine or Iran in any of his remarks during the two-day summit.

Putin said the three countries have "numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine." Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, a war that has led to significant casualties and exchanged attacks on energy facilities and other infrastructure.

Putin, left, and Xi shake hands after the meeting with Trump. (Sergei Bobylev/The Associated Press)

Trump arrived in China after Xi and Putin delivered pointed speeches denouncing Western trade "protectionism" and sanctions.

During Thursday's APEC proceedings, Xi ​called for "free and open" trade. Western leaders say China's growth model favouring industrial strength over consumers is unfair and creates destabilizing global trade imbalances.

Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said Russia was key for ⁠food and energy security in the Asia-Pacific.

'A big win for us'

Trump's talks with Xi come after an extension of their trade truce this month, but also amid growing tension over reports of Nvidia chips being diverted to China through Southeast Asia, raising questions about the effectiveness of U.S. export curbs and the future of Chinese access to advanced technology.

Trump downplayed the allegations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy. Trump in the past two years has developed a close relationship with Huang, and both the president and his Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have faced questions over when they knew about the allegations, given weighty decisions that have been made by the White House over export controls on Nvidia chips.

Asked during an interview on Fox News what he hoped to accomplish at a trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin, Trump suggested he had already secured a victory simply in the way he was received in China.

He repeatedly pointed to Xi's unprecedented decision to greet him at the airport, the elaborate military welcome, thousands of spectators and even the seating chart at the banquet that put Trump at the head table as evidence of the strength of their relationship.

"That's a big win for us. It's a big win for China too. We get ​along," Trump said.

World.title: It's costing you less to fill up your gas tank. What's behind falling pump prices?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

No, your eyes aren't deceiving you — those sky-high gas prices are coming down across Canada.

The Canadian national average for gas prices sat at $1.514 per litre for Thursday, according to price tracking site affordableenergy.ca. That's down about seven cents compared to a week ago, and about 28 cents below the national average from 30 days ago, according to the tracking site.

In some provinces like Manitoba and Saskatchewan, those average prices are down by more than 30 cents compared to last month's average, according to GasBuddy petroleum analyst Patrick De Haan.

"In fact, in some areas of Calgary, we are seeing gas stations … below a dollar a litre again," De Haan said.

He says prices could still fall by another five or 10 cents a litre countrywide over the next few weeks — so long as there are no new developments with the U.S. war in Iran, which at some points all but shuttered traffic through the vital Strait of Hormuz, sending oil skyrocketing.

While gas prices are still higher than they were a year ago, they have recently been brought down largely due to more oil moving through the strait, as well as some seasonal factors, analysts say.

Tanker traffic through the strait has been ticking up in recent months, aided by U.S. military escorts through the waterway, according to Al Salazar, head of oil and gas research at Enverus. That has helped crude oil prices come down — a barrel of Brent crude oil is now priced just under $92 US, compared to about $116 US at a high point in mid-October.

Gas prices are pictured at 222.9¢ a litre at a gas station in New Westminster, B.C., on May 1. The oil shock brought on by the war in Iran has sent gas prices way up in recent months, in some cases far past $2 a litre. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

"The U.S. military, prior to the midterms, was really [helping] improve and defend the ships getting through the strait. So that's led to a bit of a glut," Salazar said.

The International Energy Agency also said last week that the world oil market could return to a surplus in the fourth quarter, as more oil is able to make it out of the Middle East.

Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump himself has taken a de-escalatory tone on the war. And expectations that Democrats could use their newfound power picked up in the midterms to block new strikes on Iran, encouraging oil prices to fall lower, Salazar said.

Seasonal factors are also giving the industry a lot of "breathing room," according to De Haan.

The seasonal switch to the cheaper "winter blend" gas is in effect , and refinery maintenance associated with the swap is wrapping up. Maintenance at the Irving Oil plant in New Brunswick was slated to finish yesterday , while De Haan adds that more production at refineries in the prairies is contributing to the big pump price drops in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

WATCH | Here’s why you’re paying more for diesel: Here’s why you’re paying more for diesel | Duration closed caption 6:06 Crude oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz are slowly recovering, so why is the price of diesel skyrocketing? The National's Eli Glasner breaks down what’s causing the increase, and why diesel prices likely won't drop anytime soon.

There's also the fact that Canadians tend to drive less in the winter as they hunker down in the colder months, helping with demand.

And while the cost of diesel — which had been pressuring industries like trucking, farming and fishing — has also eased, relief on that front might be more short-lived, said Dan McTeague, president of the Canadians for Affordable Energy lobby group.

Diesel is similar to jet fuel and home heating oil — and the latter will be in higher demand as temperatures drop heading into winter, McTeague said.

"[With] diesel, this is probably as good as it's going to get at the end of this week," he told CBC's Hanomansing Live earlier this week.

WATCH | McTeague explains the drop in diesel and gas prices: Gas prices have dropped across Canada — how long will it last? | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 5:38 Dan McTeague believes the falling gas prices are a result of a period of geopolitical peacetime, as no significant attacks have been made on major energy infrastructure in Iran or Ukraine. He also expects the decline to last for a while, however, he does not think food prices will decline anytime soon, not until energy and input costs get lower overall.

De Haan predicts lower gasoline prices will last into early 2027, but notes some of that "artificial drop" will disappear when the suspended fuel excise tax comes back. The tax will return at a 50 per cent rate at the end of January 2027 , before returning to its full amount at the end of March.

And, De Haan and Salazar both say costs could always soar again if tensions flare with Iran. Especially since strikes on ships in the strait have already risen again over the past few days, Salazar expects the relief at the pump might not last long.

"It really is a war call. And for us, it just doesn't seem like there's a durable solution to preventing the Iranians from attacking ships," Salazar said.

"So take the swoon in prices to your advantage temporarily, but I suspect that we're going to have higher prices to come still."

World.title: Juliet Daniel changed cancer research. Students of the late Canadian scientist say she also changed lives
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Shaiya Robinson saw something she hadn't seen before — a Black woman leading a cancer research lab — when she was a student and first met Juliet Daniel at McMaster University for an interview in 2009.

Robinson, who had rarely encountered Black professors, said the meeting to join the lab was about more than an interview. It was the first time she could picture herself in that position.

"I'd never had a Black professor before."

Daniel became her supervisor, mentor and, eventually, a colleague.

Now, Robinson is an assistant professor at McMaster, carrying forward many of the lessons she learned from the woman who helped make that future possible.

Robinson was among former students, friends and colleagues who gathered Monday at McMaster University to honour Daniel's legacy. The Barbadian-Canadian professor and scientist was a longtime breast cancer survivor who died on April 28 at age 61.

"She was such a pivotal person in every step of my career journey and my personal journey," Robinson recalled.

Determined to ask different questions

Daniel joined McMaster in November 1999 as an assistant professor, the first Black woman to become a faculty member in the university's faculty of science.

Her research focused on understanding why certain cancers impact some populations more than others, and why outcomes can differ.

She was internationally recognized for her research into triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), an aggressive form of the disease that disproportionately affects Black and Hispanic women.

Her work helped advance understanding of the genetic differences behind cancer outcomes, including her discovery of a gene she named Kaiso, after a style of calypso music rooted in her Caribbean heritage.

Michele James knew Daniel for about 30 years and sits on the board of The Olive Branch of Hope (TOBOH), a breast cancer support organization.

James said Daniel was looking into health equity and reducing health-care disparities long before it became a mainstream conversation.

"She was a real trailblazer in that regard."

Daniel co-founded organizations including the African Caribbean Faculty Association of McMaster, the Canadian Black Scientists Network, the McMaster Academic Women’s Success and Mentorship Lecture Series, and the Canadian Multicultural LEAD Organization for Mentoring and Training. (Paul Smith/CBC)

Made time for students, community

Robinson said Daniel had a demanding schedule, but somehow always made students and colleagues feel they had her full attention.

"She didn't have time, but she always made you feel like there was time for you."

Daniel also mentored Kevin Kelly, who now works in biotechnology.

Kelly met Daniel in 2000, when he was an undergraduate student looking for a supervisor for his research project. He stayed in her lab through his PhD, becoming the first doctoral graduate from her research group.

Kelly said Daniel was someone who took mentorship seriously and was generous with her time.

"She was always thinking about her students."

He said he admired her willingness to pursue questions that drew little scientific attention, particularly around cancer in Black women.

Kevin Kelly and Dr. Shaiya Robinson, left to right, were both mentored by Daniel. They remember her for her scientific accomplishments and compassionate style of mentoring. (Jeffery Tram/CBC)

Daniel also helped build a stronger community for Black academics. She co-founded the African Caribbean Faculty Association of McMaster and the Canadian Black Scientists Network, along with several other initiatives supporting mentorship, inclusion and student success.

"I was really proud of her for taking that very courageous step," James said. "She was already busy and that was something else that she took on to help advance things not for herself, but for the other faculty members."

Proud to be Bajan

For Stephanie Roberts, Daniel was first and foremost a childhood friend.

The two grew up in the same neighbourhood in Barbados, meeting when Roberts was about three and Daniel was five. They remained close even after Daniel moved to Canada and Roberts immigrated to the United States.

Roberts recalled Daniel's determination to make a difference in cancer research, particularly after her mother died of the disease.

She said Daniel initially pursued medicine before choosing research as a way to help find better answers for people affected by cancer.

"It was never about the money," Roberts said. "She truly wanted a cure for cancer."

Although they were in different job fields, Daniel would sometimes invite Roberts to tag along on work trips.

She also remembers Daniel as a longtime friend from her home country.

Daniel loved calypso music, dancing, cooking and hosting friends, and was an accomplished ballroom dancer who won several awards, Roberts said.

She said Daniel never made a point of introducing herself by her title, despite her academic achievements.

"If you went anywhere with her, she always went and said, 'Hi, I'm Juliet.'"

WATCH | Juliet Daniel wanted more diversity in STEM: Pioneering cancer researcher wants more diversity in STEM fields | Duration 5:11 Juliet Daniel came to Canada from Barbados in 1983 to study medicine, but decided to pursue cancer research after a personal tragedy. After 21 years of being the only Black female scientist at McMaster University, she says she wants to encourage Black Canadians 'to aspire to more than just those traditional buckets … that Black success has been categorized into.'

Roberts says Daniel was always proud to be from Barbados and would do whatever she could to give back.

James said Daniel helped the island during the COVID-19 pandemic by connecting its government with people who could facilitate access to vaccines, medical expertise and supplies.

Daniel's contributions earned her numerous honours, including being named a Distinguished University Professor in 2025, McMaster's highest recognition for faculty members. Her research has been cited more than 6,400 times.

In 2024, the federal government's Canadian Intellectual Property Office named Daniel as one of three Black Innovators in Research and Medicine.

Roberts hopes Daniel's name will be permanently recognized, including at a potential tribute at McMaster and possibly seeing Barbados's living lab named after her.

"It's just sad that in most cases, we have to wait on some till someone passes to celebrate them."

Robinson said she wants to continue Daniel's example by making mentorship a priority for her own students.

The event to honour Daniel drew friends, colleagues, students and mentees to the McLean Centre for Collaborative Discovery at McMaster University. (Jeffery Tram/CBC)

During Monday's celebration, James shared a quote that she said captured Daniel's approach to life: "It's better to light one small candle than to curse the darkness."

James noted that the celebration drew many people whose lives were touched by Daniel.

"She was like a candle that you can just take that candle and use it to light lots and lots of other candles," she said.

"And as I looked out into the room this afternoon, I felt that there were so many candles that had been lit initially by Juliet, and that their light would carry on indefinitely."

For more stories about the experiences of Black Canadians — from anti-Black racism to success stories within the Black community — check out Being Black in Canada, a CBC project Black Canadians can be proud of. You can read more stories here.

World.title: Skipping work to play Grand Theft Auto VI? You're not alone
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Got IT problems at work? Call somebody else. Need to develop some corporate training? It'll have to wait until next week.

Gabriel Santaguida and Amberley Houseman, a Montreal couple who work as a systems administrator and e-learning specialist, respectively, would normally take care of such things, but they're taking the next two days off work to play the long-awaited video game Grand Theft Auto VI that finally arrives Thursday.

Are you playing GTA VI? What has surprised you about the game so far? Send an email to ask@cbc.ca.

"It actually started as a joke, because Gabriel had said, 'Oh, it would be funny if we took the day off for something like this,'" said Houseman.

"Then I was like, 'Wait, I think I'm picking up what you're putting down.'"

Houseman and Santaguida aren't alone. Many fans are gearing up to play the open-world action adventure video game that lets players commit a wide array of crimes as they explore the fictional world.

Montreal couple Gabriel Santaguida, 28, and Amberley Houseman, 29, who enjoy video games like Stardew Valley, are both taking two days off work to play Grand Theft Auto VI when it's released on Thursday. (Submitted by Gabriel Santaguida)

A survey by U.S. HR company BambooHR polled 1,530 employed adults in the U.S. between Oct. 9-20. It also looked at data from approved and pending paid time off requests filed on their platform by about 575,000 active employees at Canadian companies from 2024 to 2026.

It found that time-off requests were up 13 per cent in the United States and up 6.6 per cent in Canada for Thursday compared to equivalent days last year, though respondents didn't make a direct connection to the game's release.

The survey also found that of those who intended to take time off for an upcoming video game release, 50 per cent were planning to call in sick rather than schedule time off.

Some employers are just giving in.

WATCH | Gamers celebrate as Grand Theft Auto VI debuts: Grand Theft Auto VI-mania hits Canada | Duration closed caption 2:11 Gamers in Canada and around the world are celebrating the end of a 13-year wait as Grand Theft Auto VI finally lands to rave reviews. The ultra-violent video game is expected to make billions by the end of this year alone.

Tech company Logitech is giving its 7,000 employees a paid day off Friday so they can play the game, while game developer Pocket Pair announced a five-day holiday for its gamer employers. Edison Motors, the Canadian electric truck company based out of B.C., announced employees could take the two days off, though they would be unpaid.

"Everybody's got their thing that they're going to take time off for, and for some people it's gaming," said Tara Parry, director of permanent services with human resources consulting firm Robert Half Canada.

"We shouldn't shun them for that, we should find a way to embrace it and get people to be upfront about it."

Why the hype?

Grand Theft Auto VI allows players to control Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval in the fictional U.S. state of Leonida, modelled after Florida.

Like previous iterations of the game, players can steal cars, rob stores and get up to all sorts of other mischief, but it also lets them do simple things such as pet cats and hold hands with their in-game partner.

Gamers get to play as Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval in the fictional U.S. state of Leonida. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

"This is really a historic franchise. One of the biggest in gaming," said Bradly Shankar, gaming editor at the tech news website MobileSyrup in Mississauga, Ont.

Grand Theft Auto V — which was released on Sept. 17, 2013 — has sold over 235 million copies, according to its publisher Take-Two Interactive, which owns Rockstar Games. At launch it made $800 million US, and just a few days following its release, it hit $1 billion US.

Thirteen years later, Grand Theft Auto VI has already made $1.5 billion US in pre-sales, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

For Houseman and Santaguida, it wasn't as simple as just pre-ordering the game and clicking download. They had played Grand Theft Auto V on PC, but the new game isn't available on that platform at launch.

"We did actually buy a PlayStation 5 just to play this game. And it's been sitting in the living room ever since," said Santaguida.

With the price of the game and Playstation 5, he estimates it cost about $1,000. But he was able to use credit card points to pay for the gaming system.

WATCH | GTA VI is just what gamers have been waiting for, says CBC reviewer: GTA VI is an 'astonishing' open world, but no revolution in gaming, says CBC reviewer | Duration closed caption 4:35 Description: Beyond the vast, photo-realistic environment, the latest Grand Theft Auto game is mostly a familiar formula with some smart additions — and for the vast majority of players, it's exactly what they've been waiting for, says CBC video game reviewer Jonathan Ore.

Adjusting to the trend

Parry, with Robert Craft Canada, says Grand Theft Auto VI is far from the first major cultural event to have people skipping work or using vacation days.

She says millions of Americans either booked off or called in sick the Monday after the 2026 Superbowl, which she says equated to billions of dollars in lost productivity

"We aren't anticipating that level of impact with Grand Theft Auto, but it does have a meaningful impact."

But, she says businesses could be acknowledging how workers are taking part in these events rather than denying that they're happening.

"Why not embrace it and incorporate it into the corporate environment for Thursday, Friday. Call it what it is, maybe set it up so people are gaming in office as opposed to home alone," she said.

This screenshot shows Brian Heder, a character from Grand Theft Auto VI. Tara Parry says employers should prepare for and embrace cultural events such as the release of the new game. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

In Canada, Parry says many businesses set up watch parties for employees during the FIFA 2026 World Cup, especially for Canada games.

"Most employers recognize that when Team Canada was playing, productivity was going to grind to a halt. So rather than deny it or fight against it, a lot of companies leaned into it," she said.

While Houseman and Santaguida had to use their own personal days off, they say when they finally sit down to play Grand Theft Auto VI on Thursday morning, it will be a rare chance to preserve some time just for fun.

"When you become an adult with adult responsibilities, then I think the moments to just be a kid are a little more rare. And so we take them where we can get them," said Houseman.

"I think we both know it's a little silly," said Santaguida. "But that's also kind of the fun, right?"

World.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya ethnic minority, International Court of Justice rules
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In a landmark judgment, the United Nations top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.

International Court of Justice President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar "has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention."

The 15-judge panel of the World Court rejected Myanmar's defence that the 2017 campaign was a legitimate operation against insurgents.

Iwasawa said that "the court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers."

The decision marks the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide.

"This is a great day for the Rohingya, and it is a great day for all oppressed people, everywhere, who have been told that their suffering does not count and that no one is listening," said Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the court's Great Hall of Justice for the three-hour reading of the ruling.

WATCH | Rohingya survivors eagerly awaited ruling: After nearly a decade, the Rohingya community may see justice | Duration closed caption 3:24 A “clearance operation” carried out by the Myanmar military in 2017 saw the deaths of about 10,000 Rohingya people, and the displacement of more than 700,000. As Maddie Ryan reports, members of the community watched closely in the wake of landmark genocide hearings at the International Court of Justice last month.

The intent to destroy a group in whole or in part is a key element in establishing whether crimes amount to genocide under international law.

The court said that evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya.

Over 1 million refugees in Bangladesh

The Muslim-majority African nation of Gambia launched the proceedings at the International Court of Justice in 2019, asking it to rule that Myanmar has breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order the nation to end any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished.

In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.

Rohingya children are seen wading through a flooded canal after heavy rain at the Kutupalong refugee camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on June 23. Thousands of Rohingya originally from Myanmar's Rakhine state live in squalid conditions at Cox's Bazar. (Munir Uz Zaman/AFP/Getty Images)

Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court will have to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya "in whole or in part."

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox's Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

"Genocides have similarities in how they are committed so this decision will have an impact on other cases," said Melanie O'Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia.

Gambia has asked for reparations for the Rohingya, including ordering Myanmar to grant them full citizenship and the right to return home.

In a 'limbo state'

Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya human rights activist who fled Myanmar as a young child with her mother in the 1990s, said the demands in the Myanmar case are rooted in her community's desire for recognition and dignity.

"Because so far, we've just been pushed around into this limbo state," she said. "It's been almost 10 years now that Rohingya have been living in very, very precarious conditions across the Asia-Pacific."

Ko Ko Hlaing, left, Myanmar's minister of the president's office, sits in the courtroom Thursday at The Hague, Netherlands. (Patrick Post/The Associated Press)

The court's rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce it beyond reporting noncompliance to the UN Security Council.

In a previous judgment in 2007, the court said that Serbia "violated the obligation to prevent genocide" in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in the Bosnian town.

Judges at The Hague-based court have also been asked to weigh in on other allegations of genocide.

South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion.

Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

World.title: Look up and give Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk a wave! The International Space Station is flying overhead
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For the next few weeks — if you have clear skies — you can watch the International Space Station (ISS) fly overhead in the evenings.

If you see it, you could maybe give a little wave to Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk as he whizzes by at 7.66 kilometres a second.

Kutryk is just one of seven crew members working and living on board the orbiting laboratory as part of Expedition 75.

Since arriving on the ISS on Oct. 1, Kutryk has been hard at work with various experiments and tasks, including a recent one on cardiac research.

And to no one's surprise, he's also been enjoying the view.

The ISS is often visible over Canada as it orbits the Earth. But over the coming weeks it will be visible in the evening sky, rather than the early-morning passes it's been making recently.

How to find the ISS in the sky

Very simply, it will look like a very bright white dot — compared to the thousands of fainter lights you might see that are satellites — moving across the sky. It won't have any blinking lights like airplanes and it will move steadily in one direction.

Now you have to find out when the ISS will be passing overhead. There are a few ways you can do this.

One is heavens-above.com, an independent website that tracks various satellites and spacecraft. There, you can sign up with your location and find the ISS in a list of other visible objects. It will then provide you with a chart of times like the one below.

This chart shows the times the ISS will be visible over Toronto over the next couple of weeks. (Heavens-above.com)

When it comes to the brightness, the more negative a number, the brighter it will appear (it doesn't appear to make sense, but that's astronomy for you).

Click on the date, and it will show you a map of the night sky with a line crossing various constellations, representing the path of the ISS.

This map of the night sky shows the constellations and the path the ISS will take on this particular pass. (Heavens-above.com)

If you only see a short line near the horizon on the map, you can probably skip that date, as the ISS may be trickier to see.

If it’s a longer line, you can give it a try, so long as you have an unobstructed view.

The constellation map will also show you the local times when the ISS will be in the sky, which is incredibly helpful.

NASA’s Spot the Station app is another great resource.

When you open the app, it should automatically detect your location. On the home screen it will provide you with a countdown to the ISS pass. The "Sightings" button will provide you with a list of upcoming passes.

It also has a feature called AR View (augmented reality), which gives you details of the sky when you hold your phone up to it — including a line showing you where the ISS will pass.

If you can find the ISS and watch it cross the sky, just think: maybe Joshua Kutryk is looking back at you.

World.title: Ella Langley sweeps Country Music Awards as Taylor Swift returns from 13-year-absence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ella Langley and her unstoppable hit Choosin' Texas dominated the Country Music Association Awards on Wednesday at ‌a ceremony that also featured Taylor Swift's first performance at the CMAs in 13 years.

Swift, who began her career in country music before finding megastardom in pop, went into the show in Nashville with one nomination for I Knew It, I Knew You from the Toy Story 5 movie soundtrack.

In the night's first ​award, CMA voters chose Choosin' Texas over Swift's entry for single of ​the year. It was one of six awards for Langley, including the event's top honour of entertainer of the year.

"I love this song," the 27-year-old Langley said after winning the single award. "We ​just sat in a room and did our best one afternoon, and it is the ⁠gift that just keeps on giving. ⁠I can't believe this is my life, and what ‌is going on is absolutely insane. I just can't believe it's me that this is happening to."

Choosin' Texas became a cultural phenomenon. It ranked No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart for 27 weeks, breaking a record set by Mariah Carey's perennial holiday hit All I Want for Christmas Is You.

Miranda Lambert, left, and Langley, right, performed their duet Snakeskin Boots during the show. (Mario Anzuoni/Reuters)

Langley ⁠was at a loss for words as she racked up award after award, sweeping the major categories including album and song of the year.

"At this point I'm sick of me," she joked during the last of several acceptance speeches. "This has been ‌the most special night. I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life. So thank you."

Winners were chosen by more than 7,000 members of the Country Music Association, a group that includes musicians, songwriters, executives and others in the industry. The gala was broadcast live on ABC and streamed on ​Disney+.

'Dolly gave us her heart'

Midway through the show, Swift sang a mashup of I Knew It, I Knew You and her 2006 country hit Our Song. She wore a red-and-white dress with ⁠bejeweled cowboy boots and was joined onstage by Keith Urban, playing banjo.

Swift took the microphone again to present the ⁠Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award to Brooks & Dunn, a duo known for hits such as Boot Scootin' Boogie.

Taylor Swift returned to the Country Music Association Awards on Wednesday to perform a mashup of I Knew It, I Knew You and her 2006 country hit Our Song. (Mario Anzuoni/Reuters)

"They still approach ⁠their music ⁠with the mischief and excitement of little ​kids just discovering their love for this," Swift said.

The CMAs opened with a tribute to country music legend Dolly Parton, who ​died in August aged 80. ⁠Host Lainey Wilson called Parton "Tennessee's angel" and sang the ballad I Will Always Love You in a duet with Vince Gill.

"She gave us what we all need in a world where there are so many challenges, something that is even more powerful and enduring than her incredible musical legacy," Wilson said.

"Dolly gave us hope. Dolly gave us joy. Dolly gave us her heart."

World.title: Via Rail heading back to Quebec’s Gaspé region after 15 years — a partial win that brings hope
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After 15 years of lobbying for the return of passenger train service to the Gaspé region, residents are finally seeing light at the end of the tunnel.

Via Rail confirms it will resume partial service along the Baie des Chaleurs, reaching New Carlisle, Que., by spring 2028. This commitment from the Crown corporation paired with a $1.2 billion investment over three years for Via Rail are fuelling hope full service to the Gaspé region — including the city that bears the same name — could return after a 15-year absence.

But the Quebec government needs to jump on board.

"It's great news in itself," said Éric Dubé, mayor of New Richmond and president of Société du chemin de fer de la Gaspésie (SCFG), a local non-profit organization in charge of repairing and operating the tracks.

The last passenger train reached the city of Gaspé in December 2011, after the tracks were deemed unsafe. In 2013, the final stop became Matapédia, leaving a 325-kilometre stretch without service.

For residents, news of the partial return of passenger train service brings back memories of an era when travelling to and from the Gaspé region was much more accessible.

"Back in the good years of the 1990s, as many as 28,000 passengers a year would take the train to the Gaspé Peninsula — so we’d love to be able to see that happen again someday," said Dubé.

The return of passenger train service to New Carlisle will cut the driving distance in half for travellers headed to Gaspé. (Lorena Suárez del Real/CBC)

The province, which has owned the tracks since 2015, has invested $350 million so far, which enabled the partial return of freight trains to the region.

Until now, Via Rail was steadfast in its position to only bring back service to the region if the full line was refurbished, said Dubé.

"Before it was [all the way to the city of] Gaspé or nothing. Now they are agreeing to a partial return to New Carlisle , but with the objective the tracks be refurbished all the way to Gaspé."

The final stop for shipping goods is currently near the cement plant in Port-Daniel-Gascons.

WATCH | Waiting for the train on platforms across Quebec's Gaspé region: Via Rail’s partial return to Quebec’s Gaspé region — after 15 years — sparks hope | Duration closed caption 2:41 Passenger train service to the Gaspé Region came to a full halt in 2013. But people living in the area are optimistic the latest investments in the 2026 federal budget and commitments from Via Rail in the past year are finally pointing to the service’s return.

Via Rail confirmed to CBC by e-mail the service between Quebec City and New Carlisle would run two to three times a week in a "phased return of service," while "working with the g overnment of Quebec, infrastructure owners, local communities and all partners involved to move this important project forward."

Rail crucial for access to health care, local business es

Dubé hopes the next provincial budget will include money to repair the last section of tracks between Port-Daniel-Gascons and Gaspé. That is also an ongoing demand from the local citizens' committee that has been at the forefront of the battle to bring back the train.

Residents on the Gaspé peninsula have been campaigning for the return of passenger train service since Via Rail cut back service in 2011. (Julia Page/CBC)

"It's really disappointing to see how much the service has degraded in my lifetime," said Eileen Jessop, with the Coalition pour le retour des services d'un train de passagers en Gaspésie.

Jessop said going to see a show or visit family in Montreal used to be as simple as walking to the station in Chandler to board a night train. Now travelling back and forth to Matapedia adds on hours of driving.

"It's rough on the roads, it's rough on our vehicles, it's rough on our mental health."

Many people who live in the region, including seniors, don't have access to a car, said Jessop, and often need to travel to Quebec City or Montreal to see medical specialists. The coalition also wants the province and Via Rail to arrange for more comfortable wagons designed for health care transportation.

Quebec’s new Transport Minister Nicolas Girard said there were no new developments for the moment, but his office said "an update could be made further down the line."

After numerous announcements from the province over the years to finalize repairs on the tracks, the project was sent back to the 'planning stage' in Quebec's 2025 infrastructure plan. (Julia Page/CBC)

Meanwhile, the Ministry of Transport "continues to work with Via Rail with the aim of a resumption of passenger service," Girard's office said in a statement.

For Jessop, if rail service comes back, she wants to tick travelling from Gaspé to Vancouver off her bucket list.

"If the train comes back that's going to be one of my first things — taking the Canadian to the other side."

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Mexican Journalist Eduardo Flores Killed in Acapulco
World.content:
Flores, a reporter for local news website Enfoque Informativo Guerrero, was found dead on Saturday, November 14, in Acapulco, a coastal resort city in the southern Mexican state of Guerrero.(Photo: Enfoque Informativo Guerrero/Facebook)

By Committee to Protect Journalists

HAVANA TIMES – Mexican authorities must immediately, credibly and transparently investigate the killing of journalist Eduardo Flores Salado, the Committee to Protect Journalists said Wednesday.

Flores, a reporter for local news website Enfoque Informativo Guerrero, was found dead on Saturday, November 14, in Acapulco, a coastal resort city in the southern Mexican state of Guerrero.

According to a statement by the Guerrero state prosecutor’s office (FGE), published Sunday on X, the remains of Flores were found in the evening of the previous day. Authorities opened a murder investigation, but the statement did not provide any further details about the circumstances of the reporter’s death, whether his work as reporter is considered as a motive or whether the FGE has identified any possible suspects.

In an interview with Mexico City broadcaster Grupo Fórmula on November 15, Héctor Nájera, the president of Enfoque Informativo’s parent company Grupo Nájera, said that Flores had been strangled.

“The brutal killing of Eduardo Flores highlights the ongoing relentless violence against journalists in Mexico and the impunity that fuels the deadly attacks against the press that have already claimed seven victims earlier this year,” said Jan-Albert Hootsen, CPJ’s Mexico representative. “Even as the government of President Claudia Sheinbaum touts a significant drop in homicides in the country, deadly violence against the press continues unabated, as does the almost complete impunity in press killing.”

Flores, 42, was a reporter for several local outlets. He contributed for over a decade to Enfoque Informativo. He previously contributed to Novedades, a now defunct local newspaper, and Flores was also a co-founder of Prensa Rosa, a local LGBTQ+ press collective.

For Enfoque Informativo, Flores reported on local politics, crime and security, human rights and the disappearance crisis in the greater Acapulco metropolitan area, according to a statement by Grupo Nájera owner Hector Nájera the website published on its Facebook page on November 15. He most recently covered press conferences and events organized by the Acapulco municipal government.

CPJ made several phone calls to Enfoque Informativo and the Guerrero FGE for comment, but the calls were not answered.
