World.title: Data centre energy consumption could double by 2030 straining grids, IEA warns
World.content:
The amount of electricity used by data centres could double by 2030, reaching up to 1,000 terawatt-hours of electricity a year, straining energy grids and driving carbon emissions up 70%, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

 

In the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario report, the organisation warns that the rise in electricity demand could stretch power grids and even delay new projects.

The report cited data centre projects in Finland, the United Kingdom, and the United States in states such as Texas and Virginia.

It estimates that electricity would account for nearly 30% of global final energy consumption by 2035, up from 23% in the IEA’s main scenarios.

Peak electricity demand is projected to rise 40% to 50% by 2035, according to the IEA. In the report, grids should be expanded by 26 million kilometres of new lines by 2035, while about 16 million kilometres of existing lines need to be replaced or refurbished.

The IEA also warned that the supplies of copper, transformers and cables needed for data centres are already lacking and grid spending is projected to rise 75% over the next decade.

The report comes as backlash grows against data centres in the US and Europe due to their impact on local communities' public infrastructure, land, water and energy use.

World.title: French Comté crowned world's best at the 2026 World Cheese Awards
World.content:
A French cheese has been named the world's best at the 2026 World Cheese Awards, bringing the prestigious, and much coveted honour to the country's eastern Jura region.

 

The winning cheese is a 24-month-aged Comté, produced by Fromageries Arnaud under the JuraFlore brand.

It narrowly beat another Alpine heavyweight - an 18-month Le Gruyère AOP from Gourmino in Switzerland – and another worthy contender from the Basque Country and Béarn regions in southwestern France, an Ossau Iraty AOP made by Agour.

The competition brought together 270 judges from 51 countries, including cheesemakers, retailers, buyers and food experts to assess each entry on its appearance, texture, aroma and taste.

“What I liked about this cheese was the complexity,” said judge Rafa Dominguez Gonzalez, who championed the winning Comté on the final panel. “It evolves in the mouth. Those beautiful, nutty savoury flavours really left a mark on me. Sometimes you just know. The moment I tried this one I said straight away ‘This is my choice’.”

Why did Comté win?

The world beating Comté was chosen from 5,330 entries representing 45 countries at the four-day competition, held in Córdoba in southern Spain.

Aged for two years in the cellars of Fort des Rousses, a former military fortress in the Jura mountains, the presiding panel also praised its complex, savoury notes and a long-lasting finish.

Comté has been produced in eastern France for centuries, with its origins tracing back to the Middle Ages.

From the 13th century, farmers in the Jura began joining forces to make large wheels of cheese. They pooled their daily milk production in shared facilities known as fruitières.

The system allowed them to produce larger quantities of cheese that could be stored and transported, particularly through the winter months.

Today, Comté is still made according to strict geographical and production rules in the Jura massif. It received France's Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée (AOC) designation in 1958 and European Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) status in 1996.

Which other cheeses made it into the top 14?

The final shortlist featured cheeses from five European countries, with France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland and Portugal all represented.

France secured two of the top three positions, with Ossau-Iraty, a sheep's milk cheese from the French Basque Country, finishing joint secondwith 81 points.

Switzerland's Le Gruyère AOP Réserve, aged at the Village Dairy Rossens, also scored 81 points, taking third place after the tie-break.

Italy and Portugal followed closely behind. Italy's Erborinato di Capra, a goat's milk blue cheese, and Portugal's Queijo de Ovelha Curado, a matured sheep's milk cheese, both scored 79 points.

Spain's Curado Fuente La Sierra came next with 78 points, followed by Switzerland's Kaltbach Appenzeller with 77.

The remaining finalists included Italian and Swiss specialities, as well as two Spanish cheeses made from goat's and sheep's milk. Italy's Blu Notte – La Fossa dell'Abbondanza completed the top 14 with 68 points.

World.title: Fossil fuels scrubbed from COP31 draft deal despite growing momentum
World.content:
All mentions of fossil fuels have been scrubbed from the latest COP31 draft, despite growing momentum to establish an exit plan.

 

Co-host Australia unveiled a draft deal on Thursday (19 November) that removes earlier proposals that called on nations to accelerate the phaseout of coal, oil and gas – the leading driver of climate change.

Almost 200 nations involved in the annual UN climate summit have until tomorrow (20 November) to strike a final agreement but analysts expect the discussions may overrun.

COP31 agreements require consensus from all parties which means progress is often slow and incremental.

It’s a deja-vu moment from the COP30 summit in Belém last year, where the transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) was erased from the final deal following resistance from fossil-fuel exporting countries.

COP31 shies away from fossil fuels

After days of tense consultations, negotiations chair Australia published a slimmed-down text, half the original length, containing fresh language and new proposals on some of the most contentious issues.

This includes for the first time a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35 percent by 2035 – a key initiative of COP31 host Türkiye.

It also contains a recognition of the "best-available science" and a reference to the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), a key battleground at COP31.

‘You can always wish and fight’

Despite the erasure of TAFF from the draft deal, several countries have published their own roadmaps to transition to clean energy.

On 11 November, Finland affirmed its commitment to TAFF by publishing a national roadmap, following in the footsteps of France, Germany and the Netherlands.

Almost a week later (17 November), Denmark, Portugal, Luxembourg and Spain announced their own national plans.

While “you can always wish and fight” for TAFF to be anchored in the cover decision, “this is not for us the ultimate benchmark for success,” German Environment Ministry State Secretary Heike Henn told reporters on Monday (16 November), ahead of the draft’s publication. “The success is in doing, in a growing coalition,” she said.

World.title: Ukraine strikes key bridge linking Russia and Crimea for third time this week, halting rail traffic
World.content:
Ukrainian forces struck the bridge connecting Russia to the occupied Crimean peninsula again on Thursday, less than two days after a previous strike collapsed an entire section of the crossing.

 

It’s the third time in a week the key transport artery had been targeted.

“Ukrainian Neptune missiles struck the railway section of the Crimean Bridge, with hits recorded near the arch and on the tracks. The extent of the damage is still being assessed, but train traffic has stopped,” Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence wrote in a post on X.

“For Russia, the bridge is a conveyor belt for its war, carrying fuel tank cars and ammunition wagons to its forces in the south. That conveyor has broken down.”

On Tuesday, Ukraine had struck the bridge with missiles and drones, severing the road section in two.

The 19-kilometre road-and-rail link is a key symbolic target for Ukraine and has been so throughout Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-appointed head of Crimea, said railway traffic would be suspended until the afternoon following the latest attack.

"Our railroad workers are making heroic efforts to deal with the aftermath of the enemy attack," Aksyonov said.

The Russian transport ministry said on Thursday that no one was wounded in the attack and that train services across it had been temporarily halted.

Road traffic has been impossible since the Tuesday attack completely destroyed a section of the highway.

Thursday's strike came just hours before a historic meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Chinese and American counterparts, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, in China.

The bridge is seen as a symbol of Putin's rule and Russia's illegal annexation of Crimea, and functions as a key supply route for the region.

It has been struck several times, including in an October 2022 blast in which an explosive-packed truck was detonated on the bridge, causing months of disruption.

Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, one of the opening moves in what became a deadly war between Kyiv and Russian-backed separatists in the east of the country, ahead of Moscow launching its full-scale offensive in 2022.

A woman walks during a blackout in Kyiv, 18 November, 2026 AP Photo

Refineries hit

Meanwhile, Ukraine also struck two oil refineries in southern Russia, Ukrainian officials said, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised the effectiveness of domestically-produced weapons used to damage the Kerch Bridge.

Ukraine’s General Staff said the strikes hit storage tanks at the Ilsky refinery and a processing unit at the Afipsky refinery, both in Russia’s Krasnodar region.

The two refineries, also targeted on Sunday night, can together process around 95 million barrels of oil a year and supply Russian forces on the front lines in southern and eastern Ukraine, it said.

Russian officials reported attacks on two industrial facilities in the region but gave no details.

Ukraine has repeatedly targeted refineries as it seeks to hurt Russia’s oil sector, a mainstay of its economy, and Moscow presses on with the invasion of its neighbour.

“Our technologies and companies are developing very well,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post.

And Russian forces have focused on knocking out power in Ukraine before the winter, aiming to erode the morale of civilians.

Attacks last month killed at least 372 Ukrainian civilians and wounded 1,981 others, a number 95% higher than in October 2025, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said on social media.

This year, the war has brought “significantly higher” civilian casualties than in previous years, the agency said.

World.title: Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya UN court rules
World.content:
The International Court of Justice has found Myanmar guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority. It is the first time in the court’s 80-year history that it has ruled a state committed the crime.

 

"The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said on Thursday, reading the verdict in The Hague, Netherlands.

For almost three hours, Iwasawa set out the evidence from the military’s 2017 campaign against the mostly Muslim Rohingya, which drove hundreds of thousands of people across the border into Bangladesh.

He said Myanmar's security forces had killed thousands of Rohingya civilians and committed "widespread sexual violence" against women and "extreme violence" against children.

The judges found that Rohingya villages had been systematically destroyed and resettled with non-Rohingya people. They concluded that the "only reasonable inference" was that Myanmar intended to destroy the group, which is the legal test for genocide.

Compensation and return

The court ordered Myanmar to compensate the Rohingya for "the damage caused by the violations of its obligations... in so far as such damage is not made good by restitution". The amount will be decided at a later date.

Myanmar must also "allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return" of those who fled, and investigate and punish anyone suspected of taking part in the genocide.

ICJ rulings are binding and cannot be appealed. However, the court has no power to enforce them, and it is unclear whether Myanmar’s leaders will comply.

The verdict is likely to add to pressure on Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military during the 2017 crackdown. He seized power from Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in a 2021 coup, and this year he was installed as civilian president after tightly restricted elections. The ruling could complicate his push for international recognition.

Agnes Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International, called the ruling "a historic and authoritative recognition of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya and a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families".

Legal experts are watching the case for signs of how the ICJ might rule on South Africa's separate case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.

'I want justice'

More than a million Rohingya now live in the world’s largest refugee camp, across the border in Bangladesh. Refugees there have described gang rapes, mass executions and attacks on families and children.

"I want justice," said a 23-year-old survivor of rape, speaking to AFP before the verdict from the cramped shelter she shares with her family. She asked not to be named.

"There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women," she said.

Mohammed Osman, 20, said he hoped the ruling would let him go home to perform last rites for his parents and younger brother, who were killed by the military.

"They shot my father dead, forced my mother into a house with a few other women, raped them and burnt down our homestead," he told AFP.

Seven-year case

The Gambia brought the case in 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention, which allows any signatory state to take another to court over suspected breaches. It has the backing of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

"It is not about esoteric issues of international law, it is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings," said Dawda Jallow, The Gambia’s justice minister.

Myanmar has always denied genocide. It says it was responding to an insurgency after militant attacks killed about a dozen members of its security forces.

"Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein," Ko Ko Hlaing, Myanmar’s representative, told the judges at hearings in January.

World.title: UK inflation hits 12-month high: What's driving the rise in prices?
World.content:
The Consumer Prices Index increased to 3.6% from 3.5% in the year to September, the Office for National Statistics said.

 

The October reading matched analysts' consensus forecast.

"Inflation rose slightly in October, with fuel prices once again a major contributor to the increase in the annual rate," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said in a statement.

"Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively," he added.

The average diesel price at UK pumps reached a record high in October, surpassing the level seen in the wake of Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

"The conflict in the Middle East and Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine have pushed up costs around the world," the Labour government's chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said in response to the inflation reading.

In a bid to combat rising inflation, the Bank of England raised its benchmark interest rate this month for the first time in more than three years.

Alongside the increase, the central bank warned that inflation risked climbing to 6.2% in the third quarter of next year, in a worst case scenario of oil prices soaring far beyond $100 a barrel because of the Middle East conflict.

The BoE's central forecast is for UK inflation to peak at 4.9 in the second quarter of next year.

The bank's Monetary Policy Committee tightened borrowing costs by a quarter point to 4.0% in early November, catching up with the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in lifting rates since the start of the Middle East conflict.

"The MPC raised Bank Rate two weeks ago to limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the two-percent target and stays there," the Bank of England said after Wednesday's data.

Analysts said the central bank could increase the rate again as soon as December, with UK households and businesses expected to face large increases to their energy bills from January .

A further rate increase next month "is looking increasingly likely", said Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics research group.

World.title: Italy approves antisemitism law amid protests from left-wing opposition
World.content:
The Chamber of Deputies on Tuesday gave final approval to the antisemitism bill. There were 147 votes in favour, 93 against and 5 abstentions, after Democratic Party MP Piero Fassino announced that he and other Democratic colleagues would not follow the party line.

 

There has been no shortage of controversy over the definition adopted in the bill.

The text, already approved by the Senate in March, adopts the definition of antisemitism provided by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA), which has divided the opposition itself.

The Democratic Party voted against, despite defections within its reformist wing, as did the Five Star Movement and AVS, while Italia Viva and Azione backed it. All amendments were rejected.

What the definition of antisemitism approved by Italy says

The text brought before the Chamber (source in Italian), which contains five articles, states in the first that the Republic "rejects all forms of antisemitism, promotes action to counter any expression of it and prevents the spread of antisemitic prejudice in Italy, without prejudice to freedom of political criticism and freedom of expression and to freedom of assembly and association, in compliance with constitutional principles".

The subsequent articles introduce a Coordinator for the national antisemitism strategy, and the lines of action against antisemitic hatred, including educational and training initiatives.

At the heart of the measure and of the political clash, however, is the definition of antisemitism drawn up by IHRA in 2016 and above all the examples provided by the organisation (source in Italian) which, according to critics, in effect extend the definition of hate to include dissent towards the actions of the Israeli government.

Criticism from the opposition and the alternatives

It is a "gag law to cover up the crimes of the Netanyahu government and the ethnic cleansing of the Palestinians. The Meloni government chooses not to disturb those who illegally occupy Palestinian land and at the same time wants to muzzle those who denounce it. It is a disgrace", attacked the co-founder of Avs, Angelo Bonelli.

"The majority does not really want to fight antisemitism, it wants to censor criticism of the Israeli government, which is committing genocide", said Democratic Party MP and former speaker of the Chamber, Laura Boldrini. "If it had really wanted to fight antisemitism, it would have approved our amendments, which replace the IHRA declaration, which is controversial, with the Jerusalem Declaration".

In Tuesday's debate in the chamber, the opposition asked the majority, as it had on the eve of the vote, to amend this definition or replace it with less controversial documents, such as the one adopted by the Council of Europe in 2022 (source in Italian), which focuses more on tools for combating or preventing it, or the Jerusalem Declaration on antisemitism from the previous year.

In particular, the latter distinguishes between antisemitism and criticism of Israel (source in Italian), stating that opposing the Israeli government or Zionism as an ideology is not in itself antisemitic.

The response, for example from Osservatorio Israele, was that the bill "does not limit freedom to criticise the Israeli government, but distinguishes legitimate political dissent from antisemitism".

The debate in the chamber also became heated when the death toll in Gaza since 2023 was brought up, and an amendment that would have banned naming streets and monuments after figures who supported antisemitism was rejected, sparking a clash complete with insults over streets and statues in Italy dedicated to figures from the fascist era.

World.title: Portuguese families could spend 83% of average net income on rent, study finds
World.content:
A new analysis by southern Europe's largest property portal, Idealista, estimates that renting a home in Portugal would take up 83% of average net household income in the third quarter of 2026. The equivalent figure for mortgage repayments was 70%. The findings come amid protests over housing and the high cost of living.

 

"Renting or buying a home consumes a large part of household income, reflecting the difficulties that many families face in accessing adequate housing," the study says.

Idealista compared advertised rents with average net household income. For buyers, it estimated repayments on a mortgage with a typical term and interest rate.

The analysis covered 20 cities: the 18 district capitals in mainland Portugal as well as Funchal in Madeira and Ponta Delgada in the Azores. Faro was the least affordable city to rent in, with advertised rents equivalent to 92% of average net household income.

Lisbon followed at 88%, then Funchal at 85%.

Porto (66%) and Setúbal (64%) rounded out the top five. Rents took up a smaller share of income in Coimbra, Viseu, Beja, Vila Real and Bragança. Only three cities fell below the 33% affordability benchmark cited by Idealista: Castelo Branco and Portalegre, both at 32%, and Guarda, at 29%.

How much of household income goes towards buying a home?

Buying a home remains out of reach for many people in Portugal, including young buyers eligible for government support, such as a state mortgage guarantee.

According to Idealista, Funchal is the city where "buying a home represents the greatest financial effort", with estimated mortgage repayments equivalent to 96% of average net household income. Lisbon followed at 90% and Faro at 79%.

Estimated mortgage repayments exceeded Idealista's 33% benchmark in most cities, including Porto (76%), Aveiro (68%), Ponta Delgada (59%), Setúbal (57%), Braga (53%), Viana do Castelo (53%), Leiria (51%), Coimbra (47%), Évora (45%), Viseu (45%) and Santarém (43%).

Only six district capitals came in below the benchmark: Guarda (20%), Castelo Branco (23%), Portalegre (23%), Bragança (26%), Beja (29%) and Vila Real (30%).

Higher interest rates have pushed up repayments for some borrowers with variable-rate mortgages. The three-, six- and 12-month Euribor rates, used to set many mortgage rates in Portugal, all rose in March 2026.

In August, the Bank of Portugal lowered its recommended limit on total monthly debt repayments from 50% to 45% of net monthly income. The limit generally applies when lenders assess a new loan and includes repayments on any existing loans.

World.title: Pakistan minister to visit India, but no breakthrough expected
World.content:
A Pakistani minister's visit to India for a Shanghai Cooperation Organization forum marks a rare high-level contact between the two archrivals, but analysts say it does not signal a resumption of bilateral engagement.

Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Masood Malik will travel to India from November 20 to 22 to participate in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Civilizational Dialogue in New Delhi.

It marks the first India visit by a Pakistani federal minister since the two nuclear-armed archrivals fought a four-day war last year.

The fighting erupted after armed gunmen killed over two dozen tourists, mostly Hindus, in India-administered Kashmir in April 2025. New Delhi accused Islamabad of backing the attack, a charge Pakistan denied.

Since the military confrontation, diplomatic tensions have remained high, leaving little room for official engagement between the two sides.

The SCO Civilizational Dialogue was proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the SCO summit in Tianjin in September 2025.

As the forum's host, India has invited all member states to participate in the event.

The SCO is a political, economic, and security alliance established in 2001. Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan are its current members.

Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Masood Malik will participate in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Civilizational Dialogue in New Delhi Image: Dogukan Keskinkilic/Anadolu/picture alliance

A 'good sign'

Ajay Bisaria, a former Indian ambassador to Pakistan, sees significance in the fact that neither side sought to avoid the engagement. "The real takeaway is that the relationship isn't so broken that India won't invite Pakistan, or that Pakistan won't come. That alone is a good sign," he told DW.

But Bisaria cautions against assuming that the invitation followed a diplomatic breakthrough.

"The trigger was procedural. This forum grew out of Modi's proposal at the 2025 SCO summit in Tianjin, and as host, New Delhi invited every SCO member. I see no evidence of a back channel or outside mediation, and I wouldn't read much into that either way," he said.

'Being pragmatic'

The multilateral setting serves both countries, though for different reasons.

Pakistan wants to retain its influence within the organization. It currently holds the chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for 2026–27 and is due to host the next leaders' summit in Islamabad in August 2027.

Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, argues that Islamabad's decision to send a senior minister should be understood primarily in terms of its position in the grouping.

"Pakistan is keen to maintain its position and influence within the SCO and does not want to relinquish its role in the organization. The minister's visit should therefore be seen primarily in the context of Pakistan fulfilling its commitments under the SCO Charter, rather than as a gesture towards India," Siddiqa told DW.

A 'frozen conflict': India-Pakistan tensions persist To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

T C A Raghavan, another former Indian ambassador to Pakistan, shares a similar sentiment.

"Both India and Pakistan attach importance to the SCO, and Pakistan currently holds its chairmanship. This visit should be seen primarily in the context of the SCO, rather than as a development in India-Pakistan bilateral relations," Raghavan told DW.

"Islamabad is also being pragmatic in keeping channels open during its SCO chairmanship by participating in an initiative championed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. There will be no real impact on the India-Pakistan bilateral."

The bilateral freeze

Since the April 2025 attack, India has maintained that terrorism and talks cannot go hand in hand.

"Post the Pahalgam attack, we have a Pakistan policy. That Pakistan policy remains in place. There has been no change," Randhir Jaiswal, spokesperson for India's Foreign Ministry, said at the end of October.

Pakistan, meanwhile, continues to raise the issues of Kashmir and the Indus Waters Treaty, which New Delhi placed "in abeyance" following the attack.

Malik, the climate change minister traveling to India, has been a prominent voice in Pakistan's campaign over water rights. In June, he warned: "We will protect ourselves... if anyone lays a hand over our share of water, we'll cut off that hand."

Sanjay Kumar Bhardwaj, professor at the Center for South Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the SCO is part of India's "multi-aligned foreign policy."

He noted that the forum "doesn't provide any space to normalize relations with Pakistan."

The SCO Civilizational Dialogue was proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi Image: Pyotr Kovalev/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo/AP Photo/picture alliance

Unofficial channels, no formal dialogue

The absence of official talks, however, does not mean all bilateral communication has stopped.

Since the May 2025 confrontation, Indian and Pakistani former diplomats, strategic experts, parliamentarians and retired military officers have reportedly taken part in a series of informal or semi-official back-channel meetings.

Such exchanges allow participants to assess the other side's thinking, keep informal lines of communication open and reduce the risk of miscalculation.

But they do not amount to formal negotiations. New Delhi has said retired officials attending such meetings do so in their personal capacities.

An assessment by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in November said both governments appeared reluctant to resume secret talks, despite the role earlier back-channel contacts had played in stabilizing relations.

Bisaria described the visit by a Pakistani minister to India as "a modest step forward, not a breakthrough."

What happens next, he said, "depends on Pakistan."

"If it avoids grandstanding in Delhi and offers credible assurances on terrorism, publicly or quietly, it becomes more likely that Indian leaders will attend next year's SCO summit in Islamabad. That will be the real test."

World.title: APEC summit: Trump, Xi, Putin talks end with 'peace declaration'
World.content:
Donald Trump’s big theme going into the three-way summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin was "denuclearization" — saying in his opening remarks that they were "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth."

But there are no signs that that will happen.

China has long resisted US calls for three-way talks on arms control, and Xi’s reported call during the summit for a world without nuclear weapons was merely a reaffirmation of longstanding policy.

In fact, as signatories of the global Nonproliferation Treaty, all nuclear states are committed to pursuing nuclear disarmament. So the fact that the final "Heads of State Declaration toward Peace" fails to indicate any steps towards disarmament could be read by critics as just the latest failure to take that seriously.

China is engaged in a rapid buildup of its nuclear forces, from warheads to advanced theater missiles; Russia has made repeated threats to use nuclear weapons in its war in Ukraine; and the United States, despite Trump’s calls for "denuclearization," is working on as many as four new theater missiles of its own to try to catch up with the other two in what could be the decisive nukes of this era.

Neither should the Declaration’s reaffirmation of the Reagan-Gorbachev mantra "a nuclear war can never be won and must never be fought" be seen as much source of comfort — all three states last retook this oath in January 2022, just weeks before Putin launched his war.

And yet — the Declaration does have some crumbs of comfort for anyone seeking positive nuclear news. It says the three powers will "conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks." Possible areas for progress here would include commitments to notify other states when doing test launches of nuclear missiles (China has no such commitment), or keeping AI out of nuclear command and control (so far only the US and China have a very broad commitment that only humans should order a launch).

This would be the lowest of low-hanging fruit — after all, does anyone want AI to launch nuclear weapons? – but an optimist might say, it would be better than nothing. Let’s see.

World.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, top UN court rules
World.content:
The International Court of Justice has upheld large parts of a genocide case against Myanmar linked to the 2017 conflict with its Rohingya minority. It called for it to pay reparations and let refugees return safely.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide.

The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state.

The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.

"On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.

Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.

He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees, and to take measures to investigate and if necessary prosecute individual wrongdoing by its nationals and security forces.

Information on the Rohingya's legal battles is on show at the Cox' Bazar refugee camp in Bangladesh Image: Md Zakir Hossain/NurPhoto/picture alliance

What Judge Iwasawa said as he read out the verdict against Myanmar

The ICJ said that by its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.

Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa said.

"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa said.

Iwasawa also said that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But the court found that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and if anything fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.

Ko Ko Hlaing represented Myanmar's government in the court Image: Piroschka van de Wouw/REUTERS

At one point reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested."

He said this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.

How did the international community react?

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres welcomed Thursday's verdict, calling it a "powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and noting it was the first verdict of its kind against a state.

"Myanmar must act in accordance with its obligation to comply with the Court's decision," Guterres said in a statement, adding that this includes "the safe, voluntary and dignified return [of Rohingya] to their place of residence nad reunification of families."

Gambia's Justice Minister Dawda Jallow, who attended the hearing, spoke to reporters afterwards at the Peace Palace in The Hague.

"The victory belongs to the Rohingya," Jallow said. "They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe."

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband issued a statement saying the former colonial power was "taking immediate action today in light of this judgment."

Miliband said Britain would expel Myanmar's defense attache in London and was calling for a special UN Security Council session in response. He called on Myanmar to "comply fully with the judgment," and on the international community to "play its part in supporting implementation, accountability, and justice for the Rohingya."

What is the genocide case against Myanmar?

The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.

Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.

A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp.

Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.

The Gambia's Justice Minister and Attorney General Dawda Jallow attended the session Image: Piroschka van de Wouw/REUTERS

Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.

Aung San Suu Kyi, who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."

The case is likely to draw close attention from those pursuing ICJ prosecutions against Israel and Benjamin Netanyahu for the war in Gaza and against Russia and Vladimir Putin for the invasion of Ukraine.

An 18-year-old in western Germany has been held in pre-trial detention in Germany since August over the alleged plot to carry out a terrorist attack on a mosque, prosecutors have said.

The teen, who is from the town of Eslohe in North Rhine-Westphalia, allegedly held far-right extremist views and was planning the attack for late 2026 or early 2027, senior public prosecutor Alexandra Wiese said.

"He also directed his racist ideology against people of the Muslim faith," Wiese told public broadcaster WDR.

A search of the suspect's home led investigators to find numerous weapons, weapon parts and ammunition, including items manufactured using a 3D printer.

Wiese did not provide details of potential targets in order to protect possible victims.

No charges have yet been filed against the teen and Wiese stressed that the presumption of innocence applies as the investigation continues.

World.title: Denmark ratifies security deal with US and Greenland
World.content:
The deal provides the US with expanded military access, on top of what it already had based on a previous agreement. It comes after threats by US President Trump to take Greenland with force.

Denmark's parliament on Thursday ratified a security agreement with the US over Greenland, hoping to end tensions after US President Donald Trump had repeatedly demanded control over the autonomous Danish territory.

In the Danish 179-seat parliament, all 109 members present voted in favor of the text. Greenland's parliament already ratified the deal in early November.

US ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the ratification, saying in a post on X: "The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernizes our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of NATO."

What does the Danish-US security agreement over Greenland include?

The trilateral security and military access agreement between Washington, Nuuk and Copenhagen allows for expanded US military presence on the mineral-rich and strategically located island in the northern Atlantic.

It also includes permission to establish a "Golden ‌Dome" ​missile defense system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.

The island is home to some 57,000 people and is strategically located along the shortest route from Europe to North America. It already is home to the northernmost US military base.

The deal was signed in September by Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen but still needed ratification from lawmakers in Greenland and Denmark.

Trump, Frederiksen and Nielsen signed the deal in September Image: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/AFP

Trump's threats to take Greenland by force

In January 2026, Trump renewed calls for Greenland to become part of the US, threatening military action and tariffs against European allies if they opposed him.

He argued that Denmark was not able to protect the autonomous Arctic territory from threats by China and Russia. His demands strained US relations with Denmark and alarmed European NATO allies.

Tensions somewhat eased in late January when Trump and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte announced a "concept of a deal" that would expand US military access to Greenland. This then led to the agreement being signed in September.

Under a 1951 agreement, the US already has broad military access to Greenland. Denmark had repeatedly said it was open to expanding the US military presence on the island but rejected Trump's demand for full US control.

World.title: South Korea's top court overturns jail term for former PM Han
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Han Duck-so was convicted of helping legitimize the 2024 martial law declaration. The case will now return to a lower court.

The South Korean Supreme Court on Thursday overturned a 15-year prison sentence for the country's former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo for playing a key role in the 2024 imposition of martial law by ex-President Yoon Suk Yeol.

The case will now return to a lower court, the Seoul High Court, which had sentenced Han to 15 years in prison in May.

Why was South Korean ex-PM Han's sentence overturned?

Han was convicted for helping plan the insurrection by suggesting that Yoon hold a Cabinet meeting to make martial law seem legitimate.

He also allegedly tried to collect Cabinet members' signatures on a related document and reviewed orders to cut off power and water to media outlets critical of Yoon.

The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that prosecutors had not sufficiently proven the case and ordered a review of the conviction.

At the same time, the top court upheld a four-year prison term for Yoon's wife, Kim Keon Hee, on charges of corruption, including manipulating stock prices and bribery.

South Korea's Yoon Suk Yeol sentenced to life in prison To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What was the 2024 insurrection?

On December 3, 2024, former president Yoon Suk Yeol abruptly declared martial law, prompting massive protests and a showdown in parliament.

At the time, Yoon said the declaration was needed to rid the country of "pro-North Korean forces" and followed it by sending troops and police into parliament.

But enough lawmakers managed to enter the assembly chamber to unanimously vote down Yoon's decree, forcing his cabinet to rescind it.

Yoon was impeached and later found guitly of leading an insurrection and sentenced to life in prison.

World.title: Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure
World.content:
As Donald Trump seeks to tighten economic pressure on Iran, China remains its biggest oil customer and Russia a key partner. But both powers are balancing support for Tehran against broader interests with Washington.

As Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen, Washington wants to tighten its blockade of Iran, but China remains Tehran's main oil buyer and Russia offers it political and logistical support.

For Iran, relations with both China and Russia are routinely described as strategic. That relationship looks more complicated from Beijing and Moscow.

Both countries oppose Washington's efforts to isolate Iran and maintain political and economic ties with Tehran. But both have broader interests in their relationships with the United States and may see Iran partly through the prism of their own negotiations with Washington.

That raises a central question: Can Trump's strategy of economically isolating Iran succeed if China and Russia refuse to fully cooperate?

Trump hosts China's Xi for state visit To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China is now Iran's economic lifeline

China is currently the most important destination for Iranian oil.

In 2025, it was reported that Chinese buyers took more than 80% of Iran's seaborne crude exports, much of it through independent refiners and at a steep discount because of sanctions.

As China provided Tehran an economic lifeline, Iran also became increasingly dependent on Chinese manufactured goods, machinery and industrial inputs.

Mohsen Solhdoost, an assistant professor of international relations at Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, says China is important to Washington's strategy but not decisive on its own.

"If the objective is to reduce Iranian export earnings, restrict access to equipment and make economic and military recovery more difficult, the United States can achieve substantial results without Chinese cooperation," he told DW.

But forcing Iran to accept Washington's preferred nuclear or regional policies is another matter.

"The ability to interrupt trade is much easier to demonstrate than the ability to determine another government's political choices," Solhdoost said.

Sanctions enforcement raises pressure on Iran

That distinction has become more important as US sanctions enforcement and maritime blockade efforts have increased pressure on Iranian crude oil exports.

In November, Washington announced Task Force Iron Gate, an initiative aimed at disrupting the movement of sanctioned goods, military equipment and revenue through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Even so, these trade links have not disappeared. The commercial and security interests of countries including Iraq, Pakistan and Turkey mean that goods continue to move across the region, albeit under greater scrutiny.

As a result, China's role in Iran's economy remains significant, but Solhdoost argues that demand alone cannot sustain Iranian exports. The oil must be able to reach international markets.

"A Chinese buyer cannot keep Iranian export revenues flowing simply by remaining willing to buy if newly loaded tankers cannot reach the market," Solhdoost said.

Iran prepares for the worst

This economic pressure is shaping Tehran's financial planning. A senior official at Iran's Plan and Budget Organization recently said the government was preparing its 2027-2028 budget under several scenarios, including one in which oil revenue falls to zero.

That does not mean Iran has adopted a zero-oil budget, but considering such a scenario illustrates how seriously Tehran views the situation. At the same time, Chinese trade can preserve critical parts of the Iranian economy even if overall commerce shrinks.

Machinery, electronics, spare parts and industrial components can still reach Iran by rail and road. Such trade cannot replace maritime commerce at comparable scale or cost, but it can keep selected factories and infrastructure operating.

What does Beijing want?

Such Chinese support could help Iran endure pressure without preventing economic deterioration, says Solhdoost.

But even for Beijing, supporting Iran economically does not mean supporting every Iranian policy.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has maintained support for cooperation with Tehran while calling for negotiations, safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and stable energy supplies.

A prolonged conflict around Hormuz threatens wider energy supplies and global shipping. China therefore benefits from continued access to Iranian oil but also from regional stability.

Russia can help, but how much?

Russia creates another obstacle to Iran's isolation. The two countries share access to the Caspian Sea and have expanded military, transport and economic cooperation.

Iranian officials have discussed ways of using Russian and northern trade routes to reduce the impact of American restrictions. There has also been speculation about oil swaps and deeper Russian assistance, although these claims remain difficult to verify.

Trump, Xi and Putin each seek to advance competing interests on Iran, Ukraine, trade and international security Image: Sergey Bobylev/SNA/IMAGO

Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, believes the summit should be viewed within a larger attempt to manage the wars in both Ukraine and the Middle East.

"Russia, China and the United States appear to be seeking constructive dialogue and results that could shape a new security architecture in the international system," Vakhshiteh told DW.

Russia supports Iran, but limits remain

Solhdoost also warns against overstating Russian support for Iran.

The strategic partnership between Moscow and Tehran provides for security cooperation and efforts to counter unilateral sanctions, but it does not require Russia to enter a war on Iran's behalf.

Since Russia is deeply engaged in Ukraine, it likely has its own priorities in negotiations with Washington, says Solhdoost.

"Russia would prioritize its own national interests in negotiations with the US over Ukraine and Iran," he said.

Moscow could support Iran while simultaneously using its relationship with Tehran as leverage in talks with Trump over Ukraine.

How much influence do the three powers have?

For Iran, ties with China and Russia remain essential. They provide alternative trade routes, export markets and diplomatic support that complicate Washington's efforts to isolate Tehran.

Yet neither Beijing nor Moscow views Iran solely through the lens of strategic partnership. Both weigh support for Tehran against their own economic interests, security concerns and dealings with Washington.
