World.title: Vukovar Procession to Carry the Names of the Missing
World.content:
November the 18th, 2026 – The Vukovar procession will have thousands of people wearing the names of those still categorised as missing on their clothing.

Today marks the 35th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar, one of the defining moments of the Homeland War and the place of the type of massacre unseen since WWII. Index reports that in this year’s Column of Remembrance, thousands of young people will participate wearing T-shirts with the names of missing persons. This is part of the “Instead of Them” (Umjesto njih) initiative, organised for the third consecutive year by the Student Catholic Centre (SKAC) from Osijek. As part of the project, an application was also designed to permanently preserve the memories and personal stories of the people in whose name the youth will walk the streets of Vukovar.

a tribute to those still missing – all 1,725 of them

In this way, young people want to pay tribute to the 1,725 people who are still being searched for. Their message is that the memory of fallen, missing, and suffering Croatian defenders and civilians must be preserved. Many of the participants will set out on foot from Osijek toward Vukovar during the night.

“It’s a big responsibility and a very honourable role to be able to wear the name of someone who gave their life for the homeland,” said Ana Pešikan, a member of Osijek’s SKAC. Vlatka Ivančičević, head of the SKAC office, shared what motivated her to participate. “When I looked from the side and saw the faces of people searching for the name of one of their own on a T-shirt, in that moment it became very real to me,” she said.

passing on the truth about the war

Although many of those planning to march wearing the names of Vukovar’s missing were not even born during the Homeland War, today they want to pass on the truth about the events of that time. “This year on our T-shirts we’re wearing the names of missing defenders, and by wearing white T-shirts with a universal message we will pay tribute to all civilians from the Homeland War,” explained Domagoj Galić, coordinator of the “Instead of Them” initiative.

So that participants can learn more about the people whose names they wear, the organizers are recording their life stories in a special web application. “We’re aware of how grateful we should be to those people who made it possible for us to live today in a free Croatia and enjoy freedom. This is the least we can do to show them respect and gratitude,” said Ivan Galić from the organising team.

World.title: European Commission demands Estonia quickly develop AI supervision framework
World.content:
The European Commission has criticized Estonia for delays in implementing the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act at the national level and is calling for the swift establishment of an oversight framework. Pakosta confirmed that the necessary changes are underway but said the best solution would be centralized oversight at the EU level.

The EU's Artificial Intelligence Act aims to encourage the development of new technologies while preventing situations in which AI is used to make decisions that could be unfair or harmful to individuals.

Among other things, the law prohibits uses of AI that pose risks to people's health, safety or fundamental rights.

The AI Act is primarily aimed at organizations and individuals that develop AI systems, place them on the market or use them as part of their work or services.

The EU's AI Act entered into force in 2024, but its oversight and enforcement provisions took effect in early August this year.

Pakosta said preparations to implement the regulation are underway and that the necessary decisions could be made at the beginning of the next Riigikogu's term. She said the delay was partly due to the EU having amended its entire package of AI legislation in the meantime.

According to Pakosta, Estonia is exploring ways to address the oversight issue in cooperation with other member states. She said Estonia and the Finnish prime minister have been leading efforts on the issue at the EU level.

World.title: Mart Einpalu: An e-scooter isn't a narcotic whose possession is illegal
World.content:
Mart Einpalu offers six proposals for how to rein in young riders using powerful e-scooters in violation of the law.

I fully understand the police's concerns. Young people are increasingly riding more powerful electric scooters in traffic, and trying to catch them can feel like chasing the wind. They remove speed limiters, race around in groups, create dangerous situations, and the consequences of accidents can be tragic. And when things spiral out of control, everyone looks accusingly at the police and politicians: Why aren't you doing something?

It's only natural that under such pressure there is a temptation to take the scooter away from the offender and confiscate it.

Sirle Loigo, head of the Police and Border Guard Board's traffic supervision unit, compared scooters exceeding legal speed limits to weapons, narcotics and contraband cigarettes, the possession or handling of which is prohibited in Estonia. That comparison is inappropriate because possessing or handling a scooter is not illegal, whether the vehicle meets legal requirements or not. Using a noncompliant scooter is prohibited only in public traffic. These are fundamentally different situations.

Confiscation is one of the most far-reaching restrictions on property rights. Article 32 of the Constitution protects private property, and any such restriction must be necessary and proportionate. Estonia's Supreme Court has also found that confiscating an instrument used to commit an offense must be justified, among other things, by the likelihood that it could be used to commit similar violations again and that less severe measures have proven ineffective.

"Police must be given effective tools to stop violations and prevent them from recurring."

Should the police have the authority to remove a noncompliant vehicle from traffic? Of course they should. In fact, they already do. Police can seize a scooter from its user, place it in storage, process the violation and, if necessary, ask a court to order its confiscation.

A separate question is whether police should be given the power to permanently deprive someone of their property without prior judicial review. By the same logic, should police be able to confiscate a car on their own when its driver exceeds the speed limit by a factor of two? A car is also lawful property that, in a specific case, is being used unlawfully.

But let's return to the central issue: how do we bring law-breaking young riders of powerful e-scooters under control?

It is worth remembering that police have already seized such scooters and attempted to obtain confiscation orders through the courts. The courts have not granted those requests. We do not know the specific reasoning in all of those rulings, but considerations such as the inviolability of private property and the proportionality of confiscation were likely important. It is also possible that the police's applications were not sufficiently justified.

It is understandable that, eventually, a police officer may feel frustrated. You take the scooter away, return it, and before long it is back on the road. From that perspective, it is tempting to say: just give us the authority to confiscate it ourselves and the problem is solved. But is that really the right solution?

In my view, there are several underused options that could help ensure police do not feel powerless simply because they lack immediate confiscation authority.

First, fines work. The penalty must be high enough that breaking the law is not cheaper than following it.

Second, introduce a points system. Traffic violations could affect the validity of a young person's scooter permit and their future eligibility for a driver's license. Repeated and serious violations should also leave a mark on their future traffic record, including insurance bonus calculations.

Third, require community service. Young offenders could be directed to meaningful and educational work, for example at schools, the Transport Administration or the police, assisting with traffic safety programs or helping maintain bike paths and parking areas.

Fourth, involve parents more effectively. Parents are already included in the process, but results vary widely. Some immediately draw conclusions, while others remain entirely unaffected. Parents must understand that this is not a toy or a hobby but a vehicle capable of causing serious injury to both the child and others.

Fifth, return scooters only after they have been brought into compliance. Police should not return a noncompliant scooter until it has been modified to meet the requirements of the Traffic Act or there are guarantees it will not be used in public traffic. Storage and compliance costs should be borne by the owner.

Sixth, impose harsher penalties for repeat offenses. Fines should increase for repeated violations. If someone continues to break the law despite repeated penalties and other corrective measures, there is already a mechanism for petitioning a court to confiscate the vehicle.

Police must be given effective tools to stop violations and prevent them from recurring. Anyone tempted to break these rules should clearly understand the consequences. Effective law enforcement does not mean that every problem should be solved by giving the executive branch the authority to permanently take away someone's property.

World.title: Notary fees on small real estate and inheritance transactions to rise sharply
World.content:
Notary fees in Estonia will change from January, with higher charges for lower-value real estate transactions, wills and inheritance proceedings, while fees for larger property deals will decrease.

Notary fees in Estonia will change at the start of the new year following a legislative amendment passed by the Riigikogu in October.

Fees will primarily increase for lower-value real estate transactions, wills, inheritance proceedings and powers of attorney. For example, the fee for notarizing a will will rise from €32.55 to €55, while the notary fee for a €50,000 real estate transaction will increase from €83.70 to €140.

For higher-value real estate transactions, the percentage increase in notary fees will be smaller. For example, the notary fee for a €150,000 real estate transaction will rise from €237.10 to €282. Fees will decrease for transactions valued at €550,000 or more. The separate fee for remote notarization will also be abolished.

In addition to fees for notarial acts, charges for notaries providing services outside their offices will also change. Starting in January, the hourly rate for services performed outside a notary's office or regular working hours will increase from €3.80 to €14. Value-added tax (VAT) is also charged on all notary fees.

The Chamber of Notaries said in a press release that the changes are intended to ensure access to notarial services throughout Estonia, noting that some fees have remained unchanged for decades.

Chamber of Notaries Chair Merle Saar-Johanson said the new fees were established on the principle that everyone should continue to have access to essential notarial services.

"People generally need notarial services only a few times in their lives, such as when buying a home, making a will or handling inheritance matters. It is important to us that people can receive the necessary impartial legal advice at these moments, regardless of where they live," Saar-Johanson said.

She said adjusting notary fees was an essential step, as rising office operating costs over the years and outdated fees had made it increasingly difficult for notaries in rural areas to remain financially viable. This year alone, notaries in Järva County and Saare County have closed their offices due to financial difficulties.

"That is why the legislative amendment is specifically designed to help notaries in rural areas keep their offices operating, as they handle the largest number of lower-value transactions," Saar-Johanson said. "This will help ensure that notarial services remain available to people outside major cities."

People whose financial circumstances prevent them from paying for services such as notarizing a will or handling inheritance matters can apply for a fee waiver. In such cases, the Chamber of Notaries covers the notary fee.

According to notaries, the revised fees will also help keep notarial services secure and modern by supporting the maintenance and development of the digital systems and registers needed to carry out notarial acts, including the e-notary information system and the inheritance register.

A full list of changes to notary fees is available on the Chamber of Notaries website.

World.title: Hackers obtain personal data of thousands in cyberattack on TLT website
World.content:
A cyberattack targeting the public website of municipal transport company Tallinna Linnatransport (TLT) on Monday compromised the personal data of several thousand people, the company said.

The attack exploited a security vulnerability in software used on the website after a plugin update had not been installed. The attacker downloaded a copy of the website's database.

The incident affects 2,440 TLT employees. The leaked data included employees' names, job titles and personal identification numbers.

An initial investigation has also found that an additional 2,370 people who had submitted their information through forms on the tlt.ee website may have been affected. The exposed information may include names and email addresses entered into those forms.

"We take this incident very seriously. Our first priority was to close the access route used in the attack, determine the scope of the data leak and notify affected individuals and the relevant authorities. At the same time, we are strengthening the website's security measures and reviewing our personal data retention policies to reduce the risk of a similar incident occurring again. TLT has not suffered any financial losses as a result of the attack, and the leak does not affect data related to public transport ticket validation or ticket purchases," said TLT management board member Kaido Padar.

TLT immediately blocked the access route used in the attack and removed the threat from its website. The company brought in cybersecurity experts to analyze the incident and has notified the Data Protection Inspectorate, the Information System Authority (RIA) and the police.

The company said it had also checked its other IT systems and, based on current information, they have not been affected by the incident.

TLT has informed both its employees and people who submitted information via the tlt.ee website about the breach.

The company is urging affected individuals to remain alert to possible scam calls and phishing emails. Particular caution should be exercised with any requests for passwords or PIN codes.

For additional information, TLT advises people to visit its website, tlt.ee.

World.title: Study: Estonia's large-family benefit made having a third child more likely
World.content:
New research indicates women in Estonia were more likely to have a third child after the country introduced an additional large-family benefit in 2017.

The policy also appears to have accelerated plans to have a third child, with women having their next child an average of about 20 percent sooner than before the reform, researchers at Tallinn University (TLÜ) and the Estonian Institute for Population Studies found.

"We're all aware that birth rates in Estonia have fallen to very low levels in recent years," said institute junior research fellow Tanel Paas. "But that doesn't necessarily mean the major family policy measures we've introduced have lost their impact or become unnecessary."

Previous assessments of the large-family benefit tracked changes in the number of third births but could not establish whether the measure actually made women more likely to have another child or simply accelerated the birth of already planned children.

Earliest benefits substantial at the time

Paas and his colleagues analyzed registry data for women born between 1967 and 2005, covering the years 2005 to 2024.

The study compared the pre- and post-reform childbearing patterns of several hundred thousand women who had one or two children. Using a statistical model, the researchers sought to distinguish an increase in the likelihood of having a third child from a shift in its timing.

When first introduced in 2017, the large-family benefit (lasterikka pere toetus) paid families with three to six children €200 a month and those with seven or more children €400. Combined with other regular child benefits, monthly support from the state could reach €500.

Paas said the extra benefit was substantial at the time, equivalent to 41 percent of the average gross monthly wage and 106 percent of Estonia's minimum wage.

In 2023, large-family benefits were bumped to €650 for families with three to six children and €850 for those with seven or more. The following year, however, the next government cut both rates by €200, bringing them to €450 and €650, respectively.

Second children less likely, but third more likely

Paas and his colleagues used registry data to assess whether the benefit made women more likely to have a third child or simply brought forward having kids that were already planned.

Researchers found that the reform increased the likelihood of a third child by about 4 percentage points. Their analysis also found a reduction in poverty among larger families.

For comparison, they found that the likelihood of a second child among women with one child fell by 1.8 percent over the same period. Paas said the findings nevertheless suggest the benefit achieved its goal of encouraging more births.

"As a result of this reform, at least 2,000 more children may have been born between 2017 and 2024 than otherwise," he said.

Families with kids out in Tartu. Source: Airika Harrik/ERR

However, the benefit's impact has diminished over time, partly because its value has not kept pace with rising prices and wages. Subsequent changes to the system in 2023 and 2024 may have also weakened families' confidence in its stability, Paas noted.

To maintain a lasting effect, he argued, benefits need to retain their real value through either regular increases or indexation.

Cuts can undo positive impacts

Alongside domestic data, the Estonian researchers also reviewed international studies of similar family policy measures. Findings vary, with some showing lasting positive effects, others only temporary gains and some no measurable impact at all.

Measures specifically targeting third and subsequent children tend to produce more positive results, Paas said, while smaller benefits relative to the cost of raising children are more likely to have limited or short-lived effects.

International research also suggests that increasing benefits can boost birth rates, while cuts can have the opposite effect.

"Some studies have even found that the negative impact of cutting benefits can outstrip the positive effects of having introduced them," he noted.

Researchers urge greater stability

Paas urged policymakers to approach changes to family policy carefully and ensure that benefits are both substantial and predictable.

"If we want benefits to have a long-term impact, they need to keep up with the times, and families need to know they can count on these measures continuing," he said.

Paas warned Estonia's birth rate could still fall further regardless, pointing to some Asian countries with even lower rates.

Improving the situation at home, he said, will require continued development of family policy, rather than treating the introduction of one major measure as a job done.

"We cannot assume that once we've introduced one major, costly measure, our family policy is complete and we can put that issue aside," the junior research fellow said.

Paas and his colleagues Allan Puur and Mark Gortfelder published their findings in the journal Demographic Research.

World.title: Tallinn seeks designer and builder for flag square
World.content:
Tallinn's City Center Government has launched a public procurement process to design and build a flag square planned for the intersection of Narva maantee and Pirita tee.

The purpose of the flag square is to create a representative public space where the Estonian national flag will be permanently flown, the city's press office said.

The square is planned for part of the Narva maantee T18 property and will cover approximately 1,467 square meters. The flagpole is expected to be about 40 meters tall, though its final height will be determined during the design phase following a visual impact assessment.

The flag must be clearly visible from Lasnamäe, Tallinn City Center and Pirita, as well as from the sea, while not overly dominating the surrounding urban landscape, the press office noted.

The project will include walkways, landscaping, lighting and the necessary utility infrastructure. The design must improve pedestrian safety and better separate the area from nearby roadways. The Estonian national flag will also be illuminated after dark while minimizing light pollution.

"This is a highly visible location, and a tall flagpole alone is not enough. Architects have proposed a strong solution for bringing our national colors into the urban landscape. We are now looking for a company that can further develop and realize that vision. I encourage all companies that meet the procurement requirements to participate," Deputy Mayor Tiit Terik said.

World.title: K-pop's global success boosts South Korea's soft power and tourism
World.content:
Eleni Alexandri, who recently defended her doctoral dissertation at the University of Tartu, studied how the Korean pop music industry, known as K-pop, creates its own reality and how meanings and identities are formed within it.

K-pop has become one of the defining symbols of South Korea's international image. The music phenomenon, which attracts millions of fans worldwide, promotes Korean culture, boosts tourism and strengthens the country's soft power. At the same time, the glamour of the music industry can obscure the true diversity of Korean society and shape how both artists and fans perceive themselves.

Alexandri has been a K-pop fan since her teenage years, when the first generation of idols was active. By the time Psy's "Gangnam Style" conquered the world and BTS reached a global audience, she had already witnessed K-pop's international rise and the evolution of its content and aesthetics.

"I was fascinated by the genre's uniqueness and visual style, which felt both fresh and strangely familiar at the same time, especially compared with the pop culture shaped by the American entertainment industry. The blending of genres, striking fashion, creative choreography and the impeccable synchronization of the artists created a captivating whole," she said.

After moving to Estonia, Alexandri studied semiotics at the University of Tartu. She chose K-pop as her research topic because she knew the subject well and had a personal interest in it.

"I wanted to analyze something I genuinely enjoy, something I have something to say about and something that would not become tedious. At the University of Tartu, I did not encounter the stigma surrounding the study of popular culture that unfortunately remains widespread in academia," she said.

K-pop as a meeting point of reality and fiction

The central question of Alexandri's dissertation was how K-pop produces, organizes and mediates culture. She also examined how people shape and experience identities within the K-pop environment, ranging from personal and social self-images to South Korean national identity itself.

"At the University of Tartu, I did not encounter the stigma surrounding the study of popular culture."

One of the dissertation's key concepts is "place," which Alexandri clearly distinguishes from "space." Space refers to a broader structural and cultural dimension, while place is a space imbued with social meanings. She illustrates the distinction through the comparison between a house and a home: a house is a physical space, while a home is a place rich in meaning.

Another important concept is the spectacle, introduced by French philosopher Guy Debord in 1967. Alexandri does not use the term merely to mean extravagant images or entertainment, but rather a system in which reality reaches people through mediation. Eventually, that mediated world begins to shape people's understanding of what is real.

According to Debord's theory, the spectacle is a pseudo-world assembled from fragments of reality. People can observe it but may never experience it directly. This is where the danger lies: instead of living authentically, people begin observing life from a distance and become separated from one another.

In K-pop, the main actors of the spectacle are stars and idols. They offer audiences ideals of perfection and role models to aspire to. Yet they also become victims of the system, as the entertainment industry molds and transforms their personalities to serve commercial interests.

This phenomenon is not unique to K-pop. Similar mechanisms operate on social media, where algorithms feed users content based on their previous preferences. The result is filter bubbles and digital echo chambers in which people encounter only information that confirms their existing beliefs.

"When we experience life and understand culture through media, we should recognize that our understanding is based on selected and curated images that may be limited or even distorted," she emphasized.

A window into Korean culture and an eraser of nuance

K-pop's success has profoundly shaped South Korea's international image. According to Alexandri, the so-called Korean Wave, or cultural export strategy, initially emerged out of economic necessity following the Asian financial crisis of the 1990s. Over time, what began as an economic recovery plan evolved into a strategy for national rebranding and soft power.

While the K-pop industry originally borrowed expertise from Japan's idol system and the American entertainment industry, it has now become a model for others. Its training and production systems are being exported around the world.

The music industry has enhanced South Korea's global visibility, stimulated economic growth and increased tourism. Artists effectively serve as unofficial ambassadors for the country in international campaigns. Fans, meanwhile, plan trips based on locations featured in music videos and Korean television dramas.

The shiny coin has a darker side as well.

"One Korean professor pointed out that South Korea, with its long history and rich culture, is far more than just K-pop. Although the 'K' in K-pop refers to Korea, many people feel that the music actually distorts, simplifies and overshadows the country's real culture and identity," Alexandri explained.

Although K-pop introduces people to Korean culture, that does not necessarily mean Western audiences gain a deeper understanding of the country's history and society.

"Artists effectively serve as unofficial ambassadors for the country in international campaigns."

"South Korea is also the country of the 'Miracle on the Han River,' a nation that rose from devastation and whose past is marked by occupations, invasions and a devastating civil war. The problem is that the glamour of the music industry can conceal the true face of South Korean society," the dissertation author said.

When Korean culture is experienced primarily through K-pop, a complex society can be reduced to a romanticized and limited image. Alexandri also notes that the popularity of K-pop and Korean dramas influences fans' expectations of real life. Some tourists travel to South Korea hoping to encounter locals who look like K-pop idols or to experience romance similar to what they have seen in television dramas. In popular culture, this phenomenon has been dubbed the "Netflix effect." Global attention has further amplified South Korea's already strict beauty standards, making them effectively unattainable for ordinary people.

Industry-shaped idols and fans

One of the dissertation's central themes is the effect of the K-pop industry on personal identity. According to Alexandri, the industry deliberately creates emotional closeness between idols and audiences in order to generate longing and attachment among fans.

The refinement of future stars begins at a young age. Agencies shape idols' personalities, behavior and public image according to the preferences of their target audiences. Even the composition of music groups is strategically planned: members are selected to represent different personality types so that every fan can find someone to identify with or admire.

"Through media, agencies foster a sense of closeness that helps create artificial, or parasocial, relationships," the researcher explained. This carefully curated interaction creates the impression that a celebrity is directly involved in a fan's everyday life.

The emotional connection also influences fans' spending habits. They follow every move their favorite artists make, buy products they endorse and participate in promotional campaigns organized by agencies.

"Stars create pseudo-needs and encourage overconsumption by showing fans a lifestyle that appears attainable. Yet they themselves are victims of the spectacle because the machinery has drained their individuality and subordinated them to the system's goals," Alexandri noted.

Fans, however, are not merely passive consumers. They are active drivers of K-pop's spread. They share content and create new material, effectively working for entertainment agencies. In academic terminology, this is known as "love labor," meaning fans contribute their time and attention to the industry free of charge.

Alexandri sees this as a symbiosis between producers and consumers, in which audiences actively participate in content creation. In this way, fans become an essential gear in the machinery that keeps the entire entertainment industry running.

A neon-lit alleyway scene in Seoul, South Korea. Source: Pexels.com / Free licence

Artistic freedom in the iron grip of the industry

One of the central contradictions of the K-pop industry is that artists are expected to display creativity and natural talent, while their careers and public image are at the same time tightly controlled.

Most aspiring stars begin training in their early teens. They leave home for agency dormitories, where they must balance schooling, childhood and a relentless training schedule. In addition to dance, vocal and language lessons, they undergo media training that teaches them how to behave in front of cameras and on stage. Contracts can be extremely restrictive. In the recent past, they even prohibited artists from entering romantic relationships.

"Great emphasis is placed on physical appearance. Idols are expected to follow extreme diets and undergo cosmetic procedures. The intensity of this lifestyle, combined with enormous competition and the constant direction of every move, inevitably has a strong impact on identity formation," Alexandri explained.

Although artists may have a clear creative vision, agencies always retain the final say. "It is very difficult for us to assess how much singers themselves contribute to the creative process or whether their ideas make it into the final product at all," Alexandri said.

"Although artists may have a clear creative vision, agencies always retain the final say."

Pressure comes not only from the commercial interests of record labels. Artists are also expected to represent the nation's culture. Alexandri refers to literary scholar Jineang Choi, who describes the heavy responsibility placed on K-pop stars' shoulders: the public expects them to distill everything Korean into a single perfect work of art.

Yet idols are not merely puppets. Alexandri cites a BTS documentary in which members openly criticize choices made by the production team and share their own artistic doubts. This demonstrates that even within a tightly regulated system, artists retain their own creative voice.

As part of her dissertation, Alexandri developed a three-level "triptych of influences." The model is intended to analyze the impact of the K-pop industry on the broader cultural landscape, Korean society and individual people.

All three levels are closely connected. Cultural phenomena influence society, society shapes individuals and individuals in turn reshape the cultural environment. For that reason, the influence of the music industry cannot be studied in isolation but must be viewed as a whole.

The model developed by the researcher can also be applied to other popular culture phenomena. Understanding the anatomy of K-pop helps explain more broadly how modern entertainment industries produce content, shape people's desires and influence our perception of reality.

Alexandri emphasized the importance of critical thinking and media literacy throughout.

"We should critically examine the mediated images and messages we encounter every day, from products promoted by influencers and imposed beauty standards to the normalization of the sexualization of artists," she said. People should learn to ask who selects the content presented to them, for what purpose and how it influences their expectations, values and identity.

"To genuinely experience life, we must maintain a direct and immediate relationship with society and participate actively in it. The best way to understand our world and ourselves is to study culture, engage in open discussion and exchange ideas," Alexandri said.

According to her, the study of culture should not remain the exclusive domain of academia. Culture should be lived, enjoyed, interpreted and challenged. Popular culture, in her view, deserves serious academic attention because its influence extends far beyond music and entertainment.

Eleni Alexandri defended her doctoral dissertation in semiotics and cultural theory titled "The Phenomenon of K-Pop: A Place of Reality and Fiction."

World.title: Putin invites Europeans to Moscow to discuss them joining Ukraine talks
World.content:
SHENZEN, China: Russia has invited European officials to Moscow to discuss whether they should participate in US-led talks on ending the Ukraine war, President Vladimir Putin said Thursday.

“The American side is urging us to agree to the involvement of the Europeans ... Through diplomatic channels, we suggested to the Europeans to come to Moscow. And after that we will decide in what format the talks can continue,” Putin said at a press conference in China.

“We understand that discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans,” he added.

World.title: SDAIA launches Year of Artificial Intelligence initiative in universities
World.content:
RIYADH: The Saudi Data and AI Authority has launched its Year of Artificial Intelligence initiative with the aim of spreading information about new technologies, promoting their responsible use and developing national skills.

The scheme will be run in collaboration with universities across the country and comprise seminars, panel discussions, workshops and consultations.

The authority said that the initiative would help to transform academic ideas into innovative solutions that supported the Kingdom’s digital transformation and strengthen its global leadership in data and AI, in line with the goals of Saudi Vision 2030.

Muhammad Khurram Khan, a cybersecurity professor at King Saud University, said: “The designation of 2026 as the Year of AI marks an important milestone in Saudi Arabia’s journey toward becoming a globally competitive, knowledge-based economy.

“It reflects the Kingdom’s commitment under Vision 2030 to harness AI as a driver of economic diversification, technological advancement and sustainable development.”

More importantly, the initiative highlighted the country’s ambition to move beyond simply adopting AI technologies and toward developing homegrown capabilities, fostering innovation and contributing to the global AI landscape, he told Arab News.



“One of the most significant aspects of this SDAIA initiative is its potential to strengthen the link between academic research and real-world industrial applications. Saudi universities have a wealth of research talent, scientific expertise and promising ideas that could address challenges across various sectors,” Khan said.

“Stronger collaboration between universities, SDAIA, government institutions and the private sector can help transform promising research projects into market-ready technologies, intellectual property, startups and innovative products that address both national priorities and global challenges.



“Equally important is investing in human capital through specialized education, research opportunities, interdisciplinary collaboration and practical AI training,” he said.

“Developing the next generation of Saudi AI researchers, engineers and entrepreneurs will be essential to building sustainable national capabilities and strengthening the Kingdom’s competitiveness in the global AI ecosystem.



“Ultimately, the ambition should go beyond adopting and deploying AI solutions to creating indigenous technologies, generating intellectual property and producing globally competitive innovations.

“By strengthening research, development and innovation, this initiative can accelerate the Kingdom’s digital transformation, create high-value economic opportunities and position Saudi Arabia as a leading international hub for AI research and innovation,” Khan said.

Umm Al-Qura University, which is involved in the scheme, said on X that it was “honored to partner with SDAIA to implement the initiative across universities in the Kingdom, with the aim of raising awareness, building national capabilities and fostering innovation within the university community.”

Saudi Arabia designated 2026 as the Year of Artificial Intelligence, underlining the Kingdom’s emergence as a global hub for data and AI, driven by the support of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

Saudi Arabia was the first Arab nation to join the Global Partnership on AI and in September became the first to host the UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI.

World.title: The Spa at Radisson Collection Residences offers multiple services to rejuvenate, unwind
World.content:
RIYADH: We don’t know a single person who won’t benefit from a day of rest and restoration — and we have found the perfect place to do that.

The Spa at the Radisson Collection Residences is a refined wellness sanctuary designed to restore balance, strengthen vitality and elevate your lifestyle.

The health club, for both women and men, is equipped with state-of-the-art facilities, ensuring a comfortable and private workout experience. Guests can unwind in the tranquil treatment rooms of the spa, enjoy the soothing sauna and steam room, or take a dip in the pool.

We were mainly looking for a nice pool to squeeze in a last dose of sun before the summer ends, and we found it to be the perfect semi-private space to do that.

Since the property is relatively new, it isn’t overcrowded on the weekend like other accessible pools around Riyadh.

Opt for a sunbed or relax over a cup of coffee at their lounge seating — the space is lovely, whether you are looking for a bit of sun or just a nice view overlooking their glistening pool.

We had our lunch poolside from The Boulevard, one of the three restaurants on site, which offers an all-day dining selection. We went for the halloumi on fruit salad for a healthy but filling meal as we enjoyed our day of rest and relaxation. For a sweet pick-me-up, the iced caramel cloud feels like a treat while also giving you that caffeine fix. The downside is that the dining is pricier than expected; a SR50 ($13) coffee is a bit much, even for Riyadh’s market.

The pool space also offers unconventional classes at times, such as aquasculpt; a full-body water workout class taught on mats that float across the swimming pool to help with mobility, strength and conditioning.

At the health club, which overlooks some of Riyadh’s most iconic landmarks, such as Al-Faisaliah and Kingdom towers, other classes are offered daily, spanning Pilates, aerobics and Zumba. The health club also offers access to the sauna, steam room and jacuzzi.

If you are not looking for an overnight stay, access to the pool is SR200 per person, and gym fees depend on the facilities you are looking for.

After a day at the pool or gym, indulge in one of their spa services; from aromatherapy to deep muscle release, relaxation massage or detoxifying massage, the experience will give you the relaxation you need, starting from SR500 for a 60-minute service.

You could also opt for one of their many facial and body treatments, which include uncommon treatments such as prodigy oxygenation and thalassotherapy. They also offer refined services for perfectly groomed hands and feet, and salon services for both men and women.

World.title: COP31 draft climate deal removes mention of fossil fuels
World.content:
ANTALYA: COP31 co-host Australia unveiled a new draft agreement Thursday that drops any mention of fossil fuels, the leading driver of climate change.

The nearly 200 nations involved in the global climate talks in Turkiye have until Friday to strike a final agreement, though the marathon negotiations often run into overtime.

A sweeping draft pact unveiled earlier in the week laid out competing positions on flashpoint topics from energy to finance and trade, drawing criticism for its length and complexity.

After days of tense consultations, negotiations chair Australia published a slimmed-down text half the original length containing fresh language and new proposals on some of the most contentious issues.

But a proposal “for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels” was nixed in the revised text, which also made no explicit mention of coal, oil or gas by name.

Many countries have pressed for strong language on fossil fuels in Antalya after last year’s summit in Brazil ended with no mention of them in the final deal.

Nations agreed at COP28 in Dubai two years ago to transition away from fossil fuels, but language around energy sources is highly contested at the UN climate talks, where decisions are taken by consensus.

The draft “cover decision” is designed to capture the outcome of COP31 and set the course for future action as global temperatures rise and climate disasters multiply.

- Difficult backdrop —

The summit is unfolding against a record-breaking El Nino, disasters fueled by climate change from Europe to Nepal and a global energy shock triggered by the Iran war.

The latest text said that taking steps to electrify the global economy could have “significant benefits” in shoring up energy security and cutting planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

It includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35 percent by 2035 — a key initiative of COP31 host Turkiye.

The draft also proposes further discussions toward “tripling” finance for climate adaptation measures by 2035 in a nod to a key demand by developing nations.

Rich nations have resisted calls to increase support for countries struggling to adapt to climate change, citing budget constraints and insisting that big emerging economies also contribute.

The draft expresses “deep concern” about the imminent breach of the 1.5C temperature goal set under the Paris accord and underscored the importance of the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

On Thursday, Panama threatened to block any deal that did not meet its demands, including a request to cap oil global production.

World.title: Road to Esports Nations Cup 2027 gives teams more chances to compete, fans more matches to follow
World.content:
RIYADH: The Esports Foundation has announced the Esports Nations Cup’s expanded Road to ENC 2027, with events run by National Team Partners, new qualification tournaments, larger national rosters and the ENC Ranking.

The initiative gives players more chances to represent their countries and territories. National teams will have more opportunities to compete, creating new rivalries for fans, while building momentum toward the inaugural ENC finals in November next year.

Nearly 200,000 players competed in 210 regional qualifiers during the first ENC qualification season, with 2,000 players from 123 countries and territories securing ENC places. Each place earned by a national team in 2026 will be protected, with players who represented those countries and territories included in ENC’s expanded national rosters, from which coaches will select their finals squads.

Countries and territories yet to qualify will also have another route through new regional online tournaments leading into a final local area network qualifier. Regional online qualifiers will begin on Feb. 26, running over five weeks across multiple game titles. The game-specific dates and final LAN qualifier details will be announced later.

“Representing your nation is one of the proudest moments in any athlete’s career. For fans, supporting their country or territory can be their first connection to a sport and the beginning of a lasting passion,” said EF CEO Ralf Reichert.

“As we build towards the first Esports Nations Cup, we want to help national teams grow together and give fans a team to believe in. Road to ENC creates more opportunities for those teams to compete and for fans to get to know the players, follow emerging rivalries, and become a part of their team’s journey. When those teams arrive at ENC 2027, we want fans to have been part of how they got there.”

Teams on the road to the finals will be supported by four elements:



• NTP-led events will give fans more opportunities to watch and support their national team before the Finals. NTPs can organize local activations, friendly matches and multi-nation invitationals, creating more competitions while giving coaches opportunities to test new players. Supported through the ENC Development Fund, these events are designed to build national fandom and a stronger local esports ecosystem. NTPs can submit proposals for 2027 events until the end of December.



• New qualification tournaments will give countries and territories that missed out in 2026 another route to the ENC. Teams will face off in regional online qualifiers, with seven regional winners and one invited nation from the ENC Solidarity program advancing to a final LAN qualifier to compete for the remaining places.



• Expanded national rosters give coaches more flexibility to develop their teams as they can add eligible players to squads that qualified in 2026, allowing them to test different combinations before selecting their finals lineups. For solo titles, the earned slot remains with the qualifying player.



• The ENC Ranking will create year-round competitive stakes and give fans a live view of where their country or territory stands throughout the season. Players earn points for their national teams through international club leagues and tournaments, as well as national team competitions. The standings will evolve as players compete throughout the season, helping determine seeding for the ENC’s group stage draw and informing direct invitations to future ENC editions.

World.title: Britain steps up Saudi air-defense support amid Houthi attacks, UK Middle East minister says
World.content:
LONDON: Britain has stepped up military support for Saudi Arabia, with RAF Typhoon fighter jets conducting defensive counter-air missions amid continuing Houthi attacks, UK Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty told Arab News.

The British aircraft would help protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure but would not take part in offensive strikes, he said.

“We responded directly to requests from Saudi Arabia for military support and have provided refueling aircraft and sent Typhoons out, which are engaging in defensive counter-air missions,” Doughty added.

“But they are not going to conduct offensive strikes.”

The official was speaking after his first official visit to the Kingdom since becoming the UK’s minister of state for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan.

“We also have personnel working closely with the Kingdom to respond to attacks on civilian infrastructure that we have seen and that have led to a terrible loss of life, including at the airport last month,” he said.

During his visit to Riyadh earlier this month, Doughty held talks with senior Saudi officials on regional security and the additional support Britain could provide.

Asked what further assistance Saudi Arabia had requested, he said London was in daily contact with Riyadh to assess the Kingdom’s changing defense requirements. He declined to disclose specific operational details.

Describing the UK as a “close defense and security partner” of the Kingdom, Doughty said British military assistance formed part of a broader effort to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi militia.

The attacks were causing loss of life and damaging both the Saudi and global economies, he added.

“There is an impact on their economy and the global economy from disruption being wrought in not only the Strait of Hormuz, but the Red Sea,” Doughty said.

“This is hugely concerning to British citizens as well, who are looking at its impact on food and fuel prices.

“So, we have a mutual interest in ensuring freedom of navigation and standing up to those who would disrupt this and pose a threat to shipping.”

Alongside military assistance, Britain had applied diplomatic pressure on the Houthis and helped secure UN sanctions against the group, he said.

Looking beyond the immediate security crisis, Doughty said Britain wanted to deepen its relationship with Saudi Arabia in several commercial sectors, including education, pharmaceuticals, artificial intelligence, energy and defense.

The two countries were building on “strong foundations,” he added, saying that his visit had demonstrated the potential for closer cooperation in several key industries.

“It was a great pleasure to travel across the region, engage with many of my counterparts and really get stuck into dealing with some of the opportunities, but also the challenges facing us,” Doughty said.

“Those conversations revealed that there is a huge benefit to both countries from our mutual investments, and we discussed how we can grow that.

“But, of course, for growth, you need conditions of peace and stability across the wider region, and trade routes to be open.”

World.title: Iraq reaches compromise with Kataeb Hezbollah after readying forces, officials say
World.content:
DUBAI: Iraq has reached a compromise with the powerful Iran-backed militia Kataeb Hezbollah, three senior security officials said on Thursday, after Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi readied security forces to move against the group’s stronghold south of Baghdad.

Zaidi said on Thursday that Iraq would not be allowed to become “a battleground for settling scores,” and that his government would continue to fight corruption and illegal weapons.

Earlier on Thursday, Iraq’s armed forces were placed on alert as the government set up a new command to take control of Jurf Al-Sakher, which Kataeb Hezbollah has controlled for years.

“The armed forces in their various formations have entered a state of alert C,” Lt. Gen. Saad Maan, head of Iraq’s Security Media Cell, told the Iraqi News Agency.

The new command headquarters will begin operating at 6 a.m. on Friday, Nov. 20, the day of the government’s deadline for Kataeb Hezbollah to withdraw from the area, according to an executive order announced by Sabah Al-Numan, spokesman for the commander-in-chief of the armed forces.

The headquarters will report to the federal police, which come under the Interior Ministry, and will be led by Lt. Gen. Ahmed Hatem Hamid. His deputies will be Maj. Gen. Hussein Ali Nassif for defense affairs, and Adi Abdel-Imam Mussah for Popular Mobilization Forces affairs.

Under the order, the command will oversee an army brigade, a federal police brigade, two brigades from the PMF, a state-funded umbrella group of mostly Shiite armed factions, and an Energy Police regiment to protect oil pipelines in the area. It will coordinate with security commands in Babil, Karbala, Anbar and Baghdad.

The move follows a plan approved by Zaidi on Wednesday to replace the force holding Jurf Al-Sakher, after the government accused the area’s controllers of oil smuggling and referred its investigations to the judiciary.

Kataeb Hezbollah has denied the smuggling allegations and had vowed not to withdraw. On Tuesday, one of its commanders told AFP the group would not leave “not even over our dead bodies,” though he said it was keen to avoid bloodshed.

World.title: Boulevard World expands with four new cultural zones
World.content:
RIYADH: Boulevard World has introduced four new cultural zones representing Uzbekistan, the Netherlands, Portugal and Yemen, expanding its growing lineup of international experiences as part of Riyadh Season 2026.

The latest additions further enhance Boulevard World’s appeal as one of Riyadh Season’s prominent entertainment destinations, allowing visitors to explore different cultures through architecture, art, heritage, cuisine, shopping and entertainment, all in one place.

The Uzbekistan zone transports visitors to the historic cities of the Silk Road, drawing on the country’s distinctive architectural and artistic traditions. Intricate, blue-toned ornamentation and suzani embroidery motifs feature throughout the experience, reflecting Uzbekistan’s rich cultural heritage and centuries-old craftsmanship. The setting offers visitors a glimpse into the country’s historic cities and their enduring artistic identity.

Portugal’s zone brings a taste of Lisbon to Boulevard World, with colorful streets and architectural details inspired by the Portuguese capital. Visitors can encounter the country’s iconic azulejo tiles, recognized for their intricate decorative patterns and strong connection to Portuguese identity, alongside the soulful melodies of fado, introducing them to some of Portugal’s most distinctive artistic traditions.

Meanwhile, the Netherlands zone takes visitors through some of the country’s most recognizable visual landmarks, including traditional windmills, canals and tulip fields. The setting blends familiar European architecture with contemporary elements, creating an immersive introduction to Dutch culture while capturing the visual character of its landscapes and cities.

Yemen’s zone highlights the country’s longstanding architectural and artistic heritage, incorporating distinctive colors, traditional buildings and decorative details. The experience reflects Yemen’s rich history and the diversity of its cultural traditions, offering visitors an introduction to elements of its architectural identity.

The four new zones join an existing lineup representing countries including Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Egypt, Morocco, France, Italy, Spain, Greece, India and China, among others. Together, the zones allow visitors to journey between different parts of the world while experiencing elements of their cultures without leaving Riyadh.

Beyond its international zones, Boulevard World offers attractions catering to different ages and interests. Visitors can enjoy rides and adventure experiences, live entertainment, restaurants and cafes, retail outlets and dedicated spaces for families and children.

World.title: Iraq studies issuing electronic dinar to expand financial inclusion
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is investigating an electronic dinar as a digital extension of the current national currency to modernize payments, increase financial inclusion, and lessen reliance on physical cash.

Prime Minister’s financial adviser Mazhar Mohammed Saleh highlighted the initiative in remarks to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA) on Wednesday, though no launch date, technical specifications, or formal issuance decision have been announced.

The electronic dinar will serve as a digital representation equal in value to the physical paper dinar rather than a new currency issue. It will not automatically generate new liquidity but will improve the management and circulation of existing funds.

According to the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI), approximately 102 trillion dinars ($67.38 billion)—nearly 92 percent of all currency issued—is held outside the formal banking system.

The purpose of a digital currency is to direct the financial reserves into formal savings, lending, and profitable ventures.

Moving transactions onto official digital channels will help curb unregulated financial dealings, reduce cash-printing costs, and align Iraq with the CBI’s financial inclusion strategy.

The digital dinar plan is different from suggestions to eliminate zeros from the physical currency.

Although the CBI has expanded bank cards, digital wallets, and points of sale, it has not yet declared a formal launch date or technical introduction timetable.

World.title: Egypt expresses interest in Iraq’s Development Road project
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Egyptian officials have renewed their push for national firms to participate in Iraq’s Development Road project and broader infrastructure initiatives.

Egyptian Minister of Transport Kamel el-Wazir said that Egyptian companies are ready to join the Development Road and railway projects with competitive pricing, quality standards, and fast delivery.

El-Wazir’s remarks took place during his meeting with the Iraqi Ambassador to Egypt, Qahtan Taha Khalaf, in Cairo, according to a statement cited by the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).

Egypt’s Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs, Hussein Issa, also met with Khalaf to discuss expanding trade, investment, and Egyptian company involvement in Iraqi development and reconstruction projects.

During a regional transport summit held two weeks ago in Alexandria, Egypt, Iraqi Transport Minister Wahab al-Hassani said that Iraq is moving toward the early implementation of land transport agreements with Jordan and Egypt to boost regional trade and cross-border movement.

Al-Hassani confirmed that Baghdad has finalized several land transport agreements with Amman and Cairo that are expected to enter into force soon.

The deals build upon a previously signed memorandum of understanding between the Iraqi and Egyptian transport ministries covering the overland movement of both passengers and goods.

Alongside the deals with Jordan and Egypt, al-Hassani highlighted Iraq’s broader push to establish itself as a regional transit hub through the country’s strategic project of the Development Road.

The strategic corridor spans 1,200 kilometers from the al-Faw Grand Port in the southern province of Basra to the Turkish border, combining new highway and railway networks.

World.title: Baghdad replaces forces holding Jurf al-Sakhar
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered on Wednesday the replacement of the forces holding Jurf Al-Sakher, following an investigation into alleged oil smuggling.

The move seeks to end the 12-year control of the strategic Babil province area by the Iran-backed armed faction Kataib Hezbollah.

Iraq’s Supreme Committee for Security Sector Reform, chaired by Al-Zaidi in his capacity as Commander-in-Chief, ordered the replacement of the current force stationed in Jurf al-Sakhar with joint units from the Iraqi army, federal police, and other Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) brigades.

The Energy Police, an Interior Ministry force, was officially assigned to secure the three branches of the strategic Basra-Haditha oil pipeline running through the area.

Findings from a government investigative committee alleging oil theft and pipeline tampering were referred to the judiciary for legal action.

Before Wednesday’s deployment order, al-Zaidi dismissed nine senior security, intelligence, and oil ministry officials—including the director of the Oil Pipelines Company—in connection with the smuggling investigation.

The orders follow escalating tensions between Baghdad and Kataib Hezbollah, which has controlled the area south of Baghdad since recapturing it from ISIS in 2014.

The armed faction rejected the smuggling allegations, claiming the sites inspected by investigators were abandoned facilities or fuel tanks for military vehicles.

World.title: Najaf refinery expansion to raise Iraq’s refining capacity by 70,000 bpd
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s oil refining capacity is set to increase further as the expansion project at the Najaf refinery progresses.

The project aims to add 70,000 barrels per day to the country’s refining output, aligning with Baghdad’s broader plans to boost the production of petroleum products and reduce reliance on imports.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi visited the refinery expansion site on Tuesday to evaluate the progress made and to assess the technical and logistical challenges encountered during the project’s implementation.

The project is being carried out amid Iraqi efforts to improve the efficiency of its refining sector and increase its capacity to meet the domestic market’s fuel needs.

The expansion of the Najaf refinery will increase fuel production to meet the requirements of surrounding industrial projects, create new job opportunities, and boost economic activity within the province.

The Najaf refinery expansion project includes the construction of a new refining unit with a capacity of 70,000 barrels per day. This development encompasses the completion of essential facilities and services needed to support its operation.

The project includes the development of energy infrastructure, an industrial water treatment unit, oil storage tanks, and other facilities associated with the refining unit.

The refinery’s current processing capacity stands at 30,000 barrels per day. With the addition of 70,000 barrels per day from the new unit, the expansion plans aim to increase the total capacity to 100,000 barrels per day.

World.title: Iraq aims to raise non-oil revenues to 19% in 2027 budget
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s draft 2027 federal budget aims to raise non-oil revenues to at least 19 percent of total government revenues, marking the highest proportion in the country’s history.

The spokesperson for the Iraqi government, Haider al-Aboudi, announced the target on Tuesday, noting that non-oil income had never exceeded 11 percent before 2026.

According to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA), the government plans to achieve this increase and insulate the economy from oil shocks through several structural changes.

Authorities are automating customs procedures at border crossings, digitizing government operations, and strengthening tax collection.

The plan relies on tightening financial oversight to cut off sources of corruption and revenue leakage.

The bill introduces elements of program and performance-based budgeting, tying public spending to measurable goals rather than strictly to payroll and operational categories.

While the ministries of finance and planning have completed the draft, the bill has not yet been formally published or approved by the Iraqi cabinet.

The Iraqi government aims to spend 217 trillion Iraqi dinars (around $166 billion) in 2027, assuming an oil price of $58 per barrel, according to parliamentarians familiar with the draft budget.

The measures would result in a fiscal deficit of around 40 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $30.6 billion).

Members of the parliamentary finance committee told Reuters that the draft budget anticipates crude oil exports of around four million barrels per day, including shipments from Iraqi Kurdistan.

Oil exports generate the majority of the Iraqi government’s revenue, accounting for roughly 80 percent of the general budget’s resources.

The 2027 budget represents a structural transformation by allocating 150 trillion ($114.5 billion) for traditional line items and 50 trillion Iraqi dinar ($38.2 billion) for a new World Bank-coordinated program-and-performance model to measure expenditure efficiency.

World.title: Baghdad Court sentences six more French ISIS members to life in prison
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Al-Karkh Criminal Court in Baghdad sentenced six French nationals to life imprisonment on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, for membership in the Islamic State (ISIS) terrorist organization, raising the total number of French citizens convicted in the ongoing mass transfer case to 16.

According to a statement from the Supreme Judicial Council’s Media Center, the verdicts were pronounced in the presence of the defendants’ legal counsel and diplomatic representatives from the French Embassy in Baghdad.

The court issued the rulings under Article 4 (Paragraph 1)—read in conjunction with Article 2 (Paragraphs 1 and 3)—of Iraq’s Anti-Terrorism Law No.13 of 2005, applying discretionary sentence mitigation pursuant to Article 132 (Paragraph 1) of the Iraqi Penal Code to commute potential capital punishments to life sentences (equivalent to 20 years under Iraqi statutory law, subject to automatic Court of Cassation review).

The six convicts belong to a group of 47 French detainees transferred into Iraqi custody from detention facilities in northeastern Syria.

Initial inquiries were conducted by the First Al-Karkh Investigation Court with evidentiary and archival verification provided by the National Center for International Judicial Cooperation, before referring the suspects for trial.

Judicial proceedings for the group began on September 20, 2026, under tight security and without media access.

Today’s rulings mark the third wave of convictions handed down by the Al-Karkh Criminal Court in this case: on October 27, 2026, the court sentenced six French nationals to life imprisonment and a seventh defendant to 15 years in prison;two days later, on October 29, it issued life sentences to three additional French suspects, bringing the cumulative tally to 16 convicted individuals following Wednesday’s verdicts.

World.title: Fourth Arab SME Summit opens in Baghdad as CBI reveals 16.3 trillion dinar financing milestone
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) The fourth edition of the Arab Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) Summit kicked off at the Baghdad International Fairground on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, running through November 20 under the patronage of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi and co-organized by Iraq’s Ministry of Planning and the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia (ESCWA).

Participating as a strategic partner and sponsor, the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) established a dedicated pavilion within the summit’s accompanying exhibition alongside commercial banks, corporations, and economic institutions.

Through informational publications and technical briefings, the CBI pavilion highlighted the banking sector’s role in executing national development financing initiatives and walked attendees through the application procedures for accessing SME loans—which carry a financing ceiling of 20 million Iraqi dinars per project through participating banks.

During the exhibition, the Central Bank unveiled updated cumulative figures detailing the scope of its developmental lending programs since their inception in 2015 through the end of October 2026.

Over that 11-year span, total CBI-backed financing reached 16.3 trillion Iraqi dinars, supporting the launch and expansion of more than 10,000 projects across Iraq’s private sector.

World.title: Iran-backed militia torture Iraqi environmentalist who refuses to abandon marshes
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Jassim al-Asadi, an Iraqi environmentalist, has returned to safeguarding the country’s southern marshlands after being kidnaped and tortured by an Iran-backed militia in 2023, according to a November 18 article by NPR correspondent Jane Arraf.

Al-Asadi, 69, co-founded the environmental organization Nature Iraq in 2004 and has spent decades fighting to restore the marshes, which were mainly drained under Saddam Hussein and were designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2016.

Nature Iraq is an Iraqi-registered non-governmental organization accredited to the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and also Iraq’s first and only affiliate of BirdLife International, an international conservation partnership.

Speaking with NPR, al-Asadi reported that armed men kidnapped him while he was traveling from Baghdad to his village of Chibayish in February 2023.

His captors accused him of spying for Israel and using his environmental expertise to aid foreign intelligence activities.

He said he was kept for two weeks, assaulted, shocked, and brutally suffocated during questioning.

When he was asked to confess or face death, he refused and instead composed a goodbye letter to his family.

According to NPR, al-Asadi was finally released due to pressure from his Bani Asad tribe, who mobilized hundreds of armed tribesmen to demand his liberation.

He denied an offer of refuge in Europe, preferring to stay in Iraq and continue his environmental efforts.

His homecoming comes as Iraq’s marshlands begin to recover after five years of severe drought.

Recent rains have boosted water levels, enabling some displaced buffalo herders to return, but pollution, water scarcity, and diminishing fish populations remain major concerns.

Despite threats against him, Al-Asadi continues to monitor water levels, help local people, and lobby for improved environmental protection.

The NPR investigation also highlighted the dangers confronting Iraqi environmental activists, especially those working with foreign organizations in regions where Iran-backed armed groups hold significant power.

Despite his suffering, al-Asadi remains determined to preserve the marshlands and its centuries-old way of life.

Nature Iraq organization focuses on conserving and rehabilitating Iraq’s ecosystems while safeguarding the cultural traditions and heritage connected to them.

World.title: ‘I am now 80’: Siddaramaiah rules out contesting next Karnataka Assembly elections
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Former Karnataka chief minister

on Thursday said he would not contest the next Assembly election, citing his age and the physical difficulties associated with campaigning.

Speaking to reporters in Mysuru, Siddaramaiah said he was now 80 years old and found it increasingly difficult to move around as he used to.

âWhat can one say at this age? I am now 80 years old. That is why I have said I will not contest the next election,â he said.

Siddaramaiah added that while his supporters continued to urge him to contest, he had decided against it because of his advancing age.

He also rejected Union Minister H D Kumaraswamy's allegation that he was being sidelined within the Congress, maintaining that there was no such situation.



The controversy arose after Siddaramaiah was seated in the fifth row at an event in Delhi to launch Congress parliamentary chairperson Sonia Gandhi's memoir.

dismisses speculation of rift with Siddaramaiah

Meanwhile, Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar on Monday dismissed speculation of differences between him and Siddaramaiah, alleging that some people were attempting to create an impression of a rift between the two leaders.





Speaking to reporters near Mekhri Circle and Town Hall, Shivakumar said Siddaramaiah remained their leader and that he had recently met him to discuss various issues, including the upcoming local body elections.

"There is no big rift or small rift between former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah and me. Some people are trying to create an atmosphere that there is a rift between us," he said.

"In politics, there should be critics; there should be opponents.

It is only when they are there that people like us can do clean politics. Siddaramaiah is our leader. Some people, including Mahaswamiji, are projecting it differently in the media. We have already conveyed to him whatever we had to convey regarding these matters," he added.

World.title: 'Bhookh itni hai, pet bharta hi nhi': PM Modi pulls up industrialists over lack of jobs, low pay despite tax cuts
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday took a swipe at industry leaders over inadequate job creation or salary hikes despite government concessions, saying, "How much ever you give, their [India Inc] appetite is never satisfied.

"

Addressing the annual general meeting and convention of FICCI in New Delhi,

questioned whether companies had raised employee salaries or expanded their workforce.

He cited government measures to improve the business environment, including reducing the basic corporate tax rate from 30% in 2014 to 22%, simplifying tax returns and refunds, and cutting GST rates on several products.

"I know you won't applaud. I know that very well, because your appetite is so enormous that no matter how much you are given, it is never enough (

aapki bhookh itni hai, kitna hi khilao pet bharta hi nahi

)," he told industry leaders.



Referring to the income-tax relief for individuals earning up to Rs 12 lakh annually, PM Modi asked, "I have given income tax relief up to Rs 12 lakh. But have you increased the salaries of your employees? Have you increased the number of employees? No! It is always: 'Modi ji, you do it; we will see what happens.' This is how things will continue."

He also referred to the income-tax exemption for annual incomes of up to Rs 12 lakh, saying the relief had boosted people's purchasing power.





"How much ever you give, their appetite is never satisfied," PM Modi told the industry leaders and urged them do more for their employees instead of expecting the government to shoulder the responsibility for growth.

Further recalling an interaction with Income Tax Department officials in Gujarat around 2001-02, when he was chief minister, PM Modi said he had questioned the approach of treating taxpayers as potential wrongdoers.

"I did not understand much at the time; I had little knowledge and no experience either. But I delivered a speech there. This must have been around 2001-02, perhaps 25 years ago. All the senior officials of the Income Tax Department were present. I asked them: 'When will you stop treating everyone as a thief? What kind of approach is this? You, too, work for the country. Are we the only ones who have taken it upon ourselves to serve the nation? You also do your bit, and every citizen does their bit.

Everyone deserves respect,'" he said.

'Meri mat suno, par Gandhi kih toh mano'

The Prime Minister also invoked Mahatma Gandhi's call for self-reliance and (Swadeshi) indigenous goods, saying the message remained relevant even a century later.

Referring to Gandhi's 1930 message, PM Modi questioned why industry still needed to be reminded of the importance of Swadeshi and self-reliance.

"Imagine, 100 years have passed, but in 1930, Gandhi left us with this message, and today, so many years later, I too have to say the same thing.

Is this your success or your failure? Don't listen to me; at least you could have to listen to Gandhi! (Meri mat mano, par Gandhi kih toh mano bhai). He too spoke of Swadeshi before leaving; he too spoke of Atmanirbhar Bharat (Self-Reliant India). And now you have turned 100 years old, yet things remain right where they were .

.. Spread my message too to every home!" he said.

'Don't treat 140 crore Indians as assured market'

PM Modi also urged businesses not to take India's large domestic market for granted, saying companies must focus on product quality and compete with international standards.

"Do not consider the 140 crore Indians an assured market," he said, questioning the mindset that whatever companies produce will automatically find buyers in India.

He criticised the practice of marketing certain products as "export quality" for overseas consumers, asking whether Indian customers did not deserve the same standards. "My countrymen deserve quality," he said.

The Prime Minister called on businesses to invest in understanding consumer preferences in different markets, develop products suited to local requirements and build distribution networks overseas.

"Our domestic market should not be our comfort zone. It should give us the confidence to compete in global markets," he said.

Urges industry to tap trade agreements

PM Modi said India's trade agreements with several countries had opened up major international markets for domestic businesses and asked industry leaders whether they had drawn up plans to make use of the opportunities.

"Over the past few years, India has entered into trade agreements with several countries around the world.

Have you, the members of FICCI, ever sat down to reflect on this? When free trade agreements are signed with major global economies, it means that doors have been opened for you. Have you devised any plans to seize these opportunities, or will I have to come to you to address this as well?" he said.

He urged companies to look beyond the domestic market, meet international standards and strengthen their presence in overseas markets.

India is 'pharmacy of the world'

PM Modi specifically asked the pharmaceutical industry to reduce its dependence on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), bulk drugs and drug intermediates.

Pointing out that India is known as the "pharmacy of the world", he said the country continued to import billions of dollars' worth of these products every year.

"India is called the âpharmacy of the world,â yet it imports billions of dollars' worth of APIs, bulk drugs, and drug intermediates every year.

There are hundreds of categories in which we currently depend on imports. Our pharmaceutical industry must understand which ingredients we can manufacture in India. In which areas can we invest in new technology and large production plants to become competitive with other countries?" he said.

He called for investment in technology and large-scale manufacturing facilities to build domestic capacity and make Indian companies more competitive globally.

'This is a government of friends'

PM Modi also asked industry representatives to share their concerns and suggestions for further reforms, saying the government was open to feedback from businesses.

Taking a swipe at previous governments, he said the industry's past experiences had affected its relationship with the current administration.
