World.title: Ariyil Shukkoor murder case: victim’s family, IUML leadership to continue legal battle as convicts seek leniency
World.content:
Davood Muhammad, elder brother of slain Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) activist Ariyil Shukkoor, said that the family will continue the legal battle. In a Facebook post responding to the Special CBI Court verdict acquitting 18 accused, including CPI(M) leaders P. Jayarajan and T.V. Rajesh, he observed that greater will be the trial when the mission is tougher.

K.T. Sahadulla, IUML Kannur district general secretary, described the verdict as “disappointing and unexpected.” “We were expecting the court to convict all the accused and give them the maximum punishment considering the brutal manner in which Shukkoor was murdered. We have taken up the matter with the highest levels of the party and will challenge the verdict in the higher court,” he said.

Reasons cited

Earlier, those convicted in the Ariyil Shukkoor murder case pleaded for leniency in sentencing stating that they were the sole breadwinners of their families. Some of them also requested to be sent to a jail in Kannur in the event of imprisonment.

Special CBI Court judge P. Sabarinathan had found 13 accused guilty and asked whether they had anything to say before the sentence was pronounced. Each accused came forward and apprised the judge of their circumstances. Aged parents and health issues were among the reasons cited by the convicted for leniency.

Shijin Mohan, the 15th accused, said that both his father, V.V. Mohanan, and his close relative Dineshan had also been convicted in the case, and hence there was none to support his wife, young son and his mother. His income was the family’s sole source of livelihood. He sought maximum leniency and requested that, if imprisoned, he be sent to a jail in Kannur. Mohanan, the 25th accused, also made similar submissions before the court.

Pavithran, the seventh accused, said only his asthmatic wife was at home and there was nobody else to look after her. The ninth accused, Manoharan, told the court that he was diabetic and had wife and two children. The 10th accused, N.P. Dineshan, said he had his aged mother, wife and children to care for, and that he had health issues. He too requested to be sent to a Kannur jail.

The 12th accused, Bijumon, said that both his father and father-in-law were no longer alive, and there was nobody else to take care of his aged mother and mother-in-law. The 14th accused, E.P. Radhakrishnan, said there was none to take care of his wife and 13-year-old son. The 16th accused, Sajith, also cited family responsibilities before the court.

The 26th accused, M.V. Purushothaman, sought maximum leniency, citing family responsibilities and diabetes. The 27th accused, P.K. Ajith Kumar, said he had wife, two daughters and an elderly mother to support, and added that he had been involved in life-saving and rescue activities. The 28th accused, P.P. Sureshan, likewise highlighted his responsibility towards his aged mother and family.

World.title: President Zardari, PM Shehbaz agree on resolving 'all matters' through dialogue
World.content:
President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif have decided that all matters will be resolved through dialogue, the Presidency said on Thursday after the two leaders met in Islamabad.

In a statement, the Presidency said the “current situation” was discussed in the meeting, during which Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi was also present.

More to follow

World.title: US, China, Russia sign ‘peace declaration’ after historic Trump, Xi, Putin meeting
World.content:
Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin agreed on a “peace declaration” at their unprecedented three-way meeting on Thursday, in which they reaffirmed that a nuclear war should never be fought, China and Russia said.

In the declaration, the three leaders also pledged to advance reforms of the United Nations, to increase supplies of refined petroleum products for all countries and to uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.

The document was released by Chinese state news agency Xinhua and by the Kremlin. None of the presidents made immediate statements after their meeting, and Trump departed on his flight back to the US.

Earlier, the leaders of the world’s biggest nuclear powers, sitting at a round table in a villa nestled among wooded hills beside a lake in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, described their meeting as historic.

“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting before journalists were sent away.

“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”

Differences over Ukraine, Iran and trade

Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three countries had “numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine”.

Unlike Trump and Putin, Xi did not make a direct reference to Ukraine, but said: “History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace. When major powers clash, the world falls into turmoil.”

The three countries have deep differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade, casting doubts about a durable outcome. Their meeting on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit has unnerved smaller countries that fear their interests might be disregarded.

Before the trilateral, Trump met Xi and Putin separately, referring to both as friends.

Trump said both he and Xi felt strongly about oil having to flow through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been disrupted by the Iran war.

Xi did not directly mention Iran in any of his remarks.

“China, Russia, and the United States should continue encouraging parties to conflicts to sit down and engage in talks, and resolve disputes through political and diplomatic means,” Xi said.

The Kylin Villa where they met has a long history of sensitive diplomatic encounters. Its past visitors include former North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, Xi’s father Xi Zhongxun, and envoys of the Dalai Lama.

Tough nuclear arm discussion

Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit, despite China’s repeated objections in the past to joining talks with Washington and Moscow, which have far larger nuclear arsenals.

“It’s not an easy thing to do, give them up,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of their meeting.

Trump and Xi met after an extension of their trade truce this month, but also amid growing tension over reports of Nvidia chips being diverted to China through Southeast Asia, raising questions about the effectiveness of US export curbs and the future of Chinese access to advanced technology.

Airport welcome

Breaking with decades of diplomatic protocol, Xi received Trump at the airport, with the men briefly hugging before a red-carpet greeting complete with cheering children and an air-force flyover.

This reciprocated the airport greeting Trump gave Xi at Joint Base Andrews in September.

“It’s a friendship relationship. It’s a respect relationship,” Trump told Fox News.

Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes U.S. President Donald Trump upon his arrival at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting on November 18, 2026 in Shenzhen, China.

The airport welcome showed “great respect, and I appreciate that. That’s a big win for us. It’s a big win for China too,” Trump said.

Other world leaders at the APEC meeting include Japan’s Sanae Takaichi, South Korea’s Lee Jae Myung, Canada’s Mark Carney and Australia’s Anthony Albanese.

Takaichi, on her first visit since angering Beijing a year ago with comments about Taiwan, met Putin — relations are also tense — on Wednesday, Tokyo said.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin, China’s President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump, Thailand’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney and Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese pose for a group photo at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, November 19, 2026. — Reuters

Takaichi, who by Thursday afternoon had not held any formal meeting with Xi, said Thursday she wanted a “constructive and stable relationship” with China.

Despite their differences, all the leaders — including Putin — posed for the APEC “family photo” on Thursday in special scarves.

Xi opened the APEC leaders’ meeting on Thursday with a call to “reduce barriers to trade and investment”.

Trump said he opposed “any form of globalist regulation or anything to control and stifle”

World.title: DPM Dar, Asean secretary general agree to enhance cooperation to address ‘non-traditional’ security challenges
World.content:
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Secretary General of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Dr Kao Kim Hourn agreed to enhance cooperation in addressing “non-traditional” security challenges on Thursday.

Addressing a joint press stakeout with Hourn after delegation-level talks held at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, DPM Dar said that the discussions had focused on strengthening political, economic and socio-cultural cooperation.

“We agreed to enhance cooperation in addressing non-traditional security challenges, including climate change, food insecurity, disruptions to energy supplies and cyber threats,” he said.

“Our ability to respond to these challenges together is vital to the security of our people and the sustainability of our development.”

Dar added that the two sides had discussed ways to expand cooperation in trade, education, technology, climate change and food security while promoting cultural and people-to-people exchanges.

He stressed that economic cooperation was central to their discussions, including facilitating trade, improving connectivity and enhancing digital integration, with a focus on creating more opportunities for businesses and strengthening the links between Asean and Pakistan’s markets.

“Building on the Asean-Pakistan business conferences, we look forward to partnerships that connect businesses, open new markets and create more jobs,” he said.

The two sides also discussed strengthening links between universities and research institutions in order to encourage joint research, exchange of expertise and skill development, particularly in digital technologies and artificial intelligence; as well as to increase cultural, academic and youth exchanges.

They also discussed regional and international security, the deputy premier said, highlighting Asean’s role in promoting dialogue and regional integration at a time of growing political uncertainty and an evolving geopolitical landscape, including by bringing countries together around shared interests.

“Pakistan values this approach and looks forward to closer engagement with Asean to advance peace and shared prosperity,” Dar said.

He stressed the importance of secure sea routes and uninterrupted supply chains for economies and livelihoods, adding that the two leaders reaffirmed the central role of dialogue and diplomacy, respect for international law and adherence to the United Nations Charter in addressing challenges and expressing Pakistan’s continued engagement with key partners in this regard.

He also expressed concern over the continued expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank, calling for unhindered humanitarian assistance to be delivered to Gaza and reiterating his support for an independent Palestinian state.

Regarding the situation in South Asia, he also briefed Hourn on the importance of “a just, durable and peaceful settlement of the longstanding Jammu and Kashmir dispute in accordance with relevant UN Security Council resolutions”, while also expressing concern over India’s unilateral decision to hold the Indus Water Treaty in abeyance, threatening water, food and energy security for Pakistan. He also highlighted Pakistan’s concern over the continued use of Afghan soil for carrying out terrorist attacks.

DPM Dar said that Hourn’s visit — the first by an Asean secretary general in over two decades — offered an opportunity to build on the close friendly ties between Pakistan and Asean.

“We look forward to giving fresh impetus to our partnership through practical cooperation that benefits our people,” he said.

Hourn, during his address, underscored the potential to deepen Pakistan-Asean relations in the areas of economic cooperation, regional peace and security, and people-to-people connectivity, translating their longstanding relationship into “more substantive cooperation and tangible benefits”.

He called for stronger connections between the business communities and noted promising opportunities in the renewable energy sector, as well as the potential to deepen cooperation against shared international challenges including terrorism, violent extremism, human trafficking and international crime.

“I would encourage Pakistan to make greater use of Asean’s various centres and institutions as a platform for capacity building, technical cooperation and knowledge sharing, drawing on experience and expertise available between our two sides,” he said.

In addition, he welcomed Pakistan’s constructive role in facilitating negotiations between the US and Iran, which resulted in the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding in June, and acknowledged the country’s efforts to facilitate dialogue and de-escalation.

Hourn is on a working visit to Pakistan from November 18 to 20.

In their delegation-level talks, the two sides reviewed progress under the Pakistan-Asean Sectoral Dialogue Partnership, the Foreign Office (FO) said in a post on X.

According to the handout, the discussions between the two sides focused on expanding trade and investment, strengthening regional connectivity, and deepening cooperation in agriculture and food security.

Collaboration on climate resilience, disaster preparedness, and digital innovation also came under discussion.

During the talks, DPM Dar stressed the scope for closer links between the business communities of Pakistan and Asean member states as well as the significance of scholarships, student exchanges, and joint research to strengthen people-to-people ties.

FO added that the two sides also exchanged views on regional developments and appreciated Pakistan’s “constructive role” in promoting regional peace and stability.

DPM Dar reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to working closely with the Asean Secretariat and member states to advance the partnership.

A day earlier, the FO had said Hourn’s arrival marked the first high-level visit to Pakistan from the Asean Secretariat.

Pakistan has been an Asean Sectoral Dialogue Partner since 1993, and a member of the Asean Regional Forum since 2004, FO added.

Asean was founded on August 8, 1967, when Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand signed the Bangkok Declaration, setting goals for economic and other types of cooperation and regional peace and stability.

The bloc has 11 members, including Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia, and East Timor.

“The visit underscores Pakistan and Asean’s shared commitment to deepening and diversifying cooperation,” FO said in its Wednesday statement.

Earlier this year, Dar attended the 33rd Ministerial Meeting of the Asean Regional Forum in Manila, where he drew attention to key challenges threatening peaceful coexistence and stability across the world, listing the Kashmir dispute and India’s threats to Pakistan’s share of water among them.

World.title: MQM-P's Khalid Maqbool urges courts to take notice of Bilawal's 'bloodshed' remark
World.content:
Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) chief Dr Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui on Thursday urged the courts to take notice of PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s remark, which the latter made during a speech that covered the creation of new provinces, among other matters.

“We talk about the garbage on Karachi’s streets, but if Sindh is divided, we will see blood flow through its streets,” Bilawal had said, calling for a “political reset” in the same address. Asked about it a day later, the PPP chief insisted he was not issuing a threat, but rather warning of the likely reaction to Sindh’s division.

The speech drew a strong reaction from leaders of PML-N, as well as its ally MQM-P, which has been calling for the creation of new administrative units in the country, particularly Karachi.

In a fresh rebuke of Bilawal on Thursday, Siddiqui particularly took exception to the Bhutto scion’s warning of bloodshed and said it warranted that the courts take suo motu notice.

Speaking at a press conference in Karachi, the MQM-P convenor said his party expected to be countered with arguments, not threats, in response to its own arguments.

“One should pause and think carefully before threatening us and the people of Sindh’s urban areas,” he said, alleging that presently, Pakistan had “feudalistic democracy” that was a far cry from democracy.

In “feudalistic democracy”, a political worker would not transition to becoming a leader, but an individual was made a leader on the basis of their background, he explained.

“And when the leadership emerges from dynastic and feudal backgrounds, their temperament is also feudalistic,” he commented.

Siddiqui asserted that MQM-P had been calling for the creation of new provinces across the country and never restricted their demand to just Sindh or Karachi.

Directly addressing Bilawal, he questioned: “If the demand was for the creation of provinces in all of Pakistan, why would there be bloodshed in just Karachi, Hyderabad, Mirpurkhas or Nawabshah? Are you threatening us?”

He alleged that PPP’s objection to the creation of new provinces in Sindh was due to “Karachi contributing 97 per cent to the province’s budget”.

Siddiqui then reiterated his query: “The urban areas of Sindh are waiting for an answer to the question why there would be bloodshed in these areas? And who will do it? Will you get Uzair Baloch to do it?”

Commenting on PPP’s governance in Sindh, Siddiqui highlighted issues of low literacy and lack of development in the province.

“Corruption happens everywhere in the world. It is called a by-product of development. But in Sindh, development is the by-product of corruption,” Siddiqui further alleged.

He went on to point out that the PPP was not just in power in Sindh but also had governance roles in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan and Balochistan.

“Were you able to become rulers there under democratic requirements? … We have asked Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif about this as well?” Siddiqui questioned.

Again, addressing Bilawal, Siddiqui said, “We respect you and we honour your mandate, but you’re using this kind of language because we had decided that we won’t fight.

“But we will still fight the constitutional and legal battle. We will still talk in the assemblies.”

He then again urged the courts and the federal government to take notice of Bilawal’s “threat” and asked the PPP scion to respond to the MQM-P through arguments because “threats do not work on us”.

Sindh govt to contact MQM-P, others on planned rallies

On the other hand, Sindh Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon maintained that his PPP did not want any kind of tension, stressing that each person could hold a different opinion without “issuing edicts” on it.

Addressing a press conference later in the day, Memon clarified that Bilawal had “very clearly said” that his party does not incite violence or take up arms.

The minister stressed that the PPP chairman spoke considering the history of Sindh, which had witnessed communal clashes in the 1970s.

Memon said Bilawal specifically spoke of cities where different communities resided, hence heightening the risk of tensions.

Memon further announced that the provincial government has approved the procurement of 500 electric buses for Karachi, terming it “major good news”.

On plans of the MQM-P and the Sindh Taraqqi-pasand Party (STP) holding rallies in Karachi on Nov 29, Memon said the Sindh government would contact both parties and urge them not to go ahead with their gatherings.

MQM-P had earlier this month announced the rally on Sharea Faisal as part of the party’s campaign for new administrative units. Some Sindhi nationalist parties, including STP, have also announced their own gathering against new provinces on Sharea Faisal on the same day.

A day earlier, MQM-P leader Mustafa Kamal told a private news channel that his party would not hold the rally on Nov 29, but on some other date to avoid any clash.

According to Sharjeel, the nationalist party first announced the rally, following which MQM-P decided to hold their separate gathering.

“You know what happens if people with two differing opinions gather in one place on the same date,” the Sindh minister remarked, hinting at a possible law and order situation.

He stressed that the Sindh Assembly was the most powerful forum of public representatives in Sindh, adding that such decisions were to be made in the assembly, not on the streets.

“So, our request to all parties will be that you should not create such an environment,” the minister said.

World.title: Top UN court finds Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against Muslim Rohingya
World.content:
The highest United Nations court ruled on Thursday that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar’s security forces against the Rohingya Muslim minority population in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

The decision, seven years after the case was filed by predominantly Muslim Gambia, marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the legal threshold to prove genocide had been met.

It was the first time the court held a state responsible for genocide.

“The court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya,” presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa said in a reading of the decision.

The panel found “that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine State.”

Myanmar’s government did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment.

Decision is expected to influence other genocide cases

Judges found that Myanmar’s military carried out mass executions of men and boys, committed widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women and burned or razed hundreds of villages during so-called clearance operations.

The military actively spread hate speech targeting the Rohingya population, they said. The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

Genocide has rarely been established in international courts, largely because prosecutors must prove a specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

The decision by the International Court of Justice, or World Court, is expected to have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, including for South Africa’s 2023 case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.

The first major decision by the court in more than a decade on the application of the 1948 Genocide Convention will be pored over by legal experts for clues to how the bench assessed state responsibility in the alleged commission of international crimes.

Both Israel and Myanmar deny genocide and say their forces responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups.

Smoke is seen on Myanmar’s side of border as Rohingya refugees walk on the shore after crossing the Bangladesh-Myanmar border by boat through the Bay of Bengal, in Shah Porir Dwip, Bangladesh, on September 11, 2017. — Reuters

In a major legal victory for Gambia, the court found the state responsible for genocide resulting from a military offensive that drove at least 700,000 Muslim Rohingya from Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

A panel of 15 judges said “the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group namely the Rohingya population in Northern Rakhine state,” meeting the legal threshold for genocide.

The court said Myanmar had an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it had committed, to be determined at a later date.

Myanmar must also allow the “safe and dignified return to their place of residence and the reunification of families for the Rohingya displaced as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts,” it said.

International courts previously only recognised genocide during the 1994 Rwanda genocide, the 1995 Srebrenica killings in Bosnia, and atrocities by Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge in the late 1970s.

While rulings by the ICJ, which settles disputes between states and rules on alleged breaches of international treaties, are final, the court has very limited options to enforce them.

It is distinct from the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals for war crimes, crimes against ​humanity and genocide and can impose jail terms.

World.title: EY-led consortium signs financial advisory pact for outsourcing of Karachi, Lahore airports
World.content:
The Privatisation Commission and a consortium led by Ernst & Young (EY) Middle East on Thursday signed a financial advisory services agreement (Fasa) for the outsourcing of Karachi and Lahore airports.

In August, the commission had approved the appointment of a financial adviser for the outsourcing of both airports, mentioning a “consortium led by EY-Parthenon as the top-ranked interested party”.

It also constituted a negotiation committee to finalise the Fasa with the successful consortium.

“The Privatisation Commission and a consortium led by EY Middle East signed a Fasa today in Islamabad for the outsourcing of Jinnah International Airport, Karachi and Allama Iqbal International Airport, Lahore,” according to Thursday’s press release issued by the commission.

“The transactions envisage bringing in private sector expertise for the operation, management, commercial development and optimisation of both airports through a concession/management contract,” the commission underlined.

Under the Fasa, the EY Middle East-led consortium would provide “comprehensive transaction advisory services, including technical, financial, legal, environmental and commercial expertise, to support structuring and implementation of the transactions in accordance with international best practices through a transparent, competitive and market-driven process”.

The commission termed the signing an “important milestone” in the government’s privatisation programme.

The press release said the signing reflected the government’s commitment to “enhancing efficiency, service quality and long-term sustainability of both airports through private sector participation while ensuring transparency, competitiveness and value for the people of Pakistan”.

Adviser to the Prime Minister on Privatisation and Privatisation Commission Chairman Muhammad Ali, along with senior officials of the commission, witnessed the signing ceremony.

The EY team was represented by Andre Olivenca of EY International and Zeeshan Hussain, the statement added.

In December 2022, the government, under the premiership of Shehbaz Sharif, decided to outsource the management of the Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad airports under a public-private partnership.

Earlier this year, the outsourcing operation for these airports shifted from a government-to-government (G2G) mode to an open bidding process due to high investor interest, aiming for transparency and fair competition.

Both Karachi and Lahore airports are expected to attract over $500 million each in fresh investment.

In October, PM Shehbaz also approved the ex­­pansion of Allama Iqbal Inter­na­tional Airport and Jinnah International Airport to improve facilities for passengers.

World.title: PM credits economic successes to 'productive partnership' between political, military leadership
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday said Pakistan’s economic achievements were the product of a “productive partnership between the military and the political hierarchy”.

He was addressing a ceremony organised by the American Business Council of Pakistan.

The premier told the business community: “I can tell you without any fear of contradiction that this and other humble achievements couldn’t have been possible without this great team and great teamwork.

“And of course, I would say, again without any fear of contradiction, when was the last time you had struck a very productive partnership between military and political hierarchy? Never in the history of Pakistan.”

PM Shehbaz said he wished there had been such a partnership in the past, contending that Pakistan “would have completely transformed long ago” if that was the case.

“We would have touched the apex of glory through this teamwork, understanding, showing flexibility to each other in the national interest, to support the national interest, to serve the national interest,” he maintained.

The prime minister said he would refrain from taking credit for himself; rather, the credit goes to his team and the “other partners in this field” — Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and his team.

“We should make not only Pakistan’s economy stable, but make it vibrant,” he stated, adding that this required “sincerity of purpose untiring efforts, selfless service to the people and rising above your likes and dislikes”.

PM Shehbaz recalled that the country faced a serious threat of default in 2023. He then hailed his government’s efforts so far, highlighting various statistics showing macroeconomic stability.

“Despite the Gulf crisis, which has jolted even the most powerful economies around the globe, Pakistan is still passing through a period of stability,” he said, while acknowledging that the situation is “very fragile” in terms of energy requirements.

The premier asserted that despite the country importing more than 90 per cent of its energy requirements from abroad, no panic or long queues were seen at fuel stations.

“In fact, to the contrary, we have been able to carve out a subsidy programme to shelter the most vulnerable segments of our society,” PM Shehbaz said, referring to the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme.

“It all came through hard work, untiring efforts, and pain borne by the common man of this country.”

Talking about the Middle East crisis, the premier said that Pakistan was “working tirelessly” to restore peace in the region and was talking to Tehran and Washington with the support of friendly and brotherly countries.

“Difficult as it is, I have no doubts in my mind that we will be able to arrest this situation. If peace is restored in the region, we are about to take off to an altitude never seen before,” he said.

During his address, the premier acknowledged that the members of the American Business Council of Pakistan had contributed “immensely” in promoting Pakistan’s economic interests.

“I have no doubt that you are great ambassadors for Pakistan,” he said.

The prime minister said that he was present today to listen to business community members and put in place a mechanism to address their genuine grievances. He said that the government was committed to removing impediments and bottlenecks in the way of investors.

“Transparency is the primary requirement of such a system. We are trying our best to be as transparent as we possible,” he said.

He went on to say that during the last budget, the government gave tax breaks worth Rs400 billion despite being under an International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme.

He said that the tax breaks were given to the exporters, manufacturing and corporate sectors and the salaried class to ensure that “this becomes a stimulus to promote and strengthen our economy”.

“Of course, you cannot solve this problem of seven decades overnight. I think we should stand up accept the challenge and move forward in unison. That is the only way to find our last place in the comity of nations,” he said.

The premier said that Pakistan had mineral deposits worth “trillions of dollars”. He said that for the past two to three years, work has been actively carried out in this sector.

“We have together taken the first step; God willing, we’ll keep marching in the right direction. And if we do not deviate, I can assure you, without any fear of contradiction, that we will reach our destination one day soon,” he said.

PM Shehbaz also talked about the auto industry, saying that they had received subsidies for years but had very little to show for it.

“And yet they do not want to face competition. This is the time for electric vehicles […] Is it in national interest to support them or the set of policies and modern technology which will a reduce our dependence on imported energy and control climate [disasters]?” he asked.

Concluding his remarks, the premier said that the government took “difficult decisions, exercised physical discipline and embarked upon a programme of structural reforms”.

“Our task now is to consolidate these gains and put Pakistan firmly on the path of sustained export-led growth. It has to be export-led growth,” he said.

World.title: Pakistan inch closer to victory in second Test despite Sri Lanka fightback
World.content:
Sri Lanka mounted a determined rearguard to stave off an innings defeat and frustrate Pakistan on the third day of the second and final Test, reaching 309-9 at stumps at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Thursday.

The visitors, however, remain in a precarious position, with an overall lead of 82 runs and just one wicket left.

Milan Rathnayake led the resistance with an unbeaten 60, while Kusal Mendis and Sonal Dinusha contributed half-centuries to keep Sri Lanka in the contest.

Their effort ensured the match would continue into a fourth day, although Pakistan will believe they have done enough to remain favourites to secure victory.

Sri Lanka added 235 runs during the day after resuming at 74-3, still trailing by 153. Pakistan had taken a commanding 227-run first-innings lead after dismissing the visitors for 98 and then making 325 in reply.

The hosts had further strengthened their position by taking three Sri Lankan wickets before stumps on Wednesday.

They continued to apply pressure on Thursday morning, with Aamer Jamal trapping Dhananjaya de Silva lbw for 37. The batter reviewed the decision, but the original call stood, leaving Sri Lanka at 99-4.

Razaullah then accounted for Pasindu Sooriyabandara, who had battled for 116 deliveries to make 38.

The right-arm fast bowler found the edge, and wicket-keeper Ghazi Ghori dived to his left to complete an impressive catch. Sri Lanka went to lunch at 166-5, with Kusal on 32 and Dinusha on 19.

The pair provided the backbone of the recovery after the interval, putting together an 81-run partnership for the sixth wicket. Kusal, playing a patient innings, reached his 24th Test half-century, striking eight fours in his 126-ball 53.

Pakistan finally broke the stand when Salman Ali Agha dismissed the Sri Lankan captain at 215-6. Mendis attempted to sweep the off-spinner but played the ball onto his leg stump, departing after having helped steady the innings.

Dinusha continued to resist, finding support from Rathnayaka, who came in after Kusal’s dismissal. The pair added 53 for the seventh wicket, taking Sri Lanka past Pakistan’s first-innings total and into the lead. At tea, the visitors were 241-6, 14 runs ahead.

The partnership ended soon after Pakistan took the second new ball, with Aamer providing the breakthrough.

Dinusha attempted to pull a short delivery but mistimed the shot, allowing Azan Awais to take a sharp catch at midwicket. Dinusha departed for 54 from 119 balls, an innings containing seven boundaries.

Rathnayake, meanwhile, grew increasingly assured as the tail began to fall around him.

He reached his second Test half-century with a boundary off Razaullah in the 90th over and continued to attack when the opportunity arose. His unbeaten 60 came off 82 deliveries and included 11 fours.

Mohammad Abbas dealt further blows to Sri Lanka’s hopes of building a substantial lead, dismissing Prabath Jayasuriya for one and Lahiru Kumara for five.

Abbas finished with 2-54 from 33 overs, including 15 maidens, while Aamer was Pakistan’s most successful bowler with 3-67.

Pakistan’s task was complicated by the absence of Saqib Khan, who was ruled out of further bowling after suffering a left hamstring strain on Wednesday.

He had dismissed Lahiru Udara for seven in Sri Lanka’s second innings before leaving the field. The injury left Pakistan relying on their three available frontline fast bowlers for much of the day.

Speaking after play, Ghazi acknowledged the impact of Saqib’s absence but praised the remaining bowlers for their efforts.

“One of our bowlers was unfortunately injured, and that made a bit of a difference. But the other three deserve a lot of credit for the effort they put in to cover for him,” he said.

Ghazi also recognised the responsibility shouldered by Sri Lanka’s middle order.

“Their senior middle-order players showed responsibility on this pitch. The way [Kusal] Mendis batted, he stayed at the crease even though there were quite a few plays and misses. They put up a good performance,” he said.

The Pakistan wicket-keeper said the hosts would need discipline with the bat when their turn came.

“There is still a lot in the wicket for the bowlers, but you have to show a disciplined batting performance,” he said, adding that Pakistan would first look to take the remaining wicket quickly and restrict Sri Lanka to the smallest possible target.

Dinusha, whose half-century helped revive the innings, said the visitors had been determined to respond after their first-innings collapse.

“Credit must go to the Pakistan bowlers. They bowled really well in the first innings, and we struggled a little. But I am very happy with how our boys fought back in the second,” he said.

Asked whether batting had become easier, Dinusha insisted that patience had been central to the recovery.

“To be honest, it wasn’t easy. They bowled really well. We went with patience,” he said. He hoped Rathnayake could add more runs on Friday, saying another contribution from the unbeaten batter would be “very good” for Sri Lanka.

Play ended at 4:35pm after the umpires deemed the light insufficient. Sri Lanka will resume on Friday with Rathnayake and Asitha Fernando, who is unbeaten on two.

The visitors have gained the lead they desperately needed, but Pakistan require only one more wicket to begin a chase that could bring the series to a decisive conclusion.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
