World.title: COP31 negotiators publish revised deal text with no mention of fossil fuels
World.content:
Climate negotiators stripped out any reference to ending the use of fossil fuels in a slimmed down draft deal text published on Thursday, as the COP31 meeting in Antalya, Turkey, approaches its Friday deadline.

The first draft published on Monday had contained two references to fossil fuels and limiting their use — a topic that deeply divides nations in the negotiations every year.

The draft acknowledged that global warming could exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold countries have sought to preserve and the need for “deep, rapid and sustained” cuts to greenhouse gas emissions.

It also encouraged efforts to scale up the deployment of technologies that can suck carbon out of the atmosphere.

Australia, which is leading negotiations under a split presidency arrangement with Turkey, previously said Monday’s opening draft of the deal was always intended to be a broad document that would then be narrowed down.

The latest text is expected to be revised further before it can be agreed.

While the conference is scheduled to end on Friday, in recent years efforts to secure consensus among the nearly 200 countries participating have regularly blown past this deadline by more than 24 hours.

The need to limit rising global temperatures is widely accepted by participants, but they don’t all agree on the best way to do so, who should pay for it, and how quickly the world needs to act.

The talks are taking place at a time when the warming climate and its increasingly severe and regular effects, including heat waves, floods and droughts, are competing for attention among policymakers and the public with war and rising living costs.

World.title: Top U.N. court finds Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against Muslim Rohingya
World.content:
The highest United Nations court ruled on Thursday that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar’s security forces against the Rohingya Muslim minority population in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

The decision, seven years after the case was filed by predominantly Muslim Gambia, marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the legal threshold to prove genocide had been met. It was the first time the court held a state responsible for genocide.

“The court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya,” presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa said in a reading of the decision.

World.title: Rakuten Securities rushes to cope with data breach
World.content:
Rakuten Securities is working quickly to address a recent massive data breach caused by unauthorized access.

In response to the data breach, the online securities firm announced Thursday that it will postpone a plan to open a brick-and-mortar store for face-to-face consultations with customers in Tokyo’s Shibuya district next week.

The company has also decided to temporarily waive fees for transferring investment trust holdings to other financial institutions.

The data breach has raised questions about the company’s information management system.

On Monday, Rakuten Securities detected the possibility of unauthorized access. It later found that data stored in its test environment system may have leaked externally.

Up to 15.72 million accounts were potentially affected by the incident, and about 4.47 million of them contained personal information, including names, dates of birth, addresses, annual income levels and financial assets.

In the test environment, the company usually uses dummy information. However, actual customer information was included this time.

“This case is different from previous ones in that highly sensitive information, such as customers’ financial assets, has been breached,” said a senior official of a major brokerage firm.

Masayuki Endo, professor emeritus at Shizuoka University and an expert on financial information systems, said, “Tests using actual data are effective in preventing system failures.”

However, Endo noted the need to strengthen cybersecurity measures in test environments, such as swiftly deleting data after tests.

World.title: South Korea court orders retrial of ex-PM Han in martial law case
World.content:
South Korea’s top court overturned former prime minister Han Duck-soo’s 15-year sentence on Thursday for aiding a martial law declaration that briefly suspended civilian rule, sending the case back to a lower court.

The 2024 decree issued by the president at the time, Yoon Suk Yeol, plunged the country into chaos, but lasted only around six hours as opposition lawmakers scrambled to overturn it in a vote.

Han, one of several top officials sentenced over the short-lived martial law bid, was handed a 23-year jail term in January for engaging in the declaration, which the court said threatened “the constitutional order” and amounted to insurrection.

World.title: Takaichi vows to attend deliberations on tax-cut bill ‘in good faith’
World.content:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Thursday that she will attend parliamentary deliberations on the consumption tax cut bill “in good faith” and will make every effort for its early passage.

Takaichi made these remarks at a news conference in Shenzhen, southern China, following a series of diplomatic engagements in the Philippines and China. “I advanced Japan’s strong diplomacy and gained solid achievements,” she said.

Regarding the planned benefit program included in the tax cut bill, the prime minister reiterated that the government is considering offering benefits to at least 50% of workers, based on calls from opposition parties.

“We’ll attend deliberations in good faith to gain support from as many parties as possible and begin preparations for its full implementation as soon as possible,” she said.

The prime minister did not discuss the possibility of enacting the tax cut bill with a two-thirds majority in the House of Representatives if the bill is rejected by the House of Councilors, where the ruling parties lack a majority.

Ahead of the revision of Japan’s three key national security documents later this year, Takaichi said that no decisions have been made regarding the size of defense spending for the five years from fiscal 2027 and funding plans. “We’ll promote discussions while considering fiscal sustainability,” she said.

World.title: Riyadh’s tallest building damaged as Saudi reports new Houthi attacks
World.content:
A skyscraper in Riyadh housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund was damaged on Thursday, witnesses said, as the kingdom reported new attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.

Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighboring Yemen’s civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.

In the early hours of Thursday, journalists in the Saudi capital reported that a powerful blast was heard.

World.title: Japan government under fire for using conspiracy theory YouTuber in PR
World.content:
The government has come under fire for featuring a YouTuber known for spreading conspiracy theories and urban legends on an official public relations website aimed at promoting understanding of its security policies.

The government says that the use of the YouTuber is intended to deepen understanding of security policy among people in their 20s and 30s. However, opposition parties and others criticize the move, saying it undermines the credibility of government communications.

The government’s Public Relations Office website launched a special feature page on Monday titled “Kore Wa Toshi Densetsu Dewa Nai” (“This is not an Urban Legend“), explaining how national security is connected to everyday life.

The YouTuber featured on the page, Naokiman, has previously spread unsubstantiated claims, including that a major disaster would strike in July 2025 and that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is a descendant of Emperor Tenmu, a Japanese emperor of the seventh century.

In a video posted on his YouTube channel, Naokiman explained that he received a job offer from the Cabinet Office and said, “What comes out of my mouth is no longer an urban legend; it’s become official.”

At a news conference Wednesday, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the Cabinet Office selected a proposal from a contractor that won the project through a competitive bidding process.

Yuichiro Tamaki, leader of the opposition Democratic Party for the People, questioned the government’s decision, saying it “undermines the credibility of government communications and gives official backing to information that is not based on facts.”

The move has also drawn criticism on social media, with some calling the page “propaganda funded by taxpayers.”

Last month, the Public Relations Office published a feature page explaining the importance of national security in the style of a husband-and-wife comedy duo. The page was designed to target women aged 40 and older.

A Cabinet Office official said each of the two projects had a budget of ¥150 million.

Ryosuke Nishida, a professor of sociology at Nihon University in Tokyo, described the initiatives as “part of a public relations strategy adapted to the changing times.”

However, he added it is “necessary to consider whether it is appropriate for government public relations to use content creators who disseminate information mixing fact and fiction or exploit viewers’ anxieties and curiosity.”

World.title: Nearly 40% disapprove of Takaichi’s China stance, poll shows
World.content:
Nearly 40% of people in Japan disapprove of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s stance on China, a Jiji Press opinion poll showed.

The survey found that 38.4% of respondents disapprove of Takaichi’s China stance, higher than the 33.6% who approved it, while 27.9% said they were unsure or did not know.

Relations between Japan and China have remained strained since November last year when Beijing reacted angrily to Takaichi’s remarks about a potential Taiwan conflict.

Takaichi and Chinese President Xi Jinping shook hands at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.

The survey was conducted from Friday through Monday.

Among those who disapprove of the Takaichi Cabinet, 71.7% rated her stance on China unfavorably, while only 15.1% supported it.

Among supporters of the Takaichi Cabinet, 57.1% said they approve of her China stance, compared with 21.7% who said they do not.

Asked which countries and regions would be important for Japan over the next five years, with multiple answers allowed, 48.9% named China, second only to the United States, at 73.9%.

Only 1.8% selected China as their favorite country, while 63.9% identified it as a country they dislike.

In a separate question, 76.9% backed the idea of the government’s increased involvement in cybersecurity, while 9.5% were opposed and 13.6% said they had no clear opinion.

The rise of artificial intelligence has resulted in a surge of personal information breaches caused by unauthorized access. The latest survey has highlighted the spread of the view that companies are struggling to handle such threats on their own.

The interview-based survey, conducted for four days through Monday, covered 2,000 people aged 18 or over nationwide. Valid responses came from 57.1%.

World.title: AI work-ready Hong Kong graduates? It’s no longer an academic question
World.content:
Hong Kong’s tertiary institutions have long built their world-class reputations on academic rigour. Several of our universities have climbed even higher in prestigious global rankings, cementing our city’s status as an international education hub.

Yet, as we navigate a rapidly evolving economic era driven by artificial intelligence (AI), the formula for graduate success is fundamentally changing. High global rankings – largely driven by research output – are simply not adequate to future-proof our next generation against workplace disruptions.

World.title: Mark Six players could win HK$80 million jackpot in snowball draw
World.content:
Hong Kong punters buying Mark Six tickets for next Tuesday’s lottery draw could vie for a jackpot of up to HK$80 million (US$10.2 million) under a new snowball initiative that increases the prize pool as total betting turnover rises.

Unveiled by the Hong Kong Jockey Club on Thursday as part of the lottery’s 50th-anniversary celebrations, the “Hype Up. Jackpot Up.” campaign lets players collectively unlock a larger snowball reserve for the coming draw by buying more tickets.

If accumulated turnover reaches HK$70 million or above by next Monday afternoon, the club will increase the snowball amount to HK$60 million, raising the estimated First Division Prize Fund to as much as HK$80 million.

World.title: Hong Kong police arrest 123 and uncover 108 cases in anti-fraud operation
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested 123 people and uncovered 108 fraud cases involving about HK$68 million (US$8.7 million) as part of a two-week operation against phone scams and money laundering.

The citywide crackdown was conducted by the commercial crime bureau and regional units. Officers arrested 95 men and 28 women aged between 14 and 75.

Police said on Thursday that most of those detained held stooge bank accounts or were registered users of telephone numbers linked to scams.

World.title: UN intellectual property agency pledges deeper cooperation with Hong Kong
World.content:
The United Nations agency for intellectual property (IP) has pledged to deepen cooperation with Hong Kong on dispute resolution, education and commercialisation as the city’s government plans to expand a pilot scheme for lending backed by intangible assets.

At the Business of IP Asia Forum on Thursday, Shen Changyu, deputy director general of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), said the agency stood ready to help Hong Kong use IP to advance its ambitions in finance, trade and technology.

Beijing positioned Hong Kong as a regional IP trading centre in China’s 15th five-year plan.

World.title: Hong Kong’s MTR Corp probes whether back-to-back HKU station faults are linked
World.content:
Hong Kong’s railway operator is investigating whether two back-to-back signalling faults at HKU station are related, following disruptions to morning commuters for two days in a row.

The MTR Corporation apologised to passengers and said Thursday’s disruption on the Island line lasted nearly an hour, from 7.43am to 8.38am.

A separate signalling equipment fault at HKU station disrupted services from 8.27am to 10.33am on Wednesday, causing long queues at North Point station.

World.title: Treason or not, betraying one’s country won’t be tolerated
World.content:
If you ask what constitutes treason, most people would probably answer: treason is assisting an enemy to harm one’s country. If national security laws existed at the time, historical figures like Qin Hui Wu Sangui and even Wang Jingwei might all have been found guilty of treason. If you further ask whether treason applies only during times of war, the question becomes somewhat complicated.

Logically and as a matter of principle, treason is an act of betraying one’s country; the emphasis is on betrayal rather than the presence or absence of war. Betraying one’s country is doing anything that forsakes your country’s sovereignty and national interests.

World.title: Hong Kong’s ‘Symphony of Lights’ goes out with a bang: ‘end of an era’
World.content:
Hong Kong’s “A Symphony of Lights” has taken its final bow over Victoria Harbour, closing a 22-year run with rooftop pyrotechnics as tourism authorities launch an expanded WinterFest.

Thousands of tourists and Hong Kong residents flocked to the Tsim Sha Tsui harbourfront to watch the 10-minute show, which began at 8pm on Wednesday.

The crowd let out an audible gasp as the first pyrotechnics shot out from buildings across the harbour, set against the show’s familiar orchestral music.

World.title: Where Hong Kong has been hit by major data leaks, and how to protect yourself
World.content:
Multiple organisations in Hong Kong have experienced data breaches in the past few weeks, from a department store and a jeweller to a university and airlines, with experts saying artificial intelligence has enabled more targeted attacks.

The South China Morning Post rounds up what has been happening in Hong Kong, what the city’s shortcomings are in such situations, as well as how scammers have evolved using the different pieces of information they have managed to access.

Who has been hit and how hard?

On November 9, jewellery chain Chow Sang Sang had a data breach in which unauthorised parties accessed its systems, potentially compromising the personal data of both customers and employees.

Attackers may have gained access to customer records including names, contact numbers, email addresses, partial order details and the last four digits of credit card numbers, while exposed employee information may include names, job titles, corporate email addresses and contact numbers.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019293/China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
World.title: China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019293/China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
World.content:
China has proposed its first regulation on vocational skills certifications, cracking down on fraudulent credentials and tightening oversight of certification bodies.

The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security released the draft regulation on Nov. 12, with public feedback open until Dec. 12. No date has been set for when the rules will take effect.

China now has more than 220 million skilled workers — including electricians, AI trainers, and elderly-care workers — accounting for about 30% of its workforce, according to the ministry. Vocational skills certificates can bring benefits such as cash subsidies, children’s school enrollment, and fast-tracked residency applications.

Fraudulent vocational skills certificates have proliferated online in recent years, prompting a nationwide crackdown on bogus credentials in 2022.

The proposed regulation would tighten oversight of certification bodies, barring them from making misleading claims or leaking exam questions. In addition, certificates can be issued only to candidates who pass the required assessments, rather than those who simply pay to obtain them.

The draft also outlines that organizations responsible for vocational qualification assessments would be barred from offering related training. Institutions that issue certificates without first registering with the government, as well as those that forge, alter, or trade certificates, may face suspension, confiscation of illegal earnings, and fines of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan ($1,500 to $15,000).

The rules also outline penalties for examiners who engage in misconduct, candidates who cheat, and officials who fail to perform their duties properly. Employers will be encouraged to use workers’ certified skill levels as a key factor in determining pay.

Previously, workers obtained vocational qualifications through government-organized exams. Starting in 2020, however, China phased out most government-issued vocational qualifications, shifting responsibility to registered and supervised third-party organizations. By the end of 2025, 32,000 such organizations were in operation nationwide.

Cheng Xiezhong, a law professor at the China University of Political Science and Law, told domestic media that the shift had “helped expand the pool of skilled workers” but had also led to uneven standards among certification bodies and a widespread increase in bogus certificates.

An investigation by domestic media this June found vocational certificates openly advertised on multiple Chinese e-commerce platforms. In one case, a reporter paid just 300 yuan for a mechanical equipment installer certificate showing passing scores on tests they had never taken.

Previous reports also found that some training providers issued course completion certificates rather than recognized vocational credentials. Others lured young jobseekers into “training loan” scams, persuading them to borrow thousands of yuan for courses.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Heade image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019284/Bot, Interrupted: DeepSeek Users Report New Limits on Free Chats
World.title: Bot, Interrupted: DeepSeek Users Report New Limits on Free Chats
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019284/Bot, Interrupted: DeepSeek Users Report New Limits on Free Chats
World.content:
Chinese AI model DeepSeek has reportedly begun limiting use of its free chatbot by reducing the number of characters users can input and discontinuing inactive conversations after seven days.

DeepSeek users began reporting seeing an error message — “Due to server overload, the use limit has been reached” — on Monday when they tried to continue chats inactive for a week or when they tried to input larger volumes of text, according to posts on microblogging platform Weibo.

According to domestic media, users of the large language model (LLM) can now only enter around 40,000 characters at a time (a page of Chinese text typically ranges from 500 to 800 characters). Previously, the chatbot had no publicly stated text limit. Once users reach their daily limit, DeepSeek displays an error message.

It is reportedly the first time DeepSeek, headquartered in China’s eastern city of Hangzhou, has restricted free-user access since its launch in January 2025.

According to its official status page, DeepSeek has experienced 57 outages or performance degradations this year, without providing additional explanation. Domestic media reported that disruptions in the first half of the year mainly involved slower responses, delays in data generation, and occasional request failures. After October, prolonged global outages began to occur more frequently.

Usage caps apply only to individual users, but because DeepSeek has no related paid plan, those who hit their capacity cannot pay for more. App developers, who pay to use DeepSeek through an application programming interface, or API, a connection that shares data between their software and the AI model, are subject to separate limits and per-use billing.

As of Wednesday, DeepSeek had not announced a reason for the new rules or whether it might lift them. Developers who spotted references to a “Coding Plan” in the website’s code have speculated that the company may soon implement a paid subscription plan for individual users.

Online, users debated the new limits, with many expressing outrage and complaining that the company had not rolled out a paid plan option for individual users before the usage limit. “I feel like I’m a widow who just lost her husband,” wrote one user on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote.

Others sympathized with DeepSeek, arguing that data is costly or hypothesizing that the company was clamping down on users developing companion relationships with its AI, alluding to China’s ban on AI products designed to mimic human personalities that took effect on July 15.

Data from OpenRouter, a U.S.-based platform that provides access to numerous AI models through one interface, showed DeepSeek’s latest model processing 59.2 trillion tokens the week of Nov. 9 to 15, topping OpenRouter’s weekly token usage chart.

Long chats are more costly for LLM developers because models must parse more information with each reply. Industry watchers told domestic media that the higher costs mean DeepSeek may now have to choose between training new models, serving paying API customers, and providing free chats.

DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng has long said the company has moved toward developing its artificial general intelligence capabilities — the drive to create an AI that can match or surpass humans across a wide range of tasks — rather than consumer revenue.

Earlier this year, Liang said computing power is the biggest factor holding the company back. He also described near-term business opportunities targeting customers as “sesame seeds,” a Chinese turn of phrase describing small gains not worth chasing at the expense of a bigger payoff.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019257/Lu Xun’s Overlooked Translations That Shaped Modern Chinese Literature
World.title: Lu Xun’s Overlooked Translations That Shaped Modern Chinese Literature
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019257/Lu Xun’s Overlooked Translations That Shaped Modern Chinese Literature
World.content:
In 1903, 22-year-old Lu Xun, then a student in Japan, wandered into a bookstore in Jimbocho, Tokyo’s famed book district, where his attention was caught by a science fiction novel titled “A Journey to the Moon in Ninety-Seven Hours and Twenty Minutes.” Translated into Japanese by Inoue Tsutomu and believed to have been written by an American author, the novel appealed to Lu Xun’s own ambition to popularize scientific knowledge in China, where modern science education was still in its infancy. Enthusiastic about the genre’s potential, he quickly set about translating it into Chinese.

His version, “Yuejie Lüxing” (“A Journey to the Moon”), published the same year and among the earliest Chinese translations of science fiction, marked the beginning of his prolific career as a translator, long before he became celebrated as the “founding father of modern Chinese literature” for his novels and essays.

Today, we know that Inoue had misidentified the original author. The novel was, in fact, Jules Verne’s “De la Terre à la Lune: trajet direct en 97 heures 20 minutes,” published in 1865 and widely translated into English in the 1870s. Misled by its setting — in post-Civil War America, where members of the Baltimore Gun Club plan to fire a projectile at the moon — Inoue assumed the author was American. Lu Xun, following this assumption, opened his translation with original passages describing America in extravagant detail to provide context for his Chinese readers.

The curious story of this translation and mistranslation of Verne’s novel illuminates how literary forms and ideas traveled across borders at the turn of the 20th century, particularly in East Asia following the First Sino-Japanese War (1894–1895), when waves of Chinese students — including Lu Xun — went to study in Japan.

It was in Tokyo, amid the intellectual riches of Jimbocho, where he spent much of his leisure time, that Lu Xun was drawn to translation. Japan’s Meiji Restoration, which restored imperial rule in 1868, had already spurred a flood of translations from European languages into Japanese. Eager to take advantage of this wealth of material, Lu Xun, by then proficient in Japanese, with a working knowledge of German and some Russian, immersed himself in these texts. On one hand, he translated texts from cultures he perceived as more scientifically and technologically advanced, with the aim of promoting science education among his own people; on the other hand, he gradually developed an interest in writers from marginalized communities and nations, believing their experiences would resonate with China, which had endured decades of foreign invasion and exploitation. Later, recounting his decision to translate the exiled Russian writer and activist Vasily Eroshenko, he made clear that he saw translation not simply as an aesthetic pursuit, but as a means of giving voice to the oppressed.

It is worth remembering that Lu Xun, then an unknown young student named Zhou Shuren, had yet to adopt his most famous pen name that would be enshrined in modern Chinese literature. In 1918, he published “A Madman’s Diary,” a pioneering work of modern Chinese fiction inspired by a short story of the same name by Russian writer Nikolai Gogol. He later wrote the celebrated novella “The True Story of Ah Q,” published in 1921, helping establish vernacular Chinese as a language of modern literature. He is remembered as a pioneer of the New Culture Movement, which championed “Mr. Democracy” and “Mr. Science” just as China transitioned from monarchy to republic.

But in 1903, a literary career was not yet his ambition. Funded by a Qing government scholarship to study in Japan, he began by taking language courses, translating scientific essays, science fiction, and literary works along the way, before enrolling in medical school in Sendai City, 370 kilometers north of Tokyo, in 1904.

He would soon abandon medicine to pursue his own literary and intellectual revolution, with translation as his chosen medium. Back in Tokyo in 1906, Lu Xun remained enrolled at a German-language school, but rather than attend classes, he devoted his time to translating, writing, and publishing. He shared a small room with his younger brother, Zhou Zuoren (1885–1967), who had joined him in Japan.

The brothers sent their translations to publishers in China. Translation was poorly paid a century ago, just as it often is today. Zhou Zuoren later recalled with resignation: “… manuscript fees were truly meager. Typically, the translation of Western-language texts only earned two yuan per 1,000 characters — and this was a net amount, with all punctuation and black spaces excluded from the calculation.”

Nevertheless, the brothers pursued their work with passion, publishing “Collection of Stories from Abroad” in . Reflecting their intellectual ambitions, the collection featured revolutionary literature from “peripheral” nations whose experiences echoed China’s own. They hoped such works could change minds and contribute to social progress. Funded by Jiang Yizhi, a banker from China’s eastern Zhejiang province, the collection sold poorly, with just 21 copies of the first volume and 20 of the second sold in six months, according to Lu Xun’s preface to a later edition.

Like translators today, those of the past could find their intellectual lives both poor and rich: financial hardship drove them to scrimp and work harder, while literature’s riches tempted them to procrastinate. We might imagine these “revolutio.nary figures” readily sacrificing leisure for national salvation, but their personal accounts tell a more relatable, even comforting, story.

After Lu Xun returned to Tokyo from Sendai, the brothers moved to the wider Kanda-Jimbocho area. After moving a few times, they rented the former residence of renowned Japanese novelist Natsume Sōseki with three friends and named their share-house Wushe, “the house of five.” As admirers of Natsume, they even shopped at the same grocery stores he had frequented and followed his recommended reading list. Personal accounts suggest that Lu Xun spent much of his stipend on books, economizing on food and other daily necessities as a result, which also helps explain why he shared a room with Zhou Zuoren.

Tightening their belts for books while working on their envisioned projects, Zhou Zuoren described a conflict with Lu Xun when they shared a room: “He kept urging me to translate, but I brushed him off. One day, he suddenly flew into a rage, raised his fist, and beat me on the head several times.” As a translator who habitually procrastinates, I can’t bear to imagine what life would be like if I shared a room with my editor.

Translation was more than just work for the Zhou brothers. They lived a “translated” way of life. Kanda-Jimbocho, where they lived, served as a “universal library” and remains Tokyo’s most celebrated book district. Much like Chinese students abroad today who frequent bookstores such as Strand Bookstore, Daunt Books, Shakespeare and Company, or Kinokuniya, the brothers visited Jimbocho’s bookshops almost daily.

The brothers devoured texts across languages and genres. They kept detailed records of their favorite bookstores, even rating the quality of their books and service. Their daily lives involved constant movement between languages as they learned new ones and absorbed political, social, and literary theories, whether in their original languages or in translation.

This broad and intensive engagement transformed their intellectual horizons, offering access to ideas from around the world. As Zhou Zuoren later recalled, Lu Xun would read and write until dawn, sleep until late morning, get up to smoke, and then repeat the cycle.

Later, figures such as Zhou Enlai, the first premier of the People’s Republic of China; Guo Moruo, a writer, poet, and communist leader; Tian Han, the playwright who wrote the lyrics to China’s national anthem; and Feng Zikai, a pioneer of modern Chinese comics, would undergo similar intellectual journeys shaped by translation while studying in Tokyo. They, too, explored different paths toward China’s modernization through their engagement with translated texts, ideas, and ways of life.

In a 1931 letter to fellow writer and revolutionary Qu Qiubai, Lu Xun argued that “translations not only introduce new things but also new ways of expression.” By incorporating unfamiliar syntax into modern Chinese through translation, whether “ancient, dialectal or foreign,” he believed “we can later make it our own.”

His goal was to shape modern Chinese into a truly global language through translation, one flexible enough to absorb diverse forms of expression and capable of conveying ideas from around the world. Arguably, in his imagination, modern Chinese was a language born of translation, one that proudly celebrates its linguistic inheritances. Tian Han and Feng Zikai shared similar convictions, believing that drama and comics — beyond translation in the narrow linguistic sense — embodied cosmopolitan ideals and egalitarian possibilities more vividly than other forms.

To fully appreciate Lu Xun’s significance in modern Chinese literature and language, we cannot examine his fiction alone. In many ways, his identity as a translator — both in the literal sense and in the broader, metaphorical sense of absorbing influences from other cultures and passing them on — was fundamental to his intellectual and literary work.

At a time when cultural exchange has become increasingly complex and contentious, Lu Xun’s story as a translator offers a fresh perspective on what it means to be truly global.

(Header image: Lu Xun (left) with Kaizōsha publishing house president Sanehiko Yamamoto (center) and Japanese bookseller Kanzo Uchiyama (right) at Shingetsutei in Shanghai, Feb. 11, 1936. From the collection of the Lu Xun Museum.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019288/Lesson in Endurance: China’s Schools Start Later to Ease Burden on Students
World.title: Lesson in Endurance: China’s Schools Start Later to Ease Burden on Students
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019288/Lesson in Endurance: China’s Schools Start Later to Ease Burden on Students
World.content:
Parents across China have for years raised concerns about how long children spend in school each day, with some high school students logging at least 15 hours in class.

In recent weeks, education authorities nationwide have been pushing back start times for all grades to ease the burden.

Schools in Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, reportedly began introducing changes in November. A parent told the Yangtze Evening Post that their child, a high school freshman, now starts studying at 7:15 a.m. and finishes after-school study sessions at 9:20 p.m., a 45-minute reduction from the previous schedule of 6:40 a.m. to 9:30 p.m.

Jiangyin, a city about two hours east by road, also announced across-the-board adjustments on Nov. 5. Classes now start at 8 a.m. at primary schools, 7:40 a.m. at middle schools, and 7:20 a.m. at high schools.

During an edition of the show “Zhengfeng Hotline” broadcast live on Jiangsu TV on Oct. 27, Jiang Yong, director of the provincial education department, said, “The issue of excessively long school hours is severe. As the education authority, we feel a profound sense of remorse.”

Paying attention

According to the 2022 China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), a nationally representative longitudinal survey of families, individuals, and communities conducted by researchers at Peking University, 46% of full-time high school students study for more than 12 hours on a typical weekday, while for nearly 25% it’s over 14 hours. Including weekdays and rest days, high school students average 68.6 hours of study time per week.



In 2024, China’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) published its Third National Time Use Survey, which for the first time included data on how children and adolescents spend their time. In 2024, China’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) published its Third National Time Use Survey, which for the first time included data on how children and adolescents spend their time.

For a 2026 article published in Youth Studies, researchers from Renmin University of China and Peking University analyzed survey data relating to students aged 6 to 17. They found that high school students spend on average 10 hours and 54 minutes engaged in education-related activities on weekdays and six hours and 29 minutes on weekends. That adds up to about 67.5 hours.

These activities cover in-class instruction, after-class study, off-campus tutoring, and commuting to and from school.

However, for some, 67.5 hours is merely a baseline. The study reveals a direct correlation between a parent’s education level and how long their child spends studying.

For those with only a middle school education or lower, their children study an average of eight hours and two minutes a day. If the parent holds a high school diploma or a university degree, that time rises by 15 or 29 minutes, respectively.

Study time also varies by location and school quality.

The CFPS shows that high school students in China’s four municipalities — Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin, and Chongqing — as well as provincial capitals study 73.5 hours a week, nearly five hours more than the national average. Meanwhile, for students at key schools, which receive preferential funding and attract high-quality teachers, the figure rises to 75.1 hours.

Both comparisons suggest students in urban high schools and top-tier institutions endure a heavier academic burden.

But why are children spending so long in class? Xiong Bingqi, director of the 21st Century Education Research Institute, argued in an article for Southern Weekly that keeping students on campus longer makes them easier to manage, especially amid pressures to boost academic performance and meet parents’ expectations regarding supervision.

No nodding off

Children in primary education face similarly long days. The NBS’ Third National Time Use Survey shows that elementary school students spend eight hours a day on educational activities. That climbs to nine hours and 22 minutes for those in middle school.

This coincides with evidence that suggests this age group already isn’t getting enough shut-eye.

According to a 2021 Ministry of Education notice on improving young people’s sleep, primary school students should get a minimum of 10 hours a day, middle school students nine hours, and high school students eight hours. Measured against these standards, the Youth Studies research article points out that nearly 22% of 6-year-olds and 42% of 11-year-olds are getting insufficient sleep.

Although the recommended daily sleep duration is lowest for older students, about 20% of survey respondents aged 16 and 17 still weren’t getting enough sleep. Researchers explain that the relatively low proportion compared with younger age groups could be because boarding is more common at the high school level, meaning a “more fixed daily schedule.”

As more schools push back start times, some parents see a chance for change. But whether students will get more sleep depends on other factors, including homework load and the length of evening study sessions.

A later start for students will make a difference only if the time it frees up is reserved for rest.

This article, reported by Chen Liangxian and edited by Lü Yan, originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019275/China’s Basic Insurance to Cover CAR T-Cell Cancer Therapy
World.title: China’s Basic Insurance to Cover CAR T-Cell Cancer Therapy
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019275/China’s Basic Insurance to Cover CAR T-Cell Cancer Therapy
World.content:
China will include a CAR T-cell therapy in its national health insurance scheme for the first time, making a blood cancer treatment that once cost over 1 million yuan ($150,000) per dose more accessible.

The National Healthcare Security Administration announced on Nov. 14 that relmacabtagene autoleucel, or relma-cel, made by Shanghai-based biotech firm JW Therapeutics and sold under the brand name Carteyva, will be covered by insurance starting Jan. 1. The therapy has three approved uses for different types of lymphoma and costs 1.29 million yuan per dose.

CAR T-cell therapy is primarily used to treat types of lymphoma and involves extracting and genetically modifying a patient’s own immune cells to target cancer cells, before infusing them back into the body. China approved its first CAR T-cell therapy product in 2021.

Most of China’s population is covered by the country’s national insurance scheme: 1.33 billion were enrolled in basic medical insurance by the end of 2025. Only drugs listed in the national insurance catalog can be partially reimbursed through the medical insurance fund. For drugs not listed, patients must usually bear 100% of the cost.

For years, CAR T-cell drugs were excluded from the national insurance list because an unwritten industry rule held that drugs priced above 300,000 yuan rarely secured coverage, limiting patient access, according to Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper.

The rate of CAR T-cell drug use as a second-line treatment for large B-cell lymphoma in China is about one-sixth of that in the United States, while use as a third-line treatment is about one-10th of the rate in the U.S. and Europe.

Carteyva was one of five CAR T-cell therapies included last year in China’s first commercial insurance list for high-cost innovative drugs. This year, those drugs became eligible for national coverage. Two CAR T-cell drug manufacturers, including JW Therapeutics, entered insurance coverage negotiations on Sept. 6.

“Two or three years ago, we wouldn’t have dared to imagine this,” Tian Feng, JW Therapeutics chairman and CEO, told The Paper.

China records about 101,500 new lymphoma cases each year. Carteyva is available at more than 200 certified hospitals nationwide.

The updated national reimbursement list adds 107 drugs covering oncology, chronic diseases, mental illnesses, rare diseases, and pediatric medications. A separate commercial insurance list, which covers drugs outside the basic scheme, includes 12 new treatments.

“This is a historic moment for lymphoma patients in China,” Tian said, adding that when he and the company received the news, “everyone really felt that the treatment of lymphoma patients in China had entered a new, very exciting era.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG）

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019269/A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
World.title: A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019269/A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
World.content:
A TV drama about a doctor who returns to his small hometown after being fired from a prestigious city-based position has become a hit among young Chinese, who resonate with its message of finding purpose away from competitive urban areas.

“Small Town Remedy” has been hotly discussed since its Nov. 4 finale. Premiering Oct. 21, the show follows Liu Zhengliang, played by A-list actor Xiao Zhan, a young neurosurgeon who returns to his hometown in northeastern China — or Dongbei — from a major hospital following a botched surgery in which his patient dies.

The show’s popularity comes amid a broader shift in attitudes among young Chinese, who increasingly seek a more sustainable work-life balance and self-care amid growing fatigue stemming from relentless competition and conventional definitions of success.

Socially awkward and unfamiliar with local customs, Liu initially struggles to return to life at home after leaving his post in the southern metropolis of Shenzhen. The series depicts how his brother, childhood friends, and former hospital colleagues gradually help him overcome the trauma of his failed operation, among other personal struggles, such as the death of his mother.

Fans have reported being drawn to the drama’s lighthearted tone and the witty humor commonly associated with China’s Northeast, despite tackling heavy subject matter such as illness, death, and grief.

Its popularity has also sparked an online trend of learning the Dongbei dialect, with video lessons gaining traction on social media. One related hashtag — “‘Small Town Remedy’ Dongbei dialect listening test” — had amassed nearly 1.4 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Monday.

The 29-episode drama has earned an average rating of 8 out of 10 on review platform Douban and reached an audience of 148 million across all streaming platforms, according to data from domestic streaming platform iQiyi. Related hashtags on short-video platform Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, had also garnered more than 8 billion views.

Since the show’s finale, online users have been debating what Liu’s next move should be. Some suggest that as a talented young doctor, he should return to a major hospital to pursue better career prospects, while others say he’d be better off staying in his hometown, where he’d have the emotional space to continue recovering and potentially find greater purpose using his medical skills.

“Everyone wants to go to Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen, but if life away from home is too difficult, returning to your hometown is not a step backward, nor is it something to be ashamed of,” one user wrote beneath a post discussing the show on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. “One’s hometown can be a great choice, too.”

“As urbanization continues, more and more young people are facing the same dilemmas as Liu Zhengliang,” another Xiaohongshu user wrote in a comment under the same post, referring to Liu’s struggles with cultural identity and homesickness. “I think the theme of this show really suits the times.”

In one widely discussed scene, Liu and his girlfriend see off his younger brother as he leaves for Beijing in search of better job opportunities. Overwhelmed by the farewell, the female protagonist, played by Jiang Yan, questions the seemingly inevitable exodus from their hometown.

“Were we born in Dongbei only to leave it behind?” she asks. “The winters here may be cold, but people’s hearts are warm ... Will leaving Dongbei necessarily bring happiness? Don’t those who leave ever miss home?”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “Small Town Remedy.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019274/Shanghai Sacks Two Scientists Over Child’s Death in Gene Trial
World.title: Shanghai Sacks Two Scientists Over Child’s Death in Gene Trial
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019274/Shanghai Sacks Two Scientists Over Child’s Death in Gene Trial
World.content:
Shanghai authorities have dismissed two researchers after an investigation into a child’s death following experimental gene-editing treatment found unheeded safety warnings, failures in ethical review, and undisclosed payments and gifts from the family.

The child had Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder with no effective treatment, according to findings released Friday by the Shanghai investigation team. The family contributed 5.3 million yuan ($800,000) toward the research and separately gave researchers approximately 1.06 million yuan in money and gifts.

In July 2023, the family approached Qiu Zilong, deputy director of Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine’s Songjiang Research Institute, hoping his team could develop a customized gene-editing treatment, investigators said.

The child received an injection at the university’s affiliated Xinhua Hospital on March 24, 2025, and died seven days later.

At an emergency review April 2, the hospital’s ethics committee attributed the death to thrombotic microangiopathy, a complication of gene therapy, and ordered the study terminated.

The death went unmentioned in related preclinical research Qiu’s team published in Nature in February 2026, investigators said. The team reported using gene editing to correct a single error in the DNA code of mouse brain cells, restoring levels of a protein essential for normal brain development. The researchers said tests in monkeys also suggested the technique’s potential for use in humans.

Five months later, a joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch revealed the fatal human trial and reported that the Nature paper had also omitted evidence of liver and kidney damage in animal safety tests.

Shanghai authorities subsequently established a team to investigate the preclinical research, the hospital’s clinical study, and the data underlying the Nature paper.

Investigators found that Qiu’s team had failed to promptly share a safety report from experiments on nonhuman primates with the clinical study’s lead investigator, leaving warning signals unheeded.

Xinhua Hospital’s ethics committee approved the study despite insufficient toxicology and safety evidence, proceeding without additional material it had requested. The hospital also failed to independently and adequately assess the study’s scientific basis and safety.

Investigators said that although the consent form warned the family of serious complications and adverse events, it did not prominently communicate the risk of death.

Investigators found no data fabrication in the Nature paper but identified discrepancies between the research methods used and those described. Data from the same experimental batch had also been presented separately without explanation.

The Nature paper also failed to disclose financial conflicts involving four researchers. Qiu received expensive liquor and electronics worth approximately 100,000 yuan, while Xinhua Hospital associate researcher Yang Kan, the Nature paper’s first and corresponding author, received 900,000 yuan and expensive liquor. Two other members of Qiu’s team each received 30,000 yuan.

Investigators said the money and gifts had been returned or surrendered in accordance with regulations.

Qiu and Yang were both dismissed, and barred from participating in science and technology programs and awards for five years. Their names were entered into a database of serious research integrity violations.

The clinical study’s lead investigator, surnamed Yu, was removed as head of Xinhua Hospital’s research department and demoted. Yu was also barred for five years from being promoted, participating in science and technology programs and awards, and recruiting graduate students. Another official, surnamed Shi, was removed as head of the hospital’s ethics committee office and demoted.

Other officials responsible for the hospital’s ethics review and research oversight received disciplinary sanctions. Xinhua Hospital received an administrative penalty, which the investigation team did not detail.

The Shanghai Municipal Health Commission said it would soon launch special inspections of clinical research involving emerging biomedical technologies.

“As biomedical technologies advance rapidly, research institutions and practitioners must recognize the high risks associated with clinical studies involving emerging treatments such as cell and gene therapies,” the probe said. “While pursuing innovation, they must also adhere to professional standards.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: iStock/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019256/What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
World.title: What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019256/What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
World.content:
Recent exhibitions at the Shanghai Museum and Beijing’s Capital Museum have introduced Chinese audiences to the civilizations of the ancient Americas. For Chinese visitors, the importance placed on jade may feel familiar. In both ancient China and Mesoamerica, finely worked jade adorned the powerful and accompanied them into the grave, a striking similarity that has long attracted scholarly interest.

How did jade come to carry such authority? One way to explore this question is to compare the jade traditions of Liangzhu and the Classic Maya lowlands, two societies from ancient China and the Americas. Liangzhu was an early regional state near present-day Hangzhou, capital of eastern China’s Zhejiang province, around 3300–2300 BC, with a walled capital, an extensive system of dams, and a pronounced social hierarchy. In the Classic Maya lowlands, spanning parts of present-day Mexico, Guatemala, and Belize, cities ruled by royal dynasties flourished around AD 300–900. Both Liangzhu and Maya cities hold UNESCO World Heritage status.

Thousands of years separated the two societies, and there is no evidence of direct contact between them. Yet both had complex social hierarchies in which powerful ritual authorities played important roles. By tracing jade from the selection of raw stone to its final resting place, we can see how control over labor, knowledge, and materials helped establish its authority in ways that were both similar and distinct.

Jade was valued in both ancient China and the Americas long before Liangzhu and the Classic Maya. The concept of jade encompasses several kinds of stone. Liangzhu’s finest ritual jades were made from nephrite, while Maya jade was principally jadeite. Both were prized for their appearance and could be polished to a lustrous finish. Craftspeople shaped jade using abrasives such as sand mixed with water. Working with different stones helped them recognize differences in hardness and toughness and determine which materials were best suited to particular objects.

In Liangzhu, material choice was closely tied to the form and status of the finished artifact. Other stones, such as serpentine, were generally used for small, less prestigious ornaments. Among the Maya, by contrast, the symbolic meanings of stones were more closely associated with their colors. Green and blue-green evoked water, cultivating maize, and renewed life. Jadeite remained highly prized, but a wider range of similarly colored stones could also be valued for their quality and craftsmanship.

Not everyone had equal access to these raw materials or the specialized skills needed to work them. This inequality helped establish jade’s association with power.

Workshops within and immediately outside Liangzhu city made prestigious ritual objects from nephrite. A short distance away, a large workshop complex specialized in small serpentine ornaments. Despite their proximity, the workshops used different materials and produced different types of objects. The fine finish of these serpentine ornaments, however, shows that their makers were skilled.

This contrast suggests that proximity and skill alone did not guarantee access to nephrite. Access appears to have depended on a workshop’s role and status within the production system.

Evidence from the Maya suggests broader access to raw jadeite, but tighter restrictions on the skills and knowledge required to produce elaborate royal artifacts. Near the jadeite sources in Guatemala’s Motagua Valley, in the country’s southeastern highlands, households of different social ranks shaped, sawed, and drilled the stone. At Cancuén, in the country’s center, much of the waste from the early stages of production was found in modest residences. Elaborately finished objects, however, were concentrated in elite buildings, alongside some tools used to polish ear ornaments.

While non-elite households carried out the early stages of jade production, finer carving, including sacred images and inscriptions that conveyed ritual and political meanings, appears to have been largely reserved for elites or specialist craftspeople working for them. Creating these details required skills and knowledge that were less widely shared. Access to raw jadeite did not necessarily mean access to the expertise needed to produce elaborate royal artifacts.

As jade artifacts took shape, their imagery became another critical means of expressing power. This is particularly evident in elite burials, where jade objects helped convey the status and ritual authority of those buried with them.

A jade cong, or ritual tube, from Fanshan, an elite cemetery within Liangzhu city, illustrates how craftsmanship and sacred imagery conveyed authority. Its surface bears an intricately carved human-and-animal-face motif known as the Sacred Insignia. The finest versions appeared on the most prestigious ritual jades, whose material and craftsmanship signaled status.

The cong also belonged to a prescribed set of burial goods. Within Liangzhu’s political center, elite burials followed established conventions that linked the types and placement of artifacts to rank and gender, leaving little scope for personal preference. Differences in the quantity and quality of objects expressed the deceased’s rank and ritual authority within this prescribed framework.

Maya rulers, by contrast, drew on shared beliefs but had greater freedom in how they arranged jade. One example comes from the tomb of Pakal the Great, ruler of the Maya city-state of Palenque, in what is now southern Mexico. His funerary mask is a mosaic of carefully fitted pieces of jade in different shades of green. Scholars interpret its youthful face as linking the ruler to the Maize God. A cube in one hand, a sphere in the other, a bead beside each foot, and a central belt figurine have been interpreted as forming a quincunx, a five-point arrangement representing the four directions and a center in Maya cosmology, with Pakal at its symbolic center.

Pakal’s jades derived meaning from their individual forms and their placement within his tomb. Shared beliefs could guide such arrangements without requiring the standardized sets found in Liangzhu elite graves. Maya sacred imagery also appeared on multicolored ceramic vessels, carved stone monuments, and buildings. Jade was one of several materials through which rulers expressed their place in the world.

The movement and final placement of jade objects also reflected their association with power in both societies.

In Liangzhu, the movement of prestigious jade objects appears to have reinforced relationships among elites. Similarities in carving between the political center and neighboring settlements suggest that these objects circulated primarily among elites, possibly through gift exchanges. Local production continued, but the most sophisticated carving techniques remained concentrated near the political center. When finished, Liangzhu jades were deliberately buried; prestigious ritual objects were typically placed in individual elite graves, while lower-ranking burials contained smaller, less elaborate ornaments.

Among the Maya, jade served purposes beyond elite ownership. Different forms of jade circulated in different ways. Some ornaments bore inscriptions linking them to particular people and events, while plain beads and axe-shaped objects known as celts circulated more freely and may have been used as payment by the Postclassic period (900–1521). Non-elite households acquired small jade beads that could express wealth and status. At Cancuén, jade-working households buried raw or partly worked jade during house construction, suggesting that even unfinished jade material held ritual value. At Copán, in western Honduras, jade and shell artifacts were buried together in a residential courtyard, showing how different materials could serve similar ritual purposes beyond royal burials.

These differences reveal how the two societies developed distinct ways of turning jade into a symbol of wealth and authority. In Liangzhu, the quality of the stone, specialized craftsmanship, sacred imagery, and rules governing its use were brought together in a tightly regulated system. Among the Maya, jade acquired authority through a wider range of materials and ritual settings, allowing for broader participation and more flexible exchange alongside restrictions imposed by elites.

Jade’s beauty may have made it desirable, but it was people who made it precious. Through craftsmanship, sacred rituals, and control over who could possess it, ancient societies transformed stone into a symbol of wealth and authority. The treasures displayed in museums today reveal a larger truth: The value of precious things lies not just in what they are, but in who gets to decide what they are worth.

Portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: Visuals from Lin Xin, reedited by Sixth Tone)

WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
