World.title: Defense witness grilled over ‘useless’ testimony
World.content:
Lawyer Rainer Dela Fuente cites confidentiality to explain why he did not review prosecution witness Alex Cabrera's forensic report, prompting criticisms from several senator-judges

MANILA, Philippines – A defense witness admitted that he had not read the prosecution’s financial forensic report or reviewed its supporting documents before testifying in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday, November 19.

Lawyer Rainer Dela Fuente, a former Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) financial investigator, was presented as an expert witness for the defense on Day 44 of the trial.

During his direct examination, defense lawyer Mark Vinluan sought to challenge the methodology and findings of the financial forensic report prepared by prosecution witness Alex Cabrera.

Dela Fuente, however, told the impeachment court that he had not been provided copies of the report and its supporting documents before the hearing.

“No, Your Honor,” Dela Fuente said when asked whether he had received copies of AMLC records, bank statements, insurance placements, and general information sheets (GIS) of companies linked to Duterte.

Vinluan confirmed that the witness had not reviewed the entire report, saying the defense intended to focus on specific portions of the 50-page document.

“If he is to refute the report, then he should have seen the report, should have read the report,” Senator-judge Joel Villanueva said.

“Now if he cannot answer these questions then, for me, it’s going to be useless,” Villanueva added.

Other senator-judges, including Erwin Tulfo, also questioned how Dela Fuente could examine the report’s findings without reviewing the underlying documents.

“Kung hindi naman niya po nakita pala ay mga dokumento, STRs (Suspicious Transaction Reports), CTRs (Covered Transaction Reports), what good is it? Para anong tetestigo niya, eh puro ito theory sa kanyang paningin, sa kanyang paniniwala,” Tulfo said.

(If has has not seen the documents, STRs, CTRs, what good is it? What’s his testimony for, it’ll just be all his theory, his beliefs.)

He added: “The witnesses you’ve been presenting here these past few days are weak. Get somebody who can really stand up, who can really answer questions from the senator-judges.”

Dela Fuente was listed as a defense witness who would testify on fundamental legal concepts under the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA).

Explaining why he did not review the report and its supporting documents, Dela Fuente cited confidentiality concerns. He also said he was not dismissing Cabrera’s findings but was merely answering the defense’s hypothetical questions based on his understanding of the law.

“Ang akin lang pong saligan ay ang ating AMLA, ang ating batas, so I can answer based on the law… Ako personally, ayoko basahin yung report because coming here, and wala rin ako access sa report, coming here and reading that report, I will develop biases,” Dela Fuente said.

(My only basis is our AMLA, and our laws, so I can answer based on the law… Personally, I don’t want to read the report because coming here, and I also did not have access to the report, coming here here and reading that report, I will develop biases.)

Prosecution questions expertise

The prosecution tried to paint Dela Fuente as unqualified.

“Your claimed expertise as a financial expert in financial investigation only comes from the 25 months that you were an entry-level investigator for the AMLC. Is that correct?” Diokno asked Dela Fuente, who answered in the affirmative.

Dela Fuente also admitted that he was not challenging the accuracy or truthfulness of the AMLC reports, Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) records, and bank records involving the Vice President.

Diokno, like the senators, also made a big deal of the fact that Dela Fuente did not read the forensic examination report prepared by the prosecution’s witness, Alexander Cabrera.

“Let’s say that I were going to evaluate your investigation report,” Diokno said. “If in my evaluation, I decide not to read everything and pick portions only, don’t you think it will be unfair to you?”

“You didn’t read the whole report. Wouldn’t you agree that context means a lot in terms of evaluating the veracity of a financial report?” Diokno added.

Cabrera previously testified that based on his analysis of the Vice President’s bank and financial records, Duterte, and her husband, Mans Carpio, had accumulated P817 million unexplained wealth from 2022 to 2025.

Duterte is being tried for Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which involves allegations of unexplained wealth. – with reports from Dwight de Leon/Rappler.com

World.title: Dividing the Lopez empire: Who decides what a family business is worth?
World.content:
PART 1 | Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us

What months of fighting in boardrooms, shareholders’ meetings, and public statements could not accomplish, the buying and selling of shares may finally achieve: a separation of the Lopez family businesses.

Between August and November 2026, Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III’s branch sold its 25.68% stake in apex parent Lopez Inc. to Ramon Ang for ₱11.56 billion and agreed to buy First Philippine Holdings’ (FPH) controlling stake in Rockwell Land for ₱15.92 billion. In between, cousin Federico “Piki” Lopez locked down the boards of Lopez Holdings and FPH, securing his grip on the group’s energy and industrial core. (Click on these links below for the author’s special reports on these developments:

Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled it

Part 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN struggles

Part 3 | Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go

The cousins appear to be finding a way to stop running the same businesses together. But separating a family business is not as simple as dividing an inheritance, especially when the family’s interests are held through layers of private and publicly listed companies with other shareholders, employees, creditors, and business partners whose interests cannot simply be divided among the cousins.

Who decides what each business is worth? Who approves the sale? What happens when the buyer and seller are connected to rival branches of the same family? And what protects shareholders who were never part of the quarrel?

In the first story of this series, we examined why business families fight and why some choose to stay together while others separate. The Lopezes are hardly the first to confront these questions. Other families have negotiated settlements, divided companies, bought out dissatisfied relatives, or found ways to continue working together. Their experiences offer lessons on how families can manage either choice without damaging the businesses they own.

Who gets to decide?

One source of conflict in family businesses is that relatives often wear several hats at once. A person may be a grandson of the founder, a shareholder, a director, and an executive, but these positions do not give him the same authority. Being a member of the family does not automatically entitle him to run the company, just as owning shares does not necessarily give him the right to dictate daily operations. Problems arise when relatives begin treating their different roles as though they were interchangeable.

Family-business advisers Josh Baron and Rob Lachenauer explain these distinctions through their Four-Room Model. Imagine a family enterprise as a house with four rooms: the family room, the owners’ room, the boardroom, and the management room. The family discusses shared values, relationships, and what it wants to preserve for future generations. Shareholders exercise ownership rights, including electing directors. Directors oversee the company, approve major corporate decisions, and hold management accountable, while executives handle operations, employees, budgets, and the implementation of strategy.

Play Video

The same relative may enter all four rooms, but his authority in one does not automatically extend to another. Family-business adviser Enrique Soriano discussed these overlapping responsibilities during a webinar we conducted in June, when the Lopez feud was already unfolding.

The Lopez dispute illustrates why these distinctions matter. Gabby’s branch exercised ownership rights through its stake in Lopez Inc., while Piki had spent decades managing and directing the group’s energy businesses. When the cousins disagreed about investments, valuations, and corporate direction, their disagreement became a contest over who had the authority to make those decisions.

By September, Piki had secured the chairmanship of Lopez Holdings and FPH, while his brother Benjamin “Jay” Lopez became president, chief operating officer, and chief finance officer of Lopez Holdings, taking over three positions previously held by longtime executive Salvador Tirona. Piki remained chairman and chief executive officer, placing the two brothers in the principal leadership positions of the listed holding company.

The significance went beyond replacing one executive with another. Lopez Holdings sits above FPH in the ownership structure, and the people leading it exercise considerable influence over the group’s investments and corporate direction. Tirona had been a senior professional executive for decades, while Jay was a member of the controlling family branch. His appointment brought operational and financial leadership at the holding company more directly into Piki’s family circle.

Winning control of a board may settle who has corporate authority to make certain decisions. It does not necessarily resolve what the different shareholders want from the business.

Rules before the fighting

The Aboitiz family offers a useful contrast. I interviewed the late Jon Ramon Aboitiz in 2017 for a story about the Cebu-based conglomerate and how it had evolved through generations of owners and managers. When my profile of him was published in 2018, shortly after his death, the family had already established a constitution, a family council, rules governing who could enter the business, and a succession process that included preparing members of different family branches and generations for leadership.

These arrangements were part of a larger philosophy about managing family wealth. Jon Ramon recalled how his grandfather, Ramon Aboitiz, required young family members to learn the business from the ground up, sometimes literally cleaning toilets aboard the family’s ships. Relatives who wanted to become executives had to work and prove themselves. The family also learned to distinguish its attachment to one another from its attachment to a particular business.

The author interviewing Jon Ramon Aboitiz in 2017. Lala Rimando

“One of the first things my grandfather imparted was: ‘Never fall in love with your business,’” Jon Ramon told me. The Aboitizes eventually sold their shipping business under well-known brands SuperFerry and SuperCat, which were once central to the family’s identity, as they redirected capital and management attention toward businesses, such as power, which they believed had better prospects. If it was the right time to sell, for the right reason and at the right price, the family should sell and move on. (READ: Q&A with Jon Ramon Aboitiz: ‘Never fall in love with your business’)

The Po family, whose businesses include Century Pacific Food, also developed formal arrangements to manage family participation. In a 2019 Esquire profile, I wrote about Nanette Medved-Po becoming the first chairperson of the Po Family Council, a position that gave her a role in the family’s governance distinct from the management of its operating companies.

The Aboitiz and Po experiences show how family governance can provide a place for relatives to discuss shared interests and expectations without requiring every disagreement to become a corporate dispute. A family council can help relatives who are not executives remain informed and involved, while a family constitution can establish values, expectations, and policies concerning succession, employment, and the stewardship of family wealth.

Play Video

The Lopez family, however, never finalized a family constitution. Efforts were made while second generation Oscar Lopez was the family patriarch, and again after the third generation assumed leadership of the businesses. Neither effort produced a completed constitution before the cousins’ war erupted in 2026.

That is a significant distinction. The Lopezes had a long family history, established businesses, and experienced professional managers, but they did not have a finalized family constitution that could provide a common reference for the competing branches when disagreements over investments, control, and leadership intensified.

A constitution, however, would not necessarily have prevented the feud. Soriano has emphasized that a family constitution is not enough, because an agreement on shared values is different from a contract establishing enforceable rights. Families may also need shareholders’ agreements specifying how shares can be sold, how their value will be determined, whether relatives have the first opportunity to buy, and how disputes will be resolved.

The bitter dispute behind another familiar Philippine brand, Green Cross rubbing alcohol, offers a warning about relying on family trust without written agreements. Gonzalo Co It, who established the business in 1952, said he placed shares in the names of his parents and siblings when he incorporated the company, believing they were holding those shares for him. He later accused relatives of taking control and diluting his ownership, allegations that became the subject of a long-running court dispute. In a 2014 interview, Gonzalo said his mistake was failing to document the arrangements because he trusted his family.

His attempt at reconciliation brought another painful lesson. In 2011, Gonzalo withdrew his appeal before the Supreme Court, hoping to settle the dispute with his siblings. The reconciliation never materialized, and the withdrawal threatened to end his legal remedies. In October 2016, the Supreme Court allowed him to reinstate his petition, although it did not decide who owned the disputed shares. The case illustrates why families need more than goodwill when they negotiate ownership and settlement arrangements: even an agreement to stop fighting should specify what each side is giving up, what it will receive, and what happens if the promised reconciliation fails.

A family council can help relatives discuss disagreements. A code of conduct can establish boundaries on how they treat one another. A shareholders’ agreement can address what happens when they no longer want to remain business partners. None guarantees that relatives will agree, but the arrangements can establish rules before every proposed decision is interpreted as an attempt by one branch to outmaneuver another.

The best time to negotiate an exit is when nobody is yet trying to leave.

How families negotiate an exit

Some families settle their differences without dividing their businesses. Others decide that separation offers a better chance of preserving both the enterprises and whatever remains of their relationships.

In Singapore, the Kwek family’s February 2025 boardroom confrontation at City Developments Limited ended after trusted intermediaries helped broker a truce. Father Kwek Leng Beng and son Sherman Kwek retained their executive positions, while the two independent directors whose appointments had sparked the dispute stepped down. The Ortigas family, meanwhile, ended its dispute over OCLP Holdings through a 2014 compromise involving Ayala Land and SM Prime Holdings, preserving the property business while sharing influence with powerful outside investors.

India’s Ambani family chose to divide operating businesses, with mother Kokilaben mediating the 2005 settlement between brothers Mukesh and Anil. The Murdochs reached a different arrangement in September 2025, strengthening Lachlan Murdoch’s future voting control over Fox Corporation and News Corp while compensating three siblings who exited the relevant trust arrangements.

These families took different routes, but each had to confront the same practical questions: Who would control the business, what would each relative receive, who would finance the arrangement, and what would happen to the companies afterward?

The Lopezes appear to be pursuing several mechanisms at once. Gabby’s branch sold its ownership interest in the private holding company to Ang. ABS-CBN sought new investors and fresh capital. Piki secured leadership of the listed holding companies. And FPH approved a proposed sale that would move Rockwell Land from Piki’s corporate sphere to Gabby’s investment vehicle.

These are not interchangeable transactions, even if they are unfolding against the same family dispute.

A fair price for whom?

When Crème sold its 25.68% stake in Lopez Inc., to Ramon Ang for about P11 billion, it was selling shares it owned in a private holding company. It was not directly selling the assets of First Gen, ABS-CBN, Rockwell Land, or every other company associated with the Lopez group. The proceeds went to the selling shareholder, Gabby and the other heirs of second generation Lopez siblings, not automatically to the companies beneath Lopez Inc.

The proposed Rockwell transaction is different because FPH, a publicly listed company, is selling its controlling interest in another listed company to an investment vehicle associated with Gabby. The November board approval covers FPH’s 90.74% interest in Rockwell, including common and voting preferred shares, for almost P16 billion. The proposed transaction remains subject to conditions and regulatory requirements, including a mandatory tender offer.

FPH disclosed that BDO Capital & Investment Corporation provided an independent valuation range of P2.47 to P3.09 per common share, with the agreed P3 price toward the upper end of that range. The valuation provides a basis for assessing the price, but it does not automatically settle every question about the transaction.

FPH stands to receive nearly P16 billion that it could deploy toward energy, infrastructure, and other investments. But it would also surrender control of Rockwell, a mature property business that has contributed earnings and diversification to the group. Crème would acquire control of the property developer but would have to finance the purchase and comply with the obligations that accompany control of a listed company.

The question is not simply whether the cousins agree that P15.92 billion is an acceptable price. It is whether the transaction is fair to FPH and its shareholders, including those who are not members of the Lopez family. That requires examining the valuation, the handling of potential conflicts of interest, the directors’ decision-making, and compliance with corporate and securities rules.

Rockwell’s minority shareholders have interests of their own. A change in control triggers tender-offer requirements intended to provide eligible shareholders an opportunity to sell under the applicable rules. These investors did not negotiate the family’s arrangements, and their rights cannot depend on whether the cousins are satisfied with the deal.

ABS-CBN presents another example. Its P6-billion equity plan was intended to raise capital for a company that had struggled financially since losing its broadcast franchise in 2020. Issuing additional shares reduces the percentage ownership of existing investors who do not participate proportionately. Their shares are not confiscated, but they own a smaller portion of the enlarged company. Among those affected was Batangas representative Leandro Leviste, whose investment and Mother’s Day gift to Senator Loren Legarda I examined in an earlier Rappler report.

The distinction matters. The Lopez Inc., transaction allowed a family shareholder to sell an investment. The ABS-CBN recapitalization sought to raise money for the company. The Rockwell transaction would transfer control of a subsidiary and provide cash to FPH. Treating all three as one family divorce obscures the separate corporate decisions and the interests of other shareholders.

The people who did not start the fight

There is another reason a corporate divorce cannot be judged only by whether the relatives are happier afterward. The Lopezes control companies with employees, executives, lenders, and shareholders who are not members of the family. These people did not start the dispute, but its consequences can affect their investments, careers, and livelihoods.

At an April townhall, Piki told First Gen employees there was no need to take sides in the family conflict. He urged them to continue doing their jobs professionally. ABS-CBN executives, meanwhile, were trying to keep employees focused on their work while the company’s financial difficulties and changes in ownership created uncertainty. The media company had already undergone repeated rounds of retrenchment since losing its broadcast franchise in 2020, and another program affected about 200 employees in September 2026. The layoffs cannot simply be attributed to the family feud, but the employees were confronting another period of uncertainty while the company’s owners and investors were making major decisions about its future.

The dispute also unfolded alongside changes involving longtime executives Salvador Tirona and Enrique “Ike” Quiason, as well as independent directors Roberto Panlilio and Consuelo Garcia of Lopez Holdings. Tirona’s departure was particularly consequential because he had held the presidency, chief operating officer position, and chief finance officer position at Lopez Holdings, all three of which were taken over by Piki’s brother Jay. The departures and changes in corporate roles occurred amid the bitter contest for control, although the companies have not established an official reason linking each departure to the feud. It would be wrong to assume that every executive or director left because of pressure to choose sides.

Still, the timing raises legitimate questions about how professional managers and directors navigate a conglomerate when its controlling shareholders are divided. Independent directors, in particular, are expected to exercise judgment on behalf of the company and its shareholders, rather than simply follow the wishes of the family that controls it. Their responsibilities become especially important when a company is considering major transactions involving competing family interests.

There are also investors outside the family. Among the more prominent is businessman and Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste, who acquired shares in ABS-CBN as a Mother’s Day gift for his mother, Senator Loren Legarda. His investment, like those of other minority shareholders, has been affected by changes in the media company’s capital structure. When ABS-CBN issues new shares, existing investors who do not acquire additional shares can see their percentage ownership shrink. The same principle applies whether the investor is a prominent politician’s son or an ordinary shareholder who bought a small number of shares through the stock market.

Play Video

Lenders and institutional investors have their own interests. They may care about management continuity, financial stability, and whether contracts remain enforceable when control of a company changes. A family settlement may satisfy the relatives while leaving a company with insufficient capital, divided management, or shareholders who question whether their interests were properly considered.

This is why a family-controlled conglomerate cannot be treated simply as a collection of properties that relatives are free to divide among themselves. The family may control the votes, but the companies have obligations to other shareholders and stakeholders.

Beyond the family settlement

The experiences of other business families suggest that a workable settlement requires more than a willingness to stop fighting. Relatives need a credible way to value their interests, a means of financing any buyout, and clear arrangements governing who will control the businesses afterward. If they remain together, they need rules for making decisions and resolving disagreements. If they separate, they need agreements covering not only the division of assets but also debts, continuing obligations, and any business relationships that will remain between them.

For the Lopezes, the process is still unfolding. Piki has strengthened his position over the energy and industrial businesses, while Gabby’s branch has sold its Lopez Inc., stake and is positioned to acquire Rockwell if the proposed transaction is completed. ABS-CBN is raising capital to stabilize its finances. The family may be moving toward a clearer separation of business interests, but the companies still have obligations to their shareholders, employees, creditors, and business partners.

Lawyers, bankers, directors, and advisers can help value shares, prepare agreements, arrange financing, and secure approvals. They can help relatives settle who gets what, and under what conditions. What they cannot guarantee is that the businesses will prosper once the relatives have gone their separate ways. And they cannot shield controlling families from their legal and financial obligations to minority shareholders, creditors, and employees who never voted on the feud, yet have to live with its terms.

The Lopez cousins may eventually discover that running different businesses gives them the freedom they wanted. Or they may find that separating ownership and control comes with costs that become apparent only years later.

Other families have already taken that road. What happened to them after the agreements were signed, the lawsuits withdrawn, and the relatives stopped sharing the same boardroom? – Rappler.com

Part 3 on Friday, November 20 | Two cousins, two big bets: Will the Lopez split actually work?

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

World.title: ‘Filipiñana’ actress Jorrybell Agoto passes away
World.content:
The lead star of the Philippines' official entry to the 2027 Oscars succumbs to her battle with lymphoma

MANILA, Philippines – Jorrybell Agoto, the lead actress of Filipiñana, passed away, Epicmedia Productions announced on Thursday, November 19.

Epicmedia is among the film production companies responsible for bringing to life the black comedy film. Born in 1994, Agoto portrayed the main character, Isabel, a 17-year-old tee-girl for an exclusive golf club in the Philippines.

“You have touched our lives. Rest now, Belly,” Epicmedia wrote.

In September, the Filipiñana team, along with Agoto’s friends through the Instagram account “Jorrybell Beats It,” had appealed to the public for support after the actress was placed under critical care as she battled lymphoma, a type of blood cancer that affects the immune system.

The announcement of Agoto’s death comes just a day after the people behind “Jorrybell Beats It” held an acoustic night on Wednesday, November 18 to help raise funds for her hospitalization and medical expenses.

Details of Agoto’s memorial services have yet to be announced.

Filipiñana is the Philippines’ official entry to the 2027 Oscars under the Best International Feature Film category. The shortlists will be announced on December 16, while the awards ceremony will be held on March 14, 2027, at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood, Los Angeles. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Rappler Investigates] Conflict of interest
World.content:
Like a plague, this affliction has spread across both local and national offices, facilitated by the prevalence of political dynasties

It’s been a recurring theme in several stories we’ve published lately. It’s widespread, taken for granted, and its violation quite brazen among some government officials.

A conflict of interest occurs when private interests threaten to cloud or sway judgment. Public officials are discouraged from placing themselves in such a position because the temptation to exploit contracts, policies, and rulings for personal gain becomes harder to resist.

Ethics and moral principles also dictate that public officials and employees not extend favors or benefits to their relatives.

One would think the rationale is obvious: without it, government looks less like public service and more like a machine for dispensing, if not harvesting, favors.

One of our Aries Rufo Journalism fellows for 2026, Euni Barreno, with the guidance of senior editor Mia Gonzalez, reported on how public works deals involving in-laws of Caloocan City Mayor Along Malapitan raise conflict-of-interest questions.

Euni is a young, graduating journalism student at the University of the Philippines in Diliman and is a news staffer of the Philippine Collegian.

Instead of being inspired by local officials, an aspiring journalist who must report on the apparent misjudgments, if not misdeeds, of his own mayor may end up disheartened.

In his digging, Euni discovered that the recipient of multiple Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) contracts in Caloocan City, a firm named Ave-Mira Construction and Trading, is run by the in-laws of Mayor Along Malapitan.

From 2019 to 2025, according to Euni, Ave-Mira bagged 39 DPWH projects in Caloocan City worth over P731 million. During this period, Along’s father Oscar was an elected official of the city.

The Malapitans have held the mayoral post for more than a decade, with father and son taking turns after being term-limited.

Did laws on conflict of interest deter Along Malapitan and his in-laws from forging DPWH deals in Caloocan City? Apparently not. But they are not alone, unfortunately. A quick scan of recent stories yielded the following:

Like a plague, this affliction has spread across both local and national offices, facilitated by the prevalence of political dynasties.

Yet we are far from being deficient in laws and principles that prohibit these and frown upon conflict of interest in government. There’s the Constitution, Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards, Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, and even the Local Government Code. Too many laws but very poor enforcement.

No wonder they are regarded as mere suggestions rather than strictures for compliance. Besides, who has been fined or jailed for violating conflict of interest laws?

A profile by justice reporter Jairo Bolledo of newly-appointed Supreme Court Associate Justice Gamaliel Cordoba reminded me of the new magistrate’s ties to a commercial fishing company, Mercidar Fishing Corporation. It’s partly owned by his wife.

Was it coincidence that when Cordoba was still with the National Telecommunications Commission, the agency stopped issuing service numbers for trackers attached to fishing vessels? These trackers were intended to prevent illegal fishing within 15 kilometers of municipal waters because these are reserved exclusively for small fisherfolk.

It’s little protection for fishing boats that can’t compete with larger commercial vessels. But in 2023, a Malabon regional trial court allowed Mercidar to fish within the 15-kilometer zone. This was affirmed a year later by the High Court — of which Cordoba is now part.

What did I say about conflict of interest again? Till Thursday after next!

– Rappler.com

Rappler Investigates is a bimonthly newsletter of our top picks delivered straight to your inbox every other Thursday. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to subscribe.

World.title: EU Commission targeted in cyberattack – report
World.content:
EU CYEBRSECURITY. A hand is seen on a laptop with binary codes displayed in front of the EU flag in this illustration taken, August 19, 2022.

Several systems, including HR systems for payslips and time management and a system for medical reimbursements, were taken offline during the disruption that lasted around 10 days

The European Commission was targeted by a cyberattack which might have compromised large amounts of personal data, Politico reported on Thursday, November 19.

The Commission believes it has contained most of the attack, but the full extent of any damage remains unclear, Politico said, citing an EU official.

The European Commission did not immediately reply to a request for comment on Thursday morning.

Politico said several systems, including HR systems for payslips and time management and a system for medical reimbursements, were taken offline during the disruption that lasted around 10 days.

“The European Commission has taken the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told the news outlet.

“Individual systems were targeted and, in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned.”

The Commission convened its highest-level internal crisis management body for an urgent meeting about the cyber incidents, Politico said.

Tech Commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed other commissioners on Wednesday, it added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Is ‘interoperability’ the future of marketing?
World.content:
Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by Digital Marketing Association of the Philippines (DMAP) and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

The word “collaboration” has been frequently thrown around in the past years – rising influencers joining forces with brands on a series of social media postings, vloggers coming together on their individual channels, and online creators of entirely different disciplines linking for passion projects to fill in each other’s “gaps” or introduce new areas for exploration for each other’s audiences.

While it’s cool to witness these many forms of collaboration, sometimes I couldn’t help but wonder if this level of saturation makes it difficult to stand out. How can a joint creation be unique in the age of fast-paced consumption and online fatigue? How effective can partnerships be in the future?

When I attended the recent DigiCon 2026, I discovered that there’s another word for collaboration, but with a richer and clearer structure: Interoperability. At “Interoperability: Welcome to the Age of Collaboration,” the flagship program by the Digital Marketing Association of the Philippines, 2,000 leaders and professionals from the marketing, business, technology, and media industries learned about how this multilayered term means cross-industry collaboration as we tinker with new technologies. Moreover, it happens by bringing out the best in human creativity alongside benefiting from the continuous evolution of AI – not as a replacement, but a collaborator.

Integrated into human life

One of the speakers, “Connect the Dots” author Dr. Christian Busch, offered an example of this through his talk on serendipity. According to him, the difference between serendipity and luck is that the former is about having agency in what’s going to happen next.

CHANCE ENCOUNTERS. Dr. Christian Busch talked about the value of unexpected ideas in cultivating effective collaborations

We can study serendipity through interoperability, as we find the unknown connections that can bring us to fruitful situations – and this can be achieved through placing “hooks”. Simply put, these can start with the kind of questions we ask people, like, “What are you currently curious about?” or “What are you currently working on?”

DigiCon co-chair Raymund Sison described interoperability as “one of the most natural things in the world.”

ALL HANDS ON DECK. DigiCon co-chair Raymund Sison emphasized the need for collective integration in the rise of AI in the digital space

“The earliest forms of large-scale digital interoperability weren’t built for business or entertainment – they were forged by the military and early researchers to ensure that critical data wouldn’t get trapped in a single silo during a crisis. It’s about survival,” he said. “To build a resilient digital economy, we must move beyond individual capabilities and focus on collective integration.”

Empowering people’s potential is important in the event, as DigiCon co-chair Shayne Madamba acknowledges the risk of AI’s takeover of our lives. “Looking at marketing today, paradoxically speaking, as we enter the height of AI where algorithms can hyper-personalize, automate, and even segment faster than ever. Our country, our industry, everyone in this room – we’re actually becoming more fragmented.”

CRITICAL MINDS. DigiCon co-chair Shayne Madamba grounded the audience by reminding them on the risks of AI’s takeover in the marketing industry

She added, “If we allow it further, AI can build walls of data silos, isolating us, our tools, our channels, and our whole humanity. This is why interoperability is no longer just a buzzword. It is a marketing imperative.”

This year’s two-day DigiCon was divided into Innovation, Integrated, Impact, Immersive, and Interactive tracks. We got to listen to how various companies and brands define interoperability through their lived experiences – some of them, quite unexpected.

Scrupulous integration with technology

Interoperability means integrating with technology – which is common in the workplace. Thus, it’s a must to be responsible with the use of AI.

During the panel discussion, “Privacy and Data Ethics: How to Build a Culture of Responsible AI Inside Your Organization,” Don Kevin Hapal, Rappler’s Chief Data Officer, shared the importance of taking accountability in using AI.

“At the end of the day, if you generated it, you’re still liable for it. Because if something goes wrong because of the content you generated, you cannot suddenly just blame the AI for it. Because at the end of the day, it was you who decided to create that content.”

Hapal emphasized the weight of this in the context of responsible AI use in media. “The responsibility [and] accountability [are] higher if you choose to put it out into public. For example, on social media. You decided to post this information. Because at the end of the day, it doesn’t matter if it’s AI-generated – if you choose to put it out to the public. It’s carrying your name.”

Pop culture as a local movement and global soft power

During the talk of Javier Miguel “Javi” Benitez, chairperson of the House Special Committee on Creative Industries and Performing Arts, he emphasized how recent successes in our popular media often started with a “Pwede pala” (So it’s possible) thought. Think of the collaboration of previous rival networks that brought out the country’s highest-grossing film, and even the gradual worldwide rise of our underdogs SB19 and BINI.

Referencing the earlier talk, he emphasized that serendipity can’t work without the proper rails, so interoperability can happen in the form of rights, money, data, talent, and stages, among other forms of support.

Building a strong community that moves for you

On the topic of pop culture, DigiCon also highlighted fandoms as another example of interoperability in play. Ina Flores, founder of fandom platform Hey Roomie, emphasized how fans stay in fandoms because of the community they provide. It’s interoperability at work because what’s happening isn’t passive. Ellen Manalang, leader of OPM artist Maki’s fandom Zushis Official, cited an example: Maki encourages his fans to discuss his work with him, like building a lore together.

Ultimately, interoperability brings us closer together – an important aspect to preserve in the age of AI.

Frances Cabatuando of Home Buddies PH – which houses millions of active members – brought up the value of finding a “north star” for your community. This allows people to know how to utilize the space themselves; they know how to act because they see the group’s purpose. And in big communities, people also get the initiative to create smaller, closer, and more intimate communities. They move on their own.

“You are one idea away from changing the world,” said Judy John, global chief creative officer at Edelman.

INSPIRING ROOM. Edelman global chief creative officer Judy John, an influential leader in today’s creative industry, graced the event as a keynote speaker

While we’re often hounded by the “doom and gloom” image of the future, interoperability can be one of our strengths, as this inspires mobilization. We don’t just let things unfold. We’re aware that we can still make things happen the way we want to, if we’re brave enough to operate collectively. – Rappler.com

World.title: ASEAN in Manila: The arrest of activists protesting Pax Silica
World.content:
The 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, held in Manila from November 15 to 18, became a showdown between activists protesting the planned local construction of data centers under the US-led Pax Silica initiative, and police tasked with maintaining order as the Marcos Jr. administration hosts world leaders including US President Donald Trump.

Rappler videographer Jonvic Digma, with reporter Patrick Cruz, captures the gathering of the protesters, their move towards the summit venue in Pasay City, and the tense moments when they encountered Manila police who proceeded to arrest several of them, quite violently in some cases, as shown in this documentary. – Rappler.com

World.title: Taguig prosec junks raps vs 3 UMak students rallying vs Trump, Pax Silica
World.content:
Protesters gather at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila on Tuesday for a “Trump Out” demonstration ahead of US President Donald Trump’s visit for the 49th Asean Summit. (Photo from ACT-Teachers Party-list)

MANILA, Philippines — The Taguig City Prosecutor’s Office has junked the complaints filed by the Taguig City police against three students who were arrested in a lightning rally near the University of Makati last Nov. 13.

Based on the copy of the resolution dated Thursday, Nov. 19, the dismissed complaints involved alarm and scandal under Article 155.

The demonstrators were also nabbed for alleged resistance and disobedience to an agent of a person in authority, under Article 151 of the Revised Penal Code.

Article continues after this 

Alleged violation of Batas Pambansa 880, or the Public Assembly Act were also cited by the police in the young persons’ apprehension.

The prosecutor said that upon evaluation, there was no “prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction” to indict the three students.

READ: DOJ confirms release of 233 protesters during Asean Summit

The prosecutor likewise observed that evidence on record shows that the students’ actions “were made specifically to voice out certain political and social grievances.”

The state counsel also deemed that the students were joining the protest “not for the purpose of causing general disturbance or public disorder.”

Article continues after this 

The students joined the rally to oppose the visit of United States (US) President Donald Trump in time for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit.

The students were also fighting the Pax Silica initiative, which, they said, will displace indigenous communities and farmers in Central Luzon.

Article continues after this 

READ: Bayan condemns Marcos’ ‘biggest mass arrest in a single day’

US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton and President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday said that the signing of the Pax Silica initiative was not part of Trump’s agenda during the American president’s visit to the Philippines. /apl

World.title: Solons seek probe into cops’ ‘brutality’ in arresting Asean protesters
World.content:
A police barricade resulted in a fight between protesters and police officers, with the two sides violently pushing and shoving each other during a rally staged on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, in time for the opening of the 49th Asean Summit. (Photo by Zacarian Sarao / INQUIRER.net)

MANILA, Philippines — Lawmakers from Makabayan bloc on Thursday filed a resolution calling for a congressional inquiry into the string of arrests during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit in Manila.

House Resolution No. 1632 was introduced by ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio, Kabataan Rep. Renee Co and Gabriela Women’s Party Rep. Sarah Elago for this purpose.

The investigation seeks to condemn the behavior of the police in arresting hundreds of protestors demonstrating against the arrival of US President Donald Trump.

Article continues after this 

“The PNP committed gross human rights violations against the arrested protestors,” the resolution read.

The group cited incidents – such as “physical assault, kicking and manhandling,” threats for refusing mugshots, denial of legal counsel, and “filing of trumped-up charges”– as among the alleged acts of “brutality” done by members of the Philippine National Police.

READ: DOJ confirms release of all detained 233 Asean Summit protesters

Authorities have arrested more than 200 demonstrators in the lead up to the Asean Summit in Manila.

The rallyists were objecting to the participation of Trump and Washington’s Pax Silica initiative.

Article continues after this 

They were also criticizing the rising living costs amid heightened security that was put in place by law enforcement to secure the Asean-related meetings.

On Thursday, the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers said it will file countercharges against police officers who allegedly committed human rights violations.

Article continues after this 

READ: Group to sue police for protesters’ ‘illegal’ arrest during Asean Summit

The group will be suing the cops for alleged arbitrary detention and alleged violations of Batas Pambansa No. 880 or the Public Assembly Act of 1985.

World.title: Ombudsman suspends Capiz town vice mayor over alleged inaction
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman on Thursday said it had ordered the six-month preventive suspension of Sigma, Capiz Vice Mayor Stephen Alayon over his alleged inaction on a water system solar project.

The Ombudsman said the preventive suspension without pay was imposed as a precautionary measure to prevent the vice mayor from potentially influencing the proceedings while his administrative cases are pending resolution.

“Records show that there is strong evidence of guilt against respondent for the complained act of grave abuse of authority also known as oppression,” the Ombudsman said in its order.

Article continues after this 

READ: Ombudsman suspends Cavite town mayor over gambling allegation

It noted that Alayon is facing cases of grave abuse of authority, neglect of duty, conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service and Republic Act No. 6713 or the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees.

This case stemmed from a complaint filed by Sigma Mayor Dante Eslabon who claimed that Alayon, who served as the presiding officer of the municipal council, allegedly committed unlawful acts by refusing to take action on the municipality’s request to enter into a usufruct agreement with Barangays Poblacion Sur and Poblacion Norte.

The complaint also noted that the Sigma municipality needed dependable water supply, so Eslabon wanted to transfer the management of the project to the barangays. It said that the complainant shared that Sigma is a beneficiary of the Solar Water System project of the national government.

READ: Zaldy Co’s 3 co-accused declared fugitives; Ombudsman calls for action

Article continues after this 

“The transfer necessarily required a usufruct agreement stipulating that the Municipality of Sigma would retain ownership of the SWS project while allowing transfer of management to the beneficiary barangays,” the Ombudsman said in a press release.

The complainant also alleged that his request was pending for more than nine months despite several follow-ups. The Ombudsman noted that Eslabon needed authority from the municipal council to enter into an agreement with the beneficiaries. /jpv

World.title: Prosecution to Panelo: Be realistic if you want to divert attention
World.content:
Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong — Photo from Cong. Zia Alonto Adiong/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution panel has urged Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson, Paolo Panelo, to come up with more realistic stories if his goal is to divert public attention from the impeachment trial, following his claim that a no-election scenario is being floated for 2028.

In a press briefing on Thursday, prosecution spokesperson and Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said he understood why Duterte’s camp was resorting to diversionary tactics: because, in his view, the defense’s case was so weak.

READ: Chua chides Panelo: He’s just seeking attention; let’s give it to him

Article continues after this 

Thus, Alonto Adiong advised Duterte’s team to create more “believable” stories.

“I understand that there’s that incessant effort to divert the attention of the public from the impeachment trial, especially now that the defense case is so weak that they cannot even provide a single witness that can refute the case of the prosecution,” Alonto Adiong said.

“But my unsolicited advice to the camp of the Vice President, please do not stretch your imagination too much and instead create stories that are believable para naman maniwala ang mga tao kung gusto niyo lang i-divert ang atensyon ng taumbayan sa impeachment na ito,” he added.

(But my unsolicited advice to the camp of the Vice President: Please do not stretch your imagination too much, and instead, create stories that are believable so that the people would believe you, if you really want to divert the people’s attention away from this impeachment trial.)

Public prosecutor and Manila Rep. Joel Chua on the other hand urged Duterte and her team to just address the allegations raised before the impeachment court, particularly those under Article II of the Articles of Impeachment.

Article continues after this 

“Alam po ninyo, tigilan na nila ‘yong mga kung ano-anong pinagsasabi nila, siguro mas makabubuti pa sagutin na lang nila ‘yong allegations dito, hindi ‘yong kung ano-anong issue ang ginagawa nila para malihis ‘yong mga usapin,” he said.

(You know, they should stop saying these things, and maybe it would be better if they just answer the allegations here, instead of coming up with different issues to divert discussions…)

Article continues after this 

“Lahat po yan puro mga diversionary tactic lamang nila,” he added.

(All of these are mere diversionary tactics from their camp.)

Panelo claimed in a television interview that some lawmakers were supposedly discussing a no-election scenario in 2028, including possible term extensions and a shift to a parliamentary form of government.

The lawyer attributed the information to the Vice President and claimed to have independently confirmed it.

Aside from Chua and Adiong, both ranking members of the House of Representatives, Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V also denied that such discussions are taking place.

“Walang No-El plan sa Kamara. Walang planong kanselahin ang eleksyon sa 2028 at walang planong pahabain ang termino ng mga kasalukuyang opisyal. Malinaw ang ating paninindigan: tuloy ang halalan sa 2028, at ang taumbayan ang magpapasya kung sino ang kanilang mga susunod na lider,” Ortega said.

(There’s no No-El plan in the House. There is no plan to cancel elections in 2028, and there is no plan to extend the term of current officials. Our stand is clear on that – the elections in 2028 will continue, and the people will decide who their next leader is.)

Ortega challenged the Duterte’s camp to substantiate its allegations by providing evidence and naming names instead of stirring rumors.

“Kung may ebidensya sila, ilabas nila. Sino ang mga kongresistang sangkot? Nasaan ang panukala? Nasaan ang dokumento? Hindi puwedeng basta magbato ng seryosong paratang na walang malinaw na batayan at hayaang mag-alala ang sambayanang Pilipino,” he said.

(If they have any evidence, they should release it. Who are the lawmakers involved? Where is the proposal? Where is the document? They cannot just make serious accusations without a clear basis, and let the Filipino people worry about it.)

“Hindi pag-aari ng mga pulitiko ang kapangyarihan. Ang mandato ng bawat halal na opisyal ay nagmumula sa taumbayan at may hangganang itinakda ng Konstitusyon. Walang sinuman ang maaaring basta magdesisyon na hindi na magkakaroon ng eleksyon para lamang manatili sa puwesto,” Ortega added.

Panelo has been hit by several members of the prosecution panel for making supposedly outlandish statements, which some view are violations of the impeachment court’s sub judice rule.

Last September, public prosecutor and Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon offered tissue paper to critics who cannot stop crying over the Senate Impeachment Court’s ruling allowing a lower minimum vote to convict Duterte.

Ridon said that those with grievances about the Senate Impeachment Court’s decision — like Panelo — can always go to the Supreme Court to argue their case.

Panelo also claimed last September 25 that the Senate Impeachment Court has already manipulated the discussions on the minimum number of votes needed for a conviction, saying that the senator-judges are just fooling around.

However, Chua said back then that it seems Panelo’s statements are only meant to provide him a share of the spotlight and attention.

And when Panelo recently said that Duterte herself expects the trial not to reach Christmas Day as the prosecution is allegedly rushing to end the proceedings, Chua said that it would make the defense panel a “masochist,” as they seem to enjoy seeing themselves continuously ‘beaten and bloodied’ in court.

Despite the defense presenting several witnesses since the trial resumed last November 9, different members of the prosecution have been adamant that these testimonies and arguments have failed to counter evidence showing that Duterte allegedly has unexplained wealth and that she failed to disclose these in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN).

Alonto Adiong previously said that the allegations raised under Article II have not been disputed — adding that in some ways, the testimonies of defense witnesses even bolstered the prosecutors’ arguments.

READ: Prosec: Duterte’s camp in panic, still no answer to ill-gotten wealth allegations

Then last Friday, lead public prosecutor and Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro said that Duterte’s yearning for a bloodbath in her impeachment trial came true, but it seems it was not in the way she would have wanted.

Your subscription could not be saved. Please try again. Your subscription has been successful. Subscribe to our daily newsletter SIGN ME UP

Instead, Luistro said that the bloodbath happened within Duterte’s camp, or the defense panel, as the testimony of their witnesses favored the prosecution. /jpv /apl

World.title: Super-witness, supercomputer? Tulfo hits ‘omniscient’ defense witness
World.content:
Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo INQUIRER FILE

MANILA, Philippines — Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo has called out Vice President Sara Duterte’s lawyers for seemingly wanting their witness to be an expert on everything, asking whether he is a “super-witness” and later calling him a “supercomputer” as different topics were brought up during the direct examination.

Tulfo raised the point when Duterte’s trial resumed on Thursday. He interrupted defense counsel Mark Vinluan’s questioning of former Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) investigator Rainer dela Fuente, saying that the testimony appeared to be spanning different areas of expertise.

READ: Analyst: VP Duterte didn’t declare P207-M cash, total assets reach P817M

Article continues after this 

“Is he a super-witness, omni-witness? Ano bang klaseng witness itong pine-present ng defense? Pati ba naman amici curiae papaki-alaman niya, Supreme Court paki-alaman niya, Ombudsman, DOJ (Department of Justice), who is he? Who is this guy?” Tulfo asked the defense.

(Is he a super-witness, omni-witness? What kind of a witness is being presented by the defense? He is even involving himself in the amici curiae, the Supreme Court, Ombudsman, DOJ [Department of Justice], who is he? Who is this guy?)

“I’m really, really curious about the qualification of the gentleman para kahit lahat na lang na topic kayang-kaya niyang sagutin mula sa kanyang handler, or excuse me, sa defense?” he added.

(I’m really, really curious about the qualification of the gentleman because he seems to be able to address all of the topics raised by his handler, or excuse me, the defense lawyer?)

According to Tulfo, he believes that dela Fuente is not competent enough to address other topics.

Article continues after this 

“I don’t think he is capable of answering those questions kasi hindi na niya teritoryo ‘yon eh, Mr. Presiding Officer, parang nakaka-antok na, parang hindi kapani-paniwala, parang binobola lang tayo nito,” he said.

(I don’t think he is capable of answering those questions because it is no longer his territory, Mr. Presiding Officer, it’s boring already, his statements are unbelievable, we are just being taken for a ride here.)

Article continues after this 

“Anyway Mr. Presiding Officer, siguro medyo (maybe) put him (Vinluan) in a short leash,” he added.

Prior to Tulfo’s interjection, Vinluan was asking dela Fuente theoretical questions, like whether he would know if it is proper or not for a public official owning a Mercedes Benz G-Wagon to claim that another official has unexplained wealth, and on the gravity of charges that should merit a conviction against an impeachable official.

However, Tulfo’s comments did not end there, asking dela Fuente if he is a “supercomputer” since he was able to pinpoint problems in the report made by prosecution witness Atty. Alexander Cabrera despite not being able to read it before.

Cabrera is the forensic financial analyst who came up with a report on Duterte’s financial transactions, eventually concluding that the vice president has P817 million in unexplained wealth, or the amount that she did not declare in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN).

“Sabi mo, inamin mo na first time mo lang makita ‘yong report na pinakita sa screen, na isinumite ni Atty. Cabrera, ‘yong isang expert ng prosecution, forensic. Now, first time mo lang makita, and yet kino-kontra mo, nire-refute mo ‘yong nasa report without even studying it first, without having it reviewed, and then agad-agad nakakapag-bigay ka na agad ng expert opinion mo?” Tulfo asked.

(You said that the first time you saw the report submitted by prosecution witness Atty. Cabrera was when it was flashed on screen. Now, you saw this for the first time, and yet you are contradicting it, you are refuting the contents of the report without even studying it first, without having it reviewed, and then you can immediately provide your expert opinion?)

“Yes your Honor, so ‘yon po ano, kahit ho maiksi ang aking naging stint, sa isang tingin ko pa lang po kanina, alam ko na po kung ano ‘yong mga problema,” dela Fuente replied.

(Yes your Honor, so even if my stint was short, at just one look earlier, I know what the problems are.)

“Wow, so sa isang tingin pa lang, para kang supercomputer, nakikita mo agad, para kang ChatGPT, isang kita lang, alam mo na kaagad kung saan ang mali doon without even studying it, without even reading it, without even analyzing it,” Tulfo fired back.

(Wow, so in just one look you can do that, you’re like a supercomputer, you see immediately, you’re like ChatGPT, at one glance you can see what is the issue there without even studying it, without even reading it, without even analyzing it.)

Dela Fuente then clarified that he was not saying that the Cabrera report was wrong, but Tulfo still quizzed him on how he was able to pinpoint the problems when he had not even spent 10 minutes reading the document.

“So how can you tell that there’s a problem with the report if in fact you haven’t even looked at it for 10 minutes at least. Dito pinakita lang sa’yo, parang seconds lang eh. And agad-agad you were able to form an opinion and a judgment,” Tulfo said.

(So how can you tell that there’s a problem with the report if in fact you haven’t even looked at it for 10 minutes at least. It was just shown to you, for just a few seconds only. And yet you were able to immediately form an opinion and a judgment.)

“Binangga ko ho kasi ito your Honor sa aming normal financial investigation,” dela Fuente replied.

(I bumped it, your Honor, with our normal financial investigation methods.)

“Exactly, but still you have to have at least reviewed the report for let’s say 10 minutes, 15 minutes, siguro enough na pero kanina, seconds lang ata, wala pang isang minuto, agad-agad nakapag-bigay ka ng opinyon mo,” the senator-judge countered.

(Exactly, but still you have to have at least reviewed the report for let’s say 10 minutes, 15 minutes, maybe that’s enough already but earlier, it was mere seconds only, not even a minute, yet you immediately gave your opinion.)

Senator-judge Francis Pangilinan then asked dela Fuente how come he is able to analyze Cabrera’s report immediately when he previously claimed that it is extremely hard for the prosecution’s witness to come up with an extensive report on Duterte’s finances.

READ: Duterte trial: Witness says Cabrera’s 2-week financial report possible

Cabrera’s testimony is considered important by the prosecution, especially after the panel decided to drop all charges against Duterte except for Article II, which deals with unexplained wealth and non-declaration of assets in her SALN.

At one point, Cabrera said that Duterte had an “unusual banking behavior” in 2025 which included a meal at Ginza Inakaya Tokyo in Japan worth P200,007.29 with a transaction date of March 19, 2025; two transactions on December 27, 2025 with the Nike store at a Davao City mall worth P93,750.00 and P205,392.00; and another Nike store in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, worth P256,882.50.

Cabrera did not mention Duterte’s other unusual banking activities, but his Table 25 showed that she had gone shopping at two MEGA Don Quijote outlets in Japan.

Two transactions referred to a Don Quijote in Shibuya, one of the main business and entertainment hotspots in Tokyo — with one worth P62,900.95 and the other being P65,877.64, both occurring on December 8, 2025.

READ: From Donki to Nike: Analyst says VP had ‘unusual’ purchases in 2025

The other Don Quijote outlet that Duterte transacted with is in Aichi prefecture, specifically in Naka-ward. The transaction was on July 20, 2025 was worth P111,109.24

Eventually, it was revealed that the card belonged to Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

During its turn to present witnesses, the defense brought in lawyer Anel Antero to testify that the P200,000 dinner in Tokyo was for 11 individuals — noting that he was one of the persons who eventually reimbursed Carpio.

However, under cross examination, Antero admitted that he did not have any proof that he actually reimbursed Carpio.

Dela Fuente is the seventh witness for the defense panel since they started presenting their counter argument last November 9. However, different members of the prosecution have been adamant that these testimonies and arguments have failed to counter the evidence showing that Duterte allegedly has unexplained wealth and that she failed to disclose these in her SALN.

Prosecution spokesperson and Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong previously said that the allegations raised under Article II have not been disputed — adding that in some ways, the testimonies of defense witnesses even bolstered the prosecutors’ arguments.

Then last Friday, lead public prosecutor and Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro said that Duterte’s yearning for a bloodbath in her impeachment trial came true, but it seems it was not in the way she would have wanted.

World.title: 4 killed in separate Bukidnon pineapple truck accidents
World.content:
Personnel from the Kadingilan Municipal Police Station conduct an investigation at a pineapple plantation in Sitio Payao, Barangay Pay-as, Kadingilan, Bukidnon, on November 18, 2026, where two plantation workers were fatally run over by a reversing cargo truck loaded with pineapples. Photo by Kadingilan Municipal Police Station

MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — Four people were killed in two separate vehicular accidents involving pineapple-hauling trucks in Manolo Fortich and Kadingilan, Bukidnon, on Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 18 and 19).

At around 4:30 a.m. on Thursday, two unidentified women died after the Suzuki motorcycle they were riding crashed into a parked Isuzu cargo dropside truck along the provincial road in Zone 1, Barangay Sankanan, Manolo Fortich.

READ: 2 killed, 1 hurt in Bukidnon highway crashInitial investigation by the Manolo Fortich Municipal Police Station showed that the truck, loaded with newly harvested pineapples, was parked on the right side of the road while waiting for a transport vehicle bound for Cagayan de Oro City, when the motorcycle slammed into it.The still unknown victims were both declared dead on the spot by a responding barangay health worker.On Wednesday noon, two Del Monte Philippines Inc. employees died after being accidentally run over by a reversing cargo truck inside the company’s pineapple plantation in Sitio Payao, Barangay Pay-as, Kadingilan.According to the Kadingilan Municipal Police Station, an Isuzu military-type truck (locally known as kumong-kumong) loaded with harvested pineapples was executing a reverse maneuver driven by a 48-year-old male driver when it hit the victims.Police identified the fatalities as a 28-year-old single male team leader and a 57-year-old married male checker.

The victims were rushed to Sto. Niño Simbulan Hospital in Don Carlos, Bukidnon, where the attending physician declared them dead on arrival. /jpv

World.title: DBM, LGU leagues unite to fast-track local projects
World.content:
Budget Secretary Kim Robert de Leon —File photo from the Department of Budget and Management website

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) and local government leagues agreed on Thursday to strengthen coordination to speed up local development projects and address concerns regarding the 2026 Collective Negotiation Agreement (CNA) Incentive guidelines.

According to a joint statement issued on Thursday, the agreement was the result of a meeting between Budget Secretary Kim Robert C. De Leon and representatives of the League of Municipalities of the Philippines (LMP), League of Cities of the Philippines (LCP), League of Provinces of the Philippines (LPP), and Union of Local Authorities of the Philippines (ULAP).

Everyone at the meeting agreed that the CNA Incentive is not an automatic bonus, but a performance-based incentive that recognizes collective employee contributions in achieving organizational goals and prescribed performance targets.

Article continues after this 

Under previous CNA guidelines, LGUs were already required to accomplish at least 75 percent of their approved targets.

READ: DENR links with global networks to boost LGU climate action

The 2026 guidelines further make explicit the requirement for LGUs to obligate at least 75 percent of their approved appropriations for the 20 percent Development Fund as of Sept. 30. The parties emphasized that performance accountability is not a new principle in government incentive systems.

The CNA Incentive has long been linked to organizational accomplishments, while the utilization of local development funds has likewise been assessed under established governance frameworks.

In particular, the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) has included the utilization of the 20 percent Development Fund among its assessment indicators, with a 100 percent disbursement benchmark under its applicable technical guidelines.

Article continues after this 

Although the SGLG assessment is currently suspended, this demonstrates that monitoring the use of local development funds has long been part of government accountability measures.

While accomplishment, obligation, and disbursement are distinct measures, they reflect the longstanding expectation that public funds allocated for development should translate into actual projects and services for communities.

Article continues after this 

Shared commitment, joint action

The DBM and the leagues further affirmed the mandate under Section 287 of the Local Government Code ( Republic Act No. 7160), requiring LGUs to appropriate no less than 20 percent of their annual National Tax Allotment for development projects.

Recognizing this statutory responsibility, the leagues committed to encourage and mobilize their member-LGUs to accelerate the implementation of approved local development programs and projects, address avoidable delays, and ensure the timely and responsible use of development funds.

At the same time, the DBM acknowledged the concerns raised by LGUs regarding procurement delays, failed biddings, calamities, and other circumstances that may have affected their ability to meet the prescribed development fund obligation requirement.

To address these concerns, the DBM and the leagues agreed to work together on a coordinated catch-up and assessment mechanism, under which concerned LGUs may submit documented explanations, updated implementation status, and catch-up measures for evaluation.

The DBM will consider these submissions on a case-by-case basis, subject to applicable laws, budgeting and accounting rules, and the existing CNA Incentive guidelines.

Any consideration of subsequent catch-up efforts after Sept. 30, will be subject to careful evaluation of the circumstances and supporting documents, consistent with applicable laws, rules, and regulations, without automatically guaranteeing eligibility for the CNA Incentive.

READ: Most local gov’ts underspend on primary healthcare – study

Protecting employees while boosting accountability

The DBM and the leagues emphasized the need for fair and consistent implementation of the CNA Incentive guidelines, taking into account legitimate circumstances beyond the direct control of individual government employees.

They reaffirmed that the incentive recognizes collective contributions to organizational performance and efficiency, while underscoring the responsibility of LGUs to deliver their approved programs and projects.

World.title: 12 BIFF members surrender to Army in Maguindanao del Sur
World.content:
Brig. Gen. Gremel B. Brual (4th from left), commander of the 601st Infantry Brigade, receives a rifle from one of the BIFF members who surrendered during the ceremonial turnover of loose firearms at the headquarters of the 90th Infantry Battalion in Datu Saudi Ampatuan, Maguindanao del Sur on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo from 601st Infantry Brigade)

COTABATO CITY — Twelve members of the Bangsamoro Islamic Freedom Fighters (BIFF) surrendered to the government on Thursday in Maguindanao del Sur, the military said.

The former extremists used to operate in the adjoining towns of Datu Abdullah Sangki, Datu Saudi Ampatuan, Shariff Aguak, Ampatuan and Datu Unsay.

They also turned over 12 firearms.

Article continues after this 

During the ceremony, 14 other unlicensed firearms were also turned over by civilians and local officials to the soldiers.

These actions are in line with the government’s Small Arms and Light Weapons (SALW) Management Program.

Lt. Col. Loqui Marco, commander of the 90th Infantry Battalion (90IB), said the surrendered BIFF members are now described as ‘FR’ or ‘Friends Rescued.’

Marco presented the former extremists and their weapons to Brig. Gen. Gremel Brual, commander of 601st Infantry Brigade, at the 90IB headquarters in Datu Saudi Ampatuan.

In his speech, Brual underscored the importance of sustained cooperation among the military, local government units and communities in promoting peace and reducing the proliferation of loose firearms.

Article continues after this 

“The 601st Brigade will continue to work with local governments, the police and the people to ensure security and peace in the area,” Brual said.

“We welcome anyone who wishes to surrender and turn over a new leaf so they can live freely with their families,” he added. /apl

World.title: 4,500 Myanmar Refugees to Get Thai Job Training Under $3m Project
World.content:
Japan has agreed to back employment training for 4,500 Myanmar refugees and their families in Thailand under a 478-million-yen (US$ 3 million) project implemented by the International Labor Organization (ILO).

Funded by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the two-year project announced Tuesday will also incorporate training for trainers, job-matching services, and outreach to employers including Japanese companies.

It will cover residents of border camps in Tak, Mae Hong Son, Kanchanaburi, and Ratchaburi provinces, aiming to serve high labor demand in Kanchanaburi as well as Chonburi and Rayong, where Japanese businesses are concentrated.

More than 100,000 refugees are currently sheltering in nine temporary camps along the Thai-Myanmar border, according to the Border Consortium (TBC), the main provider of food and shelter in the camps.

The refugees continue to face “significant resource pressure” due to international funding cuts, leading to reduction of food rations, medical services, and other basic assistance, with “no clear sign of reversal,”

the group’s 2026 mid-year report said.

Thailand granted Myanmar refugees the right to work outside their camps in August 2025 after funding collapsed following the USAID freeze. Since then, more than 6,000 have entered the workforce. Feedback has been mixed, with some complaining of language barriers, skill mismatches and unstable working hours.

“Some don’t have steady jobs, working for just a few days every month and surviving on meager wages,” a manager at Maela Camp in Tak Province told The Irrawaddy, citing testimony from returnees.

“We interview them and ask why they returned. They mention discrimination due to the language barrier.”

He said refugees receive a one-day orientation before joining the workforce covering their legal rights, minimum wage, work permit rules, workplace safety, and how to get help if they face abuse on the job.

However, information gaps and inconsistencies between employment brokers and employers often leave workers facing unexpected working conditions.

Announcing the project on Tuesday, the ILO said employers would support both recruitment and integration of refugees into the workforce.

The project “will help displaced persons access safe and decent jobs, while supporting employers to meet their labor needs,” ILO Thailand country director Xiaoyan Qian said at the signing ceremony.

A Karenni resident of a Mae Hong Son camp welcomed the initiative as a pathway to employment. “I hope the training will instill the basic skills needed to join the workforce,” he told The Irrawaddy, admitting it was the first he had heard of the project.

Separately, the Mae La camp official said a Japanese organization was scheduled to visit for a meeting that could be linked to the project.

Thailand relies heavily on migrants from Myanmar to fill labor shortages in key industries like construction, agriculture, and hospitality. The UNHCR and rights groups have welcomed Thailand’s decision to grant refugees labor rights as a win-win for both sides.

World.title: Regime Media Censor Min Aung Hlaing’s Swipes at China, Thailand
World.content:
Myanmar’s state-run newspapers have censored remarks by junta chief Min Aung Hlaing that appeared to blame China for the initial success of Operation 1027, and accuse Thailand of facilitating “illegal trade” through resistance-held territory, despite devoting six pages to coverage of his more than two-hour address to the regime’s rubber-stamp parliament.

In Wednesday’s speech, the junta boss delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on Operation 1027, the Brotherhood Alliance offensive that led to the collapse of the regime’s Northeastern Regional Military Command in Lashio and marked one of the most humiliating military setbacks of the post-coup period.

Without explicitly naming Myanmar’s giant neighbor, Min Aung Hlaing emotionally suggested the offensive was made possible by outside backing.

Recalling the launch of the offensive on Oct. 27, 2023, he said the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) conducted the surprise attack with superior manpower, weapons and technological assistance from “certain people.”

“I was traveling at the time. I received a phone call very early in the morning saying fighting had broken out. I immediately took out a map to assess the size of their forces. The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he stated during his speech.

“There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” he said.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country involved, few observers were left in doubt about the target of his remarks. Among Myanmar political watchers and the public alike, the comments were widely interpreted as a thinly veiled swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance during the northern Shan offensive.

The comments echoed earlier complaints by Min Aung Hlaing during the height of Operation 1027, when he publicly alleged that the MNDAA had used Chinese-made drones and advanced technology in attacks on regime positions.

The junta chief also turned his fire on Thailand, accusing Thai authorities of encouraging cross-border commerce through resistance-controlled territory.

Referring to his Nov. 12 meeting with Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, Min Aung Hlaing complained that despite discussions on using official border crossings, reports of what he called illegal trade were still reaching him.

“Recently, the Thai foreign minister came and discussed border crossings with me. I said Bridges No. 1 and No. 2 at Myawaddy are open and Tachileik is open, so use those official gates and not the illegal ones. But they are still supporting the illegal gates,” he said.

He accused Thai authorities of allowing goods to move through crossings linked to what he called “insurgents” because they offered easier access for both imports and exports.

The accusation came despite Thailand being one of the strongest advocates of maintaining engagement with Naypyitaw and pushing for Myanmar’s eventual reintegration into regional bloc the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

Yet neither the China-related remarks nor the criticism of Thailand were reported in Thursday’s editions of Kyemon, Myanma Alin and the English-language Global New Light of Myanmar.

The state newspapers carried extensive coverage of the speech across six full pages. However, the politically sensitive comments about Beijing and Bangkok were conspicuously absent.
