failure to update the state register within three months of the expiry of the head of the organisation’s term of office;

expiry of an agreement with a foreign NGO branch.

New grounds for dissolution. Under the current law, a court can generally order an NGO’s dissolution if it has received more than two written warnings within a year. The draft law expands the list of grounds for dissolution. These would include posing a “threat to the interests of the state and society protected by law”, failing to hold a general meeting for three consecutive years, remaining inactive for more than three years, and carrying out activities that do not correspond to the organisation’s stated objectives.

Who will decide what constitutes “transparency” or a “threat”?

The draft law uses broad terms such as “failure to ensure transparency” and “threat to the interests of the state”. However, it does not specify the criteria for applying these provisions. If adopted, the law would allow the executive authority responsible for registering NGOs and overseeing their activities to make decisions that previously fell to the courts.

Lawyer Narmin Ahmadli told the Musavat newspaper in a comment that 30 days would not be enough for many NGOs. She said that amending their statutes would require them to draw up internal financial control procedures, which takes time. Lawyer Bakhtiyar Hajiyev, meanwhile, pointed out that the requirement would apply to all public associations and foundations registered before the law comes into force.

Raising the minimum statutory capital to 100,000 manats would make it significantly harder to register small initiatives as foundations. By comparison, this amount is around 85 times the country’s average monthly salary.

Previous tightening of NGO legislation

This is not the first time Azerbaijan has tightened its legislation governing NGOs. In February 2014, President Ilham Aliyev signed around 50 amendments into law. They prohibited banks from processing transactions under unregistered grant agreements, required Azerbaijani citizens to head branches of foreign NGOs and increased fines. The then-chairman of the NGO Forum, Gubad Ibadoghlu, said the changes would severely restrict civil society activities. US, EU and UK diplomats also expressed concern.

In July 2025, new requirements were introduced for registering service contracts funded by foreign sources, along with additional fines. In its 2024 report, international human rights organisation Human Rights Watch urged the Azerbaijani government to review its NGO legislation in line with recommendations from the Council of Europe’s Venice Commission.

Against the backdrop of the “NGO funding case”

The draft law is being considered amid ongoing criminal proceedings against NGO representatives. In February 2025, the Prosecutor General’s Office reopened the so-called “NGO funding case”, which it had launched in 2014 and suspended in 2022. According to human rights organisation Amnesty International, at least 50 civil society representatives have since been questioned as witnesses or suspects.

Asef Ahmedov, head of the Ganja Regional Public Centre, was sentenced to eight years in prison. Zamin Zakiyev, head of the Ubuntu Association for Social Work initiative, received a seven-year-and-three-month sentence. Prosecutors have requested a nine-year prison term for Bashir Suleymanli, head of the Institute for Civil Rights. The next hearing in his case is scheduled for 19 November. The defendants reject the charges and say they acted within the law.

There has been no announcement of who drafted the bill or which executive authority will oversee the re-registration of NGOs. Government agencies have also yet to explain the reasons behind the proposed changes.

Re-registration of NGOs in Azerbaijan

World.title: Deutsche Bank leak: Bank linked payments to Trump companies in Baku to ‘Azerbaijani Laundromat’
World.content:
Trump-linked companies in Azerbaijan

According to documents leaked from Germany’s largest bank, Deutsche Bank, between 2014 and 2020 the bank repeatedly flagged as suspicious payments received by two companies linked to Donald Trump‘s hotel project in Baku. Some of the funds came from companies associated with a money-laundering scheme known as the “Azerbaijani Laundromat”.

The findings were reported in an international journalistic investigation, Inside Deutsche Bank, published on 17 November. More than 200 journalists from over 50 media outlets took part in the investigation. The section focusing on Azerbaijan was published by the Russian-language investigative outlet iStories.

The journalists obtained more than 15 million internal bank files, including email correspondence, client documents and risk assessment materials. The files were provided by two whistleblowers to journalists in India and South Africa.

Trump’s unfinished skyscraper in Baku has been the subject of numerous reports in the past. This time, however, the investigation focused on a different question:

Where did the funds that the bank considered suspicious come from, and what do these findings reveal about the money-laundering scheme known as the “Azerbaijani Laundromat”?

Unfinished skyscraper in Baku

Trump International Hotel & Tower in Baku / Archive photo, 2015

The project in question is the 33-storey Trump International Hotel & Tower complex in Baku, construction of which began in 2012. However, the building was never put into operation. Trump’s partners in the project were relatives of Azerbaijan’s then Transport Minister Ziya Mammadov. As iStories notes, the family amassed a multimillion-dollar fortune through government contracts.

Trump’s company withdrew from the project in late 2016. According to Trump’s financial disclosure, he received around $2.5m for managing the project in 2015 and just over $300,000 in 2016. In 2017, the Trump Organization told The New Yorker that Trump had played a “passive role” in the project and had merely licensed the use of his name.

The project was managed by two US companies, DT Marks Baku and THC Baku Services. It is their bank accounts that are covered by the documents obtained by journalists through the leak.

Which transactions did the bank consider suspicious?

According to iStories, Deutsche Bank first flagged a payment to DT Marks Baku as suspicious in August 2014. The funds came from an unnamed client of Danske Bank’s Estonian branch. Deutsche Bank was unable to establish the purpose of the payment or the nature of the relationship between the sender and the recipient.

In April 2015, THC Baku Services received just over $141,000 from Faberlex, a UK-registered shell company. Faberlex was one of the key participants in the money-laundering scheme known as the “Azerbaijani Laundromat”.

The bank continued to identify suspicious payments in subsequent years. As reported by the Dutch investigative platform Follow the Money, Deutsche Bank’s internal analysis linked the funds to both the “Azerbaijani Laundromat” and a Russian money-laundering network associated with oligarchs close to the Kremlin.

According to an internal bank document dated May 2020, the total value of suspicious transactions involving the accounts of Trump’s companies in Baku exceeded $3m.

What was the ‘Azerbaijani Laundromat’?

The “Azerbaijani Laundromat” was a money-laundering scheme exposed in an investigation published in September 2017 by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), an international investigative journalism network.

According to the investigation, around $2.9bn was transferred through UK-registered shell companies between 2012 and 2014, primarily via the Estonian branch of Danske Bank. Journalists found that some of the funds were channelled to European politicians, while others were spent on luxury goods and other expenses of members of the elite.

The Azerbaijani authorities rejected the investigation’s findings at the time. Presidential spokesman Azer Gasimov described the investigation as “absurd and biased”. The OCCRP website was blocked in Azerbaijan.

In subsequent years, European courts handed down several sentences in cases linked to the scheme. In 2021, former member of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) and Italian politician Luca Volontè was sentenced to four years in prison for accepting bribes from Azerbaijani officials. According to iStories, the funds were transferred to him through Faberlex.

Former German Bundestag members Eduard Lintner and Axel Fischer also received suspended prison sentences for accepting bribes in connection with lobbying for Azerbaijan’s interests.

According to the documents, Faberlex and two other companies involved in the scheme, Hilux Services and Polux Management, were formally owned by Maharram Ahmadov, a driver from Baku.

What is the situation now?

The document leak comes amid closer ties between Trump and Baku. In August 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a joint declaration at the White House with Donald Trump and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan.

Deutsche Bank said that the law prohibited it from disclosing information about suspicious transaction reports. In response to journalists’ questions, the bank noted that the events in question had taken place “many years ago”, stressing that “we are a different bank today”.

The Trump Organization did not respond to journalists’ questions, while the White House referred them to the company. Danske Bank said that money laundering “should never have happened” and noted that the case had been closed in 2022 following decisions by the Danish and US authorities.

The Azerbaijani authorities have yet to comment on the newly leaked documents.

World.title: ‘Traffic jams are not caused by buildings’: Yerevan mayor responds to prime minister’s wife
World.content:
Yerevan mayor responds to Anna Hakobyan over traffic jams

“Traffic jams are caused by cars, not buildings. Armenia is experiencing economic growth and an inflow of money. People now have more opportunities – and they are buying cars,” Yerevan Mayor Tigran Avinyan said today.

He was effectively responding to Anna Hakobyan, the wife of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. A few days ago, she posted a video on social media showing traffic jams in the capital. She said Yerevan was gradually becoming “the most unfriendly city” to live in.

The prime minister’s wife asked what the authorities should do to prevent life in the city and getting around it from becoming “a reason for a heart attack”. She pointed to economic growth, the rapid construction of new buildings, a rising population, more cars on the roads and an influx of tourists.

“Some people have a professional duty to find an answer to this question. But this task is far more difficult than issuing construction permits to companies investing millions of dollars. ‘Approved’ is a magic stamp that requires minimal effort but has an enormous impact [on the situation],” Hakobyan stressed.

According to the mayor, the city authorities issued a record 108 permits for apartment blocks and residential complexes in 2021. Those are the buildings now being completed and handed over to residents. Avinyan noted that the authorities have not issued as many permits in any year since then. For example, they issued just 37 in 2025.

The mayor acknowledged that the current situation is causing a certain degree of “tension” – and said he shares those concerns. However, Avinyan called for an analysis of the problems and appropriate solutions.

Tigran Avinyan’s explanation apparently failed to satisfy Anna Hakobyan. She immediately posted another video, this time about the “catastrophic traffic jams”. In her post, the prime minister’s wife urged women drivers to stop being patient:

“Keep noisy objects in your cars. Every time you find yourself stuck in traffic for hours, make a loud noise. Make it loud enough for those who have a duty to use their brains and solve the problem to hear you.”

Prime minister’s wife: “You need an astronaut’s health to get from point A to point C”

In her first post, Anna Hakobyan said that getting around the capital required “an astronaut’s health” – in other words, a strong cardiovascular and nervous system.

She also expressed confidence that scientific disciplines exist that can help calculate how many cars Yerevan will have in 25 years, based on current development trends. They can also help determine what measures the authorities need to take now to prepare for that future.

Hakobyan suggested that, alongside the buildings springing up across the city “like mushrooms after rain”, the authorities should build flyovers, as well as elevated, underground and bypass roads.

“You have to actively seek out this knowledge yourself. Nobody will serve it up on a silver platter as a ready-made, multi-million-dollar project that only needs a ‘approved’ stamp,” she said, again alluding to the construction permits issued in the capital.

In her view, traffic planning must take into account how much the population could grow in the coming years and how many more cars the city might have.

“What will happen if between 300,000 and 500,000 people return to their homeland to live permanently over the next five years? And what if 250,000 of them bring their own cars? What are we going to do? Will the same number of people have to leave so that we can all fit on the streets?” Anna Hakobyan asked.

Mayor: “Possible solutions will be presented to the public”

According to Yerevan Mayor Tigran Avinyan, traffic congestion in the capital has three main causes: the growing number of private cars, driving culture and the need to give public transport priority.

He said the city authorities would soon present various possible solutions for public discussion. Avinyan outlined some of the measures under consideration:

fully separating bus lanes from other traffic;

introducing measures to reduce traffic violations;

restricting car use on public health grounds.

On the last point, the mayor clarified that the restrictions would not apply to vehicles coming to Yerevan from other regions. He said the aim was to reduce the overall number of cars within the city.

Tigran Avinyan believes the growing number of private cars is the main cause of traffic jams. He argues that public transport should take priority.

He expects new road construction to help improve traffic flow to some extent. However, he warned that new roads alone would not solve the problem. They would soon become congested again unless the authorities introduced measures such as restrictions on car use, dedicated lanes and tougher fines.

The mayor also addressed environmental concerns. Avinyan identified nitrogen dioxide as a specific pollutant whose levels in Yerevan are rising rapidly year after year as the number of cars increases. He said it causes lung and respiratory diseases.

“The most dangerous thing is that children are the first to suffer from these problems,” Avinyan stressed.

First lady’s appeal

In response to the Yerevan mayor’s remarks, Anna Hakobyan published a new video, saying that people had thanked her for raising the issue.

“They tell me: ‘At last, someone has had the courage to speak about this.’ Every day, hundreds of thousands of people suffer in Yerevan’s traffic jams. So does complaining about the situation now require ‘courage’?”

Hakobyan urged women drivers to stop putting up with the situation and called on men to show greater determination. She suggested that women should make a loud noise whenever they get stuck in traffic.

In her view, government institutions never hear complaints that people “do not dare to voice”.

“Otherwise, we might end up blaming the previous authorities for Yerevan’s traffic jams [the current government, led by her husband, often blames its predecessors for various problems]. If Armenia’s economy had developed in a balanced way over the past 30 years, and the number of cars had increased gradually rather than exponentially, the situation in the Armenian capital would be completely different today,” she said.

World.title: ‘Сake will be divided without us’: Analyst on Georgia’s foreign policy
World.content:
According to analyst Paata Zakareishvili, the appointment of Giorgi Zurabashvili, first deputy foreign minister, as the Georgian prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia gives the Kremlin a new channel for direct political communication with Georgia’s foreign ministry. This could pave the way for existing negotiation formats to be weakened.

Russia has already established contact with the new special representative, Giorgi Zurabashvili. His Russian counterpart will be Mikhail Galuzin, Russia’s deputy foreign minister. According to the Russian side, the main topics for discussion will include increasing trade and tourism, expanding transport links and promoting cultural exchanges between the two countries.

Paata Zakareishvili believes that placing the special representative’s post within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is a dangerous decision. In his view, the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia should be an independent figure, rather than a serving senior official in the foreign ministry.

“Georgia and Russia have not maintained diplomatic relations since the August 2008 war. At the same time, Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and the political confrontation between the two countries require a special format for relations.

“It was precisely for these reasons that the Karasin-Abashidze format was established. Under this arrangement, Georgia’s former special representative, Zurab Abashidze, met with Russia’s deputy foreign minister, Grigory Karasin,” the analyst says.

According to Zakareishvili, the format was important because it kept talks with Russia on practical issues separate from discussions about the conflicts. It also allowed Georgia’s foreign ministry to make its position clear during international negotiations.

“Russia constantly says that diplomatic relations with Georgia should be restored. The Georgian authorities remain silent on this issue. Against this background, they have suddenly taken a step in Russia’s favour. Russia needs to ‘get its foot in the door’ of Georgia’s foreign ministry and hold talks with the first deputy minister,” Zakareishvili says.

He is particularly concerned about the possible weakening of the Geneva International Discussions. Established after the 2008 war, the talks involve representatives of Georgia, Russia and the United States, as well as the European Union and the OSCE. Zakareishvili believes the Georgian authorities’ latest moves could eventually be aimed at reducing the importance of this international format in favour of direct bilateral contacts.

According to the analyst, the replacement of Lasha Darsalia as Georgia’s representative at the Geneva talks also carries symbolic significance. Zakareishvili says Darsalia clearly articulated Georgia’s position during the negotiations and regularly used the term “occupation” when referring to Russia’s actions.

“The time will come when they start singing a new tune: ‘Georgia’s foreign ministry is already dealing with Russia, so why do we need Geneva?’ Their primary aim is to weaken the Geneva format, which is visibly losing ground,” Zakareishvili predicts.

He also believes that the location of the first meeting between Giorgi Zurabashvili and Mikhail Galuzin will be particularly important. He considers holding the meeting in Moscow a disastrous political move, as it would give Russia an opportunity to symbolically demonstrate that it controls the process.

In Zakareishvili’s view, Prague would be the most logical venue, as it hosted meetings between Karasin and Abashidze for years.

“Russia needs symbolic victories. If the meeting takes place in Moscow, the message will be that Russia is in control of the process. That must not be allowed under any circumstances,” the analyst says.

Zakareishvili also links the Georgian authorities’ new approach to relations with Russia to a shift in the country’s foreign policy. In his assessment, the government is gradually moving away from the European Union and NATO, while seeking to build closer ties with Russia without making any formal commitments to direct integration or cooperation with Moscow.

In this context, the analyst also points to the possibility of Article 78 of Georgia’s Constitution being repealed. It obliges state authorities to take all necessary measures to ensure the country’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

According to Zakareishvili, the initiative to ban opposition parties and the Georgian authorities’ efforts to secure a constitutional majority are part of a broader political process that could undermine the institutional foundations of Georgia’s commitment to Western integration.

Paata Zakareishvili

“It is not Bidzina Ivanishvili who is Russia’s project, but Russia that is Ivanishvili’s project. For now, however, this suits Russia. Russia has other priorities at the moment, and it is not Russia that is working on Georgia – it is Ivanishvili who is working for Russia,” Zakareishvili says.

In his assessment, the message the Georgian authorities are sending to the Kremlin is this: Georgia no longer intends to move towards the European Union and NATO, but it also has no plans to join the political and economic blocs established by Russia. Zakareishvili believes the authorities are using this approach to preserve room for political manoeuvre while avoiding public discontent that an overt shift towards Russia could trigger.

The analyst believes that if the authorities continue with their current policy, by the time Bidzina Ivanishvili’s political influence comes to an end, support for Georgia joining the EU and NATO could be significantly weakened, leaving the political space open to groups advocating neutrality.

Turning away from Brussels and the threat to Georgia’s role as a transit hub

Another key focus of Zakareishvili’s criticism is Georgia’s absence from a ministerial meeting in Brussels dedicated to security and connectivity.

The meeting brought together representatives of the European Union, Central Asian countries, Armenia and Azerbaijan. Zakareishvili sees Georgia’s absence not simply as a diplomatic mistake, but as a significant loss for the country’s long-term economic and geopolitical interests.

He says the connectivity ministerial was not about EU enlargement. Its main focus was the development of transport, energy and economic links across the region – an area in which Georgia could play an important role because of its geographical position.

According to the European Commission’s 2026 enlargement report, Georgia’s EU integration process remains suspended, and the country’s position has deteriorated further compared with the previous year. The Commission says the Georgian authorities took no steps during the reporting period to implement the nine recommendations set out as conditions for advancing the country’s EU accession process.

Zakareishvili stresses that international transport and trade routes are constantly changing. A country that does not take part in the relevant negotiations may eventually lose the opportunity to benefit even from its own geographical advantages.

“If Georgia does not take part, someone else will take its place and share the spoils! If you do not show up to a party, the party will go on without you – and someone else will eat the slice of cake that was meant for you,” he says.

In the analyst’s view, Georgia should pay particular attention to the development of a new transport corridor through Armenia, including the so-called “Trump Route”, which could significantly reshape the transport geography of the South Caucasus.

Zakareishvili fears that if Georgia does not actively participate in regional connectivity projects, a significant share of international freight could bypass the country. Georgia would then lose the economic and political advantages built up over decades through its Black Sea ports, railway, pipelines and East-West transit corridor.

The analyst draws a historical parallel with the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan oil pipeline and the Baku-Tbilisi-Erzurum gas pipeline. He says that, as a result of political decisions made at the time, these projects were routed through Georgia rather than Armenia. But the situation could now change: new transport routes in the region could allow Armenia to become a transit country at Georgia’s expense.

Zakareishvili believes Turkey will play a particularly important role in this process. The development of new routes and the redistribution of transport flows could increase the importance of Turkish ports and Mediterranean routes, affecting the competitiveness of Georgia’s Black Sea ports.

“As long as Georgia has pipelines and ports, and still has a chance to take part somewhere, to get a foot in the door and claim a share – if not a piece of the cake, then at least a seat at the table – it should do so. Otherwise, these processes will move forward without Georgia,” Zakareishvili says.

In his view, the authorities’ refusal to attend international meetings, justified on the grounds of protecting the country’s dignity and sovereignty, could in reality damage Georgia’s economic interests.

“EU candidate status is becoming little more than a formality”

Zakareishvili identifies the Georgian authorities’ decision to suspend political dialogue with the European Union as one of the main reasons for the country’s growing distance from Brussels.

In November 2024, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Georgia would not put the opening of EU accession talks on the agenda until the end of 2028. The announcement came after the EU had effectively suspended Georgia’s accession process and stepped up its criticism of the government’s policies.

Zakareishvili believes that instead of meeting the conditions set by the European Union, the Georgian authorities chose political confrontation. He says candidate status alone does not mean progress towards membership: the country must fulfil specific commitments.

The analyst points to Ukraine, Moldova, Albania and Montenegro as examples of countries that continue to implement reforms as part of their efforts to move closer to the EU.

“The European Union did not write an application saying, ‘I want Georgia to join.’ It was Georgia that said it wanted to join the European Union. It is all very well to want to join the EU, but you need to look at its standards, its economy and its relations. The EU’s conditions include judicial reform, de-oligarchisation and many other things that the ruling Georgian Dream party does not like,” Zakareishvili says.

In his assessment, the EU’s declining political attention to Georgia is not limited to deteriorating diplomatic relations. The country could also gradually be left out of regional developments in which its geographical position and transit potential once gave it a significant advantage.

The analyst warns that Georgia’s international role is not determined by geography alone. A country may lie on a transit corridor on the map, but to gain real economic and political benefits, it must take part in the processes shaping the region’s future transport, energy and security architecture. Otherwise, Georgia risks finding itself surrounded by new political and economic partnerships while remaining on the sidelines.

World.title: Part of Crimean Bridge collapses into sea: what damage to one of Kremlin’s key propaganda symbols means
World.content:
On 17 November 2026, the Crimean Bridge, which spans the Kerch Strait, was severely damaged in another Ukrainian attack. Video footage and photographs circulating online appear to show a large metal arch and a section of the road deck collapsing into the sea. Both road and rail traffic across the bridge have been suspended.

The attack is particularly significant because the Crimean Bridge is a vital land corridor linking the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed in 2014, with Russian territory. Moscow has also used the bridge to supply its military forces.

For years, the Crimean Bridge was regarded as one of Vladimir Putin’s largest infrastructure projects and a symbol of Russian control over Crimea. Its damage creates several problems at once: it complicates Russian military logistics, increases the cost of supplying Crimea and shows how difficult it is for Moscow to secure one of its most heavily protected strategic assets.

It is important to note that the collapse on 17 November was preceded by an attack on 16 November, which also reportedly damaged the bridge’s structure. This means the bridge has been hit in a series of successive strikes rather than in a single isolated incident.

According to Anton Herashchenko, an adviser to Ukraine’s interior minister, the attack involved a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. Russian authorities confirmed the attack and the suspension of traffic across the bridge, but have yet to issue an official statement about its collapse.

The Russian outlet Agentstvo reports that federal television channels did not mention the attack on the Crimean Bridge in their morning news bulletins. Instead, they covered strikes on several bridges in Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine.

The collapsed Crimean (Kerch) Bridge

What does the collapse of the bridge arch mean from an engineering perspective?

To understand the scale of the damage to the Kerch Bridge, it is important to know how it is constructed.

The bridge is approximately 19 kilometres long and consists of two independent parallel structures: one carries road traffic and the other railway traffic.

Both structures rest on concrete supports. However, the navigable section of the Kerch Strait features large metal arch structures that support the corresponding spans and provide sufficient clearance for ships to pass underneath.

According to reports published on 17 November, a roughly 227-metre-long arch of the road bridge collapsed into the sea, along with the section of road deck connected to it. The adjacent railway arch was also damaged but has not collapsed.

Why does this matter?

The arch is not a decorative feature of the bridge but a key load-bearing element. Its damage means that the load in the affected section can no longer be safely distributed.

This creates several technical problems:

Damage to the load-bearing structure: After the arch collapses, the affected section of the bridge can no longer support the weight of cars and heavy vehicles.

After the arch collapses, the affected section of the bridge can no longer support the weight of cars and heavy vehicles. Risk of damage to adjacent elements: The failure of one major structural component can place additional stress on neighbouring supports and spans.

The failure of one major structural component can place additional stress on neighbouring supports and spans. Safety of the railway infrastructure: The road and railway sections are separate structures, but they form part of the same transport corridor. Suspending rail traffic until the damage has been assessed is therefore a logical safety measure.

The road and railway sections are separate structures, but they form part of the same transport corridor. Suspending rail traffic until the damage has been assessed is therefore a logical safety measure. Possible disruption to shipping: Debris from the collapsed structure could also obstruct the shipping channel used by vessels.

It is important to stress that the collapse of the arch does not mean the entire 19-kilometre bridge has been destroyed. However, one of its most important sections has been damaged. Restoring traffic will require a detailed structural assessment, the removal of debris and the necessary engineering and repair work.

Rebuilding such a large load-bearing element is a far more complex, time-consuming and costly process.

What does the collapse of the Kerch Bridge mean symbolically?

For Russia, the bridge is one of the most visible political symbols of the annexation of Crimea.

When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, one of Moscow’s main challenges was establishing a land link between the peninsula and Russian territory, as the Kerch Strait separates Crimea from Russia’s Krasnodar Krai. By building the bridge, the Kremlin overcame this geographical barrier.

Vladimir Putin personally championed the project. In May 2018, he drove a lorry across the bridge and officially opened its road section. The event was broadcast on Russian state television and became an important part of the Kremlin’s propaganda narrative.

For Moscow, the bridge carried several key messages:

Consolidation of the annexation of Crimea: The bridge served as a demonstration of Russia’s integration of the peninsula into its own territory.

The bridge served as a demonstration of Russia’s integration of the peninsula into its own territory. Putin’s political project: Its construction was presented as a personal achievement of the president and a showcase of Russia’s engineering capabilities.

Its construction was presented as a personal achievement of the president and a showcase of Russia’s engineering capabilities. Demonstration of Russian control: The bridge signalled that Moscow intended to maintain a long-term presence in Crimea and had no plans to return the peninsula to Ukraine.

Russia decided to build the bridge in 2014, following its annexation of Crimea. Construction began in 2016. The road section opened on 15 May 2018, while rail traffic began in December 2019.

The bridge is considered one of the longest in Europe. Its construction cost around 228 billion roubles (approximately $3.5–3.8 billion at the exchange rate at the time).

The project involved extensive engineering work. The structure includes supports on both land and underwater, while specially designed high arches allow ships to pass through the navigable section of the strait.

After the first explosion in 2022, the damage to the bridge was seen in Ukraine as an important moral and symbolic victory. At the time, Al Jazeera reported that the attack had heightened the perception of Russia’s vulnerability.

Crimean (Kerch) Bridge

How many times has Ukraine attacked the Kerch Bridge before?

Before the attack on 17 November 2026, Ukraine had carried out three major successful operations against the Kerch Bridge. Ukrainian officials subsequently confirmed or acknowledged responsibility for them.

The strike on 16 November 2026, which directly preceded the attack on 17 November, should also be treated as a separate incident.

8 October 2022: First major explosion

A lorry travelling across the bridge exploded, damaging several road spans and causing some of them to collapse. The blast also set fuel tankers on a passing railway train on fire. Four people were killed.

Ukraine subsequently acknowledged its involvement in the attack. Repairs to the damaged sections took several months.

Damage to the Kerch Bridge on 8 October 2022

17 July 2023: Sea drone attack

Ukraine attacked the bridge using Sea Baby naval drones. The road section sustained damage, and one of its spans collapsed. Two civilians were killed in the attack, and their child was injured.

Vasyl Maliuk, head of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), later confirmed that Ukrainian forces had carried out the operation.

Sea drone attack on the Kerch Bridge in 2023

3 June 2025: Underwater explosion

Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) detonated explosive devices near the bridge’s underwater supports. According to the Ukrainian side, the blast had an estimated force of 1,100 kilograms of TNT.

The SBU said the operation had been in preparation for several months and that the bridge’s supports had sustained significant damage. The agency claimed that the structure had been left in a critical condition.

Underwater explosion on the Kerch Bridge in 2025

16 November 2026: Another strike

The Ukrainian drone attack damaged the bridge’s structure. Russian authorities initially described the damage as minor, but traffic across the bridge was temporarily suspended and later partially restored.

16 November 2026: Another strike on the Kerch Bridge

What did Russia use the Kerch Bridge for?

For Russia, the bridge was not just a transport link for Crimea’s population. It was also one of the key logistical routes used in its war against Ukraine.

Military role

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the bridge acquired particular strategic importance. It allowed Russia to transport military supplies from its territory to Crimea and then onwards to the occupied regions of southern Ukraine.

These supplies included:

military equipment and armoured vehicles;

ammunition and weapons;

fuel and other military supplies;

military personnel and logistical resources.

The bridge allowed Russian forces to move military supplies relatively quickly from Russian territory to Crimea and then distribute them towards the front line in southern Ukraine.

In March 2024, Vasyl Maliuk, head of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), said Russia had significantly reduced its use of the bridge to transport military equipment following Ukrainian strikes.

According to Maliuk, 42–46 trains carrying weapons and ammunition crossed the bridge every day before the attacks. After the strikes, that number fell to four or five.

Civilian and economic role

The bridge is also an important transport route for Crimea’s residents and tourists.

It was used to deliver:

food;

fuel;

consumer goods;

construction materials;

various industrial products.

The bridge also carried passenger trains and cars travelling between Russia and Crimea.

A prolonged disruption would therefore affect not only military supplies but also everyday economic life in Crimea, the cost of delivering goods and the tourism industry.

The collapsed section of the Kerch Bridge

What alternatives does Russia have?

Disabling the Kerch Bridge does not mean that Russia will lose the ability to supply Crimea altogether.

Moscow can use the land corridor through the occupied parts of southern Ukraine. It links Russia’s Rostov region with the occupied territories of Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, and Crimea.

However, this route has several drawbacks. It is significantly longer, runs close to active combat zones and is itself vulnerable to Ukrainian strikes.

Russia could also use the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, but it would not be able to fully replace the bridge’s capacity.

Disabling the Kerch Bridge therefore represents a serious logistical blow to Russia, even if Moscow continues to supply Crimea via alternative routes.

Why is this attack significant?

From a military perspective, Russia is losing – at least temporarily – one of its most important transport corridors, which it used to supply its forces in Crimea and southern Ukraine.

From an economic perspective, a prolonged closure of the bridge will increase the cost of supplying Crimea and put additional pressure on alternative transport routes.

From a political perspective, it is another blow to Putin’s project, which has become a symbol of Russia’s annexation of Crimea.

It is also particularly significant that the bridge was considered one of Russia’s most heavily protected strategic assets. It was guarded by air defence systems, maritime barriers and other security measures. Yet Ukraine has managed to strike it repeatedly.

However, the ultimate strategic impact will depend on how long the bridge remains out of service, how severe the damage is to its supports and the adjacent railway structure, and how quickly Russia can increase the capacity of alternative routes.

One thing is clear: the Kerch Bridge is one of the most important symbols Putin has created since the annexation of Crimea. Its repeated damage sends Moscow a clear message: in its war against Ukraine, no infrastructure asset is safe or beyond reach.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan discuss drought-resistant grapes and organic farming
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan have explored opportunities to expand agricultural cooperation, focusing on the cultivation of drought-resistant grape varieties, greenhouse farming and the development of organic agriculture.

The discussions took place during a meeting between Kyrgyz Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers and Minister of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry Erlist Akunbekov and Turkmen Agriculture Minister Charyyar Chetiyev, held during Akunbekov's working visit to Turkmenistan, according to the Kyrgyz Cabinet of Ministers.

The sides considered the possibility of applying Turkmenistan's experience in cultivating drought-resistant grape varieties under Kyrgyzstan's climatic conditions, as well as conducting joint research on fruit, berry and vegetable production.

They also discussed expanding organic farming, improving certification procedures and promoting organic products in foreign markets. The talks covered the introduction of modern technologies for processing, storing and packaging such products.

Another area of potential cooperation is strengthening direct business ties between agricultural producers and processing companies in the two countries. The sides discussed holding bilateral business meetings to establish new partnerships, expand trade and increase mutual supplies of agricultural products.

Akunbekov also highlighted Kyrgyzstan's interest in establishing direct supplies of high-quality mineral fertilizers produced in Turkmenistan at competitive prices and on mutually beneficial terms.

The parties confirmed their readiness to deepen practical cooperation, exchange agricultural expertise and pursue joint initiatives.

World.title: Armenia allocates $44,000 for preparatory work on TRIPP project
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Armenia has allocated 16 million drams ($44,000) for the procurement of services and works related to the TRIPP project.

The corresponding decision was adopted at a meeting of the Armenian government on November 19.

The funds will be used for preparatory work to clear the project site.

The planned work includes clearing tunnels of rocks and debris, removing accumulated soil from the site, and carrying out other related tasks.

On August 8, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan signed a joint declaration in Washington in the presence of US President Donald Trump. As part of efforts to restore regional ties, the document provides for the commissioning of the Zangezur Corridor, also known as the “Trump Route.” In addition, the foreign ministers of the two countries initialed the Agreement on Peace and Inter-State Relations.

World.title: Korean Air plans to launch Seoul-Almaty flights in summer 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. South Korea's Korean Air aims to launch scheduled flights between Seoul and Almaty in summer 2027, Kazakhstan's Vice Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev said, according to the ministry.

The issue was discussed during a meeting between Lastayev and Jeong Chae-gyo, Deputy Minister for Civil Aviation at South Korea's Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, on the sidelines of the 7th ICAO Worldwide Air Transport Conference (ATConf/7).

Lastayev welcomed the airline's plans, noting that the arrival of a new carrier would help increase passenger traffic, expand tourism ties and provide additional travel options.

The sides also discussed Korean Air's interest in exploring the possibility of launching flights between Seoul and Astana.

Currently, Kazakhstan and South Korea operate 12 scheduled passenger flights per week on the Astana-Seoul, Almaty-Seoul and Shymkent-Seoul routes.

Lastayev also emphasized the importance of finalizing the draft Air Services Agreement between Kazakhstan and South Korea and confirmed Kazakhstan's readiness to sign it. The agreement is expected to provide a solid legal framework for further expanding air connectivity, strengthening cooperation between the aviation authorities and creating additional opportunities for airlines from both countries.

At the end of the meeting, Lastayev reaffirmed Kazakhstan's interest in further strengthening its partnership with South Korea. He expressed confidence that the current level of cooperation creates favorable conditions for implementing new initiatives and further developing civil aviation in both countries.

World.title: Kazakhstan seeks to expand civil aviation cooperation with Australia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Kazakhstan is interested in expanding cooperation with Australia in civil aviation through technical consultations, professional exchanges and training for aviation specialists, Kazakhstan's Vice Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev said, according to the ministry.

The issue was discussed during a meeting between Lastayev and Rebecca Udvardi, Director at Australia's Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications and the Arts, on the sidelines of the 7th ICAO Worldwide Air Transport Conference (ATConf/7) in Montreal.

Sarah Millard, Australia's Representative on the Council of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), also attended the meeting.

The sides exchanged views on prospects for developing international cooperation in civil aviation. Lastayev noted that closer interaction between the aviation authorities of the two countries could facilitate the exchange of best practices and contribute to the development of the international aviation industry.

The meeting also highlighted Kazakhstan's progress in civil aviation development, including structural reforms to the state oversight system. Kazakhstan has operated an open skies regime since 2017, providing foreign airlines with additional opportunities to operate international flights.

The sides expressed interest in further strengthening cooperation between their aviation authorities, developing professional contacts and expanding engagement on international aviation platforms.

The 7th ICAO Worldwide Air Transport Conference (ATConf/7) is taking place in Montreal from November 16 to 20 under the theme "Air Transport: Powering Global Connectivity, Economic Development and Resilience in a Dynamic World."

The conference provides a global forum for ICAO member states and key stakeholders to discuss the future of international air transport. Topics include regulatory frameworks, industry resilience, financing for civil aviation infrastructure, innovation, institutional capacity, and sustainable growth.

The event brings together senior officials from member states and representatives of international and regional organizations involved in the economic development of air transport.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan discuss China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan route to Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan have discussed plans to develop a multimodal transport corridor linking China, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan and Europe, with the launch of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway expected to create additional opportunities for cargo transportation along this route.

According to Kyrgyz Cabinet of Ministers, the issue was discussed during a meeting between Kyrgyz Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers and Minister of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry Erlist Akunbekov and Turkmen Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers overseeing the transport and communications sector Mammed Akmammedov, who met as part of Akunbekov's working visit to Turkmenistan.

The sides noted the potential for expanding transport cooperation and improving regional connectivity. Akunbekov described Turkmenistan as an important transit partner for facilitating Kyrgyz cargo access to the Caspian region and Europe.

He said more effective use of the two countries' transport and logistics capabilities could expand cargo destinations, increase mutual trade and strengthen Central Asia's transport links with other regions.

The officials also discussed the construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, which is expected to provide the basis for a new multimodal route continuing through Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan to European markets.

They noted that the corridor could increase freight volumes, reduce delivery times and improve the competitiveness of international transportation.

Another topic was the use of the International Seaport of Turkmenbashi. Kyrgyzstan expressed interest in making greater use of the port to organize freight shipments along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (Middle Corridor).

Akmammedov said Turkmenistan was ready to offer Kyrgyzstan preferential conditions for using the port, adding that the agreements reached would be advanced through practical cooperation between the relevant agencies.

The two sides agreed to step up cooperation in international freight transportation, logistics infrastructure development and the use of their transit potential.

World.title: Central Asian states sign deal to establish regional environmental platform
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan have signed a memorandum of cooperation to establish a regional digital platform for best available techniques (BAT), aimed at promoting cleaner industrial production and strengthening environmental cooperation across Central Asia during an international session titled "Digital Platform and Regional Programme of the Central Asian Bureau for Best Available Techniques," held at Kazakhstan's National Pavilion on the sidelines of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) on Thursday, November 19.

According to Uzbekistan's Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, organized by Kazakhstan's International Center for Green Technologies and Investment Projects, the session brought together representatives of environmental authorities from Central Asian countries, international organizations and industry experts to discuss industrial modernization and the adoption of best available techniques.

Uzbekistan was represented by Vyacheslav Shi-syan, deputy director general of the Center for State Environmental Review under the National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change.

During the session, the Uzbek delegation highlighted the role of BAT in improving industrial environmental performance, promoting the efficient use of natural resources and reducing pollutant and greenhouse gas emissions.

Participants also discussed the development of modern environmental regulatory mechanisms based on technology-specific standards, comprehensive technological audits and the gradual adoption of more environmentally efficient production processes.

The proposed regional digital platform is expected to facilitate the exchange of advanced technological solutions, support the development of BAT reference documents and promote coordinated approaches to industrial environmental modernization across Central Asia.

Particular attention was given to cooperation with international expert organizations, including the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), as well as drawing on the experience of South Korea and European countries in technology-based environmental regulation and pollution prevention.

In addition to the four-country memorandum, the Kazakh International Center for Green Technologies and Investment Projects and the Uzbek side exchanged documents expressing their intention to cooperate on comprehensive technological audits and the implementation of best available techniques.

The agreements are intended to combine the countries' scientific, technical and expert resources, strengthen regional environmental regulation and accelerate the modernization of industrial facilities.

Uzbekistan's participation in the initiative is part of its broader efforts to improve environmental standards, promote cleaner industrial technologies and advance its national climate objectives.

World.title: Deepfakes emerge as key tool in hybrid warfare - Azerbaijani expert
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Fake images and voices generated using deepfake technology have become an integral part of hybrid attacks, Murad Balayev, head of the Computer Incident Response Center of the State Service of Special Communications and Information Security, Trend's correspondent reports.

He made the remarks during a panel discussion titled “Information Warfare and Deepfakes: Defending the Truth in the Digital Age,” held as part of the Second International Conference on Cyberdiplomacy.

“Generative artificial intelligence has made cyberattacks cheaper, faster, and more convincing, shifting their focus from systems to people,” Balayev said.

He explained that generative AI has transformed cyberattacks in three main ways: they have become cheaper and faster, their targets have shifted from systems to people, and disinformation has become more widespread and persuasive.

According to Balayev, complex cyberattacks previously required significant resources and were typically carried out by advanced persistent threat (APT) groups operating with state support. However, artificial intelligence has now expanded the range of possibilities available to attackers.

Citing a threat report published by Anthropic in September, Balayev said that one of the incidents described involved attackers intercepting more than 2,100 access tokens across more than 40 organizations in just 34 hours. Virtually the entire operation was carried out by AI agents.

He also noted that the first AI-driven cyber-reconnaissance campaign was recorded last November. Approximately 30 organizations were targeted, with 80–90% of the operation conducted by an AI model without human intervention.

Balayev also referred to Microsoft's October report, noting that newly discovered vulnerabilities begin to be exploited in attacks within less than 24 hours. He added that the share of phishing attacks used as an initial access method had increased from 7% to 23% in just one year.

“For us, the conclusion is clear: the time available to patch vulnerabilities has shrunk from days to hours, and the complexity of an attack no longer indicates who is behind it,” Balayev emphasized.

He said that as security systems become more sophisticated, attackers increasingly seek to deceive people rather than hack systems directly. Artificial intelligence makes such attacks more convincing by reproducing familiar faces and voices.

Citing CrowdStrike data, Balayev noted that the number of voice phishing attacks doubled in the first half of this year. He also referred to a September report by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), which received approximately 61,000 complaints about fraud attempts carried out in the names of government officials. The losses from these incidents exceeded $1.6 billion.

According to Balayev, Interpol estimates that AI-enabled fraud schemes are 4.5 times more profitable than traditional methods.

He cited several cases involving the use of deepfake technology. In May this year, a businessman in Singapore was invited to a meeting on Zoom, where the faces of people presented as the prime minister, president, a government minister, and a Central Bank representative appeared on screen. However, their images had been fabricated using deepfake technology.

Balayev added that the discussion concerned the actual geopolitical agenda at the time, specifically the situation in the Strait of Hormuz. Available data put the damage caused by the incident at at least 4.9 million Singapore dollars.

He also described an incident directly related to cyberdiplomacy. In June 2025, an unidentified individual used an AI-cloned voice of the US Secretary of State to contact three foreign ministers, one governor, and one member of Congress through the Signal app. Following the incident, the US State Department issued a warning to all diplomatic missions.

According to Balayev, a similar scheme was carried out in January this year using the identity of Japan's Minister of Defense.

“In both cases, no systems were hacked. Instead, people's trust, including their trust in diplomatic channels, was undermined. This represents a new category of risk for cyberdiplomacy,” he emphasized.

Turning to the role of deepfakes in information warfare, Balayev explained that hybrid warfare involves states pursuing their objectives not only through military means but also in the economic, political, and informational spheres. Disinformation is the main tool of information warfare, while deepfakes have become one of its most convincing forms.

“Deepfake technology spreads lies not through text, but through faces and voices that people recognize. This, in turn, makes it easier for people to accept false information,” he said.

Balayev also cited fake content circulated in connection with the war that began in February this year in a neighboring region. According to estimates by The New York Times, more than 110 AI-generated fake videos and images were recorded during the first two weeks of the war. One disinformation campaign attracted 125 million views in 14 days.

He added that a fake video showing Dubai's Burj Khalifa skyscraper on fire was viewed tens of millions of times. The day before the war began, one individual also hacked 31 social media accounts and used them to spread fake videos depicting combat operations.

“In other words, a cyberattack and disinformation were combined into a single operation,” Balayev said.

He also highlighted the use of deepfake technology during elections. According to him, fake videos targeting one of the candidates were circulated this fall in connection with the US Senate elections. The video received more than 850,000 views in just 24 hours, and researchers linked the incident to a foreign influence operation.

Balayev stressed that these examples demonstrate how different aspects of hybrid warfare are interconnected. In one case, the target is citizens' financial resources; in another, it is relations between states. In both cases, disinformation is the main tool.

“Generative AI has not created a new type of attack. It has made existing attacks cheaper, faster, and more convincing. Deepfakes are the face and voice of disinformation in hybrid warfare,” he concluded.

World.title: SOCAR, US-based SLB sign agreement on seismic data processing
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Azerbaijan's state oil company SOCAR and US-based energy technology firm SLB have signed a cooperation agreement covering seismic data processing and imaging.

According to SOCAR Exploration, the agreement establishes a framework for technical cooperation between SOCAR Exploration and SLB on selected hydrocarbon exploration, development and production projects.

The partnership will enable the application of advanced seismic data processing techniques to improve subsurface imaging accuracy, reduce geological uncertainties and support more informed decision-making, the company said.

"The cooperation will also facilitate knowledge exchange, strengthen in-house capabilities in seismic data processing, particularly through the application of full-waveform inversion (FWI) and advanced depth imaging technologies, as well as support the professional development of young Azerbaijani geophysicists.

"We congratulate both teams and thank them for their efforts in bringing this agreement to fruition. We look forward to productive and mutually beneficial cooperation," SOCAR Exploration said.

SLB is an international technology company that has operated in the energy sector for more than 100 years and has a presence in over 100 countries.

Its core business areas include developing and deploying technologies for the oil and gas industry, digitalising the energy sector, reducing industrial carbon emissions, and developing and scaling new energy systems.

The company focuses on supporting the energy transition by combining technological advances in traditional energy with solutions designed to reduce the industry's environmental impact.

World.title: ABC wins scoop of the year at 2026 Walkley Awards
World.content:
The ABC has won seven gongs at this year’s Walkley Awards, including the coveted Scoop of the Year prize for coverage of ASIO’s failures ahead of the Bondi terrorist attack.

The 71st Walkley Awards for Excellence in Journalism was hosted in Sydney, Thursday night, with 30 categories.

The Walkley Foundation’s chief executive, Shona Martyn said: “Once again the Walkley Awards have proved the excellence and breadth of Australian journalism."

"Public interest journalism is in good hands with these Australian journalists who are working against a backdrop of challenges to journalism, press freedom and news organisations in a shifting world."
