World.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingyas, UN court says
World.content:
The top United Nations court has ruled that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar's security forces against the Rohingya Muslim minority population in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

The decision, delivered seven years after the case was filed by predominantly Muslim Gambia, marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the legal threshold to prove genocide had been met.

It was the first time the court held a state responsible for genocide.

"The court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya," presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa said in a reading of the decision.

The panel found "that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine State."

Genocide has rarely been proven in international courts because judges must find that crimes were committed with the specific intent "to destroy, in whole or in part" a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

It carries major implications for the genocide case against Israel over its war in Gaza, which South Africa filed at the court in 2023.

A campaign of 'clearance'

Muslim-majority The Gambia filed the case with the backing of the 57-member Organization of Islamic Cooperation.

The Rohingya are not from The Gambia, and no atrocities took place there, but under international law any state can bring a case at the ICJ if it believes another country has violated the Genocide Convention.

The case centred on a violent military campaign in Myanmar's western Rakhine state almost a decade ago, after a Rohingya militant group carried out guerrilla-style attacks on army posts.

The army responded with massive "clearance operations" that targeted Rohingya villages. Survivors described a sweeping campaign of massacres, rape, arson and looting in northern Rakhine that forced more than 740,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, according to the United Nations and human rights groups.

The United Nations calls Rohingya refugees "the most persecuted minority in the world". (Reuters: Jorge Silva)

Nur Sadek, a 15-year-old student living in Ngan Chaung village, said he witnessed soldiers gun down his neighbours.

"Their homes were being burned, people were being chased, and they started shooting. They did not care whether they were women, children, or elderly people. And due to the fear of being shot or killed, people started fleeing," he told the ABC.

Survivors from the village of Tula Toli told journalists that unarmed civilians were executed and children thrown into a river.

Satellite images later showed the village had been razed. The nonprofit Médecins Sans Frontières estimated that at least 10,000 people died in the pogrom, and hundreds of Rohingya villages were burned to the ground.

The Gambia also said sexual violence, including mass gang rape and genital mutilation, was integral to the campaign and was itself evidence of genocidal intent. It pointed to the extreme brutality of the attacks, official tolerance for hate speech, and Myanmar's failure to investigate the alleged atrocities.

Fears over renewed US-Myanmar talks The United States has been holding secretive talks with a regime it has accused of genocide, and experts believe it could come down to rare earths.

Antonia Mulvey, a UN investigator on the Myanmar-Bangladesh border from 2017 to 2018, probed sexual violence and crimes against Rohingya children.

"I recall one woman, a mother like I am, who recounted how she was eight months pregnant. She was stripped naked by the Myanmar military soldiers. She was hung from a tree, and she was repeatedly raped by nine soldiers. Her unborn child died," she told the ABC.

Ms Mulvey, who is now the Executive Director of Legal Action Worldwide and worked with Rohingya witnesses and victims after the genocide case was filed, said women and girls were targeted with brutal sexual violence in public, gang rape and sexual enslavement.

"Myanmar's argument in brief was that it was a lawful counter-terrorism operations under which they killed men," she said.

"No counter-terrorism operation in any country at all allows for sexual violence."

Myanmar's defence

Myanmar rejected the allegations throughout the seven-year legal process, arguing that the 2016–2017 operations were counterterrorism measures in response to attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).

The military insisted the Rohingya had burned their own homes and that there was no direct evidence of genocidal intent.

It also disputed evidence and reports gathered by UN agencies, humanitarian organisations and journalists, including the fact-finding mission's reports, which were presented to the court.

Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar's civilian leader at the time and a Nobel laureate, dismissed the allegations, saying refugees may have exaggerated abuses and that the international outrage was based on "unsubstantiated narratives". She travelled to The Hague in 2019 to defend Myanmar in person.

Myanmar's leader Aung San Suu Kyi addressed the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, Netherlands in 2019. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

In 2021, her elected government was toppled in a military coup led by military chief Min Aung Hlaing, and she has been held in detention ever since.

The International Court of Justice said Myanmar had an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it had committed, to be determined at a later date.

Myanmar must also allow the "safe and dignified return to their place of residence and the reunification of families for the Rohingya displaced as a result of Myanmar's wrongful acts," it said.

These orders are legally binding, but the ICJ's judgment is not linked to any criminal trial, and no individuals will be held accountable or go to prison.

"One of the features of the international legal system is that we don't have much in the way of enforcement of judicial decisions," said William Schabas, a professor of international law at Middlesex University in London and an expert on genocide and international criminal law.

"It's a great shortcoming, and quite frankly, if someone were to propose that there be a mechanism to enforce the judgements, I think most states wouldn't 

However, if Myanmar fails or refuses to comply, the matter can be referred to the UN Security Council to help with enforcement.

"One of the problems at the Security Council is getting the five permanent members to agree. I don't know whether that would even be possible in the case of Gambia versus Myanmar, and it certainly wouldn't be possible in the case of South Africa versus Israel," Professor Schabas said.

A benchmark for Gaza

For many observers, the judgment's significance extends well beyond Myanmar.

It offers the strongest hint yet of how the court might approach the South Africa v Israel case, which alleges that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Israel denies the charge.

Streets lay in rubble across Gaza three years after the war. (ABC News)

"Without wanting to diminish the suffering of the Rohingya in Myanmar, the question of the Palestinians and Israel has been at the centre of the global agenda since the United Nations began," Professor Schabas said.

"Everybody knows that the pronouncements by the court will ricochet into the South African case."

A related case, Nicaragua v Germany, filed in March 2024, alleges that Germany failed to prevent genocide in Gaza by providing aid, including military equipment, to Israel.

The Myanmar ruling is likely to shape both cases, although the court is not expected to make its decisions for many years.

Refugees welcome ruling as sign of 'hope'

For the more than one million people forced to escape Myanmar's brutal campaign against the Rohingya, the ruling is a milestone.

Rohingya refugees gather to take part in a protest rally inside a refugee camp to mark the ninth-year anniversary of their exodus. (Reuters: Piyas Biswas)

"We have been waiting for decades to be recognised for our suffering and what we have gone through. And we have not seen anyone in the world take a step to stop this," said Nur Sadek, 24, who has been a refugee for almost a decade now.

He said he was forced to leave his family and make the dangerous boat journey from Bangladesh to Malaysia in 2022 after gangs kidnapped him for ransom in the Rohingya camps.

"I am staying in Malaysia in a country where they do not recognise refugees," he said.

"I have no right to get an education. I can't get work. I have very limited health care; I can't decide my own future.

"That's why the legal proceedings in the ICJ give me hope that the situation might change in our country so that we can go back some day."

ABC/wires

World.title: FIFA unveils Diallo and Tashima as challengers to Infantino's presidency
World.content:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino's re-election bid will be challenged by the French and Japanese federation presidents Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima, the global soccer body has confirmed.

The election, set to be held in March 2027, will be the first time Mr Infantino faces a challenger after being re-elected without opposition in 2023.

Mr Infantino has faced repeated calls for his resignation since his FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, a bid to sell stakes in the World Cup and other major competitions, failed.

How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded The FIFA president has faced international turmoil, embroiled in a World Cup sell-off saga that sparked loss of confidence in his leadership.

But the 56-year-old Swiss native, who has been the FIFA president since 2016, maintains that he has enough support from member associations around the world to get him re-elected.

French Football Federation (FFF) president Mr Diallo announced his candidacy on Monday, with the support of UEFA member associations represented on the executive committee and the FIFA Council.

Mr Tashima had declared his bid earlier this month and formally submitted his nomination on Wednesday.

"The candidatures have been forwarded to the electoral committee for examination and for passing a decision on the admission of the candidates," FIFA said in a statement.

"Member associations will be notified of the names of the proposed and admitted candidates no later than 18 February 2027."

Mr Diallo, who took over as FFF president in 2023, played a leading role as France and other European associations withdrew support from Mr Infantino last year over the FFE controversy.

"Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of FIFA, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community," UEFA said on Monday.

Reuters

World.title: Trump, Xi and Putin release joint statement after historic talks
World.content:
The official account of a landmark trilateral meeting between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin does not mention the war in Ukraine, despite the US president saying the conflict would be on the agenda.

Instead, the three leaders emerged from their historic talks in Shenzhen with a broad statement on nuclear security, global energy supplies and potential reform of the United Nations, but few concrete details about how those ambitions would be achieved.

Hours before the meeting, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used his speech at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China to directly call on Mr Putin to end his illegal invasion of Ukraine "now".

The meeting between Mr Putin, Mr Xi and Mr Trump on the sidelines of APEC lasted about 90 minutes on Thursday evening.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump during their trilateral meeting. (Sputnik: Vyacheslav Prokofyev via Reuters)

A readout published by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV after the talks wrapped up made no reference to Russia's invasion of Ukraine, but included an agreement that the International Criminal Court (ICC) and similar bodies should not abuse their jurisdiction.

The declaration was particularly significant for Mr Putin, who remained subject to an ICC arrest warrant over the alleged unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children during Russia's invasion.

The three leaders also recognised the immunity of state officials, a potentially contentious position given the ICC's role in prosecuting alleged war crimes.

The leaders pledged to work together to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation, reiterating that a nuclear war "cannot be won or fought".

They also agreed to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, emphasising the importance of stable global energy flows, although no specific targets or timelines were announced.

At the start of the trilateral, the leaders gathered in front of flags from all three nations at the sprawling Kylin Villa in China's tech hub of Shenzhen and stood for a photo, without shaking hands, before entering the meeting room.

Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin ahead of their meeting in Shenzhen. (Reuters: Win McNamee)

Trump confirms Ukraine talks before trilateral

"This is the first time the heads of nations from China, Russia, the US meet; it has groundbreaking significance," Xi said, according to Chinese news agency Xinhua.

Mr Trump was effusive in his praise of Mr Xi, congratulating him on hosting a successful APEC, while he also described it as an "honour" to be meeting with Mr Putin.

Ahead of the meeting, the US president confirmed Ukraine was on the agenda for the meeting, and said the conflict had "already" been discussed with Mr Putin earlier in the day.

"I think he [Mr Putin], and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war," he said.

Mr Trump also used his opening remarks to attack the International Criminal Court, which he described as "out of control".

Australia supporting ICC staff A senior official has told the ABC Australia and other countries have provided public support and help through "quiet diplomacy".

"I believe we all agree [it] has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," he said.

Mr Trump also said that, as the three largest nuclear powers, the US, China and Russia were "uniquely positioned" to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth.

"It's quite frankly a very hard thing to do because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard not to have them," he said.

"You have thousands of weapons, and you're supposed to give them up."

Mr Putin said Russia, China and the United States "hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace and security" during his opening remarks.

"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine," Mr Putin said.

"I am convinced that Russia, the US and China, our people are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening peace and stability over the world, if we cooperate constructively on the basis of mutual respect, equality, and a balance of interests."

US President Donald Trump called Russia's President Vladimir Putin his "friend" during a meeting on the sidelines. (Reuters: Sputnik/Vyacheslav Prokofyev)

Ahead of the meeting, Mr Trump referred to Mr Putin as his "friend".

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk immediately took to social media.

"God, protect us from such friends," he wrote on X.

Albanese directly calls on Putin to end Ukraine war

Hours before the high-stakes meeting was due to begin, Mr Albanese used his allotted speaking time at APEC to single out Mr Putin over Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine.

"I say very directly to President Putin: end your war, end it now," Mr Albanese said.

Anthony Albanese at the plenary meeting at APEC. (Reuters: Ng Han Guan)

The prime minister was looking directly at Mr Putin as he delivered the words, but the Russian leader did not look up when addressed.

Mr Xi and Mr Trump were also in the room during the prime minister's APEC speech.

Mr Albanese warned global conflicts, including in Ukraine and the Middle East, were driving up inflation and putting pressure on household budgets.

"Military conflict, disrupted global supply chains, and increasing challenges to the international rules that have underpinned decades of growth are impacting our national economies," he said.

"I welcome the meeting being held this afternoon between President Xi, President Trump, and President Putin, and we hope for positive outcomes in the interests of the world."

Meeting sparks 'Yalta 2.0' fears

The gathering has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, when US president Franklin D Roosevelt, British prime minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met to discuss the future of Europe as World War II ended.

That summit helped shape the post-war international order and became synonymous with powerful countries making decisions about the future of smaller nations without their involvement.

In the lead-up to the Shenzhen meeting, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned against Mr Trump, Mr Xi and Mr Putin using the meeting to carve up spheres of influence, amid concerns Russia could seek concessions over its ongoing invasion of Ukraine.

"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4,' with a redistribution of influence," Mr Zelenskyy said last month.

World.title: Kimberley man who whipped and beat partner to death jailed for 10 years
World.content:
A West Australian man has been jailed for 10 years for killing a woman in a sustained and violent assault in the state's remote Kimberley.

CONTENT WARNING: This story contains descriptions of domestic violence that some readers may find distressing.

Craig Charlton Rastus faced the Supreme Court in Derby for sentencing today over his fatal assault of the 39-year-old woman last year.

The woman, who cannot be identified for cultural reasons, was found unresponsive in Mowanjum Community, 2,240km north of Perth, on April 20.

She was taken to Derby Hospital, but died as a result of her injuries.

Rastus was initially charged with her murder, but the charge was subsequently downgraded to manslaughter.

He pleaded guilty in July.

When the sentence was announced, members of the woman's family in court yelled out, "He should have got more."

Craig Charlton Rastus killed the 39-year-old woman in the Kimberley community of Mowanjum in April last year. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Argument over alcohol sparked violence

Prosecutor Tracy Tan told the court Rastus started assaulting the woman in the early hours of the morning after "an argument over alcohol".

She said it was a sustained physical assault lasting about 30 minutes, with the woman receiving blunt force injuries to the head and face.

Ms Tan said Rastus also used a power cord to repeatedly whip the woman.

The Indigenous community of Mowanjum is on the outskirts of the Kimberley town of Derby. (ABC Kimberley: Erin Parke)

The attack happened outside a Mowanjum property, with Rastus later moving the woman's unresponsive body inside.

He called authorities for help at 7am the following day, with the woman pronounced dead at Derby Hospital at 9am.

Not an isolated incident

In his sentencing remarks, Justice Matthew Howard said the killing "could not be regarded as an isolated incident".

Craig Rastus was sentenced in the Derby Supreme Court in Western Australia's north. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Justice Howard said Rastus was issued with a 72-hour order prohibiting him from contact with the woman about 11:20pm on April 19 last year, "some three hours before the incident occurred".

"At the time of your assault there were in effect two orders binding on you to protect the deceased; you ignored both of them," he said.

"Importantly you were subject to a protective bail order and were serving a suspended imprisonment order."

Justice Howard applied a 25 per cent sentence discount for Rastus entering a plea at "the earliest possible opportunity".

Family says sentence not enough

The small public gallery of Derby Courthouse was packed by the 39-year-old victim's family and friends.

Speaking outside court, her sister, Yelonda Donation, said Rastus's 10-year sentence was not enough.

"We're still grieving, we're still processing," she said.

"Today was a hard one to swallow … 10 years is not enough for us; it feels very unfair."

Yelonda Donation, the victim's sister, said her family felt Rastus's 10-year sentence was insufficient. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

Ms Donation said her sister's absence was felt deeply across Derby and surrounding communities.

"She was a beautiful, loving, caring … strong family woman," she said.

"She loved her kids and her family; she loved outings and family gatherings.

"Wherever she'd been, she made friends and family as well."

World.title: 'Does it come with a chef?' rental price causes a stir within community
World.content:
A rental  asking $2,300 a week for a four-bedroom, two-bathroom home in Western Australia's South West has sparked an online debate over the equity of the local rental market.

The property, built in 1976 on an 806sqm block, is located in the coastal suburb of Abbey in Busselton, 230km south of Perth.

The eye-catching price tag triggered a wave of reaction after the listing was posted online on Tuesday, with commenters questioning who could realistically pay that amount.

Local property data shows the median rent for a house this size in Abbey is $880 a week, meaning the listing is roughly 160 per cent above the going rate.

The high-priced property is a four-bedroom, two-bathroom house. (ABC South West: Kalani Bate-Henry)

The online comments included: "Does it come with a chef, butler, gardener, electrician, plumber, handyman, and cleaning lady?" and "How is the next generation ever going to be able to afford to buy a house?"

Agent calls property premium

Local property agency Acton Belle South West is responsible for the listing and said the house was a premium property and not reflective of the current market.

"This particular property sits firmly within the premium end of the market. It offers an exceptional location, high-quality fixtures and fittings, and a level of finish and presentation that distinguishes it from a typical rental property," director Lyn Perks said.

" It should not be viewed as a representative of rental pricing across the broader region. "

The agency said they understood the struggles people face in the current rental market.

"We appreciate that the advertised rental price has attracted attention, particularly at a time when housing affordability is a significant concern for many West Australians," Ms Perks said.

Property values in Busselton recorded the nation's steepest regional decline of 4.1 per cent in the July quarter of this year, according to property data from analytics firm Cotality.

Abbey Beach is just around the corner from the property. (ABC South West: Kalani Bate-Henry)

'Ridiculous' rental price

Busselton local Renee Guthridge said the price seemed ridiculous, adding that rent at that level felt out of reach for families and risked pushing longtime Busselton renters out of town.

"I just don't understand how people can sleep at night charging that amount," she said.

Local property investor David Newman owns two similar four-bedroom, two-bathroom rentals in the area.

He said while the price looked steep, owners were free to ask for whatever they liked.

Mr Newman said rising house prices, mortgages, and interest rates had pushed costs up across the sought-after region, though plenty of comparable homes were available for around $900 a week.

David Newman says he doubts whether a long-term tenant would pay double the market rate. (ABC South West: Kalani Bate-Henry)

"It is a premium area to live in, and it does cost a lot more than other parts of Australia to live in, but that's part of living in the luxury of the South West," he said.

Supply shrinking while demand rises

While some see high prices as the cost of coastal living, frontline support services warn the rising prices are leaving a growing number of locals behind.

Not-for-profit housing organisation Accordwest's Matt Wilson described this rental listing as an outlier, though he noted it reflected broader affordability pressures across the region.

The property has attracted debate online over the cost of renting in the South West. (ABC South West: Kalani Bate-Henry)

"The availability of the rentals as well is shrinking, so you've got hundreds of people and families trying to compete for a much smaller pocket of what's actually out there, and hence you kind of see the increase," he said.

Those housing pressures are also rippling through Busselton's tourism and hospitality sector, making it harder for local employers to keep staff in town.

Siesta Park Holiday Resort owners Greg and Jane Tickle said the $2,300 rental figure sounded more like a short-term summer rate than a standard lease, warning high long-term rents hit local workers hard.

Siesta Holiday Park owners Jane and Greg Tickle. (ABC South West: Kalani Bate-Henry)

"We find that our staff find it hard, and they're just needing more work to be able to pay their rent and afford anything else," Ms Tickle said.

Mr Tickle said holiday businesses often adjusted prices dynamically during peak summer demand, but pushing long-term residential rents to similar heights makes it harder for local businesses to find year-round staff.

World.title: Almost-forgotten Australian author uncovered in biography that just won $40K
World.content:
A biography of the late Australian author Elizabeth Harrower, who was described as Patrick White's "most important successor", has won the $40,000 Mark & Evette Moran Nib Literary Award (the Nib).

Elizabeth Harrower: The woman in the watch tower by journalist Susan Wyndham is a richly detailed account of the life of the writer admired by White, Shirley Hazzard and Christina Stead.

Born in 1927 in Newcastle, Harrower was the author of five novels between 1957 and 2014, including Down in the City and The Long Prospect, and occupied the same postwar Sydney milieu as artist Sidney Nolan.

When White declined the Miles Franklin, Australia's most prestigious literary award, in 1966, he even suggested Harrower in his stead, for what many believe is her best book, The Watch Tower, about two sisters, Laura and Clare, living under the tyranny of Laura's overbearing husband, Felix.

Yet Harrower remains relatively little known, both in her time and now. Her books sold few copies and fell out of print before they were reissued by Text Publishing in 2012.

Wyndham hopes her book, and winning the Nib, a prize for research-based literature, will help the "mysterious, sensitive, tenacious" Harrower reach more readers.

As she explains in her introduction: "She lives on most of all in her own remarkable books, and I hope this biography will lead readers to them."

A former literary editor at The Sydney Morning Herald, Wyndham says it's a joy to be on the other side of a prize she once wrote about.

"Maybe it'll help me write something else," Susan Wyndham says of what she'll do with the prize money. (Supplied: UNSW Press)

"I used to have to get up far too early to go to many breakfasts at Bondi where they gave the prize," she says.

"But I always recognised it as unlike any other because it is about research and it also recognises writing and readability and relevance to today, but it's across all genres.

"It's a great honour to be in a shortlist and a longlist of books that are history, biography, First Nations writers, queer writers, poetry [and] fiction."

Judge Kirsten Tranter praised Elizabeth Harrower: The woman in the watchtower as "rigorous, insightful, and beautifully written".

She said the book stood out for "its depth of research, accessible, distinctive literary voice, and the way the book illuminates this under-appreciated figure and places her in the context of Australian literary culture in such interesting and compelling ways".

Depth of research

In Elizabeth Harrower: The woman in the watch tower, Wyndham blends close literary study of Harrower's novels and short stories with archival research to show how her life fed into her fiction.

Elizabeth Harrower, pictured in Sydney in 1961, moved to London in 1951, where she published her first two novels. (Supplied: Jill Crossley)

A recurring figure is a manipulative man, like Felix, seemingly inspired by Harrower's stepfather, a "shady character" often on the wrong side of the law.

"One always has to be careful about reading novels as autobiography and I tried not to fall into that trap," Wyndham says.

"However, the more I learnt about her life, the more I saw she had used episodes and created characters out of people from her life.

" I wanted to show how life had become art. "

Following Harrower's death in 2020, at the age of 92, her archive, held by the National Library of Australia in Canberra, became public. That's when Wyndham was able to begin researching the book in earnest.

The book also won the Magarey Medal for Biography, for a book by a woman author about an Australian subject. (Supplied: UNSW Press)

There, she found letters to and from the author and her literary friends.

Wyndham had first realised Harrower might make a good subject for a biography long before 2020, having first interviewed the author in 1996 when she won the Patrick White Award.

With the release of Harrower's final novel In Certain Circles, written in the late 1960s but only published in 2014, Wyndham read her novels for the first time and spoke to her again.

They would go on to form an easy acquaintance, sharing many afternoon teas over the final years of her life.

"She was in her mid-80s and still sharp-minded but elusive about her earlier life," Wyndham says. "She said she'd never read the books since she wrote them so couldn't talk about them.

"I felt that she was a lovely, interesting person, and interested in talking about my life and work and books.

"I got to know her as far as she would let anyone."

Same for writers today

In Elizabeth Harrower: The woman in the watch tower, Wyndham quotes writer Geoffrey Dutton, in 1966, describing Australian authors as a "depressed class, in terms of finance and prestige".

It feels akin to the dire financial position facing most Australian authors today, with a 2022 survey finding writers earned an average of $18,200 a year from their creative work.

"[Harrower] liked to tell people that when she was trying to be a writer, there weren't many writers in Australia," Wyndham says.

"It was hard to be seen and heard.

" I think she would sympathise with any writer today who's struggling to make a career and a living. "

Like most authors today, for most of her career, Harrower needed a job to support her creative work. She then stopped writing in the late 70s and withdrew from public life.

Elizabeth Harrower wrote five novels, including The Watch Tower and Voss winner In Certain Circles. (Supplied: Text Publishing)

"Everyone always asked her, 'Why did you stop?'" Wyndham says.

"I think she got a bit sick of answering that question.

"She said, 'Well, actually, I did write quite a lot of books.'"

Wyndham suggests Harrower "ran out of puff" as she began to realise "she wasn't going to be able to fund a career that would keep going for a long time".

"She decided it was easier not to write and to enjoy her life, and that's when she really turned to friendship and politics during the Whitlam years."

What she did write was, Wyndham suggests, "almost a portrayal of what feminism needed to fix for women".

Her novels were championed by people such as Anne Summers.

"I think her goal in life was not to be under the thumb of a man or anyone else," Wyndham says.

"It was important to her to live alone and work and have life on her own terms."

World.title: Sydney Marathon winner banned for three years, stripped of title
World.content:
This year's Sydney Marathon winner Peres Jepchirchir has been handed a three-year doping ban after testing positive for EPO.

The 33-year-old returned the adverse finding in an out-of-competition test in Kenya before travelling to Sydney in August.

One of the all-time greats of marathon running, Jepchirchir claimed victories in four of the World Marathon Majors; New York (2021), Boston (2022), London (2024) and Sydney (2026), the 2025 World Athletics Championships, as well as winning gold at the 2021 Olympic Games.

Her Sydney Marathon victory has now been stripped, and legacy trashed, following her doping result.

"In an interview on [September 17], the athlete denied using EPO and said she had no knowledge of how the AAF (adverse analytical finding) had occurred," the Athletics Integrity Unit said.

"Despite her explanations in the interview, the former world record-holder in the half-marathon subsequently signed an admission of anti-doping rule violations and acceptance of consequences form."

Peres Jepchirchir won in New York in 2021. (Getty images: Elsa)

Sydney Marathon race director Wayne Larden said he was disappointed the race had been won by a doper.

"We're disappointed for every athlete, partner and fan affected," Larden said in a statement.

"But this outcome shows the system works. Alongside our fellow [World Marathon Majors], the Sydney Marathon has voluntarily invested in additional out-of-competition testing, above and beyond what is required of us, and this case is exactly why that investment matters.

"There is no place for doping at the Sydney Marathon or in the sport at all, and anyone who cheats should know they will be caught."

Jepchirchir was provisionally suspended in October after an out-of-competition sample collected in Kenya ahead of the race returned an adverse analytical finding for EPO.

She was also tested on race day in Sydney and returned a negative result, highlighting the importance of out-of-competition tests.

The Sydney Marathon announced that Kenyan runner Irine Cheptai, who finished second behind Jepchirchir on the day, will be elevated to champion.

Irine Cheptai came home second in Sydney, but is now a Marathon Major winner for the first time. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng)

Cheptai endeared herself to the Sydney crowd, handing her drink to Australian Paralympian Michael Roeger during the race, earning her a nomination as a finalist for World Athletics' 2026 International Fair Play Award.

It is the 34-year-old's first win in one of the eight World Marathon Majors: London, New York, Boston, Chicago, Berlin, Tokyo, Sydney and Cape Town.

"Today we get to celebrate Irine Cheptai, who raced clean and with real sportsmanship, and we're proud that Sydney will be where she claims her first [World Marathon Majors] title," Larden said.

Sydney Marathon organisers said that all other tests from the event had now been cleared, meaning there would be no more disqualifications.

Cheptai finished three minutes and 40 seconds behind her Kenyan teammate, running 2:22:11.

Two Ethiopians will step up onto the podium as well; Shure Demise Ware will be credited with second after running 2:22:33, with Haven Hailu Desse up to third in 02:22:57.

Jepchirchir is yet another high-profile Kenyan athlete to test positive for doping, with more than 140 sanctioned for doping offences since 2017, when the AIU was established.

Last year, Kenya's ⁠women's marathon world record holder Ruth Chepngetich was banned for three years after admitting anti-doping rule violations involving hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), a ‌prohibited diuretic.

Chepngetich's world record of 2:09:56 remains on the books, however, because it ​was set before her positive test.

"Out-of-competition testing is one of the most powerful tools we have in protecting clean sport," Athletics Integrity Unit chief executive Brett Clothier said.

"It reaches athletes when and where they least expect it. This case is a clear example of that, and it would not have been possible without the Sydney Marathon's voluntary investment in additional testing this year.

"We're grateful to have such a committed partner in the fight for clean athletics."

World.title: Cody Walker lands safely with Carlton as new draft rules bite premiers in night one shock
World.content:
SportAFLDraft Cody Walker lands safely with Carlton as new draft rules bite premiers in night one shock Marc McGowan November 19, 2026 — 11:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cody Walker was right not to worry. The father-son jet officially became a Blue on Thursday night when Carlton matched Richmond’s bid on the 18-year-old at the No.3 pick, ending all fearmongering under the AFL’s new rules that he might not make it to his dad’s old club. However, those same rules – announced in April to make it tougher for clubs, particularly higher-performing ones, to match father-son and academy bids – cost Brisbane dearly in the shock of night one. Sydney placed a successful bid on Lions academy dasher Caylen Murray at No.9, with blindsided Brisbane – who had hoped a bid would not come for several more picks – unable to conjure up the draft points required to match. AFL draft - first round Dougie Cochrane (Port Adelaide match Essendon bid) Ethan Drever (Essendon) Cody Walker (Carlton match Richmond bid) Arki Butler (Richmond) Heath Mellody (West Coast) Ethan Matthews (GWS match Melbourne bid) Mitch Harris (Melbourne) Harry Van Hattum (Richmond) Caylen Murray (Sydney) Leo Steed (Gold Coast) Gus Teixeira (St Kilda) Sam Gayfer (Collingwood) Jake Eime (GWS) Toby Krasna (Adelaide) Lochie Burrows (Melbourne) Tyson Bradley (St Kilda) Archie Elliott (Essendon) George Dimer (Fremantle) Clancy Snell (Port Adelaide)



Walker’s father, 202-game ex-Carlton player Andrew, who was among those to condemn the change to father-son rules, and mother Kylie were in attendance at Marvel Stadium to celebrate their family’s milestone moment. “It’s so surreal. It’s everything I’ve ever wanted to be, coming up as a junior footballer,” Walker said, 16 months after he nominated as a father-son candidate. “To go to a team that I supported, and also the team that my dad played for, is pretty special.” Cody Walker quickly gets used to the Carlton colours. Joe Armao There were four bids on club-tied prospects in the opening nine selections, starting with Port Adelaide matching Essendon’s bid at No.1 on their next-generation academy prodigy and supersized utility Dougie Cochrane, who was delighted to join his father Stuart’s old club.



Cochrane did not qualify to be a father-son draftee because Stuart played only 54 of his games for the Power, but his Indigenous background made him a late addition to the club’s NGA – and rubber-stamped him to Alberton. The Bombers pivoted to big-bodied midfielder Ethan Drever before using their second pick of the night, No.17, on his GWV Rebels teammate, Archie Elliott, who was visibly shocked to be selected, at least in the first round. Elliott had to quickly switch into a Rebels polo to walk on stage with. Essendon’s bid on Cochrane triggered a start-of-second-round compensation pick, not only for them, but also the Tigers and Eagles, as part of rules for bottom-five clubs that have their first selections pushed back. Other key adjustments included ladder-related loadings and discounts on draft points, which descend in value from the top pick, depending on where clubs finished in the preceding season, and being able to match bids with a maximum of two selections.



Brisbane making another grand final ended up being the deciding factor in them missing out on Murray because they had to pay a 20 per cent loading on the Murray bid. Murray, from the Maroochydore Roos, was one of four Indigenous players selected in the first round, alongside Cochrane, Walker and Toby Krasna, who Adelaide picked at No.14. “I didn’t realise Sydney were that keen,” a shocked Murray said. “I was a bit shocked at the start, but now it’s sunk in that I’m a Sydney Swans player, and I’m stoked.” Caylen Murray was stunned to become a Sydney Swan. Joe Armao The Swans’ draft twist delivered an unexpected win for St Kilda, who secured Sandringham Dragons teammates Gus Teixeira, a powerful midfielder-forward, and Tyson Bradley, a key defender, with their two first-round selections.



Saints recruiter Simon Dalrymple, who formerly worked at Sydney, revealed they rated both players in the top seven of the draft. “It is an unbelievable and unexpected result. I’ve never seen it – I’ve been going 18 years to have a night like that,” Dalrymple said. “[To get] the dynamic mid and the key defender, and both in the bayside region, was an unbelievable result. Thanks to my mate at the Swans, [list boss] Chris Keane, numbers man. That opened it up.” Related Article Draft AFL draft as it happened: Port land Cochrane as top pick; Cult figure Van Hattum a Tiger The Blues began the draft with picks 13 and 18 – enough to match any bid on Walker outside the opening two selections, including the ability to go into points deficit at next year’s draft, which will include Tasmania for the first time.



A pre-draft trade agreed with Adelaide went through once Walker made it past Essendon’s selections, where Carlton sent picks 13 and 58 to the Crows for selections 15, 35 and 53. That deal still left the Blues with enough points to match any Walker bid, while adding an extra second-round choice and moving up five places later in the draft. For Adelaide, the benefit was getting ahead of Melbourne’s second selection in the first round to snare Northern Knights winger Krasna. “I think Cody complements the people we’ve got, so not only is he a good player, but he’s going to come into a team where the people around him could complement him as well,” Carlton football boss Chris Davies said. “We think he’s a player of high talent.”



Walker, likened to Patrick Dangerfield for his power and burst out of stoppages, graduated from school last year and relocated to Melbourne soon after to train regularly with Carlton. The teenage midfielder joins a new era at the Blues under Josh Fraser, who won the coaching job after guiding Carlton back from a 1-8 record to the finals as a caretaker after replacing Michael Voss. Related Article Draft AFL draft round one: Tears flow for new Bomber who came to support a mate and got picked himself They also matched a bid on a father-son prospect at No.3 last year, key defender Harry Dean, who made an instant impact to finish runner-up in the Rising Star award – behind another young Blue, ball magnet Jagga Smith. Richmond’s consolation prize after missing out on Walker was Sandringham forward Arki Butler, who is compared to Tom Papley and considered one of the most gifted players in this year’s class.



They also caused a ripple in the draft when they chose athletic ruckman Harry Van Hattum over Teixeira with their second selection, No.8. “It was close, and it was close between a number of players,” Tigers national recruiting manager Rhy Gieschen said. “There was a little bit of tinkering with our order, based on what we knew other clubs were doing, and we did have some really serious conversations about it, but ultimately, we found Harry really hard to pass up on.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Trump, Putin and Xi talk nuclear weapons and Ukraine
World.content:
WorldAsiaChina relations Trump, Putin and Xi talk nuclear weapons and Ukraine Lisa Visentin November 19, 2026 — 11:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Shenzhen: Seated at a large round table, US President Donald Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, cast themselves as peace brokers capable of ending wars, reining in the nuclear arms race, and securing global stability as they sat down for historic talks. The leaders spoke behind closed doors for around 90 minutes, with Xi hosting the unprecedented three-way summit at the lakeside Kylin Villa in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday afternoon. The historic trilateral meeting took place at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein “We are really making history,” Trump said in a brief statement before reporters were excluded from the room. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.” Following the meeting, China and Russia released a broadly-worded four-point joint statement that they said the three leaders had agreed to during their talks. It included an agreement to reform the United Nations, increase the supply of petroleum, and affirm the view that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought”.



It said the leaders also agreed that the International Criminal Court must not abuse its authority and that state officials must have immunity. The ICC in 2023 issued an arrest warrant for Putin, and Trump has been repeatedly critical of the body. However, it is unclear whether they landed any major concrete commitments, including on the wars in Ukraine or Iran, or agreed to hold future trilateral discussions. Experts have generally held the low expectation that the summit would produce little more than a photo-op. The US side has not yet released its summary of the meeting. Both Trump and Putin put Ukraine on the agenda in their opening remarks, while Xi called for a “world without nuclear weapons”, according to China’s official Xinhua news agency. Trump said the US, Russia and China were uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons stockpiled by countries.



Putin, Xi and Trump walk towards the Kylin Villa where they held talks. Getty Images “It’s quite frankly a very hard thing to do because once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard to not have them. It’s very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump said. Positioned at the centre of the table, with Trump and Putin seated on either side, Xi projected the image of a coordinating powerbroker, as he opened the talks by saying history showed that when major powers were at peace, the world was safe. “When major powers fight, the world falls into turmoil,” Xi said. He notably avoided mentioning Ukraine, reflecting Beijing’s reluctance to be seen as brokering a deal without Kyiv at the table — an image that would undermine China’s assurance to the world that it doesn’t seek to be a hegemonic superpower carving up territories.



Xinhua cited Xi as telling the other two leaders that nuclear weapons should be “comprehensively prohibited and completely destroyed,” describing them as a “Damocles Sword” hanging over humanity, according to a state media readout of his remarks. However, Xi’s remarks will be met with scepticism by Western analysts, who say Beijing has previously shown little interest in curbing its stockpile of 600 nuclear warheads when the US and Russia possess more than 5000 warheads each. Related Article China relations ‘End your war, end it now’: Albanese gives Putin a serve at APEC In his opening remarks, Putin said the three countries had “numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine.” He was widely expected to push for favourable terms to end his war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year. Trump revealed he and Putin had already had a “long discussion” on the issue when they held impromptu bilateral talks for 40 minutes earlier on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.



The meeting overshadowed the two-day APEC forum, which Trump used as a platform to project his camaraderie with his authoritarian rivals. The men shook hands and exchanged small talk and smiles ahead of a group photo at a gala ball on Wednesday evening. Xi and Trump hugged on the tarmac as the US president arrived in Shenzhen. The warm exchanges continued on Thursday. “You’re my friend, and we have a very special relationship,” Trump said before a one-on-one meeting with Xi ahead of the trilateral talks. “I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we will never have a problem.” A few hours earlier, Trump greeted Putin with a playful “who’s that” while pointing at him and saying “my friend”, before they sat down for their own talks. The Kremlin said Putin left the meeting in an “excellent” mood. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Second Gold Walkley for McKenzie as Age scoops nine awards
World.content:
Breaking NationalMedia & marketing Second Gold Walkley for McKenzie as Age scoops nine awards Cassidy Knowlton November 19, 2026 — 11:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Age investigative journalist Nick McKenzie has won the highest prize in journalism, the Gold Walkley, for the second time. McKenzie, the most decorated journalist in the nation, also won the award for investigative journalism for his work “Gatto's rise and a premier's fall”, which exposed evidence that the Victorian government was warned of union misconduct and criminal infiltration in the state’s construction sector. The Age editor Patrick Elligett described McKenzie as the best journalist in a generation. Sam Mooy They were two of the nine awards won by journalists at The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald at the 2026 Walkley Awards, held in Sydney on Thursday night. The two awards take the number of Walkley Awards McKenzie has won to 22, including the Gold Walkley in 2024 alongside journalists David Marin-Guzman and Ben Schneiders. McKenzie’s relentless Building Bad investigative series was instrumental in the downfall of premier Jacinta Allan and Premier Ben Carroll’s establishment of a royal commission into corruption on government building sites.



"A second Gold Walkley in the space of two years reinforces Nick's position as the best journalist in a generation," Age editor Patrick Elligett said. Nick McKenzie won the Gold Walkley for “Gatto’s rise and a premier’s fall”, published in this masthead and on 60 Minutes. The Age Long-time Age writer Tony Wright, who recently stepped away from daily writing but continues as a columnist, was also honoured at the ceremony for his outstanding contribution to journalism. Wright spent years in the Canberra press gallery and has covered everything from state politics to foreign wars to personal reflections over more than 30 years. Tony Wright watches on as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese paid tribute to his incredible career earlier this year in the House of Representatives. The Age “The Age’s investment in high-quality journalism continues to deliver benefits for readers, and we’re thrilled to have this recognised by our peers,” Elligett said.



“Our journalists are the best in the country, and they deserve every one of the accolades they received tonight. “I was particularly thrilled for Tony Wright, who has never sought recognition or fame throughout his decades-long career, but deserves both. I look forward to welcoming him back as a columnist next year.” Editor Patrick Elligett described The Age’s journalists as the best in the country. Justin McManus Chris Vedelago, Marta Pascual Juanola and the Visual Stories Team were recognised with the Walkley for explanatory journalism for their compelling visual story about the nation’s booming illegal tobacco trade. “Congratulations to winners from all outlets. Our work as an industry is so important to the country, and it is great to be reminded of its robust health,” said Elligett.



Cartoonist Megan Herbert’s insightful work Discarded, which satirised the Albanese government’s response to domestic violence, won the cartoon of the year category. Herbert’s cartoon was featured in a July 2026 edition of The Age. Megan Herbert Good Weekend senior writer Melissa Fyfe and WAtoday journalist Carla Hildebrandt won the long feature writing category for their investigation into the death of prominent Jeffrey Epstein victim Virginia Giuffre. Photographer Sam Mooy won the category for his photographic essay on the riots in Alice Springs that followed the killing of Kumanjayi Little Baby. Sam Mooy won the Photographic Essay category for his coverage of riots in Alice Springs. Sam Mooy



Contributor David Leser was honoured in the opinion category for his reflections on the Bondi massacre, and Julie Hare won the Walkley for specialist and beat reporting for her coverage of former deputy prime minister Julie Bishop’s catastrophic legacy at Australian National University. Luke McIlveen, executive editor of The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald, was thrilled by the results for the mastheads. “Our incredible journalists at The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald have once again shown why they’re the very best – fearlessly exposing corruption, keeping governments on the hook and telling the stories of their cities with heart and purpose,” he said. World.title: Herald journalists, photographers dominate 71st annual Walkley Awards
World.content:

The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age’s investigative journalist Nick McKenzie has won the Gold Walkley for exposing alleged links between underworld figure Mick Gatto and the Victorian government’s infrastructure programs, as this masthead’s photographers swept the 71st annual awards on Thursday night.



McKenzie’s investigative series, “Gatto’s rise and a premier’s fall”, published in this masthead and on 60 Minutes, beat the rest of the Walkley winners to the top prize, marking another illustrious achievement for the star reporter.

Nick McKenzie won the Gold Walkley for “Gatto’s rise and a premier’s fall”, published in this masthead and on 60 Minutes. The Age

Executive editor Luke McIlveen said the Gold Walkley was “due recognition” for McKenzie, whom he called the “finest investigative reporter in the country”.

Herald editor Jordan Baker described McKenzie as a “brave, relentless advocate for truth and accountability” who deeply deserved the award.



Also among the winners were Herald photographers Sam Mooy, Edwina Pickles and Steven Siewert. Mooy took out the feature/photographic essay prize for his work covering the death of Kumanjayi Little Baby and the ensuing riots in Alice Springs.

Pickles won the Nikon Photo of the Year for her harrowing photograph of the Bondi Beach massacre, taken moments after police arrived.

Follow along for the all picks from night one of the 2026 AFL National Draft. 1. Dougie Cochrane, Port Adelaide What Cochrane said: “Feeling pretty cool and so grateful to be a Port Adelaide player.” The young star said he was ready to attack the pre-season and was eager for a big 2027. Former No.1 Pick and Port Adelaide star Jason Horne-Francis presented Cochrane with his jumper. Knee surgery to fix a persistent patella tendonitis issue wiped out most of Cochrane’s draft year, but he was always considered the standout prospect.



2. Ethan Drever, Essendon What Drever said: “It’s pretty awesome, I still can’t believe it’s real, obviously a boyhood dream.… it’s just a buzz, I don’t know what to say.” Drever said some of his favourite players were from Essendon, highlighting Nate Caddy. Drever is a big and powerful midfielder who wins contested possessions for fun and bursts away from stoppages before driving long kicks inside 50. 3. Cody Walker, Carlton



What Walker said: “The amount of work that the academy boys have put into me, the players such as Harry Dean… I can’t thank them enough… they’ve turned me from a good player to an even better one.” When his name was announced, the budding star embraced his family and friends and walked up to the stage with a huge smile. Walker will now follow in his 202-game father Andrew’s footsteps. 4.Arki Butler, Richmond



What Butler said: “I can’t wait to get started, I can’t wait to be a Tiger.” The young Tiger vowed to try and keep his banter with rivals down to a minium to avoid fines. “We’ll have to wait and see, I hope not,” he said when asked if he intended on break Toby Greene’s fines records “Mum and dad are pretty keen on me saving my money so I’d like to not spend it at the tribunal.” 5. Heath Mellody, West Coast



What Mellody said: “I was really happy with that and super grateful to be a West Coast player.” His whole family are Fremantle supporters, but Mellody joked they would all have to convert now. 6.Ethan Matthews, GWS What Matthews said: “I’m so happy to be with the Giants, I wouldn’t want to be anywhere else.” Matthews said GWS coach Adam Kingsley “isn’t as scary as he looks”.



The western Sydney academy product grew up supporting Collingwood but says he’ll be “Giants all the way” now. 7. Mitch Harris, Melbourne What Harris said: “I’m looking forward to it,” when asked how he’d feel moving to Melbourne. The tall defender said he models his game on Brisbane Lions star and co-captain Harris Andrews. Harris gobbles up intercepts, is an effective lockdown defender, and had an impressive SANFL finals series



8. Harry Van Hattum, Richmond What Van Hattum said: “Probably a couple of years ago, I stopped playing basketball because it just got too much of a commitment with both [footy and basketball].” The athletic ruckman with rare kicking skills said he models his game on fellow big man Luke Jackson. 9.Caylen Murray, Sydney



What Murray said: “It’s a great place [Sydney] ... but first and foremost I want to say thanks to Brisbane.” Many expected Brisbane to get Murray, but Sydney swooped on the Lions Academy player with a top-10 bid. Murray’s favourite player is Hawks star Cyril Rioli. 10. Leo Steed, Gold Coast



What Steed said: “I’m over the moon, I’ve worked so hard, so it means a lot.” Steed was in tears during the interview and said this is “all I have wanted since I was three” and embraced his family before he went on stage. Steed said he had worked on being more damaging with the ball and was thrilled to be selected by the Suns. 11. Gus Teixeira, St Kilda What Teixeira said: “Every year I get back to Brazil, hopefully I can get there next year.”



The youngster has Brazilian heritage and said he grew up supporting Essendon but could quickly convert to the Saints. 12.Sam Gayfer, Collingwood What Gayfer said: “It’s a childhood dream come true, I’m just so happy.” The big man smashed the combine’s running vertical jump record and wouldn’t be out of place in the NBA draft. His uncle Mick was a 1990 premiership Magpie.



13. Jake Eime, GWS What Eime said: “I’m over the moon - to be honest I didn’t really know [if GWS would select him], but I’m ready to get to work.” Eime’s friends and family jumped on top of him when his name was called out. 14. Toby Krasna, Adelaide



What Krasna said: “I think I just want to get to training and earn the respect of all my coaches and my teammates.” Another fantastic Zoom celebration – all of Krasna’s friends jumped on top of him ruffling his hair and almost knocking him off the chair. 15. Lachlan Burrows, Melbourne



What Burrows said: “I started off pretty nervous as the picks kept going through, but couldn’t be more grateful now.” The new Demon was surrounded by primary school and high school friends. 16. Tyson Bradley, St Kilda What Bradley said: “I’m so excited to stay in Melbourne with my family, St Kilda is down the road.”



Bradley put together an outstanding season in the backline, including winning Victoria Metro’s MVP award and being the recipient of Sandringham Dragons’ best finals player 17. Archie Elliott, Essendon What Elliot said: “I’m super pumped I don’t even know what to say.” The young forward was in tears during his interview and said 15 clubs had spoken to him, but he wasn’t invited tonight as he wasn’t considered one of the leading prospects to go early. He joked when Essendon met with him, the coach wasn’t even there.



18. George Dimer, Fremantle What Dimer said: “I’m literally shaking right now, just to share this moment with the people I love the most and all my closest friends, it’s so special to me.” The small forward said it was “such a nerve-wracking night” but said hearing his name was such a relief. Dimer is also planning to go to university next year and says he’s “undecided on law or engineering”.



19. Clancy Snell, Port Adelaide What Snell said: “It’s been in the back of my head [moving to Adelaide] but super keen to move”. Snell’s friends jumped on top of him before and after the interview, embracing the new Power star and sending him crashing to the floor. World.title: AFL draft as it happened: Port land Cochrane as top pick; Cult figure Van Hattum a Tiger
World.content:
Port Adelaide have landed highly touted utility Dougie Cochrane as the AFL’s No.1 draft pick, matching Essendon’s bid on their next-generation academy product.

The Bombers, last season’s wooden spooners, used their top selection on Cochrane, the top player in the draft pool.

But the Power swiftly matched that bid to claim the 195cm son of former North Melbourne and Port player Stuart Cochrane.

Cochrane is the first No.1 draft pick in Port’s history and appears destined for stardom.

Especially after Zak Butters’ move to the Western Bulldogs, the 18-year-old is seen as the figurehead for generation next at the Power under coach Josh Carr.

Cochrane was presented his first Power jumper by new teammate Jason Horne-Francis at Marvel Stadium on Thursday night.

Dougie Cochrane. Getty Images

“I’m feeling pretty good,” Cochrane told Fox Footy moments later.

“I’m just so grateful to be a Port Adelaide player once and for all. I couldn’t be happier, to be honest.”

Cochrane was largely unsighted on the field this year because of lingering patella tendonitis, but made it back after surgery for four SANFL appearances late in the season.

“It was definitely a challenge, but I was also very lucky to go to Port Adelaide and do my rehab there,” Cochrane said.

“I got a little bit of a scrape-out there and felt pretty good by the end of it.

“I’m now ready to attack the pre-season and ready for a big 2027.”

Cochrane not only follows in his father’s footsteps at Port, but will call brother Tom a teammate.

Tom has played six senior games for the club since joining in more humble fashion through the 2024 rookie draft.

Dougie admitted his older brother usually won the backyard fights when they were kids.

“He was a bit bigger than me and I still need to get that frame behind me,” he said.

“But no, it was a good battle back in the day, that’s for sure.”

Cochrane shot to prominence by winning the MVP award at the national under-16 championships in 2024, and has long been touted as a future star.

“He’s thrived under that spotlight,” Port coach Carr said.

“He’s embraced it, he hasn’t shied away from it ... his attitude really has been more about how he can be better as a player and be ready to play AFL football.”

AAP

World.title: Pat Cummins is under siege. His manager blames ‘hysteria unfounded in reality’
World.content:
Pat Cummins’ position as Australian Test cricket captain is under intense scrutiny after former teammates rallied around ball tamperer Cameron Bancroft and backed his revelations about the team’s cheating in South Africa in 2018. Nothing epitomised a state of siege more than how Cummins was chased by cameras outside his Sydney home, then again as he tried to enter the SCG for a training session. Pat Cummins with his back to the wall on Thursday. Kate Geraghty While his manager Neil Maxwell described the criticism of the Test captain as “hysteria unfounded in reality”, Cummins has now been Australian captain for five years, and will have to weigh up whether he wants to carry on as the team’s leader and spokesman amid the current conflagration. Cricket Australia’s board and executive were on Thursday working furiously to try to settle terms of reference for the “independent truth forum” meant to be convened to provide players and staff with an outlet for their divergent memories of the 2018 South Africa tour and the sandpaper scandal.



Noted barrister Fiona McLeod, SC, is a leading contender to preside over the forum, but declined to comment when contacted by this masthead on Thursday. While initially characterised as a voluntary avenue for players to speak “their truths”, state associations contacted by this masthead on Thursday believe the truth forum needs both greater powers and greater transparency while running fully at arm’s length from CA. Federal Sports Minister Anika Wells fired a similar message across CA’s bows in late afternoon. Loading “Integrity in the game matters for every kid with a bat or a ball,” a spokesperson for the minister said. “This is Cricket Australia’s process to run, and it is a matter for them to work through. Australians will expect this to be run independently and as openly as possible.” Cummins remains adamant he did not know of the plot to use sandpaper in South Africa, while Cameron Bancroft, in his first public appearance since his explosive account, declined on Thursday to say whether Cummins should retain the captaincy.





“When you go through it all calmly and in detail, Pat’s eight-year long position and 68-minute Q&A stands up. “There is no serious case he was an architect of ball tampering or knew sandpaper was going on the field. Loading “Its also true that the players who were suspended paid far too high a price. Year long bans for ball tampering that players in other countries did and were suspended for just a few games – they have always been right to feel aggrieved by that.” Bancroft gave a short interview in Perth on Thursday, his first public comment since the publication of his statement.



“Obviously, yesterday was a really big day for me. Really emotional day, and [I’ve] obviously been carrying a lot of this stuff for a long period of time,” Bancroft told Nine. “I feel really freed and really happy to be able to do that. Now there’s a process in place which Cricket Australia and [chief executive] Todd [Greenberg] have put [in place]. I look forward to being a part of that process.” Bancroft did not comment when asked if he believed Cummins should step down as captain. Usman Khawaja, who relit the sandpaper bonfire now ablaze in Australian cricket with the release of his autobiography last week, backed Bancroft when approached by reporters on Thursday.



“There’s no reason for Cameron to lie,” Khawaja said. “I’m really happy that Cam felt safe enough to go out there and tell the story that he told about what happened. “I fully support Cameron and what he said. As a friend, I will always have his back.” Cummins and fellow paceman Josh Hazlewood were both at NSW training on Thursday morning at the SCG.



Steve Smith, the former Australian Test captain who copped a 12-month ban for his role in the ball-tampering scandal, hasn’t appeared, and this masthead has been told he won’t be training on Thursday with the main NSW group, despite Sunday’s looming Sheffield Shield fixture at the SCG – the last first class match before the December 9 Test against New Zealand in Perth. Smith is expected to play in that game, but it’s not expected that Cricket NSW will ask the Test vice captain to fulfil media duties during that game. Related Article Ball tampering Lehmann dodges question on Bancroft claims, leaves commentary box Nathan Lyon, who was one of the four bowlers who denied knowledge in 2021 that sandpaper was used to tamper with the ball, along with Hazlewood, Starc and Cummins, isn’t expected to be in attendance. Lyon’s partner gave birth recently. Bancroft’s extraordinary statement was released on Wednesday night, hours after Cricket Australia announced an independent forum for members of the 2018 tour to speak honestly and privately about the events of the infamous series.



Bancroft revealed at length how he became involved in the use of sandpaper on the ball, at the initial suggestion of David Warner. He also detailed meetings showing how widely the team knew about what he was doing, including repeated feedback conversations with all the bowlers about how much he was doing. Matt Golding Sayers, Warner, Khawaja and Bancroft remain at odds with Cummins about the controversy. Sayers said he wished he had spoken out before last Sunday, when he contradicted Cummins’ denial that the Australia’s whole touring party in 2018 knew of the ball tampering Bancroft conducted against the Proteas.



“Knowing what happened is not great and knowing a lot of people were telling the truth and some weren’t,” Sayers told SEN on Thursday. “But I was pretty comfortable that it had moved on. But now knowing what Cameron Bancroft actually had gone through and all the different scenarios that had happened, I probably wish I did come out a bit earlier.” Related Article Opinion

Australian cricket Eight years of carrying the burden of the country on my shoulders. Now it’s time I told the truth Cameron Bancroft Australian cricketer Sayers’ only Test came in the match after Bancroft was caught with sandpaper in his trousers during the Cape Town game. “It obviously took a lot of courage for Cameron Bancroft to come out and tell his story,” he said. “It has obviously been sitting with him for eight years and taking most of the brunt for what occurred.”
